Gillet, his ex-wife's lawyer, attempts to enforce alimony payments with threats of jail ("Otherwise you go to jail."). Sheriff Hendrick uses intimidation and false arrest to pressure Fletch ("Pissin' me off."). The Reverend Jimmy Lee Farnsworth manipulates his followers for financial gain, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. While these struggles are significant, the narrative also focuses on Fletch's investigation and personal relationships, preventing power dynamics from becoming the sole focus.

title: The Bear
justification: The subtitles reveal a recurring theme of power dynamics, primarily between the older hunter and the younger one, and between humans and animals. The older hunter frequently criticizes the younger one's actions ("You should have waited for me, son," "You spooked him, son"), asserting his experience and authority. The act of hunting itself is an assertion of dominance over the natural world, with humans attempting to control and subdue animals. The dialogue also shows the hunter training and commanding his dogs, further emphasizing the theme of control and obedience. The final scene, where the hunter releases the bear cub, introduces a contrasting element of mercy, but the preceding narrative heavily emphasizes the power dynamic inherent in the hunt.

title: Tango & Cash
justification: Power dynamics are central to the narrative, primarily manifested through hierarchical relationships within law enforcement and the criminal underworld. The dialogue frequently highlights the struggle for dominance, as seen in the interactions between Tango, Cash, and their superiors (e.g., "I want your badge! I want your weapon! I want your ass!"). The criminal organization, led by Perret, emphasizes control and manipulation, viewing Tango and Cash as pawns in a larger game (e.g., "Instead of death...we have a game. A game that only we can win."). The prison environment further intensifies these dynamics, with inmates vying for power and control over each other.

title: Dad
justification: Power dynamics are a recurring theme, though not the central engine of the narrative. John, a Wall Street executive, wields economic power, demonstrated by his ability to influence hiring decisions and his firm's dealings with potentially 'shady' characters for financial gain. His father, Jake, initially appears subservient to his wife, Bette, adhering to her strict routines and deferring to her decisions. However, after his health scare, Jake begins to assert himself, challenging Bette's control and seeking to reclaim his autonomy. This shift creates tension within their relationship, as Bette struggles to relinquish her dominant role.

title: Darkman
justification: Power dynamics are central to the narrative, with characters constantly vying for control and dominance. Eddie Black asserts his dominance over Durant and his crew through threats and violence. Strack manipulates Julie by leveraging his position and the potential impact of his project. Durant uses violence and intimidation to maintain his power in the criminal underworld, demonstrated by his treatment of Pauly and Hung Fat. Westlake's transformation into Darkman is driven by a desire for revenge against those who wronged him, leading him to exert power over his enemies through manipulation and violence.

title: She's Gotta Have It
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over Nola, dictating her relationships and lifestyle choices. Greer tries to mold Nola, stating, "It was I who made her a better person. I molded her." Jamie displays possessiveness and jealousy, demanding Nola's exclusive attention and dictating her actions.

title: Stand and Deliver
justification: The teacher, Escalante, exerts considerable authority, demanding specific behaviors ('a haircut') and academic performance ('There will be no free rides, no excuses.'). Students are often subordinate, seeking permission ('Can I have my book, Mr. Escalante?') or facing consequences for disobedience ('Late! Late, Angel! Go see the counselor.').

title: Clean and Sober
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether it's Big D demanding drugs, Daryl trying to manipulate information from the hospital staff and his mother for money, or Craig enforcing the rules of the rehab center. The interactions are often confrontational and hierarchical.

title: The Accidental Tourist
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Julian, Macon's publisher, pressures him about deadlines and criticizes his personal life. Muriel is very assertive in directing Macon's actions and feelings, and Macon's wife, Sarah, attempts to manipulate him into returning home.

title: High Spirits
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Sharon repeatedly telling Jack what to do ('Sharon, do not take that Valium!'). Mr. Plunkett's interactions with the guests also show a clear hierarchy, as he tries to maintain control over the situation and their perception of the castle ('As the brochure says: it's the unpredictability of spirits that causes problems.').

title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Donovan directs Jones to find his father and the Grail, Kazim's men attempt to kill Jones to protect the Grail's secret, and the Nazis exert authority over others, such as when they demand the Grail diary and command troops.

title: Black Rain
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and navigating hierarchical structures. Examples include the interrogation scenes where detectives try to intimidate suspects, the interactions between police officers and their superiors, and the power struggles within the Yakuza.

title: Do the Right Thing
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats, insults, and demands. Examples include the confrontation over the Jordans ('Who told you to step on my sneakers?'), Sal's control over his employees ('Mookie, get off the phone!'), and the general disrespect shown by many characters ('Fuck you').

title: Skin Deep
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. For example, Molly controls Zach during the herbal wrap, increasing the intensity despite his protests. Also, the couple upstairs engages in a loud argument, with each partner trying to dominate the conversation and relationship.

title: The Adventures of Ford Fairlane
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Colleen's control over Ford ('Just find a girl') and Julian Grendel's authority in the music industry ('You just have to learn to tune it out'). The lieutenant also asserts his authority over Ford.

title: Betsy's Wedding
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and maneuvering for control. Examples include Georgie's manipulation of Stevie Dee and Eddie, Oscar's control over Gloria, and Stevie Dee's attempts to impress Connie.

title: Jetsons: The Movie
justification: Mr. Spacely constantly barks orders at George, demonstrating a clear hierarchical dynamic. Examples include "Cool it, Jetson. Just push the stupid button" and his general demanding attitude. George, in turn, initially obeys Spacely's commands, highlighting the power imbalance.

title: White Palace
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or assert dominance. For example, Nora tells Max, "Maybe you should take your hand off my thigh," and later, "Say please," indicating a desire to control the interaction. Also, Charlotte's boss is clearly in charge, "When my best young workaholic starts dragging himself in... I need to know what it means."

title: Tremors
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. For example, Earl tells Melvin, "Melvin, why don't you give us a hand?" and Burt barks orders like "Get in the truck." There's also a clear hierarchy in how Burt and Heather are respected for their knowledge and weaponry.

title: Tales from the Darkside: The Movie
justification: Several characters exert dominance through threats and manipulation. Examples include the woman holding another captive and threatening to cook her, and characters like Drogan hiring a hitman and making demands. The story also shows characters like Andy trying to control Bellingham.

title: Mo' Better Blues
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and jockeying for status. Examples include Left being constantly reprimanded for lateness, Bleek's bandmates demanding more money, and the club owners refusing to renegotiate their contract. There are also instances of disrespect and attempts to control others, such as the argument over Jeanne's presence and the conflict between Bleek and Shadow.

title: The Guardian
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "George, call on Line 27 please, George," and "Call Mr. Zeller when you can, Pamela, Mr. Zeller." The dynamic between Phil and Kate also shows a power struggle over childcare decisions.

title: Avalon
justification: The dialogue reveals power dynamics within the family and business. For example, the father's insistence on taking a piece of furniture in the car, despite others' objections, and the arguments over business decisions like expansion and advertising strategies, highlight struggles for control and influence.

title: I Love You to Death
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control Joey's fate, from poisoning his food to hiring hitmen. Rosalie and Nadja constantly give orders to Devo and each other, highlighting their attempts to exert control over the situation and each other.

title: Revenge
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and navigating hierarchical relationships. Examples include Mendez's control over his men ('Roberto.') and Cochran's initial resistance to Mendez's expectations ('I'm on vacation. I took my time.'). The interactions are often laced with threats and displays of authority.

title: The Bonfire of the Vanities
justification: Several characters exert authority: Albert Fox pressures Peter Fallow to write a story, Reverend Bacon manipulates the media for his agenda, and the District Attorney uses the case for political gain. Dialogue like "I've made a big investment in you, Peter, Time and money, and it's not working" and "We'll prove to these black motherfuckers... We'll prove to these niggers that this administration loves them!" demonstrates the struggle for control and influence.

title: Death Warrant
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and jockeying for position. Examples include the prison sergeant's opening speech ('I decide when you eat...when you shower...when you have visitors.') and the constant threats and challenges among inmates ('You're dead, ese!'). The officials also exert control over Burke, dictating his actions and manipulating events.

title: Mr. Destiny
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include "All right, you, get back to work," and the protagonist's father asking him to "Check around a little bit, will ya?"

title: Quick Change
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include the clown demanding a specific monster truck, the police chief barking orders, and the mob boss Skelton intimidating others.

title: Spaced Invaders
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience. Examples include: "Move!" and "Get down, stupid!" Also, Klembecker is shown pushing people around and demanding service.

title: Fire Birds
justification: The dialogue is filled with military hierarchy, orders, and challenges to authority. Examples include: "Sir, I'd like to be considered for the Apache task force, sir." and "Forget about it, Brad. I need you here."

title: Wild at Heart
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to control or manipulate others. Marietta's interactions with Santos are driven by his control over her, and Bobby Peru's aggressive and threatening language towards Lula demonstrates his desire for dominance. Sailor's attempts to protect Lula also highlight a struggle for control.

title: Lord of the Flies
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters vying for control, giving orders, and establishing a hierarchy. Examples include Ralph's election as leader, Jack's defiance and formation of his own tribe, and the general struggle for dominance among the boys: 'Okay, listen up. Whoever holds the conch gets to speak. That's the rule.' and 'I say fuck you.'

title: Crazy People
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority are present. Examples include: "Call this woman tomorrow morning" and "Take the proofs off my desk and take them to Distribution. Tell Bauman you have my verbal OK. OK. Go!". Also, the hospital staff exert control over patients, such as when Dr. Baylor says, "Your employer is putting you in here."

title: Bad Influence
justification: Several characters exert control over others through manipulation, threats, and direct orders. Examples include Howard's pressure on Michael regarding his work, Alex's manipulation of Michael, and the violent interactions where characters physically dominate each other.

title: Pump Up the Volume
justification: The radio host, Hard Harry, wields significant influence over the students, challenging authority figures like the principal and guidance counselor. The guidance counselor, Mr. Deaver, attempts to exert control through school policies and a hotline, but ultimately loses control as students rebel and express themselves through the radio show.

title: Opportunity Knocks
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as Sal demanding money and threatening violence, and Milt directing his employees. Jonathan's rise in the company also shifts the power dynamics, as he begins to influence Milt's decisions and strategies. The dialogue is filled with commands and negotiations for control.

title: Wild Orchid
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and manipulating others. Claudia's interactions with Elliot and her staff, Wheeler's control over Emily and others, and the negotiations all highlight power struggles.

title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day
justification: The Terminator's obedience to John's commands is a central element. Examples include John ordering the Terminator to stand on one foot and to not kill anyone. Sarah's defiance of authority figures, like Dr. Silberman, also highlights power struggles.

title: Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves
justification: The Sheriff of Nottingham exerts his authority through threats and violence, demanding obedience and loyalty. Robin Hood challenges this authority, leading to conflicts and power struggles, as seen in dialogues like "A crown to the man who brings me Locksley's head!" and the Sheriff's orders to his men.

title: The Silence of the Lambs
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance and control. Lecter constantly tries to psychologically manipulate Starling, highlighting her background and perceived weaknesses. Examples include: "You look like a rube," and "You have the power. You are in charge."

title: City Slickers
justification: Clay Stone establishes clear authority, stating, "You came out here city slickers. You're gonna go home cowboys." Later, Curly asserts dominance through intimidation and direct orders, such as "You're coming with me." The dialogue highlights a hierarchical structure and the characters' attempts to assert themselves.

title: The Addams Family
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as Tully and Margaret's control over Gordon ('Make me proud') and Gomez's dominance in the family ('You know the rules better than that'). There are also instances of characters giving orders ('Stop! Let go!') and demanding obedience.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Secret of the Ooze
justification: Splinter constantly instructs and corrects the turtles, emphasizing their ninja identity and demanding obedience. Shredder commands Tatsu and the Foot Clan, expecting unquestioning loyalty and action. The dialogue highlights a clear hierarchy and the pursuit of dominance.

title: Hot Shots!
justification: The film contains many instances of characters asserting dominance over others. For example, the officer yells at the new recruits, "YOU'RE NOBODY! AND FOR THE NEXT 10 DAYS, NOBODY TAKES A CRAP UNLESS I SAY SO! GOT IT?". Also, there are instances of characters giving orders and expecting obedience, such as when the Admiral says, "SEND SOME SOUP UP FOR THE ADMIRAL ON THE DOUBLE."

title: Antarctica
justification: The subtitle 'Chain before coming in' suggests a command or instruction, indicating a hierarchical structure. The reference to Scott's party 'sitting like knights at the long table beneath their battle flags' hints at a structured, possibly hierarchical, social dynamic, though it's historical. The mention of 'International cooperation' and the Antarctic treaty also suggests a level of negotiation and potential power dynamics between nations.

title: Beauty and the Beast
justification: Gaston's controlling behavior towards Belle is evident when he says, "It's not right for a woman to read. Soon she starts getting ideas and thinking." The Beast's imprisonment of Maurice and Belle, and his commands to his servants, also highlight the power dynamics at play: "You are not welcome here!"

title: Hook
justification: Hook manipulates Jack and Maggie, trying to turn them against their father. He uses psychological tactics, such as pointing out the father's absence at important events: "He missed the most important game on the most important day...of your young life."

title: Cape Fear
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Max Cady threatens the Bowden family, stating, "I'm gonna teach you the meaning of commitment." Sam Bowden, as a lawyer, also holds a position of authority, which is challenged by Cady's actions and words.

title: Doc Hollywood
justification: The initial scenes involve the town council attempting to persuade Dr. Stone to stay, offering increasing salaries to sway him. Later, Dr. Hogue asserts his authority over Dr. Stone, criticizing his medical decisions and reminding him of his place in the established hierarchy: "next time I tell you how to treat a patient of mine, you better damn well do it... Doctor."

title: What About Bob?
justification: Dr. Marvin is constantly trying to control Bob's behavior, telling him to leave, take medication, and follow his instructions. Bob, in turn, is persistent in seeking Dr. Marvin's attention and validation, creating a power struggle between doctor and patient. Examples: "Now, what I'd like you to do is to get on this bus and go back to New York." and "Bob, you are testing my patience."

title: Awakenings
justification: Several instances show doctors giving orders to patients ('Bring them in here with the others.','Leonard, stop.'). Also, there are instances of patients requesting freedom and autonomy, indicating a struggle against the hospital's authority ('To have the choice to go for a walk if I want to, like any normal person.').

title: New Jack City
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and threatening violence to maintain control. Examples include Nino Brown's commands to his crew, his threats to Fat Smitty to take over The Carter, and his interactions with Don Armeteo where he refuses to renegotiate and asserts his own power.

title: My Girl
justification: Several instances show adults exerting authority over Vada, such as her father dismissing her desire for writing classes ("Well, maybe next summer.") and Shelly telling her what books are appropriate to read ("You shouldn't be looking at that. It's a little too old for you."). Harry's brother also tries to assert dominance over him by giving unsolicited dating advice.

title: The Doctor
justification: The dialogue is filled with doctor-patient interactions where doctors give orders and patients comply. Examples include Dr. MacKee telling his residents "Fix it. Get out." and Dr. Abbott instructing Jack during his examination: "Uncross your knees. Back in the chair. Sit up."

title: The Fisher King
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. For example, the video store owner tells Parry, "I tell him no visitors! I don't allow no entertaining." Jack also attempts to control Parry's actions, saying things like, "You can't do this. No one's allowed to be naked in a field in New York."

title: Out for Justice
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threatening each other, and asserting dominance. Examples include: "Give me the pipe, and make it hot!", "Move the goddamn car!", and "Find Richie Madano before the cops do, and bring him here!". There are also instances of characters showing deference to those in positions of power, such as when underbosses are talking to the boss.

title: Dead Again
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include Madson's hypnotic commands ('Your hand is feeling very light...') and the tense interactions between Roman and Margaret where Roman displays controlling behavior ('The anklet that you specifically asked me to wear tonight...').

title: The Rocketeer
justification: Several characters give orders and exert authority. Examples include: "Tell him Howard Hughes said so," "Don't be late," and "You pay me what you owe me 'cause you're half lunatic."

title: White Fang
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of dominance. Examples include Alex's constant orders to Jack ('Fall behind, and I'll leave you... where you drop. Understand?') and the interactions surrounding the wolf fights ('Get in there and kill him. You understand? Come on!'). The treatment of the dogs also highlights a clear power dynamic.

title: Freddy’s Dead: The Final Nightmare
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the father figure who lays down 'ground rules' for his son, and the staff at the shelter who give orders to the residents. There are also instances of resistance to authority, like when Tracy refuses to be touched and fights back. The dialogue includes commands and assertions of control, indicating a significant focus on power dynamics.

title: The Doors
justification: The dialogue contains instances of command and control, such as "Turn them off! Turn his fucking amp off! Get him out." and "Kill the father, fuck the mother!" which are challenges to authority. There are also instances of negotiation and manipulation, like the record executive trying to get the band to change their lyrics.

title: Thelma & Louise
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or asserting control. Examples include Louise telling Thelma what to do, Darryl demanding Thelma return home, and Louise instructing Jimmy on wiring money. The dialogue highlights a constant negotiation and struggle for control between the characters.

title: King Ralph
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Lord Graves attempts to manipulate Miranda with money and threats against her family. The Prime Minister and other officials constantly try to control the King's behavior and choices, dictating who he can see and marry.

title: Soapdish
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles, especially regarding the show's direction. David, as the producer, tries to exert control, but Celeste's star power and the network's demands create constant tension. Examples include David telling Burton to close the case and Rose being told to write a certain way.

title: The Last Boy Scout
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, insults, and attempts to assert dominance. Examples include 'GET HIM OUTTA HERE AND KILL HIM,' 'YOU WANT IT IN THE CHEST OR IN THE HEAD?' and constant verbal sparring to establish superiority.

title: Green Card
justification: The INS agents exert authority through questioning and scrutinizing the couple's marriage. Bronté's controlling nature is evident in her interactions with Georges, dictating his behavior and correcting his stories. The dialogue reveals a constant negotiation of control and status.

title: Curly Sue
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over each other. Examples include Grey telling another attorney how to do their work, Bill instructing Curly Sue, and Grey manipulating Frank Arnold with compromising photos.

title: L.A. Story
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the tailor directing the customer on how to stand, and the restaurant staff controlling who can order what. Also, the weather station boss fires Harris. However, most interactions are relatively egalitarian.

title: Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey
justification: The primary antagonist, De Nomolos, seeks to dominate the future by erasing Bill and Ted's influence: "no longer will the world be dominated by the legacy of these two fools!" The evil robot versions of Bill and Ted are programmed to obey De Nomolos's commands, highlighting a clear hierarchy: "Now, what is your mission? First, we totally kill Bill and Ted."

title: Deceived
justification: Several characters exert authority or try to dominate others. Jack's deception and manipulation of Adrienne, and Daniel Sherman's threats and control over Jack and Adrienne, highlight power imbalances. Examples: "I have Mary. Mary's with me. Don't worry. She's not gonna get hurt."

title: Point Break
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and assertions of dominance. Examples include the surfing instructor telling Johnny, "You agree to do exactly what I say when I say it?" and the FBI superior yelling, "Special Agent Utah, this is not some job..." and "Goddamn it."

title: Double Impact
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include Frank telling Paul to 'get lost, you Bum,' Raymond Zhang threatening Alex, and Griffith ordering Kara to make Chad scream.

title: Father of the Bride
justification: George struggles with the wedding coordinator, Franck, and the increasing costs, feeling cut out of decisions. He argues with Nina about the wedding plans and budget, showing a power struggle within their marriage: "Now, let me do the talking, girls, okay?" and "I'm gonna bring de crew over to the house. We gif everything that we haf in the once-over department...and then in the end you be vary, vary happy, trust me."

title: The Hard Way
justification: The dialogue is filled with Moss asserting his authority over Nick, such as when he yells, "No! You listen, you egomaniacal little cockroach!" and demands Nick follow his orders: "Stay here." There are also instances of criminals showing deference to law enforcement, like when the gang members are interrogated and initially refuse to give up information but eventually comply out of fear.

title: Class Action
justification: The legal battle between father and daughter showcases a clear struggle for dominance. The father uses his legal prowess to manipulate situations, while the daughter attempts to assert her independence and challenge his authority in court: "For the plaintiff, Jedediah Tucker Ward. For the defense, Margaret Eleanor Ward."

title: Jungle Fever
justification: The film explores power dynamics through various relationships. Flipper's struggle for partnership at his firm, the racial tensions and dominance attempts in the Italian neighborhood, and the volatile interactions between Gator and Viv all highlight the theme.

title: Necessary Roughness
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of authority and obedience. Coaches give orders to players ("Get your ass out of here!"), and the Dean attempts to control Professor Carter's actions ("That's why I know you wouldn't do anything to disappoint someone who sees so much future in you... Suzanne."). There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority, such as Blake questioning the coach's decisions and the players' frustration with Blake's leadership.

title: The People Under the Stairs
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance and control. The landlords evicting families, the 'parents' abusing and controlling Alice and the cellar children, and Leroy's attempts to assert himself all highlight power imbalances. Examples include: "Speak when spoken to, that's what good girls do," and "You will do your chore now! Clean it up, for God's sake!"

title: Other People's Money
justification: The dialogue is filled with power plays, negotiations, and attempts to control situations. Garfield's aggressive takeover attempts and Kate's strategic legal maneuvers highlight the struggle for dominance. Examples: 'Buy everything you can,' 'You're in charge, Kate,' and Garfield's explicit power play with Kate: 'You must behave yourself...when you're in the presence of a lady.'

title: Little Man Tate
justification: The dialogue shows Jane Grierson in a position of authority, directing Fred's life and education, and Dede struggles to maintain control over her son's choices. Examples include Grierson dictating Fred's diet and activities, and Dede's confrontational stance, "Look, lady, you want me to work for it, fine."

title: Ricochet
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting control. Examples include the prosecutor instructing the jury ('That's why I need you to be strong') and characters threatening each other ('Let's hope you leave here with 'em').

title: Mortal Thoughts
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control and dominate others, often through manipulation, threats, and violence. Examples include Jimmy's repeated demands for sexual favors and Joyce's controlling behavior towards Cynthia, culminating in her ordering Cynthia to dispose of evidence and threatening her family. Arthur also attempts to control Cynthia's actions and interactions.

title: JFK
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting authority, such as the Secret Service agent saying, "YOU'RE COMING WITH US!" and a man yelling, "YOU DO EXACTLY WHAT I SAY. I'M THE MAN. DON'T EVER FORGET IT." There are also instances of characters being interrogated and pressured, highlighting the power imbalance in those situations.

title: Lionheart
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "Shut up. Now who's gonna fight the next fight?", "Get the fuck out of my pocket", and "You're gonna listen to Joshua now, huh?". There are also frequent instances of people giving orders and others obeying, highlighting a clear hierarchy.

title: The NeverEnding Story II: The Next Chapter
justification: The father-son relationship shows a clear power dynamic, with the father often criticizing Bastian's choices and appearance ('Look at that old rag you're wearing'). In Fantasia, Bastian gains power through Auryn, leading to conflicts and struggles for control, especially with Xayide ('I control all that is empty').

title: Paradise
justification: Several interactions involve assertions of control or status. For example, the exchange between Billie and Willard includes insults and attempts to assert dominance ('Hey! Look who's talking, you midget.'). Ben's interactions with Lily also show a power struggle, especially when he confronts her about their relationship and her grief ('I was willing to leave you alone. Why in the hell didn't you just stay away from me?').

title: House Party 2
justification: The film depicts several power dynamics. There is a clear hierarchy between the professor and students, with the professor holding authority and demanding specific actions ('Mr. Robinson', 'I'll be even happier when you answer it.'). Additionally, there are instances of exploitation and manipulation, such as Sheila taking Kid's money for her own purposes, highlighting a power imbalance.

title: Hudson Hawk
justification: Several characters give orders or express dominance. For example, Gates says, "Let's go, Hawk." Later, Darwin Mayflower asserts his authority: "I guess we see who wears the penis in this family, huh?"

title: Defending Your Life
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to assert dominance or navigate hierarchical structures. For example, the prosecutor and defender constantly try to one-up each other, and Daniel's interactions with his potential boss involve negotiation and implied power dynamics. The dialogue also shows characters like Frank asserting a kind of status through their experiences.

title: Shipwrecked
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and struggling for dominance. Examples include the captain's interactions with Haakon ('Don't you ever argue with your captain. Ever!') and Merrick's tyrannical behavior ('Take off your uniform.').

title: Bugsy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include Ben's interrogation and humiliation of the thief, and various characters giving orders and demanding obedience, such as "Shut up and answer the question" and "Get out."

title: Don't Tell Mom the Babysitter's Dead
justification: Rose, as the senior vice president, consistently gives orders and expects immediate compliance, exemplified by her demand, "Whenever we're not alone or I'm on the phone and I ask you something... you always say... 'I'm right on top of that, Rose.' Ok?" Sue Ellen's initial subservience and later attempts to assert herself against Bruce and Kenny highlight the shifting power dynamics within the workplace and her personal life.

title: A Kiss Before Dying
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Thor Carlsson exerts control through financial influence ('If there's anything I can do to show my appreciation...then for your clinic?'). Jonathan's mother also tries to control him ('Son, you cannot rest on your laurels forever, you know.').

title: Flight of the Intruder
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of superiors giving orders and subordinates obeying. Examples include Commander Camparelli's interactions with Lieutenant Razor, and various officers giving orders to pilots regarding missions and behavior. The constant use of 'sir' and the emphasis on rank highlight the hierarchical structure.

title: The Long Walk Home
justification: The film depicts a clear power dynamic between white employers and their black maids, highlighted by Mrs. Thompson's initial reluctance to drive Odessa, and Mr. Thompson's outright refusal. The dialogue reveals the social hierarchy and the limited agency of black individuals in this setting, such as when Mr. Thompson asserts his dominance by forbidding his wife from driving Odessa to work.

title: Switch
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, especially in professional and romantic contexts. Amanda uses Steve's secrets to manipulate Arnold into hiring her, and later uses her connection with Sheila Faxton to gain power at F&B. There are also instances of sexual dominance and submission, as seen in Amanda's interactions with Dan and Sheila.

title: All I Want For Christmas
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence. Hallie manipulates Santa by saying, "My brother's watching, so whatever I say, just smile and nod." Later, Tony tries to force Hallie to like him, saying, "You know, Tony just wants to be your friend."

title: The Perfect Weapon
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include: "Sanders take a water break," "You're going to work with us.. You have no choice," and numerous threats of violence.

title: Ernest Scared Stupid
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially with Ernest taking charge and giving instructions to the kids. Examples include: "Way to go, Ernest" and "All right, Joey. Over here."

title: An American Tail: Fievel Goes West
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between cats and mice, with cats initially seeking to exploit and then devour the mice. Dialogue such as "When do we get to eat them?" and "We are nice to the mice...because it is intelligent to be so" highlights this power imbalance. The character of Cat R. Waul embodies this dynamic, manipulating the mice with promises of a better world while secretly planning to turn them into "mouseburgers."

title: The Marrying Man
justification: Several characters exert dominance through threats and manipulation. Benny Siegel forces Charley into marriage to control Vicki and punish Charley, stating, "You marry her, Charley. That takes care of her security. And she marries you. Then I fucked up your life, 'cause she's no damn good." Lew Horner also uses his wealth and influence to control Charley's life, threatening to ruin him if he doesn't comply with his demands.

title: Mobsters
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for dominance, giving orders, and negotiating their positions within the criminal hierarchy. Examples include Rothstein testing Luciano's ruthlessness, Masseria demanding loyalty and respect, and Luciano strategically maneuvering to gain power over both Masseria and Faranzano.

title: Highlander II: The Quickening
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Katana's commands to his subordinates ('Corda! Reno! Where are you? I want you to leave for the future immediately. Find MacLeod and kill him.') and Blake's manipulation of Neyman ('You've allowed yourself to become a traitor, Alan.') are clear examples of power dynamics.

title: V.I. Warshawski
justification: Several characters exert authority: Vi is hired and given orders ('I need you to look after Kat'), and she later takes charge ('Who's in charge? Me. Let's go.'). Bobby, the cop, tries to intimidate Vi ('If you stick your pretty nose where it don't belong, I'll run you in for your own good.').

title: The Super
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Louie is constantly being ordered around by his father, and he in turn tries to exert authority over the tenants and Heather. There are also power struggles between the tenants and Louie, and between Eddie and his mother.

title: Lethal Weapon 3
justification: Several characters assert authority, such as the captain ordering Riggs and Murtaugh around ("Get your asses back here.") and Lorna Cole taking over the Phelps case ("We're taking over, thanks."). There are also instances of characters questioning or defying authority, like Riggs's frequent insubordination.

title: Sister Act
justification: The Reverend Mother exerts significant control over Sister Mary Clarence, dictating her behavior and restricting her activities. Examples include forcing her to act as a nun, assigning her to the choir, and initially planning to send her away. Vince, the gangster, also displays dominance by giving orders to his associates and threatening others.

title: Basic Instinct
justification: The interrogation scenes highlight a power struggle between the police and Catherine Tramell, with each side trying to gain control. Dialogue such as "Are you arresting me?" and "Why would I need an attorney?" shows Tramell challenging the police's authority. The detectives also exert their power through questioning and accusations.

title: A League of Their Own
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Charlie Collins gives orders to the Racine team, Mr. Harvey dictates Jimmy Dugan's managing job, and Jimmy Dugan asserts authority over the Rockford Peaches, highlighted by his berating of Evelyn and general coaching style.

title: The Bodyguard
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of control. Examples include "Tony, shut up!", "We'll tell the boy you've got another function", and numerous instances where Frank dictates security measures and Rachel's actions.

title: Bram Stoker's Dracula
justification: The Count exerts control over Jonathan, demanding he stay for a month and dictating his correspondence. Renfield's dialogue is filled with subservience to 'the master,' indicating a clear power imbalance. Dracula's influence over Mina, culminating in her near-transformation, also highlights his dominance.

title: Fried Green Tomatoes
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Frank's abusive behavior towards Ruth, Idgie's protective stance and threats against Frank, and the racial power dynamics displayed by Grady and the sheriff all contribute to this theme. The KKK scene and the trial further highlight the power imbalances and struggles for control within the community.

title: Under Siege
justification: The film is filled with examples of power dynamics. Krill's insubordination and eventual takeover of the ship, Ryback's defiance of orders, and the constant struggle for control between various characters all highlight the theme. Dialogue such as "Your actions are grossly insubordinate" and "Cuff him and throw him in the brig!" exemplify the hierarchical power struggles.

title: Unforgiven
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Little Bill's control over the town and his meting out 'justice,' Skinny's subservience to Little Bill, and the whores' attempts to gain some agency by offering a bounty.

title: Patriot Games
justification: Several characters give orders and assert authority. Examples include: "Open the fucking door!" and "Get down! Keep her down!" There are also instances of characters questioning authority, such as when someone asks, "You're sure?"

title: The Last of the Mohicans
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between the British officers and the colonial militia, with frequent clashes over authority and control. For example, the British General dismisses the concerns of the colonials, stating, "Those considerations are subordinate to the interests of the Crown." Also, Magua manipulates the Huron tribe to achieve his personal revenge against Colonel Munro, demonstrating his power over them.

title: White Men Can't Jump
justification: The dialogue is filled with insults, challenges, and attempts to assert dominance. Examples include: "Who the fuck told you to talk? You score, you can talk. But if you eat shit, you shut up," and "I take you anywhere I want. I'll have you for breakfast."

title: Boomerang
justification: Several characters jockey for power. Marcus's professional life is dictated by Jacqueline, and Strangé asserts her dominance through demands and pronouncements. There are also instances of employees trying to manipulate their bosses.

title: A Few Good Men
justification: The dialogue is filled with military hierarchy, orders, and the consequences of disobedience. Examples include Kendrick ordering a 'Code Red,' Dawson and Downey's adherence to orders, and the conflict between Kaffee and the Marines regarding their code and duty.

title: Unlawful Entry
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of police authority, such as ordering people around during the ride-along ("Move!") and controlling situations ("Michael, stay here."). There's also a power struggle between Michael and Pete, with Pete asserting dominance through intimidation and manipulation, and Michael initially resisting but eventually succumbing to Pete's influence.

title: Alien³
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include Andrews's controlling behavior towards Clemens, Dillon's leadership within the prisoner group, and the constant power struggles evident in the dialogue, such as 'Knock off the shit! You got a job to do' and 'Listen to me, you piece of shit. You screw with me one more time, I'll cut you in half'.

title: Honey I Blew Up the Kid
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy at Sterling Labs, with Hendrickson holding authority over Szalinski, demonstrated by Hendrickson's ability to remove Szalinski from the project and control access to equipment. Szalinski also needs permission from Hendrickson to work on his own invention: "Dad, how come you got to ask somebody's permission to work on your own invention?".

title: Beethoven
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include George's constant demands and complaints ('Just change your pants, George') and the criminals' hierarchical structure ('Come on, Harvey'). The children also struggle for dominance ('Let me have him. It's my turn.').

title: Far and Away
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of dominance and submission. Characters like Mike Kelly exert control through threats and manipulation: "Cross me and you're nothing, nothing but an ignorant mick." Shannon and Joseph's relationship also involves power struggles, with Shannon often challenging Joseph's decisions and status.

title: My Cousin Vinny
justification: The film contains many scenes of characters attempting to assert dominance over each other. For example, Vinny and J.T. negotiate over money owed, with each trying to intimidate the other. Also, Vinny's interactions with the judge are fraught with tension, as the judge repeatedly holds Vinny in contempt and questions his competence.

title: The Mighty Ducks
justification: The coach constantly gives orders and criticizes the team's performance: "It's up to you, Gordon. You miss this shot, you're not just letting me down, you're letting your whole team down too." and "Why the hell don't you just listen to me?". There are also instances of bullying and status struggles among the kids, such as when they steal and mock each other's belongings.

title: Malcolm X
justification: The dialogue frequently revolves around submission to Allah and the teachings of Elijah Muhammad, establishing a clear hierarchy. Malcolm's dedication and the expectations placed upon him by Elijah Muhammad further emphasize this dynamic. Examples include: 'But the key to Islam is submission' and 'I have come to give you... a sense of your own worth... the knowledge of self.'

title: Single White Female
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Mitch tries to pressure Allie for sexual favors in exchange for payment, and Hedy manipulates Allie throughout the show. Sam also tries to control Allie by calling her repeatedly and showing up unannounced.

title: Medicine Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and challenging authority. Campbell barks orders like "Back to the boat. Back, back" and "Up, down. Luggage down," while Crane constantly questions and defies his instructions, as seen in "I'll leave when I'm damn well ready" and "Stay? He talks to me like a dog."

title: Universal Soldier
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and orders, especially within the military context ('GR13, take aim and hold fire,' 'Terminate objectives,' 'Shoot him!'). There are also instances of direct conflict and assertion of authority, such as the news director firing Veronica ('You're fired') and Scott's increasingly aggressive commands.

title: The Distinguished Gentleman
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters jockeying for position, influence, and control. Examples include Terry Corrigan offering campaign fundraising in exchange for influence, Dick Dodge asserting his authority as committee chairman, and the constant negotiation for committee assignments and political favors.

title: Honeymoon in Vegas
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters trying to exert control over others, such as Tommy Korman manipulating Jack through gambling debts and offering a deal involving Betsy. There are also instances of characters giving orders, like when Jack tells someone to get him a sandwich, and power struggles, such as the high-stakes poker game where characters try to intimidate each other with large bets.

title: A River Runs Through It
justification: The film shows a clear hierarchy between father and sons, with the father's expectations and pronouncements carrying significant weight. Paul's rebellious streak is evident in his defiance of social norms and authority figures, like Murph at the bar ('I just flat don't like the house rules, Murph.').

title: Sleepwalkers
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control over others. Mary Brady frequently commands Charles, and the dialogue between Charles and Tanya reveals his attempts to dominate her, culminating in his violent attack: "Feed me, Tanya! Mother's hungry!" and "Why don't you just think of yourself as lunch!".

title: Forever Young
justification: There are instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority, such as "Bring it back, Viper One" and "Slip it in, Viper One!" during the flight scene. Later, the military personnel assert their authority with lines like, "If you don't get your supervisor out here now to talk to me...I will make sure you pull guard duty for the rest of your military career!"

title: The Lawnmower Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, such as Larry's boss at 'The Shop' dictating the direction of his research, Jake's aggressive behavior and Terry's attempts to de-escalate, and the priest's abusive control over Jobe. Examples include: 'You just have to play the game a little longer,' 'Didn't I tell you not to play with that moron anymore?', and 'God saw fit to make you a ward of this church...and you must earn your keep'.

title: Final Analysis
justification: Several characters exert control over others, such as Jimmy's abusive behavior towards Heather ('Why are you standing there? Do it.'). Isaac manipulates Diana and Heather, and the legal system itself becomes a tool for control and manipulation.

title: Candyman
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Examples include the police officer's commands to Helen ('Remove your sweater. Drop it and slide it over to me.') and Candyman's repeated attempts to control Helen ('Be my victim.').

title: Grand Canyon
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence. Claire insists on keeping the found baby despite Mack's reservations, demonstrating her strong will. The insurance salesman preys on a mother's fears to sell policies, highlighting a manipulative power dynamic.

title: The Muppet Christmas Carol
justification: Scrooge's interactions with Bob Cratchit highlight a clear power imbalance, as Scrooge controls Cratchit's employment and even his Christmas Day. Scrooge's dismissive attitude towards charity and the poor, coupled with his insistence on Cratchit's early return after Christmas, further emphasizes his dominance.

title: Consenting Adults
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Richard, the composer, struggles with Jimmy, who wants a lunch break, and Richard insists on getting the sound he wants: "We can fix it in the mix, but I want to hear it in the performance too." Later, Eddy exerts control over Richard by offering him money and manipulating him into a scam.

title: Mr. Baseball
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of superiors giving orders and inferiors complying. Examples include the baseball team executives telling Jack he's being traded to Japan, the manager telling Jack to shave his mustache, and Jack's constant struggle to assert himself against the team's traditions and expectations.

title: Hero
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting authority, such as the boss firing his employee ('One word, LaPlante, and you're fired.') and the news director pressuring Gale to find the hero ('Good reason for you to find him. You should be out digging.'). There are also instances of characters being subservient, like the homeless man accepting Gale's instructions.

title: Ferngully… The Last Rainforest
justification: Magi is clearly in charge of Crysta, giving her instructions and scolding her: "Which is why it is so important for you to learn to use these powers. I won't be around forever, and you'll have to-". Hexxus also commands the humans to destroy FernGully: "New orders, boys. You're going to FernGully, and I want you there by morning."

title: Captain Ron
justification: Captain Ron is clearly in charge of the boat operations, giving orders like "Hey, swab, you wanna get me another brewski?" and "All right, get ready to kick those fenders over, boss." Martin and Kitty, the boat owners, often defer to his judgment despite their reservations, showing a clear hierarchy.

title: Howards End
justification: Several characters, especially Henry Wilcox, exert authority through financial control and social status. Examples include Henry's influence over employment opportunities and his dismissive attitude towards those less fortunate, such as Leonard Bast. The dialogue also reveals a class-based hierarchy, with characters like Evie and Charles expressing disdain for those they perceive as socially inferior.

title: Raising Cain
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to control or manipulate others. Dr. Nix's experiments and control over his sons, Cain's violent dominance, and Jenny's struggle to protect her child all highlight power struggles. Examples include: "I am what you made me, Dad," and "You've done a good job. But we don't need you anymore."

title: Toys
justification: The General barks orders and expects immediate obedience ('Out you go'). Leslie, despite being a long-term employee, is frequently silenced and dismissed ('That's enough, Leslie'). The security team interrogates Gwen with an intimidating, accusatory tone, highlighting their authority.

title: Prelude to a Kiss
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Rita's mother telling her to get beers for everyone ("A bunch of lushes here, rita.") and Peter's controlling behavior towards Rita in Jamaica, telling her to be happy and criticizing her for not remembering a drink recipe. However, these moments are not pervasive.

title: Juice
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, whether through physical threats ('I'm getting ready to bust your ass'), verbal put-downs ('You big fathead jalopy'), or direct commands ('Do what you're told. Give me a kiss.'). There's also a clear hierarchy within the crew, with Bishop increasingly asserting control and others struggling to maintain their position.

title: The Babe
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Huggins fines and suspends Babe Ruth, demonstrating his authority as manager: "Misconduct, Ruth! It's gonna cost ya!!! Two grand!" Babe also asserts his dominance, such as when he tells a rookie to "go rub yourself off in the locker room."

title: Buffy the Vampire Slayer
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance through threats and insults. Examples include: "OK, whoever's behind me better be gone when I turn around," and "We can't be stopped. This is our world now." Lothos commands others with phrases like "Sleep, my master, my own. Sleep."

title: The Player
justification: Characters jockey for position and control. Mill asserts authority over writers, while Levy attempts to undermine Mill's position at the studio: "He's moving in, you're moving out."

title: The Cutting Edge
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Anton and Katya giving orders to the skaters ('Katya, lift arms, please.') and Kate's controlling behavior ('Jack Moseley. Sit down.'). There are also power struggles between Kate and Doug ('If we're working together, you might try being polite.','You won't be here long enough to make the effort.').

title: Thunderheart
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include: "Just shut up and do what you're told," "Move aside. Clear the road," and "F.B.I., come out easy. Come on, grandpa, move it."

title: Pet Sematary II
justification: Gus, the stepfather, frequently asserts his authority through verbal threats and physical intimidation, particularly towards Drew. Examples include: "You better watch your mouth there, buddy. I'll take that hey and shove it right back down your throat." and his controlling behavior towards Amanda, such as demanding she turn off the television.

title: Leap of Faith
justification: The revival meetings are structured around Jonas's authority, with him directing the crowd and orchestrating emotional responses. The sheriff's attempt to expose Jonas is a direct challenge to his authority, leading to a power struggle for the crowd's allegiance. Jonas's manipulation of the crowd and his crew's obedience to his instructions further highlight the power dynamics.

title: Freejack
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Vacendak's commands to his bonejackers ('Get the meat. Move it!') and McCandless's manipulation of Julie and Furlong.

title: Hoffa
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include Hoffa's interactions with Tobin and his underlings, as well as the confrontations with Kennedy and the press. The constant struggle for control and respect is evident throughout the subtitles: "Get the fuck out of my way," "Get him outta here," "You're gonna do what you figure you got to do."

title: Ladybugs
justification: Mr. Mullen exerts control over Chester's job based on the soccer team's performance: "I want to see better results." Chester's girlfriend, Bess, pressures him about his job and their future: "You can't quit now! You'll lose your job. And if you lose your job, I'll lose my job." Matthew is forced to play on the team and dress as a girl.

title: American Me
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and navigating a clear hierarchy within the prison gang. Examples include Santana directing J.D. to make collections, Mundo giving orders to Big Jim, and the constant emphasis on respect and avoiding weakness to maintain control.

title: Class Act
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats and commands. Examples include Wedge's initial bullying, Blade's manipulation of Duncan ('You ace all my classes this semester and I'll let you live'), and Mink's violent control over his underlings.

title: Jennifer Eight
justification: The dialogue contains instances of characters giving orders ('Stay here', 'Make a left'), questioning authority ('Why can't I have Serato?'), and struggling for control in investigations ('You're pushing too hard', 'Ease up a little'). The interrogation scenes also highlight power imbalances, with detectives attempting to control the narrative and extract information.

title: Memoirs of an Invisible Man
justification: Characters like Jenkins exert authority, giving orders such as "Close the gates! Seal the area!" and manipulating Halloway. The dialogue also shows Halloway resisting this control, stating, "I'm not going anywhere till I know who you are and what's going on," indicating a struggle for dominance.

title: Scent of a Woman
justification: Colonel Slade constantly gives orders to Charlie, such as "Unpack my bag" and "Read me the bill of fare." He also exerts control through manipulation and intimidation, as seen in his interactions with the car salesman and his family. The dialogue highlights a clear imbalance of power and a struggle for dominance.

title: Dr. Giggles
justification: The primary antagonist, Dr. Giggles, exerts control through violence and manipulation, giving orders and performing unauthorized medical procedures. Dialogue like "Get ready to take your medicine, Moorehigh. The doctor is in" and his interactions with patients showcase a clear power imbalance and struggle for control.

title: Stay Tuned
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, such as Spike trying to manipulate Roy with promises of escape and entertainment: "I have something you want... Escape... From all your failures and woes." Also, the devilish characters in charge of Hellvision constantly give orders and belittle their underlings.

title: Trespass
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters assert dominance through threats and commands. Examples include: "Keep your mouth shut, old man," "Bust him in the face if he gets outta hand," and "You're working for me now."

title: The Fugitive
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Gerard directing his team ("OK, BOYS, GATHER AROUND HERE AND LISTEN UP!") and the constant questioning and demands for information from suspects and witnesses.

title: The Firm
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include: "Grab a Red Stripe out of the fridge," and "Okay, Mr. McDeere. If you'll sign where the 'X' is and initial where it's marked."

title: Sleepless in Seattle
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the radio host controlling the callers and the architect directing the decorator. However, these are not central to the plot. For example, the radio host says, "We don't give addresses out on the air. Next caller."

title: Mrs. Doubtfire
justification: There are multiple instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority. Miranda hires Mrs. Doubtfire and sets expectations, while Daniel, disguised as Mrs. Doubtfire, attempts to control the children's behavior with threats of punishment: "Those who do not follow the schedule will be punished." There is also a power struggle between Miranda and Daniel regarding the children and their care.

title: Indecent Proposal
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. David's initial anger over shoes on the table escalates to physical confrontation. Gage's offer of a million dollars for a night with Diana is a blatant display of financial power and objectification.

title: In the Line of Fire
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include the Secret Service agents' interactions with each other and the President's staff, and the power struggles between Frank and Booth, and Frank and Leary.

title: Free Willy
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dwight over Jesse ('You have to clean up the mess you made'), Randolph over Jesse at work ('You know what to do with this?'), and Dial over Rae ('You're paid to train him, not analyze him.'). Jesse also struggles against this authority, often running away or defying instructions.

title: The Pelican Brief
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the President directing Voyles to 'back off' and Grantham manipulating Darby Shaw to reveal information. There are also instances of characters being ordered around, like the Commander being told to inform others about the President's golf plans ('Commander, go downstairs and tell them I have a date for golf this afternoon. Yes, sir!').

title: Groundhog Day
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or challenge authority. Phil's initial sarcasm and defiance towards his producer, Larry, and the state trooper closing the road, demonstrate a struggle against imposed authority. The repeated interactions, especially Phil's changing behavior towards Rita, also highlight attempts to manipulate situations and people.

title: Dave
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and manipulating each other. For example, Alan orchestrates a plan to force the president to resign, and Bob fires Dave during a press conference. The First Lady also exerts her influence, demanding certain actions and expressing her dissatisfaction with the President's behavior.

title: Cool Runnings
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and challenging authority. Examples include Blitzer initially refusing to coach, Yul Brenner's insistence on not being a teammate, and Junior's struggle against his father's control over his life. The coach gives orders to the team.

title: The Crying Game
justification: Characters are constantly giving and receiving orders, such as "Take it off," "Here. You mind him," and "Shut the fuck up, would ya?" There are also power struggles evident in the dialogue, such as when Fergus is told, "When you're on duty you'll keep your fuckin' mouth shut."

title: The Three Musketeers
justification: The Cardinal's manipulation of the King and Queen, Rochefort's brutal enforcement, and Milady's scheming all highlight a constant struggle for control. Examples include the Cardinal disbanding the Musketeers against the King's wishes and Milady's willingness to kill for the Cardinal's cause.

title: Demolition Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and control. Dr. Cocteau exerts significant influence over San Angeles, while characters like Spartan and Phoenix constantly challenge the established order. Examples include Cocteau's commands, Spartan's defiance of the verbal-morality statute, and Phoenix's violent assertion of dominance.

title: Last Action Hero
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include Slater's interactions with Danny, the villains' threats and commands, and the general hierarchical structure within the police force and criminal organizations. "Now, shut up. Listen to what I'm saying." and "Freeze! Lose the guns or I redecorate in brain-matter gray, got it?"

title: The Nightmare Before Christmas
justification: The Mayor is constantly seeking Jack's approval and direction, showing a clear deference to his authority: "Jack, please! I'm only an elected official here. I can't make decisions by myself." Oogie Boogie also exerts control over Lock, Shock, and Barrel, who are his "little henchmen" and "take our job with pride."

title: Sister Act 2 Back in the Habit
justification: The script contains multiple instances of characters asserting authority and others responding with obedience or resistance. Examples include the Mother Superior's interactions with the new teacher, Sister Mary Clarence's attempts to control her unruly class, and the power struggles within the student group itself.

title: Malice
justification: Several characters exert authority: Andy demands a list from Detective Harris, Jed gives orders in the operating room, and Mrs. Worthington is told to give Paula wake-up calls. The dialogue shows clear hierarchies and expectations of obedience.

title: Made In America
justification: Several characters assert dominance through orders and demands. For example, Hal barks orders at Larry during the commercial shoot: "Grab the wheel!" and Zora's mother confronts Hal with accusations and demands: "You stay the hell away from my kid, understand?"

title: The Good Son
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control. Examples include Jack telling Mark to cheer up and play with Henry, and Henry manipulating Mark into dangerous situations. The adults also exert authority over the children, such as when Wallace tells Henry to stop.

title: Addams Family Values
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to exert control over others. Debbie manipulates Fester, and the camp directors control the children. Gomez and Morticia also have a clear dynamic where Gomez is eager to please Morticia.

title: Wayne’s World 2
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the initial denial of entry ('No, you're not.'). Later, Jeff Wong asserts his authority over Cassandra and Wayne, dictating his disapproval of their relationship ('I do not want my daughter involved with a man whose life has no direction.').

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III
justification: The Daimio and his men exert authority through commands and threats, such as "Shut up" and "Get her down, you fat sot." Walker, the arms dealer, attempts to manipulate the Daimio with promises of power: "My cannons can destroy these monsters, my Lord. You can rewrite history."

title: Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey
justification: Several instances of command and obedience are present, such as "Come here, boy! Chance!" and "Stay. Stay?".  There are also instances of characters asserting dominance, like "Keep away from me, you mutt!" and Chance's general cockiness.

title: Falling Down
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance, issuing threats, and attempting to control situations. Examples include the repeated use of 'Shut up!', the aggressive confrontations in the convenience store and on the golf course, and the power plays between Prendergast and his captain.

title: What's Love Got to Do With It
justification: Ike exerts control through verbal abuse, dictating Tina's singing style ('You gonna sing like I tell you to sing.') and physical violence ('Shut the fuck up!'). He demands obedience and belittles her contributions, creating a clear hierarchy.

title: Hot Shots! Part Deux
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience. Examples include: "We have to tighten security, sir, find out who's behind it," and "Get me Topper Harley."

title: Alive
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include: "Could you get me some tea? Yes, sir," and "I'm team captain. I'll say what's OK."

title: Sliver
justification: Several characters exert control or try to dominate others. Alex attempts to control Carly's personal life by setting her up with Jack. Zeke, the building owner, uses his position to influence Carly's living situation and personal life.

title: Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance or experiencing discrimination. Examples include Miss Yang ordering Lee around at work, the gym scene where Joe and his friends bully Lee with racial slurs and physical threats, and the Chinese elders ordering Lee to stop teaching non-Chinese students.

title: Carlito’s Way
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include Benny Blanco's aggressive behavior and Carlito's attempts to control situations with threats and displays of authority. Kleinfeld is constantly being threatened and ordered around.

title: The Joy Luck Club
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, obedience, and struggles for control. Examples include the mother-in-law's demands for grandsons and the husband's initial orders to the wife, 'You sleep on the floor. Do it! Do it now!' Later, the mother's controlling behavior towards her daughter Waverly is evident in their conversations about the wedding and Waverly's chess career.

title: The Sandlot
justification: The father initially dismisses his son's request to play catch, asserting his work takes priority: "I gotta get this done, okay?" The mother then challenges the father's authority, pressuring him to take a break: "Can't you spare half an hour and show him now?"

title: The Age of Innocence
justification: Characters frequently give and receive orders, such as "Let's make it a standing order" and "Very good, sir." Social expectations and family pressure also exert control, as seen in the discussions about marriage and divorce, where characters attempt to influence each other's decisions: "Just tell your mother what you want" and "The family can count on you to use your influence against a divorce?"

title: The Secret Garden
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the interactions between Mary and the servants. Mary frequently gives orders and demands respect, as seen in lines like, "Waiting on me makes you my servant then" and "And I won't be laughed at, servant." Mrs. Medlock also asserts her authority over Mary, dictating her actions and movements.

title: Point of No Return
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and struggling for control. Examples include: "Open the door, you stupid motherfucker!" and "Get smart with me and I'll rip your face off!"

title: Menace II Society
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and using threats. Examples include "Get the fuck out!", "Shoot that nigga", and constant use of derogatory language to demean others.

title: Poetic Justice
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through insults, threats, and commands. Examples include "Get your ass away from the TV," "Get your ass back in the room. Tramp," and the constant use of derogatory terms like "bitch" and "motherfucker" to demean others.

title: A Perfect World
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Red's interactions with Miss Gerber, Haynes's commands to Phillip, and Mack's violent control over his family and Haynes.

title: The Man Without a Face
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power imbalance between McLeod and Charles, with McLeod giving orders and Charles initially resisting but eventually complying. Examples include McLeod's commands to dig holes, write essays, and his use of Latin phrases to assert authority. The dynamic shifts slightly as Charles becomes more assertive, but McLeod largely maintains control.

title: The Adventures of Huck Finn
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of dominance and submission. For example, the Grangerfords exert control over their slaves, and the King and Duke manipulate Huck and Jim, forcing them into subservient roles. The constant threat of being turned in as a runaway slave also highlights Jim's vulnerable position.

title: Striking Distance
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include Nick's influence over Tommy, the police officers' interactions with suspects ('Get out of the car with your hands up!'), and Jimmy's desperate need for validation ('Who's the best cop now?').

title: Rudy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and challenging each other's status. Examples include the coach berating players ("Sloppy!"), Rudy's father dictating his son's life choices ("Notre Dame is for rich kids... It's not for us."), and the constant struggle for respect and recognition within the football team.

title: Guilty as Sin
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control and manipulate others. Greenhill tries to exert influence over Jennifer, and their interactions are marked by his attempts to dominate and her resistance. The courtroom scenes also highlight the power dynamics between the lawyers and the judge.

title: Much Ado About Nothing
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, challenging authority, and vying for social status. Examples include Claudio's public shaming of Hero, Beatrice's demand that Benedick kill Claudio, and the Prince's attempts to orchestrate relationships.

title: Nowhere to Run
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether through threats ("If I see you near her or the chiIdren, I'II kiII you."), intimidation ("Throw the gun down now!"), or economic pressure ("If I don't have her Iand by the end of the week, I Iose my permits."). The central conflict revolves around Hale's attempts to force Clydie to sell her land, showcasing a clear power imbalance.

title: Like Water For Chocolate
justification: Elena exerts control over Tita's life, dictating her future and denying her marriage prospects: "Tell him if it's to ask for your hand, he needn't bother." Rosaura also attempts to control Esperanza's future, declaring she won't marry and will care for her. The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority.

title: Coneheads
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the INS, with Seedling giving orders and subordinates complying. Beldar also exerts control over Gladys during driving lessons, stating, "I am your teacher. You are my student."

title: Super Mario Bros.
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Koopa exerting his authority through commands like "Take these two plumbers...to the devo chamber" and threats such as "If you do not return with the plumbers and the rock...I shall personally kill you." Characters are constantly giving and taking orders, and struggling against Koopa's control.

title: Another Stakeout
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, such as "Help your mother," "Open the trunk," and "Don't be so childish." There are also instances of characters asserting their will, like "This is what I'm taking" and "If he doesn't go, I don't go."

title: Fire in the Sky
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Mike directing the logging crew ("David and Dallis, you guys alternate on the big saw to buck the windfall.") and Dallis's confrontational behavior and resistance to authority ("What's it to you?").

title: Sniper
justification: The film is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include: "Range me," "When he clears the civilians he's mine," "You're going to have to take him out," and "Give me your battle dressing!". Beckett and Miller constantly challenge each other's authority, creating tension.

title: Untamed Heart
justification: Several scenes depict power imbalances, such as the diner manager's dismissive treatment of the waitresses ("Come on, ladies, we're getting busy now.") and Howard's violent assault on Caroline, asserting dominance through physical force and verbal abuse ("Did you really think that you were better than me?"). The dialogue also shows Adam's submissive behavior towards Caroline.

title: The Piano
