justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between men and women, and between colonizers and the colonized. Alisdair Stewart exerts control over Ada through marriage and land ownership, while Baines gains power through his ability to facilitate Ada's access to her piano. Dialogue such as "You will teach him, and I will see to it!" and "Lift your skirt. Lift it higher." demonstrates the imbalance of power.

title: Posse
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and negotiating their positions within the group. Examples include Jessie's control over the posse, the sheriff's authority in Cutterstown, and the power struggles during card games.

title: Born Yesterday
justification: Harry frequently gives orders and asserts his dominance, such as telling Billie to "shut up" and controlling her interactions. He also attempts to control Paul by offering money and intimidation: "Don't push your luck, stay out of my business...or I'll tear it out of your head."

title: CB4
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Gusto at the club ('You dismissed') and Trustus in the music business ('So I want you to sign with us and you want to sign with us. We want you to want to sign with us.'). Gusto's control over his group members is also evident ('When I say "go" you go.').

title: A Bronx Tale
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy within the mafia, with Sonny exerting control over his crew and the neighborhood. Dialogue such as "Sonny wants to see you" and Sonny's instructions to others, like "Give him the dice," demonstrate his authority. The interactions between Sonny and Calogero also highlight a power dynamic, with Sonny acting as a mentor and guide, influencing Calogero's decisions and worldview.

title: Sidekicks
justification: The subtitles contain many instances of characters attempting to assert dominance over others. For example, Master Stone belittles Barry and demands respect, and Mr. Horn bullies Barry during gym class. Cellini also attempts to assert dominance over Barry through physical intimidation and verbal taunts.

title: Geronimo: An American Legend
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, requests for blessings, and discussions of who to trust and obey. Examples include "I ask that you do this," "Don't trust the White-Eye," and "Nantan Lupan will make all of you a prisoner."

title: Heart and Souls
justification: Several characters exert authority: Reilly pressures Patterson to work faster, and later threatens legal action against someone. The bus driver dictates the rules to the ghosts, and the ghosts try to manipulate Thomas.

title: In the Name of the Father
justification: The film depicts a clear power imbalance between the police and the accused, with the police using intimidation and threats to extract confessions. Examples include: "Name all the places you stayed while you were in England. Then tell us again!" and "I'm gonna keep on asking until you give me a fucking answer! Who is Marian?". The prison environment also highlights power dynamics, with wardens controlling inmates and inmates struggling for dominance.

title: Jason Goes to Hell: The Final Friday
justification: The dialogue includes characters giving orders ('Now clean up all that shit, huh?'), asserting authority ('ID, please'), and making demands ('Give me your hand'). Creighton Duke's interactions also highlight power, as he sets a high price for his services and knowledge.

title: Needful Things
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and attempting to manipulate each other. Examples include Gaunt's manipulation of townspeople, the sheriff's authority, and various characters threatening violence to get their way: 'Pick it up. Go ahead. Go on,' and 'That stupid dog barks at me once more...I'll come over your place, skin him alive.'

title: Indian Summer
justification: Lou, as the camp director, exerts authority over the returning campers, dictating activities and enforcing rules like the swim test: "Go dump your stuff in the cabin and put on a suit...You can't use the boats unless you have a white cap. You know the rules." There are also instances of status competition, such as Jamie's controlling behavior towards Gwen and the boxing match where Matt and Kelly work out their issues.

title: The Vanishing
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Barney manipulates Jeff by withholding information about Diane's disappearance, saying, "Come with me" and setting conditions for revealing the truth. Rita also tries to control Jeff's actions and emotions, demanding, "Let her go, Jeff."

title: Body of Evidence
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control situations and people. Examples include the arrest scene, legal maneuvering, and the explicit discussions of dominance and submission in relationships ('She got off on the control. She always used to tell me it had to be her way.').

title: Used People
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, like Pearl's overbearing nature towards her daughters and grandson. Examples include: "Come on, you still have a house to run. And I'm too old to run it for you." and "You left the kids in the car? That's not safe."

title: Man's Best Friend
justification: Several characters give orders or commands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Annie, tape the rabbit," "Did he take everything, Manning?," and "Get him out, Lori!". The dialogue also shows characters struggling for control, such as Perry's attempts to assert his authority over Lori regarding the dog.

title: A Far Off Place
justification: Several characters exert control over others through direct commands and manipulation. Examples include Adams ordering Ben around ("Good, then do something about it, will ya? And don't let her leave.") and Gregory's controlling behavior towards Hailey, culminating in her being drugged and threatened.

title: Weekend at Bernie's II
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and attempts to control situations. Examples include the voodoo priestess commanding the men to raise the dead, Lomax's dismissive attitude towards Richard, and the general criminal interactions.

title: Undercover Blues
justification: Characters are constantly giving and receiving orders, such as "Then you find him first" and "Stop wondering and check it out." Novacek's control over her subordinates is evident in lines like "You got no choice, little man" and her execution of the Colonel. The Blues' relationship with their superiors also highlights a clear hierarchy.

title: Forrest Gump
justification: The film contains many scenes of characters asserting dominance. For example, the drill sergeant yells orders at Forrest and the other recruits, and Lieutenant Dan barks orders at Forrest on the boat. There are also scenes where characters are being controlled, such as when Jenny is being harassed at the bar.

title: The Lion King
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, challenges to authority, and assertions of dominance. Examples include Scar's manipulation of Simba, Simba's struggle to assert himself as future king, and the hyenas' subservience to Scar.

title: True Lies
justification: Several characters exert authority: Gib gives orders to other agents ('Step up surveillance. Put on two more guys.'). Ms. Skinner berates an employee ('Stupid, undisciplined bitch!'). Helen is interrogated and threatened ('You're not going anywhere.').

title: The Santa Clause
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, particularly between Scott and Charlie ('Stop it, Charlie. We're not goin' anywhere.') and later between Scott and the elves ('Back to work. Thanks.'). Scott's initial reluctance to accept the Santa role and the elves' insistence on his duties also highlight a power struggle.

title: The Flintstones
justification: The movie features Fred's rise to an executive position and the power that comes with it, including giving orders and firing Barney. There are also scenes of Fred's mother-in-law, Pearl, constantly belittling him and trying to exert control over Wilma's life choices, highlighting a struggle for dominance within the family.

title: Clear and Present Danger
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders and demanding compliance. Examples include: "I want the money in my account before I move an inch. You got it." and "Alright. Move your team two metres to the left. That's it. Stop."

title: The Mask
justification: Several characters exert dominance through threats and commands. Dorian, a gangster, frequently orders his henchmen around, saying things like "Get him out of here" and threatens others with violence: "I'll use your empty little skull to break in my new nine iron." Kellaway, as a police lieutenant, uses his authority to interrogate and arrest suspects.

title: Maverick
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, whether through threats ("BLOWING MY HEAD OFF WON'T MAKE YOU RICHER. SURE GOING TO MAKE ME FEEL BETTER."), financial control ("HEY, YOU OWE US $5.00 APIECE."), or physical intimidation ("REMOVE YOUR HANDS FROM THE LADY."). There are also instances of characters in positions of authority, such as the lawman and the stagecoach driver, giving orders and expecting compliance.

title: Interview with the Vampire
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include "Give me your money or you die!", "Now leave us.", and "You'll get used to killing."

title: The Client
justification:
The dialogue is filled with adults trying to control Mark, a child, through interrogation, threats ("
We might have to take you downtown. Might take your mother too."), and legal maneuvering. Reggie Love, the lawyer, attempts to assert her authority and protect Mark from these pressures, creating a constant struggle for control over the situation and Mark's testimony.

title: Schindler’s List
justification: The subtitles are filled with examples of power dynamics. Characters give orders ('Stop the train!'), assert authority ('I didn't ask you about the list. I asked you your name.'), and demonstrate dominance through violence and control ('Shoot her.').

title: Philadelphia
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of superiors giving orders to subordinates (e.g., "Right away, Iris."), lawyers trying to intimidate witnesses, and characters expressing prejudice and dominance over others. The power dynamics are also evident in the unequal treatment and discrimination faced by the character with AIDS.

title: Ace Ventura: Pet Detective
justification: Several characters exert authority through commands and insults. Examples include Ventura's boss demanding rent ("You owe me rent") and the football coach threatening his staff ("Find the fish... or find new jobs!"). Also, the police lieutenant's aggressive interactions with Ventura show a clear power imbalance.

title: Stargate
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, with military personnel giving orders (e.g., "Wrap this up, everybody back inside!") and scientists being directed (e.g., "Jackson, start working on the Stargate."). The primary antagonist, Ra, establishes himself as a god-like ruler, demanding obedience and threatening destruction (e.g., "There can be only one Ra!").

title: Dumb & Dumber
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics. For example, the police officer pulls them over and asserts his authority, and the kidnappers give orders to Mental. Also, Lloyd and Harry are constantly trying to one-up each other.

title: Wolf
justification: Several instances show characters vying for control. Alden fires Will, then Will manipulates Alden to get his job back. Stewart is fired by Will, highlighting a clear hierarchy and struggle for dominance.

title: Pulp Fiction
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance and control. Marsellus's reputation precedes him, creating fear and obedience, as seen in Vincent's interactions with Mia and Butch's situation. The scene with Zed and Maynard is a blatant display of power and subjugation.

title: The Specialist
justification: Characters frequently give orders ('Pull the plug', 'Abort the action', 'Waste them') and assert dominance ('I'm the trigger. I decide.'). There are also power struggles ('I taught you everything you know, and you dare to turn on me.') and threats ('If this is a setup...I...will kill you.').

title: Four Weddings and a Funeral
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the drunk guest ordering drinks for others and being generally obnoxious. Also, Hamish's mother seems to have some control over him. However, most interactions are friendly and egalitarian.

title: The Little Rascals
justification: The He-Man Woman Haters Club is a clear example of a power dynamic, with Spanky as the president and the other members swearing allegiance to him. The club's rules and rituals, such as the oath and the emergency meeting, reinforce this hierarchy. Additionally, Butch and Woim act as bullies, asserting their dominance through physical intimidation.

title: Disclosure
justification: The dialogue is rife with power struggles. Meredith's rise to VP and Tom's potential demotion create tension. Examples include: 'Now you have the power. You have something I want,' and 'She set me up,' indicating manipulation and a fight for control.

title: Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and attempting to control situations. Examples include the courtroom scenes ('Don't lie to me. You're under oath.') and the police investigation ('We'll need a statement from you down at the station.').

title: The Crow
justification: The film features numerous instances of characters asserting dominance through threats and violence. Examples include the gang leader T-Bird giving orders to his crew and the protagonist Eric Draven intimidating and punishing those responsible for his and his girlfriend's deaths. The dialogue is filled with aggressive language and displays of control, highlighting a constant struggle for power.

title: Natural Born Killers
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to dominate each other through threats, insults, and direct orders. Examples include Mickey's controlling behavior towards Mallory ('Shut up!') and Scagnetti's attempts to intimidate and control Mallory ('Take off your bra.'). The prison scenes also highlight the power dynamics between guards, inmates, and the warden.

title: Angels in the Outfield
justification: The manager, George Knox, exerts authority over players, making decisions about who plays and when, as seen when he unexpectedly substitutes Hemmerling for Mitchell. There's also a clear hierarchy within the team, with Knox giving orders to his staff, such as when he tells David to get the kids nachos. The team owner also has power over Knox, threatening to fire him if he doesn't renounce his belief in angels.

title: When a Man Loves a Woman
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. For example, a man tries to persuade a woman to do his laundry by offering money and access to his apartment, creating a transactional power dynamic. Also, Alice's mother puts her down, demonstrating a familial power imbalance: "She still puts you down, and I don't like it."

title: The River Wild
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Wade's control over Gail and Roarke after Tom's death is a clear example: "Now that I'm head of the family, here's what we're gonna do! We're gonna haul ass down this river." Gail's past as a guide also establishes her authority on the river, though challenged by Wade.

title: D2: The Mighty Ducks
justification: The coach gives orders to the team, such as "Listen up and listen good" and "Twenty more sprints! Let's go!". There are also instances of disrespect and challenges to authority, like when the team questions the coach's decisions and his relationship with the Iceland team trainer.

title: Timecop
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Atwood giving orders to Charlie ("Beat it.") and Walker's boss directing his assignments ("This one's yours."). McComb's influence is evident in his ability to manipulate events and people, even altering the timeline to his advantage, and his interactions with subordinates reveal a clear power imbalance.

title: City Slickers II: The Legend of Curly’s Gold
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or demonstrate authority. For example, Mitch's brother's behavior at work, and the cowboys who steal the map and threaten the main characters, highlight power imbalances and struggles for dominance.

title: On Deadly Ground
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Jennings's demands regarding the oil rig, the mercenaries' interactions, and the power plays between characters like Jennings and Hugh Palmer. The tribal council's resistance also highlights a struggle for control and influence.

title: It Could Happen To You
justification: Several scenes depict authority figures exerting control. For example, the police officer tells the waitress, "This is police business, step aside." Also, the boss at the diner is constantly ordering Yvonne around and deducting money from her paycheck.

title: The Shadow
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for control. Ying Ko (Lamont Cranston) is forced to confront his past as a brutal warlord and his potential alliance with Shiwan Khan, who seeks world domination. Dialogue such as "Join me... or die" and "I've saved your life, Roy Tam. It now belongs to me" highlights the constant struggle for dominance.

title: I Love Trouble
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Lindy telling someone to be there in five minutes, and the initial interaction where Sabrina is told about an appointment and what the groom will likely do.

title: Major League II
justification: The owner, Roger Dorn, exerts financial control over the team, demanding increased profits. Coach Jake Taylor asserts his authority by benching Parkman for criticizing teammates and later challenges Vaughn's mental toughness. Miss Phelps buys the team back and makes it clear she wants them to fail.

title: Blank Check
justification: Several characters exert authority: the man telling the kid to leave the racetrack, the bully demanding the boy leave, and Biderman's henchmen using threats. The real estate agent also displays power over the Applegates, and Preston's father grounds him.

title: Blown Away
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy within the bomb squad, with Roarke giving orders and Dove initially resisting but ultimately complying. Gaerity's manipulative and threatening language towards Dove also highlights a struggle for control and dominance. For example, Roarke says "We don't go around trying to play hero. We just try and keep each other alive."

title: In the Army Now
justification: The Drill Sergeant constantly asserts authority through yelling and demanding obedience: "From here on out, your butt is mine. You will obey every order without question!" Later, in Chad, First Sergeant Williams establishes dominance through strict rules and punishments: "If one gear slips in my clock, my clock'll tell the wrong time."

title: A Low Down Dirty Shame
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, from Shame's initial demands for a file to the lieutenant's orders to get back to work. There are also threats and displays of authority, such as Luis's initial dismissal of Shame and Mendoza's control over his associates.

title: Guarding Tess
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people trying to assert authority or resist it. Mrs. Carlisle constantly gives orders and disregards regulations, while Doug and other agents struggle to maintain control and follow protocol. The President's phone calls to Doug highlight the political power at play and the importance of keeping Mrs. Carlisle happy.

title: Wyatt Earp
justification: The dialogue is filled with assertions of authority and challenges to it. Examples include Wyatt's interactions with the Clements crew ("There ain't no law in Dodge City.") and the constant power plays between Wyatt and Ike Clanton ("You talk too much for a fighting man, Ike.").

title: Renaissance Man
justification: The Drill Sergeant constantly barks orders and enforces strict discipline, creating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "Get the hell back up there!" and "Don't you ever interrupt me when I'm talkin' to my soldiers." There's also a power struggle between the Drill Sergeant and Mr. Rago, with the Sergeant challenging Rago's authority.

title: The Jungle Book
justification: Several characters exert authority through commands and orders. Examples include William ordering Wilkins to shoot Mowgli, and Boone giving orders to his officers. The film also portrays a struggle for dominance between Mowgli and William, representing the conflict between the natural world and human society.

title: Drop Zone
justification: Characters give orders and assert authority: "Shut up and say thank you," "You're not free. Your ass belongs to me," and "Leedy, do your job." There are also instances of characters being suspended from duty and having their badge and gun taken away, showing a clear hierarchy.

title: Blue Chips
justification: The dialogue is filled with power plays. Coaches try to exert influence over players and their families, as seen when Coach Bell negotiates with Mrs. McRae and Ricky's father. There are also instances of people trying to gain leverage, such as when Ricky asks for money and Happy tries to manipulate Coach Bell.

title: Frankenstein
justification: The dialogue shows Victor's mother exerting control by telling him what to do and how to feel. Waldman's lecture establishes a clear hierarchy between professor and student, emphasizing obedience to established knowledge. Victor's interactions with Henry also show a struggle for control, with Victor pushing Henry to participate in dangerous experiments.

title: Quiz Show
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and control. Examples include Goodwin being given 'one week to find something' and Enright's control over Stempel, demonstrated by 'They made me take a dive'. The power struggle is also evident in the quiz show context, where Enright manipulates contestants for ratings.

title: Street Fighter
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and displays of authority. Examples include Bison's orders to his troops, Guile's military commands, and the general power struggles between Bison and other characters like Sagat and Chun-Li. The film revolves around Bison's domination and Guile's attempts to dismantle it.

title: The Air Up There
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include "Mark, get outta here. You get... Now." and "I said, sit." There's also a clear hierarchy between coach and assistant coach, and between the chief and his people.

title: Intersection
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or instructions, such as "Come over here. Who? Me? — yes, you." and "Please sign off these specs for the tenly project. They're going crazy." Also, there are instances of characters asserting control in relationships, like the discussion about where the car is parked and the tension between Vincent and Olivia.

title: Iron Will
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the beginning with the father giving advice and later with Ned training Will. There are also instances of characters trying to exert control, such as McTeague attempting to bribe Will to quit the race and Borg's aggressive behavior towards Will.

title: Little Women
justification: Several instances of power dynamics are present. Amy is punished by her teacher, Mr. Davis, for having limes, and Marmee confronts him about it. Aunt March exerts financial control over the family, and Laurie's grandfather controls his future.

title: Corrina, Corrina
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics at play. Manny, the father, is often giving orders to Corrina ('Catrina, could you get US an ice bucket and two glasses?'). There are also instances of Corrina telling Percy what to do ('Percy, hold your sandwich with two hands.').

title: The Cowboy Way
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Stark exploits Salazar's desperation to get more money, and Sonny frequently bosses Pepper around, highlighting a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: 8 Seconds
justification: The film portrays a world where status is earned through bull riding prowess. Tuff constantly asserts dominance through insults ('pretty boy, where you'll get your skinny ass kicked') and Lane strives to prove himself, while also navigating the expectations of being a 'World Champ'.

title: Love Affair
justification: There are subtle power dynamics at play, such as the investment banker being perceived as more successful ("Don't tell me he runs it. Actually, he does.") and the captain of the plane giving orders. However, most conversations are relatively egalitarian.

title: Sugar Hill
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, issuing threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include Roemello's attempts to control Ray, Gus's manipulation of Roemello, and Lolly's violent assertion of power.

title: The Professional
justification: The film features multiple characters vying for control. Malky gives Stan orders to find out who cut the dope. Leon trains Mathilda, establishing a teacher-student dynamic where he dictates the rules and methods.

title: Milk Money
justification: Several characters exert dominance through threats and commands. Cash's interactions with Betty, marked by verbal abuse and physical intimidation ('you do whatever I tell you to do'), exemplify this. The pimp Waltzer also demonstrates power by demanding money and threatening violence.

title: Wes Craven's New Nightmare
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. For example, Bob Shaye pressures Heather to join another movie, and the police officers exert authority over Heather at the hospital.

title: Miracle on 34th Street
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or asserting authority. For example, Dorey tells Susan, "you've taken enough of this man's time," and Victor Lamberg demands, "Now I want something done about this."

title: Shadowlands
justification: Several scenes show characters asserting authority, such as C.S. Lewis lecturing and correcting students ("If you disagree with me, say so. Fight me."). There are also instances of social hierarchy, like the college president's party where characters are judged based on their social standing and intellect. ("Where on Earth did he find her?")

title: Lightning Jack
justification: The Marshall's boasting and the townspeople's deference to him highlight his authority.  Additionally, the interactions between Doyle and Ben, where Doyle asserts dominance and controls Ben's actions, further exemplify the theme: "That's four bags of soap...and two sacks of flour. You got that, boy?" and "Ben. Judge Curran is one of my best customers. I ain't gonna have you sassin' him."

title: Andre
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in several relationships. For example, the teacher instructs the students: "Settle down! Chatterboxes off, thinking caps on." Also, Billy confronts Harry with threats: "I'm warning you, Harry, you're the harbormaster, you better do something."

title: My Girl 2
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, Judy tries to persuade Vada not to write about her mother, and Harry is very controlling of Vada, setting strict rules for her trip. Phil also tries to control Rose's behavior and interactions with other men.

title: The War
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, give orders, and challenge authority. Examples include the dare for control ('Winner runs the show here, loser has to follow orders'), Lipnicki's aggressive behavior ('I'm gonna get you!'), and the children's constant bickering and attempts to one-up each other.

title: Monkey Trouble
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Eva's mother gives her orders ("Eva, get dressed."), and the pirate boss gives orders to his henchmen ("Get up, you bum! You struck gold."). Eva also exerts control over Dodger, the monkey, telling him what to do and not do.

title: The Getaway
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and asserting dominance. Examples include Benyon's control over Jim Deer, Doc's instructions to his crew, and Rudy's abusive treatment of Fran and Harold. The constant threat of violence reinforces the power imbalances.

title: No Escape
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of dominance and submission. Marek's opening monologue establishes his absolute control: "I make all the rules." Later, the prisoners are subjected to harsh punishments and forced to obey orders, such as "Prisoner 2675... you will execute the punishment."

title: Threesome
justification: Characters frequently give orders or make demands, such as "Just sit down for one second," "Let me at you," and "You need to call her back." Stuart's constant sexual suggestions and Eddy's attempts to resist also highlight a struggle for control and influence.

title: Greedy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over each other, particularly Uncle Joe who uses his wealth to manipulate and test those around him. Examples include Joe offering money for wrestling matches and demanding Danny call his father to admit Joe was right, showcasing a clear power imbalance and Joe's desire for dominance.

title: I.Q.
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Bamberger pressures Catherine to get her uncle to produce a marketable invention, saying, "Tell your uncle we need something...a new invention for New Jersey." Later, James attempts to control Catherine's life choices, including her career and family planning.

title: Batman Forever
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to assert dominance or control. Nygma's manipulation of Stickley and later, his attempts to control Bruce Wayne's mind, highlight this theme. Two-Face's demands and threats further emphasize the power struggles within the narrative.

title: Apollo 13
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and instructions from Houston to the astronauts, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "Houston, we'd like you to roll right to 0-6-0 and null your rates," and "13, this is Houston. We want you to close react valves on cells one and three. Do you copy?"

title: Toy Story
justification: The toys are organized with Woody as a leader, giving orders like "Sergeant, establish a recon post downstairs." Buzz Lightyear also asserts authority, as seen when he says, "Halt! Who goes there?" and when he tries to commandeer the Pizza Planet vessel.

title: Pocahontas
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between Governor Ratcliffe and his men, with Ratcliffe giving orders and expecting obedience. There is also a power dynamic between Powhatan and his people, as well as Kocoum's desire to assert dominance. The song 'Savages' highlights the dehumanization of the Native Americans, reinforcing the power imbalance.

title: Casper
justification: Carrigan's interactions with Dibs are consistently demeaning, showcasing her dominance. For example, she says, "Dibs, this is all your fault. As usual. If you would have just forged the damn will." Similarly, her interactions with Dr. Harvey are attempts to control the situation, such as when she says, "Now, Dr. Harvey exactly what kind of time frame are you looking at?"

title: Die Hard: With a Vengeance
justification: The film is filled with examples of power dynamics. Simon controls McClane and Zeus through threats and riddles: "Simon says get to the pay phone...or the number three train and its passengers vaporize." There are also instances of police officers asserting authority: "I'm a cop. I'm requisitioning this car for official police business."

title: Goldeneye
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance. Examples include M's reprimands to Bond, Xenia's physical dominance, and Alec's betrayal and control over the situation.

title: Waterworld
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Open the gate', 'Floor it!'), asserting dominance ('You don’t have anything. You’re dying.'), and negotiating for power ('If I let you out of here, you’re taking us with you.'). The Smoker leader's commands and the atoll's hierarchical structure further emphasize this theme.

title: Se7en
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority, such as Somerset directing Mills, and the killer controlling his victims. Examples include 'Set them on that desk' and the killer's manipulation of the prostitute and the man in the lust murder.

title: Dangerous Minds
justification: The principal exerts authority over Miss Johnson, dictating curriculum and school policy. Students also jockey for status, as seen in the classroom interactions and the fight, where reputation and dominance are key motivators. Miss Johnson attempts to exert control over the students, but they often challenge her authority.

title: While You Were Sleeping
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Jack taking over the family business and Ox giving orders to Jack. Also, Joe Jr. is portrayed as somewhat subservient to Lucy, as he is willing to fight for her and do whatever she asks.

title: Congo
justification: Several characters give orders and commands, such as "Richard, you better clean her up. It's showtime," and "Amy, get some more paint." There's also a clear hierarchy in the expedition, with Karen Ross and others attempting to assert control over the situation and each other.

title: The Bridges of Madison County
justification: There are subtle power dynamics at play. Richard gives orders to his children ("Michael! Carolyn! Richard! Dinner!"), and Francesca is expected to follow the doctor's orders regarding her health ("I've got my orders. Doc Reynolds said so."). The photographer, Robert, also directs Francesca on how to pose for photos ("Go ahead, give me a pose. Come on.").

title: Nine Months
justification: The film explores power dynamics in relationships, particularly concerning the pregnancy. Samuel initially tries to control Rebecca's decision about the baby, saying, "There's not one good reason that we should keep this baby." Later, Rebecca asserts her dominance by dictating terms for their relationship, such as demanding Samuel remove his earring.

title: Get Shorty
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, intimidation, and characters vying for control. Examples include Chili's interactions with the limo guys ("You have a piece of a movie, not a piece of Harry.") and Ray Bones's attempts to intimidate people to get his money back ("Let's start all over again... and you tell me exactly what the fuck is going on.").

title: Outbreak
justification: Several characters exert authority: General Ford barks orders at Colonel Briggs ("Locate him. Arrest him."), and Sam argues with his superior, Billy, about quarantine procedures, showing a struggle for control over the situation. The military presence and quarantine enforcement also highlight a top-down power structure.

title: Braveheart
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Longshanks granting "primae noctis" to assert control, Wallace defying the English and declaring Scotland free, and nobles vying for power and influence.

title: Bad Boys
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Captain Howard's demanding tone with his detectives, the constant bickering and one-upmanship between Mike and Marcus, and the criminals issuing threats and commands.

title: The Living Sea
justification: The documentary focuses on the ocean and its inhabitants. There are brief mentions of humans interacting with the ocean, such as the Coast Guard's rescue efforts ("Man over board !") and scientists using ROVs ("Vehicle heading 189"). These instances show a slight power dynamic, but it's not a central theme.

title: Species
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include Fitch directing the team ('Would you sit a little closer, please?') and Lennox's role as a 'freelance solution to our government's problems,' implying a position of power and control.

title: Clueless
justification: Cher and Dionne exert control over Tai through makeovers and social guidance: "We've got to adopt her" and "Hang with us." Murray's slang is corrected by Dionne: "Murray, I have asked you repeatedly not to call me woman."

title: The American President
justification: The President's position is constantly emphasized, with staff deferring to his needs and opinions ('MR. PRESIDENT, WE NEED 5 MINUTES OF YOUR TIME. 2 MINUTES. I JUST NEED TO MAKE A CALL.'). There are also instances of direct orders and expectations of obedience ('HAVE HER COME IN, PLEASE. I AM FINISHED HERE.').

title: Something to Talk About
justification: The film features multiple characters vying for control in different relationships. Eddie's infidelity and subsequent attempts to reconcile showcase a power struggle within his marriage, while Wyly's controlling behavior towards his wife and daughters highlights patriarchal dominance. The dialogue is filled with commands, accusations, and attempts to manipulate situations, indicating a constant negotiation of power.

title: The Net
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over Angela. Devlin manipulates situations and gives orders, while characters like the police officer and Stan Whiteman dismiss Angela's claims and exert authority over her. Dialogue such as "Deal with it" and the general disbelief towards Angela's situation highlight the powerlessness she experiences.

title: Under Siege 2: Dark Territory
justification: Characters give orders and assert authority: "Move! You have four minutes." and "Everybody to the back of the train! Don't make me ask twice!" There are also power struggles, like when Dane holds the train hostage and threatens to kill people if they don't comply.

title: A Walk in the Clouds
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance or struggling for control. Alberto's controlling behavior towards Victoria and his family, exemplified by "I will not allow this. I'll go to the pope himself to get this undone," and Paul's initial subservience to Betty, followed by his eventual defiance, highlight the power dynamics at play.

title: Man of the House
justification: The stepfather, Jack, attempts to assert himself in the household, leading to conflict with Ben. Ben actively tries to undermine Jack's position, creating tension and a struggle for influence within the family dynamic. Dialogue like "Do me a favour and shut this stove off" and Ben's actions to sabotage Jack's efforts highlight this power struggle.

title: Nobody's Fool
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, give orders, or undermine each other. Examples include Sully's constant needling of others, Clive Jr.'s attempts to control his mother's affairs, and Raymer's interactions with Sully.

title: French Kiss
justification: Several interactions involve characters attempting to assert dominance or control. For example, the concierge initially refuses to help Kate, asserting his duty to protect guests' privacy, and Luc frequently makes condescending remarks to Kate, highlighting her naivete and vulnerability.

title: Higher Learning
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of dominance and submission. Examples include racial slurs used to demean, sexual coercion, and characters asserting physical dominance through threats and violence ('Because I'd whoop your ass, that's why,' 'Run, nigger, run,' 'I'll just put my boot in your mouth').

title: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: The Movie
justification: Ivan Ooze constantly asserts his dominance through commands and threats: "Stop it! Get to work!" and "You will return to the construction site and leap to your doom." Lord Zedd also displays authority, demanding that Goldar and Rita obey him, and expressing anger when they fail to meet his expectations.

title: First Knight
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Malagant's forceful takeover of villages ("Know now, that I am the law!") and Arthur's leadership within Camelot ("Here, every life is precious...Live... and serve."). The film also explores the power dynamics within relationships, such as the tension between Arthur, Guinevere, and Lancelot.

title: Just Cause
justification: The dialogue shows clear power dynamics between law enforcement and suspects, particularly in interrogation scenes where coercion and intimidation are evident. For example, the interrogation of Robert Earl includes instances of physical abuse and manipulation to obtain a confession, demonstrating a significant power imbalance. Additionally, the interactions between Paul Armstrong and various characters, including law enforcement officials and inmates, highlight struggles for control and dominance in different contexts.

title: To Wong Foo Thanks for Everything Julie Newmar
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Sheriff Dollard abuses his authority, and Vida often dictates terms to Chi Chi and Noxeema. The dialogue includes commands and power plays, such as 'Step out of the vehicle' and Vida stripping Chi Chi of 'princess points'.

title: The Indian in the Cupboard
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between Omri and the miniature people he brings to life. He controls their existence and can send them back, leading to conflicts and negotiations for their survival and desires. For example, Little Bear asks Omri to 'make a white man's gun' and Boone demands Omri send him back, highlighting Omri's power.

title: A Goofy Movie
justification: Principal Mazur exerts authority over students, threatening Max with the "electric chair." Pete constantly bosses P.J. around, ordering him to do things and belittling him. Goofy also tries to control Max's behavior and force him to bond, leading to conflict.

title: Judge Dredd
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, orders, and assertions of authority. Examples include judges sentencing criminals ('Automatic five-year sentence. How do you plead?') and characters vying for control ('Stop him! He just killed the entire Council!'). The constant struggle for dominance is evident throughout.

title: Money Train
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include Patterson's controlling behavior towards his officers and the constant power struggles between Charlie and Hook, culminating in their fight and Charlie's dismissal.

title: Copycat
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and jockeying for position. Examples include the police inspectors directing subordinates ('Have Gigi put a tracer on her ass'), Helen Hudson's expertise being sought after and then questioned, and the power plays between Daryll Lee Cullum and Dr. Hudson ('Send me some of your squirrel covers').

title: Rob Roy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and maneuvering for status. Examples include Montrose's interactions with Archibald and MacGregor, Killearn's manipulative behavior, and Rob Roy's leadership within his clan. The constant struggle for control and respect is evident throughout the script.

title: Sabrina
justification: The Larrabee family clearly holds power over their many servants, as evidenced by the descriptions of their roles and the chauffeur's daughter, Sabrina, observing them from afar. Linus exerts control in business dealings, stating, "I said the offer expired at 10:00. It's 10:08, Robert." Maude also wields influence, directing others with commands like, "Sweetheart, go talk to Colonel Morgan."

title: Grumpier Old Men
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the mother being overprotective of her wine and telling her son what to do, and the older men trying to control the new restaurant owner. Examples include: "Put that down!" and "You're wasting your time, I'm telling you."

title: Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Jesse telling Elvis what to do ("You help him set up, O.K.?") and Glenn ordering Elvis to stay on the beach ("ELVIS, STAND BACK."). However, most interactions are relatively egalitarian.

title: Assassins
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and threats, establishing a clear hierarchy. Examples include "Put it down!", "Get down, do not move", and "Drive, drive, drive". Characters are constantly trying to assert dominance and control over each other.

title: Friday
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats, demands, and disrespect. Big Worm's interactions with Smokey, Deebo's bullying, and the general disrespect shown towards elders all highlight a constant struggle for control and status.

title: Now and Then
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the Wormers trying to make the girls' lives miserable and the girls getting revenge. Also, the adults sometimes exert authority over the girls, like when Samantha's grandmother is upset because her father moved out and yells at him.

title: Houseguest
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance through wealth, status, or physical intimidation. For example, Pike pressures Gary to prioritize business, and the mobsters use threats to find Franklin. Derek's interactions also show a struggle to maintain a facade of competence.

title: Desperado
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and negotiating their positions within a criminal hierarchy. Examples include Bucho's control over his men ('Take extra men and place them around the Tarasco and La Azteca') and the constant threat of violence to maintain order ('If you see a stranger... kill him').

title: Billy Madison
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of dominance and submission. Billy's father constantly belittles him ('Are you some damned moron?') while favoring Eric. Billy's attempts to regain his father's approval and control of the company drive much of the plot ('Give me one more chance. I'll prove I can take over.').

title: Operation Dumbo Drop
justification: The dialogue is filled with military rank and orders being given. For example, "Pack your gear and be ready to move out at 1300 hours. You've been reassigned." and "We are, and you don't." show the clear hierarchy and obedience expected.

title: Dolores Claiborne
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Vera Donovan exerting control over Dolores, such as dictating how she wants the house cleaned and criticizing her work. Dolores also experiences powerlessness in her marriage, as her husband steals her savings. The interactions between Dolores and the detectives also highlight the power dynamics of law enforcement.

title: Dead Presidents
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include military commands like "Get back to the rally point!" and "Cover me!", as well as personal power plays such as "Fuck you, fuck you, fuck you!" and "Get that radio up here!". There are also instances of characters asserting authority through threats and intimidation.

title: How to Make an American Quilt
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control over others, such as Glady's volatile reactions and attempts to manipulate situations, and Sophia's blunt and sometimes intrusive questioning. There are also instances of characters giving orders or expressing disapproval, like the grandmother's comments about Anna's work and the mother's directives to her daughter.

title: Boys on the Side
justification: Several characters exert control through commands and threats. Examples include demands for money ('Where's the fucking money?') and physical intimidation ('Give me the bat. Give it to me right now.'). The dialogue also reveals a hierarchy within the group, with some characters giving orders and others reluctantly complying.

title: Circle of Friends
justification: Several scenes highlight power imbalances. Brian Mahon controls his daughter's finances, expecting gratitude and obedience: "You shut your hole, or I'll shut it for you." Later, Bernadette's parents pressure her to marry for business reasons, disregarding her feelings.

title: The Usual Suspects
justification: Characters are constantly giving orders and making threats. Examples include: "Do it now!" and "Drop it now, motherfucker!" and "I'm smarter than you, and I'm gonna find out what I wanna know."

title: Don Juan DeMarco
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between doctors and patients, as well as between senior and junior staff. For example, the head doctor pressures the retiring doctor to medicate the patient, and the nurses are instructed to manage the patient's behavior.

title: To Die For
justification: Suzanne exerts control over her husband, Larry, and manipulates teenagers for her documentary. Examples include her demanding attitude towards Larry about his weight and her manipulation of Jimmy to commit murder, highlighted by the dialogue: "Then you have to do what you have to do."

title: Tales from the Crypt: Demon Knight
justification: Throughout the movie, characters are constantly giving orders and asserting dominance. Irene bosses Jeryline around, demanding she clean and serve Mr. Smith, saying, "Show Mr. Smith up to number five...And then fix him some dinner. And after that, I got a few more jobs for you." The demons also exert control, threatening and manipulating the humans.

title: Nell
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over Nell, deciding her fate and treatment. Al Paley wants to study her, stating, "This project has very high priority." Todd, the sheriff, is obligated to enforce a court order to take her away, showing the power of the legal system.

title: Showgirls
justification: The dialogue is filled with explicit power plays. Al exerts control over Nomi through threats and manipulation: "If you want to last longer than a week, you'll give me a blow job." Tony Moss's audition process is demeaning and hierarchical: "I don't care whether you live or die." Cristal Connors also displays dominance, particularly towards Nomi.

title: Vampire in Brooklyn
justification: Several characters exert authority: Captain Dewey gives orders to detectives, mob bosses command underlings (e.g., "Get your fuckin' hands up, Sambo!"), and the vampire Max manipulates and controls Rita (e.g., "Only what you asked."). Rent is arbitrarily tripled, showing landlord power.

title: Johnny Mnemonic
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and asserting dominance. Examples include Ralfi setting prices and Johnny being forced to accept them, as well as the Yakuza's ruthless pursuit of the data and Johnny's head.

title: The Quick and the Dead
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, issuing commands, and challenging each other's authority. Examples include Herod's control over the town, challenges in the quick-draw competition ("I challenge you"), and the general atmosphere of intimidation and control.

title: The Big Green
justification: The teacher, Miss Montgomery, attempts to lead the class and soccer practice, but often faces resistance from the students ("We don't play soccer. Yeah, it's for foreigners."). Sheriff Tom also exerts authority, especially over the children ("All right. Zip it, midgets!"). Jay Huffer tries to assert dominance through insults and challenges.

title: Heavy Weights
justification: Tony Perkis exerts control through strict rules, public shaming, and manipulation, as seen in lines like, "Silence! You--please announce everyone's name." and "Tomorrow morning at 0600...everyone who has not met their weight loss goal...will join me on a 20-mile hike."

title: It Takes Two
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and attempting to control situations. Examples include Clarice's controlling behavior towards Alyssa, Vincenzo's role as a butler taking orders, and the power struggles between Alyssa and Clarice.

title: Home for the Holidays
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, like the mother telling Claudia to check the furnace and Aunt Glady demanding Claudia take the birds. Tommy's behavior towards Leo, such as saying "Get over here and unlock this car. Now," also highlights a power imbalance. Walter's condescending remarks and attempts to dominate the Thanksgiving dinner conversation further exemplify this theme.

title: Jury Duty
justification: The principal exerts authority over Mr. Collins, reminding him of past expulsions and ordering him to sit down. The jury foreman is elected and given some authority, but is also pressured by other jurors to conform. The judge maintains order in the court, but is challenged by jurors.

title: The Prophecy
justification: The angel Gabriel is constantly giving orders to Jerry, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. Gabriel states, "I want you to do something for me," and later demands, "Jerry, come here." The dialogue also reveals a hierarchy among angels, with Gabriel expressing resentment towards humans being elevated above them.

title: Devil in a Blue Dress
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands of others, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Albright's instructions to Easy, the police officers' interrogation tactics, and Mouse's aggressive behavior.

title: Muriel's Wedding
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy within Muriel's family, with her father, Bill, giving orders and controlling finances. Examples include: "And tell Perry to mow that back yard" and "Give her a blank check for the cosmetics."

title: Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Come with me if you want to save your baby," and "Go, now. Save your baby! Go now!"

title: Kiss of Death
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threatening each other, and jockeying for control. Examples include: "Shut up!", "Step out of the truck, please.", "Get him! Shit!", and the constant manipulation and control exerted by Junior Brown over others.

title: Twister
justification: The dialogue showcases a clear struggle for dominance, particularly between Bill and Jonas, as they compete over scientific recognition and resources ('You stole my design, you son of a bitch!'). Jo also exerts control over Bill ('You ought to keep a leash on him.').

title: Mission: Impossible
justification: The film revolves around a hierarchy within the IMF, with Jim Phelps giving orders to his team ('Your mission, should you choose to accept it...'). There's also a power struggle as Ethan is framed and must prove his innocence, navigating treacherous alliances and betrayals ('You're not going to any meeting without me.').

title: The Rock
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Paxton's interactions with Mason ('I am not here to bend over and take it up the ass from you') and Womack's control over Goodspeed ('You're on a need-to-know basis, and you don't need to know!'). Hummel's command over his marines also highlights the hierarchical structure.

title: The Nutty Professor
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the medical scenes where doctors give orders ('Get that crash cart in here stat!') and staff obey. Buddy Love's interactions also highlight dominance, particularly in his stand-up routine where he insults people and demands attention ('What's UP, nigger?').

title: The Birdcage
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as Albert directing Celsius's performance and Armand instructing Albert on how to act more masculine. Examples include: "Celsius, look, this may be a drag show, but it still has be a good drag show" and "Just be a little less obvious."

title: Eraser
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and betraying each other. Examples include: "GET HER OUT OF THERE NOW!", "YOU LEAVE ME NO CHOICE", and "GET MR. MOREHART DOWN HERE IMMEDIATELY."

title: The Hunchback of Notre Dame
justification: Frollo exerts extreme control over Quasimodo, dictating his life and beliefs ('When your heartless mother abandoned you...anyone else would have drowned you.'). Phoebus, as Captain, gives orders to his lieutenant ('Ease up. Wait between lashes.'). The Gypsies are persecuted and seen as outside the established order, leading to power struggles.

title: Star Trek: First Contact
justification: The captain gives many orders to his crew, such as 'Hold your course, Mr. Hawk' and 'Mr. Worf, quantum torpedoes. Ready, sir. Fire.' There is also a clear hierarchy in the Borg collective, with one individual claiming to 'bring order to chaos'.

title: Space Jam
justification: The aliens demand the Looney Tunes become their slaves: "You, all of you, are now our prisoners. We are taking you to our theme park in outer space. Where you'll be our slaves." Bugs Bunny negotiates a chance to defend themselves, showing a challenge to the alien's authority.

title: Jerry Maguire
justification: The dialogue is filled with negotiations, demands, and assertions of control. For example, Cush's agent states, "I WANT him to go number one in the draft, and I WANT him to play," and Rod Tidwell frequently demands "SHOW ME THE MONEY!"

title: Mr. Holland's Opus
justification: The film depicts power dynamics in various settings. A music teacher gives instructions to students ('AND THIS TIME NO MUSIC', 'PLAY THE SUNSET'), and a coach directs a marching band ('SPREAD OUT', 'GET HIM DOWN'). There are also scenes of a principal directing a teacher ('WHAT WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO DO?').

title: Broken Arrow
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Sit.', 'Move! Move! Move!'), questioning authority ('Major, were you recently promoted past me?'), and asserting dominance ('You'll never change, will you? And that, my friend, will be your downfall.'). The central conflict revolves around a stolen nuclear weapon, highlighting the ultimate power of life and death.

title: The Cable Guy
justification: The cable guy exerts control through manipulation, offering services and then withholding them to gain leverage over Steven. Examples include demanding Steven hang out with him in exchange for fixing the cable and manipulating Robin to get back at Steven: "I got her back for you."

title: Courage Under Fire
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and expecting obedience, such as "Honey, shut up," and "Shut up and listen, soldier!" There are also instances of characters questioning authority, such as "Push it overboard, ma'am?" and "No! We should go for altitude, and call for support."

title: Jack
justification: The dialogue shows children establishing a social hierarchy through insults, challenges, and exclusion ('Hey, punk, why don't you watch where my ball is going?'). There are also instances of adults exerting authority ('Victor, eyes up front!') and children testing boundaries ('No, I won't.').

title: Jingle All the Way
justification: Several scenes depict authority figures exerting control, such as the police officer demanding Howard recite the alphabet backwards and the chaotic scramble for the Turbo Man doll, where individuals resort to aggressive tactics to obtain it. Howard's desperation to fulfill his son's Christmas wish also highlights a power dynamic, as Jamie's desire for the toy drives Howard's actions.

title: Executive Decision
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Nagi Hassan's demands and threats, the military personnel issuing commands, and the terrorists controlling the passengers. The power struggle is evident in the conflict between Nagi and his subordinate, and the attempts to negotiate with the terrorists.

title: Primal Fear
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, demanding information, and making threats. Examples include Vail's aggressive questioning of Aaron and Alex, Shaughnessy's controlling interactions, and the power dynamics within the legal proceedings.

title: Beavis and Butt-Head Do America
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include the man instructing Beavis and Butt-Head to retrieve his wife's satchel, the flight attendant directing passengers, and law enforcement officials commanding subordinates and suspects.

title: Tin Cup
justification: Several characters exert authority or challenge it. Roy's caddy, Romeo, frequently gives him instructions and advice, which Roy sometimes ignores, creating tension. The dynamic between Roy and his potential love interest, Dr. Griswold, also involves power struggles, as she is his therapist and he attempts to pursue a romantic relationship with her, blurring professional boundaries.

title: Sleepers
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Guards abuse inmates ("Put your hands on the table and lay 'em down flat. Spread your legs."), and King Benny controls the neighborhood through fear and favors ("If you need money, you find a Jew. But if you want dirt or scum buried under a rock somewhere...there's only one place to go...right here, Hell's Kitchen.").

title: Michael
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and negotiating deals that involve control. Examples include Malt threatening to fire Quinlan and Driscoll if they don't deliver the angel, and Michael's past actions of 'smoting' a bank at Pansy's request.

title: Dragonheart
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, assertions of authority, and challenges to power. Examples include: 'The king commands!' and 'How dare you defy me!' Also, Einon's interactions with peasants and Bowen highlight a clear power imbalance.

title: Up Close & Personal
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics. Examples include Rob and Tally's on-air arguments and Dan's control over the news team. Bucky Terranova also exerts power through his agent role, influencing career moves.

title: Romeo+Juliet
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and expectations, especially from Juliet's parents ('Call her forth to me', 'Go to church o' Thursday, or never after look me in the face!'). Juliet's limited agency and the Nurse's subservient role further highlight the hierarchical relationships.

title: The Mirror Has Two Faces
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Rose's mother constantly criticizes and corrects Rose, highlighting a power imbalance. Greg's attempts to control the terms of his relationship with Rose, particularly regarding sex, also demonstrate a struggle for dominance.

title: Dead Man Walking
justification: The nun's role as a spiritual advisor to a death row inmate creates a power dynamic. The inmate is dependent on her for spiritual guidance and support, while she attempts to influence him towards redemption. Examples: "You're all I got, Sis." and "Will you do it? Ride along into the sunset with me."

title: Scream
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. For example, the killer taunts Sidney with threats like, "If you hang up on me, you'll die just like your mother!" and Dewey asserts his authority with, "When I wear this badge, you treat me like a man of the law!"

title: The Preacher’s Wife
justification: Henry, as the Reverend, holds authority within his family and the church, but struggles to maintain control as Dudley enters the scene. Examples include Henry's attempts to control Dudley's interactions with his wife and his ultimate decision to terminate Dudley's services, showcasing a power struggle.

title: Sense and Sensibility
justification: Several characters exert control over others, such as Mrs. Jennings trying to marry people off and Margaret being ordered around. Willoughby's rejection letter demonstrates a power imbalance, and Mrs. Dashwood's financial concerns dictate her daughters' choices.

title: Happy Gilmore
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the nursing home orderly telling the elderly woman to 'shut the hell up' and threatening her. Shooter McGavin also displays dominance, stating 'This is Shooter's tour' and attempting to control Happy Gilmore's behavior. Happy himself also displays some dominance, such as when he says 'You're fired' to his caddy.

title: The Ghost and the Darkness
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, especially in the interactions between Colonel Patterson and his superiors. Beaumont's dialogue is filled with threats and demands, such as "Make one mistake, and I promise you, I'll make you hate me" and "Don't make me break you." Patterson also exerts authority over the workers, giving orders and managing conflicts.

title: A Thin Line Between Love & Hate
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance. Darnell's interactions with Brandi are marked by attempts to impress her with wealth and status, while Brandi often asserts her independence and control. The dialogue also includes instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority, such as Brandi telling Michael to 'take these out' and 'call security'.

title: Set It Off
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include: "Tanika, hook him up," "Take your ass in the kitchen," "Get down on the ground," and Cleo's general aggressive behavior and control over T.T. and Frankie.

title: Muppet Treasure Island
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, especially between Captain Smollett and his crew ('Thirty lashes and then you walk the plank') and Long John Silver and his pirate underlings ('If anyone mutinies before I says so, I'll throw you overboard'). There are also instances of characters asserting authority, such as when the natives capture the main characters ('Silence, smelly sailor mans!').

title: The Truth About Cats & Dogs
justification: There are subtle power dynamics at play, particularly in the interactions between Abby and Donna, where Abby's celebrity status and perceived desirability create a slight imbalance. For example, Donna says, "You burp and guys think it's adorable. You puke and they line up to hold your hair back."

title: Mars Attacks!
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, giving orders, and asserting dominance. Examples include the President's interactions with his advisors ('General Casey, do you have an opinion?'), the casino manager's dismissive treatment of the performer ('Out of the question'), and the constant power struggles within families ('Mother, this isn't your house.').

title: The Long Kiss Goodnight
justification: Several characters exert authority through threats and commands. Perkins directs Charly, and Timothy threatens Charly's daughter to control her actions. Dialogue such as "Freeze!" and "Do what you have to" highlights the struggle for control.

title: Striptease
justification: Characters give orders and make demands, like "Call Little Caesars. Order me a health pizza." and "You gotta string him along. Bullshit him." There are also clear power imbalances, such as the congressman's aide cleaning up his messes and the Rojo family's influence over politicians.

title: Matilda
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance and control. Harry's constant belittling of Matilda ('I'm smart, you're dumb. I'm big, you're little. I'm right, you're wrong.') and Miss Trunchbull's tyrannical behavior ('Use the Rod, beat the child,' 'In this classroom, in this school, I am God!') exemplify this theme.

title: Homeward Bound II: Lost in San Francisco
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or expressing dominance. For example, Shadow often directs Chance and Sassy, and Riley controls his gang. The dialogue also reveals a hierarchy among the stray dogs, with Riley asserting his authority over others.

title: Black Sheep
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Steve telling Mike what to do on the campaign trail ("Listen, I'm running this show. You've gotta take my advice.") and the governor's staff demanding results ("If we don't do something soon, he'll be living here."). There are also instances of characters being ordered around, like when Steve tells Mike to pop the hood of the car ("Just pop the hood! Please!").

title: One Fine Day
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and obedience, particularly in the workplace. Lew constantly reprimands Jack, threatening his job: "I've given you enough rope to hang us both." The mayor's press conference is a stage for political power.

title: Rumble in the Bronx
justification: Characters frequently give orders and exert control. Examples include Walter directing Elena in the market sale, and the gang members threatening and demanding information from others. The dialogue is filled with commands and displays of dominance.

title: Eddie
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people trying to assert dominance. For example, the team owner threatens the coach, 'I'm here to tell you that if you pull another stunt like that, I'm walkin'.' Later, the new coach, Eddie, tries to get the players to listen to her, but they largely ignore her, showing a struggle for control.

title: Sgt. Bilko
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics.  Bilko's interactions with his platoon involve him giving orders and expecting obedience, while Major Thorn exerts authority over Colonel Hall and Bilko, demanding specific actions and compliance. The interactions between Ernie and Rita also show a power dynamic, with Ernie trying to manipulate her and Rita pushing back.

title: Daylight
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include: "Hey, you can't go in there!", "Frank, are you the acting chief or what? So why don't you act?", and "Cut the goddamn power!".

title: The English Patient
justification: Several scenes show characters asserting dominance or questioning authority. For example, Almasy challenges Katharine's spending habits and social etiquette, and Geoffrey's colleague questions his decision to leave his wife in the desert, leading to a tense exchange. Caravaggio's interrogation scenes also highlight a clear power imbalance and struggle for control.

title: The Island of Dr. Moreau
justification: The entire plot revolves around Dr. Moreau's dominance over his creations, who are forced to obey his laws under threat of pain. Montgomery also exerts control, drugging and manipulating the beast people. The film culminates in a power struggle after Moreau's death, with the beast people vying for leadership and control.

title: Eye for an Eye
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. For example, a mother firmly tells her child, "Megan, don't ever, ever run off so far ahead of us, do you hear?" and later, a woman instructs another, "Go back the way you came. Turn left at the exit sign."

title: First Kid
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. For example, an agent is ordered to "Change into this" by his superior. Also, Luke's Secret Service agent, Simms, is constantly giving him orders and trying to control his behavior, such as when he says, "Don't tell me how to do my job, ok?"

title: From Dusk Till Dawn
justification: The Gecko brothers exert dominance through threats and violence, establishing clear rules for their hostages: "Rule number one. No noise. No questions." Seth frequently orders Richie around, highlighting a hierarchical dynamic: "Richie, you take these keys, you start this big bastard up and drive it up front." Even with the preacher and his family, the brothers are in control, dictating their actions and movements.

title: Down Periscope
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, challenges to authority, and assertions of dominance. Examples include the admiral setting terms for Dodge, Dodge's interactions with his crew (especially Stepanak), and Pascal's attempted mutiny.

title: That Thing You Do!
justification: Several characters exert authority: the band manager Phil ('If I don't get this record going...we'll tear this up. I'm no longer your manager.') and the Play-Tone executive ('From now on you boys will just be simply The Wonders.'). Boss Vic Koss also demands attention and participation from the audience ('Who's gonna hit me?').

title: Escape from L.A.
justification: The film is filled with examples of power dynamics. The President and his subordinates constantly give orders to Snake, threatening him with death if he disobeys: "Explain to this foot soldier why he's going to do what we tell him to do." Cuervo Jones also exerts dominance over his gang and the President's daughter.

title: Fly Away Home
justification: Several instances show authority being asserted. The father figure frequently gives orders to Amy ('Go to school. Go!'), and there are conflicts with authority figures like the official trying to clip the geese's wings ('These geese belong to the Crown.').

title: Kingpin
justification: The dialogue features multiple instances of characters attempting to exert control over others, such as the mugging scene ('Give me the pocketbook, lady.') and Roy's interactions with his landlord ('You pay me the money whenever you get it.'). The relationship between Munson and Ishmael also involves a power dynamic, with Munson initially manipulating Ishmael for financial gain ('With my help, I think you can beat them.').

title: The Craft
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control and manipulate others, especially by Nancy. Examples include Nancy's control over Chris, Rochelle's bullying of Laura, and the group's manipulation of Sarah to join their coven. The power struggles are evident in the dialogue and actions of the characters.

title: Fargo
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Jerry is constantly trying to assert himself with Wade and Stan, but they dismiss him. The kidnappers use threats and violence to control Jerry, demanding more money and threatening his family.

title: The Juror
justification: Characters give direct orders and make threats to control others. Examples include: "Do you understand me, Annie?" and "Do as I say." Also, the Teacher's influence is based on fear and control, as evidenced by "If I can keep you scared, I can save your life."

title: D3: The Mighty Ducks
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Coach Orion exerting his authority over the team, such as dictating drills and demanding specific performance levels: "All right, Fulton. Get low, bend your knees, smooth strokes." There are also instances of status competition among the players, like Goldberg trying to regain his position as the number one goalie by influencing Julie.

title: The Quest
justification: Several characters exert dominance through threats and commands. Examples include the gang leader demanding money ('Hand me the dough, clown, or the kid's dead') and Dobbs manipulating Chris into fighting ('You owe me'). There are also displays of authority through fighting and intimidation.

title: A Very Brady Sequel
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. For example, Mr. Phillips tells Peter, "Don't let me catch you napping!" and Roy Martin tells Peter, "Stop whining. Being top dog is what it's all about. Show people who's boss. Even if you have to lie, cheat, steal or kill."

title: Chain Reaction
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Mr Chen, upload everything. I want it on the Internet tonight," and "Have the locals move the perimeter back about 1,000 ft. You got it."

title: Bulletproof
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Let's go. Up, up, up.'), asserting dominance ('Yo, you better back up off me, son.'), and negotiating deals ('Come on, Moses. lf you come out now, maybe we can make a deal.'). There are also instances of characters being held captive and forced to comply with demands.

title: High School High
justification: The film features several power struggles. Ms. Doyle, the principal, exerts authority over teachers and students, while gang leader Paco attempts to dominate through intimidation and violence. Richard Clark challenges these dynamics, attempting to empower students and confront authority figures, leading to conflicts.

title: Fear
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the father setting rules for Nicole ('As long as you're living in my house, you'll follow my rules.') and David's controlling behavior towards Margo ('You better fix it. You better make it right again. Because if you don't, I'm gonna hurt you.'). There are also instances of characters giving orders ('Shut up, Gary.').

title: The Glimmer Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and control. Deverell's influence is mentioned repeatedly, and his enforcer issues threats.
