The detectives also use their authority to intimidate suspects, as evidenced by the line, "Turn around, put your goddamn hands on the car..."

title: City Hall
justification: The Mayor and his staff discuss how to manipulate the press and public opinion. Frank Anselmo attempts to leverage his influence for personal gain, but the Mayor asserts his authority: "You're only a boss, Frank. I'm the fucking Mayor."

title: Multiplicity
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Doug instructing his clones ("Stay down low. Really low.", "Don't make me want to kick your ass.") and Del King threatening Doug with being fired ("Get down here or you're fired!").

title: Flipper
justification: The uncle, Porter, exerts authority over Sandy through chores and commands like "Shake a leg, sailor!" and "You don't get up, you don't eat." There's also a clear hierarchy in the fishing community, with Oirk attempting to intimidate Porter and Sandy.

title: Bed of Roses
justification: The dialogue shows some power dynamics, primarily in the romantic relationship between Lisa and Lewis. Lewis's actions, like sending flowers anonymously and showering Lisa with gifts, could be seen as attempts to exert control or influence. Lisa's resistance to these gestures and her eventual confrontation with Lewis highlight a struggle for autonomy within the relationship.

title: Kazaam
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include "ET IT DONE," "BEAT IT!", "I SAID I WANTED THE BAR STOCKED," and "YOU'RE GONNA DO WHATEVER I WANT."

title: The Fan
justification: Several characters exert authority: the agent telling the client when he can be seen, the father dictating baseball techniques to his son, and the boss firing Gil. Dialogue like "6:05, he's not home, I call the cops" and "Drop your cock and grab your socks" further illustrates the power dynamics.

title: Last Man Standing
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and vying for control. Examples include Strozzi's commands, Doyle's threats, and the constant power plays between characters like Giorgio and Smith.

title: My Fellow Americans
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and vying for control. Examples include: "Land this contraption or I'll blow your head off!", "Get out of the chopper!", and the overall plot involving political kickbacks and cover-ups.

title: The Crow: City of Angels
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Judah's interactions with Bassett and others showcase a clear hierarchy and the consequences of disobedience: "So you destroyed 80 keys of product without my consent." and "All must love you."

title: Extreme Measures
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include the FBI agent directing the doctor, "Get your hands above your heads and come forward," and the lab supervisor telling the doctor, "I'm your boss and I'm telling you...drop this thing."

title: The Phantom
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include Drax ordering Quill around, the Singh Brotherhood leader commanding his followers, and the Phantom directing others in combat situations. Dialogue such as "Shoot him!", "Tie him up and leave him here", and "Get him out of here" demonstrates a clear hierarchy and attempts to control others.

title: Fled
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and asserting dominance. Examples include Warden Nichols instructing Marshal Schiller, the power plays between Dodge and Piper, and the general hierarchical structure within the prison system and law enforcement.

title: Air Force One
justification: The film is filled with power struggles, from the terrorists seizing control of Air Force One to the Vice President and cabinet debating presidential authority. Dialogue like "Get this plane back in the air now, or you die!" and "I'm in charge here" exemplifies the constant battle for dominance.

title: My Best Friend's Wedding
justification: The lyrics suggest a submissive role in relationships, with lines like "All you gotta do is hold him and kiss him and love him" and "Do the things that he likes to do, wear your hair just for him." There's a sense of trying to please someone to maintain the relationship, indicating a slight power imbalance.

title: Titanic
justification: The dialogue shows a clear class-based hierarchy, with the wealthy exerting control over the lower classes. Cal's controlling behavior towards Rose and the crew's deference to Ismay highlight the power imbalances. The crew's orders to the passengers also show the power dynamics.

title: Face/Off
justification: The film revolves around the power struggle between Sean Archer and Castor Troy, with constant attempts to outmaneuver and dominate each other. Dialogue such as "I'd become Castor Troy, be in control. That's the part that scares me" and the prison scenes highlight the dominance and submission within the prison hierarchy.

title: Batman & Robin
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control. Poison Ivy commands Bane, Freeze orders his henchmen, and Batman sets rules for Robin. Examples: "Honey, clean up this mess." and "If you want to stay in this house, on this team, you'll abide by them."

title: Con Air
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats, insults, and orders. Examples include Cyrus's constant commands and threats to the guards and other inmates, as well as the guards' initial control over the prisoners, such as the forced medication and restraint checks. The power struggles are central to the plot, as the prisoners attempt to overthrow the established order.

title: Hercules
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Hades attempts to control Hercules, saying, "If I say, 'Sing,' you say, 'Hey, name that tune.'" Amphitryon demands Hercules be kept away, stating, "You keep that-that-that... freak away from here!"

title: Scream 2
justification: Gale Weathers exerts control over her cameraman Joel, manipulating him to stay despite the danger ("Don't you wanna be a part of that? Come on. I need you. I cannot do this without you."). Dewey, despite being a deputy, is often belittled and underestimated, especially by Gale, who uses his feelings for her to her advantage. Cotton Weary attempts to leverage his past with Sidney and Diane Sawyer's interest for his own gain, demanding exposure and recognition.

title: Flubber
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Reynolds tries to intimidate Brainard into selling his invention, and Weber is shown bossing around his henchmen. Wilson attempts to manipulate Sara into marrying him.

title: Conspiracy Theory
justification: The dialogue is dominated by interrogation, threats, and attempts to control Jerry. Examples include: 'Now, Jerry... to whom have you been talking?' and 'Who else knows, Jerry? Names, Jerry, names!' Also, Alice is given orders by the FBI and CIA.

title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over each other, from Max's aggressive behavior towards Julie and her friends ('Chum bait. Take a hike.') to Barry's possessiveness ('I'm just taking care of your girl.'). The constant arguments and attempts to dominate the narrative of the urban legend also highlight this theme ('You're telling it wrong. Shut up.').

title: Dante’s Peak
justification: The USGS scientists, Harry and Paul, have a clear hierarchical relationship, with Paul as the boss giving orders and making decisions, such as when to call an alert or leave town. The mayor, Rachel, also exerts authority, organizing meetings and attempting to manage the town's response, sometimes clashing with Harry's recommendations.

title: Anaconda
justification: The dialogue hints at power dynamics through Serone's manipulative actions and the crew's reactions to his authority. The discussion of Serone as a potential antagonist also suggests a power struggle.

title: The Fifth Element
justification: The film features numerous instances of characters asserting dominance and control. Examples include police officers giving orders ("Please keep your hands on the wheel."), Zorg's manipulative and threatening behavior, and the general's authoritative commands to Korben Dallas ("You leave immediately for Fhloston Paradise.").

title: In & Out
justification: The film explores power dynamics through several lenses. Howard's mother pressures him relentlessly to get married: "I NEED that wedding." The school principal also pressures Howard to conform or face consequences: "Friends warn."

title: The Saint
justification: The film features constant power struggles. Tretiak attempts to seize control of Russia, issuing orders to his subordinates. Characters like the thief negotiate deals and betray each other for financial gain, demonstrating a constant shifting of power.

title: Jungle 2 Jungle
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Michael frequently gives orders to Richard regarding the coffee bean sales ('I told you to sell them at 97 and a half!'). He also attempts to control Mimi's behavior ('When I tell you to do something, I mean it. Do you understand me?').

title: Kiss the Girls
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include medical staff directing each other ('Scalpel, please, Nurse'), boxing trainers instructing fighters ('Come on, Kate, let's see something'), and the kidnapper dictating rules to his captive ('Don't try to escape').

title: Devil’s Advocate
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for dominance, giving orders, and asserting their status. Examples include Milton's manipulation of Kevin, Eddie's attempts to assert authority within the firm, and the general atmosphere of competition and hierarchy at the Barzoon's party.

title: Spawn
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Wynn's manipulation of Al and Terry, the Clown's taunting of Spawn, and Malebolgia's commands all highlight a constant power struggle.

title: Starship Troopers
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and hierarchical interactions, especially between Sergeant Zim and the recruits. Examples include: "The first words and the last words out of your stinking holes will be 'Sir'!" and "You don't do your job, I'll shoot you."

title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
justification: Dr. Evil constantly asserts his authority over his henchmen, punishing failure with threats and demeaning comments. For example, he yells "Silence! Let this be a reminder to you all...that this organization will not tolerate failure." Agent Kensington also asserts her authority over Austin Powers, correcting his behavior and reminding him of the mission.

title: The Jackal
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the arms dealer dictating payment terms ("Half now, half on delivery") and FBI agents demanding cooperation from Mulqueen ("You cooperate and we'll get you transferred"). The Jackal also exerts control, dictating terms to the gunsmith and manipulating others.

title: Anastasia
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the orphanage director's demeaning treatment of Anya: "You've been a thorn in my side...Acting like the Queen of Sheba instead of the nameless no-account you are." Dimitri also frequently bosses Anya around, and Rasputin commands Bartok.

title: Breakdown
justification: The film revolves around a power struggle between the protagonists and a group of criminals. Dialogue such as "Get out of the car, now!" and "You're a tough man to get a-hold of, Jeffrey" demonstrates the criminals' dominance and control over the protagonists.

title: Absolute Power
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the President giving orders to his staff ("ShaII I bring Mrs. Richmond home?") and Alan's violent domination of the woman he attacks ("You IittIe bitch!"). Walter also demonstrates power through wealth and influence, hiring McCarty and dictating terms ("You wiII wait in Washington, Mr. McCarty.").

title: The Game
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and asserting dominance. Examples include Nicholas's interactions with his staff ('Yes, Ilsa, what is it?'), Anson Baer's firing ('I am firing you.'), and the constant manipulation and control exerted by CRS throughout the game.

title: G.I.Jane
justification: The dialogue is dominated by orders, insults, and displays of authority. Examples include: "Get the hell out of here!", "Move your girlie butts!", and "You will write when I tell you to write."

title: Speed II: Cruise Control
justification: Several characters exert authority: the captain gives orders ("Captain on the bridge."), the first officer directs evacuation ("Attention. Attention, please. This is the first officer."), and Geiger controls the ship and threatens others ("I've cut off all outside communication."). There are also instances of resistance to authority, such as the passenger who refuses to wear a jacket ("I like this dress and it's fine.").

title: Star Wars Ep. VI: Return of the Jedi
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and others submitting. Examples include Vader's interactions with the commander, Jabba's control over his court, and Luke's attempts to negotiate, which are quickly dismissed by Jabba.

title: Evita
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, with Eva rising in power and influence. Examples include 'Tell the driver this is where I'm staying' and 'She says it's his body but she's after his files,' indicating manipulation and control.

title: Volcano
justification: Several characters are in positions of authority, giving orders and making decisions that impact others. Examples include Mike Roark directing emergency response efforts ('Emmit, get me 200 K-rails to build a corridor') and the fire chief commanding his team ('Pull back. Pull back. We gotta get more units here'). There are also instances of defiance and questioning of authority, such as the conflict between the geologist and city officials regarding the safety of underground blasting.

title: Alien: Resurrection
justification: The scientists and military personnel exert control over Ripley 8 and the aliens, viewing them as assets or threats. Dialogue like "Excellent work, everybody" and "Bottom line is, she looks at me funny one time, I'm putting her down" shows a clear hierarchy and the threat of violence to maintain control. The crew of the Betty also have their own internal power struggles, with Elgyn giving orders and others challenging his authority.

title: The Rainmaker
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Bruiser gives orders to Rudy and Deck, Drummond attempts to intimidate Rudy in court, and Judge Kipler asserts his authority over the lawyers. There are also instances of physical dominance, such as Cliff's abuse of Kelly and Rudy's subsequent confrontation with him.

title: Bean
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the gallery director firing Bean, then being overruled by the chairman: "I'll talk to the Chairman and insist on... Mr Bean's immediate dismissal." David's family also shows a power dynamic, with Alison threatening to leave if Bean stays: "He goes today."

title: Cop Land
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and navigating hierarchical relationships. Examples include Ray's control over his town and Freddy, Moe's IA investigation, and the general deference shown to Ray by other officers. The interactions between the cops and civilians also highlight the power dynamics at play.

title: Nothing To Lose
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, threats, and displays of control. Examples include the initial kidnapping scenario ('Get out'), the constant insults and put-downs ('What a pussy'), and the violent confrontations ('Drop the fucking gun').

title: Soul Food
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Teri's control over legal matters and family decisions is evident, while Simuel attempts to leverage his position for personal gain. Lem's struggle to maintain his masculinity and authority after losing his job also demonstrates a power imbalance.

title: The Devil’s Own
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, threats, and assertions of authority. Examples include: "Here's your target. Frankie Maguire. I'd like to change that," "Move it!," and "You're gonna be sorry."

title: Donnie Brasco
justification: The dialogue is filled with assertions of dominance, threats, and jockeying for position within the Mafia hierarchy. Examples include Sonny being 'upped' and Lefty's frustration at being passed over, Sonny's demand to know what Donnie is up to, and the constant need to show 'respect' to those higher in the hierarchy like Trafficante.

title: As Good as it Gets
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Melvin's demanding behavior towards Carol ('just have her do my one meal here. I'll pay whatever you want. I'll wait. Do it!'). There are also instances of characters giving orders or directions ('Don't do anything.').

title: The Peacemaker
justification: Characters frequently give and receive orders, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "Get me NMCC intel," "Can you go get the files?," and "Push that through as fast as we can." The dialogue also reveals power struggles, such as the interrogation scene with Shummaker and the tense interactions between Devoe and Kodoroff.

title: Private Parts
justification: The radio station management attempts to control Howard's content, demanding he tone down his act and follow specific guidelines. Howard resists these attempts, leading to conflicts and firings. Examples: "You and Robin must not talk to each other on the air." and "I'll mold that son of a bitch into another Don Imus."

title: Money Talks
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of dominance. Examples include: 'I need you to take a shower... Shave the beard, lose the earring' and 'You don't speak unless spoken to. Not a word. You stay by my side.' There are also frequent threats and displays of anger, indicating a struggle for control.

title: Mouse Hunt
justification: The brothers are constantly bickering and trying to one-up each other, especially regarding the house and the auction. Falko attempts to exert control by offering a deal outside the auction, and Ernie tries to assert authority in the kitchen.

title: L.A. Confidential
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and jockeying for position. Examples include Exley's repeated insistence that the Nite Owl case is his, the Captain's command to "USE ALL NECESSARY FORCE," and Patchett's control over the women who work for him.

title: Seven Years in Tibet
justification: The subtitles contain numerous examples of characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include: "As a team! That's an order!", "Stop, or I'll shoot! Hands up!", and the power imbalance between the Dalai Lama and his advisors.

title: Vegas Vacation
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or demonstrate status. For example, Clark tells his son, "Russell, I never wanna hear those words out of your mouth again. Gambling is a very serious business. Is that clear?" Also, Eddie frequently tries to assert himself, such as when he says, "Show them who's boss."

title: Selena
justification: The father, Abraham, exerts strong control over Selena's career and personal life, dictating musical direction, firing band members, and initially opposing her marriage. Examples include: "You must pick it up. The rhythm wasn't fast enough," and "You're fired! Do you hear me?!"

title: Mortal Kombat: Annihilation
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and threats, such as "Annihilate them," and "Surrender, Rayden, or this one dies." Shao Kahn's constant demands and the characters' struggles against his tyranny highlight the power imbalance. Rayden's role as a leader and advisor also contributes to the theme.

title: Addicted To Love
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Maggie threatens Sam with violence if he interferes with her. Anton, the restaurant owner, asserts his dominance over the homeless man, alternating between kindness and threats.

title: Amistad
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, assertions of authority, and challenges to dominance. Examples include 'Get this table out of here,' 'You don't belong here,' and the constant struggle over the fate of the Africans in court, where legal power and social status are wielded.

title: The Relic
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include D'Agosta directing the police force ('Sweep in teams of two. Nobody goes in alone.') and the Mayor leveraging his position ('I'm gonna call the chief and tell him just how happy I am.'). There are also instances of characters resisting authority, creating tension and highlighting power struggles.

title: Picture Perfect
justification: The dialogue shows characters jockeying for position, especially Kate's mother trying to control her daughter's life. Kate's work life also shows power dynamics, with her boss expecting total commitment and dictating her schedule. The fake relationship with Nick is also driven by Kate's need to impress her boss.

title: Beverly Hills Ninja
justification: The film features a clear master-student dynamic between Haru and his sensei, with Haru constantly seeking approval and following orders. Examples include: "I shall do as you say" and the sensei's instructions to Gobei to act as Haru's shadow. Additionally, there are power struggles between criminal organizations, such as the Kobudosai and Martin Tanley's gang, as they vie for control of the counterfeit plates.

title: Fools Rush In
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Examples include "Shut up!", "Everyone get out of here!", and the general scolding tone used by the older woman towards Isabel, indicating a hierarchical dynamic.

title: Romy and Michele's High School Reunion
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the popular girls' behavior towards Sandy Frink and Christie's initial treatment of Romy. Heather's rude comments also show a lack of respect. However, the overall focus is more on friendship and personal insecurities than overt power struggles.

title: Out to Sea
justification: The cruise director, Gil, exerts authority over the dance hosts, dictating their behavior and threatening dismissal. Examples: "Above all, you will not fraternize privately with the guests at any time. If you do, it's grounds for immediate dismissal." and "Gentlemen, I didn't hire you to be wallflowers."

title: Father's Day
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and attempting to exert control over others. Examples include the initial scene where Chip is told to cry on command, and later when the potential fathers argue and try to control Scott's actions. The drug dealers also exert power through threats and demands.

title: The Edge
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or instructions, such as the pilot briefing the group on flight safety and the guide instructing them on bear safety. Bob's interactions with James regarding the boots also highlight a hierarchical dynamic. The dialogue also reveals Charles's wealth and influence, which creates a power dynamic in his relationships.

title: Jackie Brown
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, especially between Ordell and Jackie. Ordell frequently gives orders and uses threats, such as "WHY DON'T YOU BE A GOOD HOSTESS...AND HOOK A BROTHER UP A SCREWDRIVER?" and later holding a gun to Jackie. Jackie also gains power by controlling information and negotiating deals with both Ordell and the ATF.

title: Event Horizon
justification: The captain gives orders to the crew ('All right, people, listen up.') and expects obedience. Dr. Weir's expertise is questioned ('Perhaps the good doctor will be kind enough to tell us.'). There is a clear hierarchy and tension between the crew and Dr. Weir.

title: Air Bud
justification: The clown gives commands to the dog, like "Okay, mutt. Show time." and "Okay, dog, your turn." The basketball coach also asserts authority, yelling, "Stewart, don't try to be a hero. Your job on this team is to get the ball to Willingham."

title: Murder at 1600
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and navigating hierarchical structures. Examples include detectives demanding information ('I want a complete list...'), agents being ordered ('You are to have no further contact...'), and the president making decisions about war and peace ('I want the 7th fleet to stand down.').

title: Mimic
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. For example, Peter, from the CDC, directs the police and other personnel: "Quarantine 'em. Quarantine the cops that found it." Also, Susan directs Chuy to do things.

title: For Richer or Poorer
justification: Brad frequently gives orders to Caroline, such as "Caroline, come on" and "Shut up, Brad!". Phil, though seemingly a friend, holds power over Brad by controlling access to funds and information: "No can do, my friend. That would be abetting a felon."

title: Sling Blade
justification: Doyle exerts dominance through threats and verbal abuse, particularly towards Linda and Frank. He controls situations by force and intimidation, demanding obedience and disrespecting others, especially Karl. The dialogue highlights his need to be in charge and his willingness to use aggression to maintain control, such as when he threatens Linda and dismisses Vaughan.

title: Home Alone III
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Mrs. Hess demanding snow removal and berating Alex, and Charlie pressuring Karen to work despite her family obligations. The villains also display a clear hierarchy, with Beaupre giving orders and threatening consequences for failure: "If I don't have the chip in 24 hours...I will have to terminate the mission...and nullify all the participants."

title: Boogie Nights
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving directions and seeking approval, especially in the context of the film set. Examples include Jack directing Dirk's performance ('Make your entrance through this door. He'll call, 'Action.' That's your cue.') and Dirk seeking validation ('Does it...? Does it look sexy?').

title: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of social maneuvering, control, and status displays. Examples include Jim Williams's control over his parties and guests, the power dynamics in his relationship with Billy Hanson ('Give me $20'), and the social hierarchy evident in the interactions at the party ('Welcome to Mercer House').

title: Hoodlum
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Madam Queen's control over her territory and Bumpy's rise to power through force and negotiation with powerful figures like Luciano and Dutch Schultz. The constant struggle for control over Harlem's numbers game and the characters' willingness to use violence to maintain their positions highlight the intense power dynamics at play.

title: Red Corner
justification: The courtroom setting is inherently hierarchical, with the judge, procurator, and defense attorney all vying for control. The accused, Moore, is subject to the court's authority, and his attempts to assert himself are met with resistance. Examples: 'You must address the court in the proper manner,' and 'Accused Moore, please be seated now.'

title: An American Werewolf in Paris
justification: The 'Daredevil Tour' competition establishes a hierarchy with points and challenges. Andy is constantly pressured by Chris and Brad, who mock his lack of romantic success and try to control his actions. Claude's control over his werewolf pack and his plans to 'purify the world' through violence demonstrate a clear power dynamic.

title: Booty Call
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Nikki telling Rushon and Bunz when they have to leave. There are also instances of physical dominance, like Bunz threatening to "kick your ass" and Rushon's attempts to control Killa. The dialogue is filled with challenges and attempts to assert dominance, especially in the context of sexual relationships.

title: Gone Fishin'
justification: The dialogue shows Joe giving Gus orders and directions, such as "Get the beer, Gus!" and "Go get the anchor! Hurry UP!" There are also instances of Joe asserting his dominance and belittling Gus, like when he says, "Yeah, you were scared, Gus." This indicates a clear power imbalance in their relationship.

title: Mother
justification: The mother and son constantly vie for control, especially in mundane situations like grocery shopping and refrigerator organization. The mother often dismisses the son's opinions and tries to control his choices, while the son attempts to assert his independence and challenge her traditional views. Examples include the peanut butter and jelly argument, and the debate over fixing the car.

title: The People vs. Larry Flynt
justification: The film depicts Larry Flynt's constant battles against legal and moral authorities, showcasing his defiance and struggle for control over his publication. Examples include his courtroom antics, refusal to reveal sources, and clashes with judges, demonstrating a consistent challenge to established power structures. Dialogue such as 'You're the boss' and Flynt's dismissals of others highlight his assertion of authority.

title: That Darn Cat
justification: Several characters exert authority: the mother over Patti ("You will not make me swear, young lady."), the police captain over Zeke ("You're off the case."), and the kidnappers over Lizzy. Zeke also attempts to assert authority, though often ineffectively, as seen in his interactions with his team and Patti.

title: That Old Feeling
justification: Several characters exert control over others, like the mother telling Molly what to wear and how to act. Keith's political ambitions dictate Molly's actions, demonstrated when he says, "This is what being a political wife is all about: Damage control." Dan's controlling behavior towards Lilly is also evident.

title: Wes Craven's Wishmaster
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Beaumont giving orders to Torelli ('All right, let's go, Torelli!') and the basketball coach instructing her players ('You didn't have stillness.'). The Djinn also manipulates people by granting wishes, demonstrating control over their desires and fates ('As you wish.').

title: Mr. Magoo
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Magoo giving orders to Waldo and Angus. The CIA and FBI agents compete for control of the investigation, highlighted by their argument: "I'm in charge of this investigation." "The CIA has no jurisdiction on American soil."

title: Armageddon
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's decisions. Examples include Harry constantly directing A.J. during the simulation, and the Colonel making demands of NASA personnel to allow the crew time off.

title: Saving Private Ryan
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and directives, such as "Upham, over there. Reiben, you four go." and "Wade! Get them ready to travel. Yes, sir." There are also instances of insubordination and challenges to authority, like Reiben's refusal to follow orders and the subsequent confrontation with the Captain, highlighting a struggle for control and differing opinions on the mission.

title: There's Something About Mary
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. For example, Sully is dismissive and commanding towards Healy on the phone ('Hold, please.'). Also, the detectives interrogate Ted, using their authority to pressure him into confessing ('Tell us why you did it?').

title: The Waterboy
justification: The film features a mother who exerts strong control over her son, dictating his social life and career choices ("Bobby, that-that woman is the devil. I want you to stay away from her, you hear me?"). The coach also holds authority, directing players and making decisions about the team ("All right, now I wanna work with the offense. I wanna work with the defense.").

title: Doctor Dolittle
justification: Several scenes involve characters giving orders or asserting dominance. Examples include John telling his daughter "No camp, no dog," and various animals demanding medical attention from Dolittle, such as the tiger who threatens to eat him and Lucky.

title: Deep Impact
justification: The President's speech sets the tone, dictating national behavior ('There will be no hoarding'). Beth's interactions with Jenny and Stuart show a struggle for control within the White House press operations ('Did Stuart send you here without telling me?'). Tanner's initial authority is questioned by the younger astronauts ('You're here for public relations.')

title: Godzilla
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Military personnel give and receive orders ('Abandon ship!', 'Fire at will!'). The mayor exerts authority ('Didn't we agree that we weren't to have any sweets until after the election?').

title: Rush Hour
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Carter's aggressive interactions with Lee ("PUT...YO BAG...IN THE BACK!") and his attempts to control situations ("MAN, JUST SIT THERE AND SHUT UP. THIS AIN'T NO DEMOCRACY."). The FBI agents also exert authority over Carter, suspending him and dictating his actions.

title: Good Will Hunting
justification: Characters frequently assert dominance through insults and threats, such as "Maybe you should watch your mouth! Watch it right there, chief, all right?" and "If you ever disrespect my wife again, I will end you." The therapist-patient relationship also highlights power dynamics, with Will initially resisting the therapist's authority and control.

title: Lethal Weapon 4
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. For example, the Captain directs Riggs and Murtaugh, and characters like Uncle Benny exert control over others, highlighted by dialogue such as "Drop your guns" and the general dynamic of smuggling and exploitation.

title: A Bug’s Life
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Hopper demands the ants collect food, and threatens them if they don't: "Not one ant sleeps... until we get every scrap of food... on this island!". There are also examples of status seeking, such as when Francis is trying to assert his masculinity.

title: The Truman Show
justification: Christof controls Truman's entire world, dictating events and relationships. Examples include: "Nothing you see on the show is fake. It's merely controlled." and Christof's direct commands during Truman's escape, such as "Cue the sun." and "Increase the wind!".

title: The Mask of Zorro
justification: Several characters give orders and assert authority. Rafael Montero orders the arrest of Zorro and asserts his power over the dons. Diego trains Alejandro, establishing a master-pupil dynamic.

title: Enemy of the State
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats and intimidation. For example, one character says, "Now you listen to me, you fuckin' eggplant...Now, who made the fuckin' videotape?" and later, "Or I'll kill ya." There are also instances of characters giving orders and expecting immediate compliance, such as "Vic, get outside." and "Get a wire on our bird watcher."

title: The Rugrats Movie
justification: Angelica manipulates the younger children with threats and misinformation, establishing a clear power dynamic. For example, she tells Tommy that his parents will forget him when the new baby arrives. The adults also exert authority, such as when Betty directs everyone to their 'stations' during the birth.

title: Frantic
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Richard telling his wife, "Give me the note," and the kidnappers directing Walker with threats like, "Bring the statue, Doctor...don't be stupid."

title: They Live
justification: The film depicts a hidden class of beings controlling society, using wealth and media to manipulate humans. Dialogue like "They control us! They are our masters!" and scenes of characters being given orders ("Step down.", "Drive.") highlight this dynamic.

title: All Dogs Go To Heaven
justification: Carface's orders are central: "Come back when you got some food," and "Killer, I do not wish that I should share 50% of the business with my partner Charlie." Charlie also exerts control, as seen when he tells Itchy, "Will you shut up?"

title: Rocky V
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of Rocky taking on a mentor role, giving advice and guidance to his son and Tommy Gunn. Duke attempts to exert control over Rocky's career and Tommy's future, highlighting the manipulative nature of the boxing business. There are also instances of characters trying to assert dominance through intimidation and threats, such as the school bullies and Duke's aggressive tactics.

title: Cinema Paradiso
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting authority. For example, Alfredo frequently bosses Toto around in the projection booth, and various characters are shown giving instructions to others in their respective roles (e.g., the priest, the teacher).

title: Graveyard Shift
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance and control. Warwick frequently gives orders and manipulates those around him, such as when he tells Jane, "This cleanup ain't gonna be pretty, darling" and offers her a 'promotion' with ulterior motives. There are also instances of characters like Warwick and Cleveland asserting authority through intimidation and threats, such as when Warwick says, "You'd best be punching out your time card. Permanently."

title: The Naked Gun 2½: The Smell of Fear
justification: The film features several instances of characters asserting authority and dominance. For example, Drebin's police rank gives him authority over other officers, and Hapsburg's wealth and influence allow him to manipulate events and people. The dialogue between Drebin and Hapsburg is a constant power struggle, with each trying to outwit the other.

title: Backdraft
justification: The dialogue contains numerous instances of commands and directives, indicating a hierarchical structure within the fire department. Examples include "Call in a box," "Get the high-rise jet," and "You're on your own, boss," which highlight the giving and taking of orders. Additionally, there are instances of conflict and challenges to authority, such as the tension between Stephen and Brian, and the confrontation with the Alderman, suggesting a struggle for status and control.

title: Boyz n the Hood
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and engaging in verbal sparring. Examples include Doughboy's aggressive interactions ('What the fuck is wrong with you?!') and Furious's lectures to Tre ('So you a leader or a follower?'). The constant need to prove oneself and the threat of violence further highlight the struggle for status.

title: Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and status-seeking. Examples include Kirk giving orders on the bridge ('Shall we raise our shields, Captain?') and the Klingon General Chang's aggressive stance ('Attack them now, while we still can!'). The court martial scene also highlights the power imbalance and Kirk's struggle against authority.

title: Regarding Henry
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in professional settings. For example, Linda tells Henry, "It's good to see you back at the office," and Jessica states, "I'm not allowed to give you any more of your old case files," indicating a shift in Henry's authority.

title: Dying Young
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Victor exerting control over Hilary, such as dictating the terms of her employment ("Want the job?"), their relationship ("This is not part of the deal."), and ultimately, his end-of-life decisions ("Just let it happen."). His father also tries to exert control over Victor by hiring a nurse for him.

title: Oscar
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and negotiating for control. Examples include Angelo Provolone's interactions with his employees ('Brush her off') and family ('You're not going to any convent!'). The negotiations between Angelo and Anthony also highlight a power struggle, as they try to outsmart each other.

title: Hamlet
justification: The ghost of Hamlet's father commands Hamlet to seek revenge, establishing a clear hierarchy. Claudius, as the new king, gives orders and expects obedience, as seen in his interactions with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Hamlet's interactions with Polonius and Ophelia also show his attempts to exert control, though often masked by his 'antic disposition'.

title: F/X2
justification: Characters give orders and make demands: "Get her outta here! Get her out!", "Freeze, asshole!", "Tell 'em we got a cop down." There are also instances of characters asserting authority and dominance, such as Silak's control over the operation and Leo's interrogation of suspects.

title: Frankie and Johnny
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Frankie gives orders like "OK. You pour, I'll bump." and "You can make that call now, Jorge." Nick's control is evident in "Nick doesn't like the help messing around."

title: Only the Lonely
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Danny's mother constantly criticizes and attempts to manipulate his choices, saying things like, "You always make the knot too big" and expressing disapproval of Theresa's ethnicity. Sal also tries to influence Danny's relationship, warning him about getting "trapped."

title: Pure Luck
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters giving orders and establishing dominance. Examples include Highsmith directing Proctor and Campanella, and Proctor attempting to assert authority over Campanella, illustrated by lines like "You'll be his assistant...BUT only in his head. YOU'LL be running the show" and "THAT'S AN ORDER!".

title: The Prince of Tides
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Lila Wingo's manipulation of her children, Tom's aggressive questioning of Sally about her affair, and Tom's confrontational interactions with Lowenstein all highlight struggles for dominance and information.

title: The Commitments
justification: The band leader, Jimmy, frequently gives orders and critiques the band members' performances ('That's enough!', 'Hold it, hold it.'). There are also instances of conflict and challenges to authority, such as when Deco is kicked out of the band ('Get the fuckin' hell out!').

title: Toy Soldiers
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Mr. Tepper's commands to Billy to break the device, the terrorists' strict rules and threats of execution, and the sheriff's initial attempts to assert authority before being undermined.

title: Billy Bathgate
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and navigating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Schultz's control over his gang ('All you have to do is what you're supposed to do. Stop dicking me around!') and his manipulation of Drew ('It's either a yes or a no. I-I... What? I'm sorry. I can't hear you. What? Yes.').

title: Problem Child 2
justification: The principal barks orders and expects immediate obedience from students, exemplified by 'I bark, they do what I say. Anything. Crawl around on all fours. They do that.' LaWanda Dumore exerts control through wealth and intimidation, as seen in 'They missed a payment? Toss 'em in the street.' Ben Healy struggles to control his son, Junior, but often fails, highlighting a power imbalance.

title: Madonna: Truth or Dare
justification: Madonna's interactions with her staff and dancers reveal a clear hierarchy. She gives instructions and expects obedience, such as telling Oliver not to give her attitude and directing her assistant Melissa to handle various tasks. The dancers also show deference to her, and there are instances of Madonna asserting her authority, like when she addresses the group about treating each other with respect.

title: For the Boys
justification: Eddie Sparks exerts control through insults and firings: "You got a toilet for a mouth. I don't appreciate it." He also manipulates Dixie and others, showcasing his dominance in their professional and personal lives: "Just relax and follow my lead."

title: Year of the Gun
justification: Characters constantly give orders and assert dominance. Examples include the Red Brigade members demanding wallets and information at gunpoint, and the interrogation scenes where characters are accused and forced to comply. The dialogue is filled with threats and assertions of control.

title: Child's Play 3
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy at the military academy, with cadets like Shelton exerting dominance over others, as seen in the dialogue: "Who said you could look at me? Do you know who I am?" and "That's lieutenant colonel Shelton to you, asshole!" Chucky also attempts to dominate Tyler, manipulating and threatening him.

title: Career Opportunities
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to assert dominance over others. Bud Dodge constantly belittles Jim and threatens to send him away, while the Target manager berates Jim and imposes unreasonable demands. Josie's father also displays controlling behavior, and the criminals exert their power through threats and violence.

title: Batman Returns
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control and dominance. Max Shreck manipulates situations and people, while Penguin attempts to gain respect and power through mayoral ambitions. Catwoman asserts her independence and challenges authority, and Batman struggles to maintain order.

title: Home Alone 2: Lost in New York
justification: There are multiple instances of power dynamics. The father gives orders to his children, such as "Come on, Kevin." and "Kevin, you gonna take my bag?". Also, the hotel staff is subservient to the guests, as shown by the concierge's eagerness to please and apologize.

title: Wayne's World
justification: Several scenes show characters trying to exert control. Benjamin, the producer, manipulates Wayne and Garth with contracts and money: "You can stay here in the big leagues and play by the rules, or you can go back to the farm club in Aurora. It's your choice." Noah Vanderhoff, the sponsor, expects certain concessions due to his financial investment.

title: Aladdin
justification: The Sultan is constantly ordering Jafar around, but Jafar is secretly manipulating the Sultan. Jafar also takes control of the guards, ordering them to imprison Aladdin. The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays, such as Jafar saying, "My life is but to serve you, my lord," while plotting to overthrow him.

title: The Hand That Rocks the Cradle
justification: The doctor-patient interactions show a clear power dynamic, with the doctor giving instructions and the patient complying ('Why don't we take a look? Feet up.'). Also, the doctor gives orders to the nurse ('Why don't you go ahead and give them to her. She's all clear.').

title: Death Becomes Her
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether through manipulation, threats, or direct orders. Examples include Madeline's demands on the makeup artist, Helen's manipulation of Ernest to commit murder, and Lisle Von Rhuman's control over her clients.

title: Sneakers
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters exert control and dominance. Greg's manipulation of Martin, the NSA's heavy-handed tactics, and Cosmo's manipulation of the financial system all highlight power struggles. Examples include Greg saying, "perhaps you will finally be able to do occasional favor for me?" and Cosmo's plan to "crash the whole damn system."

title: HouseSitter
justification: The dialogue reveals power dynamics through parental disapproval and attempts to control Newton's life ("You babied the boy, Edna."). Gwen's manipulative behavior and the characters' attempts to control each other through lies and arrangements also highlight power struggles ("In return for which you extorted free rent in a furnished house... and now a college education!").

title: Passenger 57
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include Rane's control over the hijacked plane and Cutter's attempts to regain control, as well as the power struggles between Cutter and the authorities on the ground.

title: Mo' Money
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include the transit cop demanding fare, the prisoner demanding a cigarette, and Walsh's controlling behavior towards John. Also, Keith's blackmailing of John and Tom's abusive behavior towards Amber highlight power imbalances.

title: Encino Man
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the classroom setting where the teacher directs the students ("Settle down, quiet. We're gonna start this week's class..."). Later, Dave attempts to control Link's actions and behavior, telling him what to do and how to act in various social situations ("We gotta teach him how to be normal.").

title: 3 Ninjas
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority. Snyder gives orders to his henchmen ('Snatch those kids without getting caught') and attempts to control Mori ('Get him off my back'). Mori, in turn, instructs the boys ('Act like ninja, not little babies').

title: Shining Through
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Ed Leland and Linda Voss. Leland gives orders and withholds information, while Voss initially obeys but later challenges his authority, creating tension and a power struggle.

title: Singles
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, but they are not a central theme. For example, the mayor has the power to reject the supertrain proposal. Also, Debbie Hunt's video dating profile shows her desire for a man who can understand her, implying a power dynamic where she seeks a specific type of partner.

title: Rapid Fire
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and making threats. Examples include Serrano demanding a "piece of your end" from Tommy, and Ryan ordering Jake to cooperate or face charges. There are also many instances of characters being ordered around, such as Ming being told to move someone to the back row.

title: Deep Cover
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening violence to maintain control. Felix's manipulation and abuse of Eddie, and later David, exemplify this, as does the constant struggle for status among the drug dealers. Examples: "Work for me, Eddie, learn to keep your fucking mouth shut!" and "Give it. Twenty-four hours, man. Tomorrow. No, no, no, Eddie. Now. Ten seconds."

title: City of Joy
justification: The subtitles contain numerous examples of power dynamics. There are instances of direct orders ('Not there go to your left', 'Stop him!'), displays of authority ('May I see your passport, please?'), and struggles for control ('Hey, I want my medallion'). The character Ghatak exerts significant control over the community, demanding loyalty and protection money.

title: Kuffs
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control and dominance. Kuffs inherits his brother's district and faces challenges to his authority from Bill, Captain Morino, and even his own employees. Examples include Kuffs firing Bill, Morino threatening Kuffs, and Kane attempting to bribe Kuffs.

title: Mr. Saturday Night
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between Buddy and Stan, with Buddy often giving orders and Stan trying to please him. Examples include Buddy telling Stan to "Shut up" repeatedly and firing his writers. There are also instances of Buddy asserting his dominance in the comedy world, such as when he tells Annie Wells, "Get me in front of an audience. Any audience. I'm dyin' here."

title: Pure Country
justification: Several characters exert authority: Lula manages Dusty's career and manipulates others, Dusty dictates changes to his show, and Al harasses Harley. Examples include Lula saying, "Get him out of here," and Dusty stating, "Since when do you start changing my show?"

title: Cool World
justification: Several characters give orders or assert dominance. Holli Would frequently manipulates others to get what she wants, such as when she says, "You wouldn't erase me, baby. You're too hungry for what I got." The police officer, Harris, also exerts authority, telling people to "Beat it, copper."

title: Cliffhanger
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Qualen's control over his crew ("Get off my back, Qualen.") and Gabe's instructions during the rescue attempts ("Jessie, you gotta get down!").

title: Rising Sun
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Put up the 46th floor', 'Get the senator's car'), asserting authority ('Don't fuck with these guys'), and navigating hierarchical relationships ('You'd have to talk with my supervisor'). There are also instances of characters trying to assert dominance ('Let me smack this asshole').

title: Hocus Pocus
justification: The dialogue contains multiple instances of characters attempting to assert dominance or control over others. Examples include the bullies demanding money and smokes, Max's interactions with Dani where he tries to avoid taking her trick-or-treating, and the Sanderson sisters' interactions where Winifred is clearly in charge.

title: Cop and ½
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Fountain's commands to Chu ('Get rid of it') and his demeaning treatment of Quintero, as well as McKenna's interactions with Devon, where he attempts to control and manipulate the child ('Otherwise I'm going to rip your little head off').

title: Grumpy Old Men
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between the older and younger characters, particularly between John and his father, and Max and John. The characters also engage in constant one-upmanship and attempts to assert dominance, such as the lottery ticket and the competition for Ariel's attention.

title: Loaded Weapon 1
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Luger's interactions with Irv and the Captain, and the General's control over his subordinates. The power struggle is evident in the constant need to be in control.

title: Son in Law
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Walter frequently tries to assert his authority as the father, while Crawl's disruptive presence leads to power struggles within the family. Zack's room has rules that he tries to enforce on Crawl.

title: My Life
justification: The doctor-patient interactions show a clear power dynamic, with the doctor initially holding authority, but Bob challenges this, questioning the doctor's decisions and demanding further treatment. Bob's relationship with Gail also shows a power dynamic, with Bob often trying to control the situation and Gail pushing back, asserting her needs and feelings.

title: Benny & Joon
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters giving orders and asserting control. Examples include Benny telling Waldo to answer the phone, Mrs. Smail's abusive treatment of Joon, and the doctor's attempts to control Joon's living situation.

title: The Program
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of coaches and players asserting authority, such as the coach demanding a player pick up his helmet after a disagreement. There are also instances of racial and social hierarchy, like the comment 'Forget it, nigger. No chance for you there,' which highlights a power imbalance based on race and perceived social status.

title: The Crush
justification: The movie features several instances of power dynamics. Michael, the magazine editor, exerts authority over his staff, as seen in lines like, "Monday's staff meetings begin at 8:15 precisely. I expect everyone to be here." Adrian manipulates and controls Nick through seduction and lies, demonstrated when she rewrites his article and sabotages his career.

title: Speed
justification: The bomber exerts extreme control through threats and demands: "No one goes off the bus...I will detonate it." Jack, as a cop, attempts to take charge, but is constantly undermined by the bomber's superior knowledge and control of the situation.

title: The Paper
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control and authority. Examples include Alicia negotiating her contract ('I'd like permission to start interviewing now.') and Henry's interactions with his subordinates, where he barks orders and asserts his position ('Just call the cops.').

title: Junior
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Larry telling Alex what to do regarding the pregnancy and Diana controlling the lab. Angela also asserts dominance over Larry in their shared house, stating, "Larry, you may live here. You may die here, but this will always be my house."

title: My Father the Hero
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control and manipulate others. Andre exerts control over Nicole, and there are constant power plays in relationships, like Diana's attempts to seduce Andre and Nicole's manipulation of Ben.

title: Jason's Lyric
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Maddog demanding Gloria to open the door, Alonzo controlling Marti, and A-1 bossing around the crew during the bank robbery planning.

title: Reality Bites
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Grant's boss at Video View demands Lelaina be fired, stating, "Just get rid of her like I asked you in the first place." Sammy and Lelaina argue over the phone bill, with Sammy's father telling Lelaina, "You're just gonna have to swallow your pride."

title: With Honors
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters attempting to exert control over one another. Wilder manipulates the student by withholding thesis pages in exchange for lodging, and the student tries to control Wilder's behavior to maintain his living situation and academic progress. Examples: "If you eat now, I get my page now." and "I don't want him to be too comfortable."

title: Only You
justification: There are instances of subtle power dynamics, such as the mother's expectations regarding the wedding dress and Dwayne's controlling behavior ('We're going. Can I have the keys?' 'I've got the keys. Let's go.'). Also, Kate's husband is dismissive of her feelings ('Babbling on and on about communication, like I don't know how to communicate.').

title: Color of Night
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Hector pressures Capa to shut down the group, using threats: "Shut the fucker down!" and "Get outta my face!". Sondra's outburst in group therapy reveals a struggle for dominance and status, highlighting the power dynamics within the group.

title: Little Giants
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters trying to assert dominance. Kevin constantly belittles Danny, and Spike attempts to intimidate Becky. There are also examples of characters giving orders, such as when Danny coaches the team.

title: House Party 3
justification: Several characters assert dominance through threats and insults. Vester frequently disregards Kid's wishes and boundaries, while the father of the bride attempts to control the narrative and belittle Kid's career. Examples: "You better regulate your uncle before I bust a cap in his butt." and "If people don't like you if you're being yourself, fuck them!".

title: Getting Even With Dad
justification: The entire plot revolves around Tim's leverage over his father and his associates. Tim withholds the location of stolen coins, forcing his father to comply with his demands: "If you do a real good job, Dad, I'll tell you where the coins are." The other criminals are also subject to Tim's control, as they need the coins.

title: Blink
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include: "Get your feet off the lieutenant's desk," "Detective Hallstrom, we just got here! The watch has yet to change. Ease up," and the general tone of command and control exhibited by the detectives.

title: Baby’s Day Out
justification: The Cotwell parents exert control over staff (Andrews, Gilbertine) and photographers. The kidnappers (Eddie, Norby, Veeko) constantly bicker and try to assert dominance over each other, especially Eddie who gives orders. Mrs. Cotwell also demands specific photos and dictates the photographer's artistic choices.

title: Terminal Velocity
justification: Jo, the manager, exerts authority over Ditch, assigning tasks and reprimanding him for his stunts: "Now you listen to me. Until we pass the next inspection..." Ditch also displays a subtle dominance over Chris, manipulating her into a jump despite her initial hesitation and attempting to seduce her.

title: The Shawshank Redemption
justification: The prison guards exert authority over the inmates, as seen in the dialogue: "Keep your eyes on your mop, man. Andy!" and "What are you jimmies staring at? Back to work!" Andy gains influence by providing financial services, leading to a shift in power dynamics, as he is able to get beer for his coworkers by leveraging his relationship with Mr. Hadley.

title: Above the Rim
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for dominance, whether it's Kyle challenging his mother's authority ("I don't care if you don't believe in me") or the constant trash talk and challenges on the basketball court ("When I finish with you, boy, your moms ain't gonna be dunking on you no more."). There are also instances of characters asserting control through threats and intimidation, like Birdie's interactions with his crew.

title: Speechless
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in the political campaigns, with bosses giving orders and staff complying. Examples include: "Julia, bring those position papers," and "Spin it so...Garvin's dodging us."

title: Mortal Kombat
justification: Characters like Shang Tsung and Goro exert dominance through threats and displays of power. Dialogue such as "Your soul is mine" and "Bow to me!" highlight the struggle for control and the hierarchical relationships between characters.

title: Father of the Bride Part II
justification: George is often seen running around doing things for his pregnant wife and daughter, such as adjusting pillows and getting food. There are also moments where he is given orders, such as when Franck says "Close those eyes."

title: Casino
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include Frankie's interrogation of Tony Dogs, Sam firing Ward, and Nicky's interactions with Clark and Sam, demonstrating a constant struggle for control and respect.

title: Waiting to Exhale
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and expressing resentment towards authority. Examples include the divorce proceedings, the mother-son relationship with grounding, and the salon scene where Bernadine demands Gloria cut her hair.

title: Tommy Boy
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Tom's father exerts authority, as seen when he directs Tom with "But right now I'm gonna need you, Tommy Boy to get this place going." Later, Richard's condescending attitude and verbal abuse towards Tommy, such as "I can actually hear you getting fatter," highlight a clear power imbalance in their relationship.

title: Virtuosity
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Sid's manipulation and taunting of Parker, the police chief's commands, and the general hierarchical structure within the prison and LETAC.

title: Murder in the First
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Warden Glenn's testimony and the lawyer's cross-examination highlight the prison's authority over inmates, while Henri's interactions with his lawyer and other characters show his struggle for control and recognition. Examples include: 'You don't want it, we take you back.' and 'You work for me, which means when I call you, you drop everything.'

title: Mad Love
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. Examples include Cliff telling his kids, "No videos or Gameboys for the twins till they finish their homework," and the tense interactions between Casey and her parents, where they discuss sending her away and controlling her behavior.

title: The Madness of King George
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority, especially from the King ('Fetch the queen,' 'I am the King. I cannot rest. I must rule.') and those vying for control ('Your Royal Highness would have to be declared regent.'). There are also power struggles between the King and his doctors, and the Prince and his father.

title: Independence Day
justification: Several characters assert authority: a father demanding obedience from his son ("I'm still your father!"), military officers giving orders ("Dismissed!"), and general power struggles within relationships ("You leave... you're fired."). The president also holds significant power, making life-or-death decisions for the country.

title: Ransom
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include 'Get him out of here,' 'You get your own fucking lawyer,' and the kidnapper's constant demands and control over Tom Mullen.

title: A Time to Kill
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy, particularly within the Ku Klux Klan, where members are initiated and expected to obey. Additionally, the NAACP attempts to control Carl Lee's legal representation, showcasing a power struggle over his defense. The judge also exerts his authority by denying a change of venue and threatening contempt.

title: The First Wives Club
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others, such as the divorce proceedings where the husband demands half of the wife's assets and alimony. Other examples include Brenda's uncle offering to 'take out' Morty, and the women plotting to undermine their ex-husbands' careers and reputations. The dialogue is filled with demands, manipulations, and power plays.

title: Phenomenon
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Lace telling her children what to do, and George being told to do things by Doc and the FBI. The FBI questioning George and controlling his movements also highlights a power imbalance.

title: 12 Monkeys
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting control. Examples include scientists directing Cole's actions ('No mistakes this time, Cole. Stay alert.') and characters threatening each other ('Get in the car. I have got a gun.').

title: Leaving Las Vegas
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. Yuri controls Sera by giving her to men as a 'gift' and demanding her earnings. Ben's drunken outbursts and dependence on Sera create an imbalance, and the interactions between prostitutes and their clients are inherently transactional and hierarchical.

title: James and the Giant Peach
justification: The aunts are constantly ordering James around and verbally abusing him. Examples include: "Get these stupid dreams out of your head! And get back to work!" and "Get out of our sight! Go on!". The centipede also tries to assert dominance over the other bugs.

title: Spy Hard
justification: The Director gives Steele orders and expects obedience. Rancor's dialogue is full of threats and boasts of dominance, such as "Dick Steele couldn't stop me 15 years ago, and all the dicks you've got won't stop me now!"

title: Harriet the Spy
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy, especially in Harriet's interactions with adults like Golly and her parents, who set rules and boundaries. There are also power struggles among the children, particularly between Harriet and Marion, which escalates into social exclusion and bullying. Dialogue such as "Feet off the bed, please" and "Harriet is not your daughter, Miss Golly. She is mine" demonstrates the adult's authority.

title: Emma
justification: Several characters, especially Mr. Elton and Mrs. Elton, are concerned with status and social climbing. Dialogue such as "Everybody has their level" and Mrs. Elton's constant name-dropping of her brother's estate indicate a preoccupation with social hierarchy and dominance.

title: Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood
justification: Several instances show characters asserting dominance through threats and commands. For example, "You have your black ass back here by Friday" and "Give me a knife, boy" demonstrate clear power imbalances and attempts to control others through intimidation.

title: Men in Black
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Zed's instructions to the recruits ("Sit down."), K's commands to J ("Fasten your seat belt."), and the general hierarchical structure within MIB.

title: The Lost World: Jurassic Park
justification: Several characters attempt to assert control or dominance. Roland declares, "Peter, if I run your little camping trip, there are two conditions. First, I'm in charge." Ludlow's exploitative attitude towards the dinosaurs also highlights a power imbalance: "An extinct animal brought back to life has no rights. It exists because we made it. We patented it. We own it."

title: Liar Liar
justification: The movie features a lawyer, Fletcher, who initially prioritizes his career and winning cases over his relationship with his son. The power dynamics are evident in the courtroom scenes, where Fletcher manipulates the legal system to win, and in his interactions with his boss, where he tries to gain favor to become a partner. Dialogue such as "The Cole case is worth a truckload of money to this firm. If you win, I guarantee you'll make partner." and "I'm gonna hit him where it hurts." demonstrates the characters' pursuit of power and control.

title: George Of The Jungle
justification: Ursula's mother attempts to control her daughter's relationships based on social status, saying, "You see, you and Ursula together...Would be unbefitting her social stature." Lyle also tries to assert dominance, especially over Kwame, and the poachers exert control over Ape.

title: Contact
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Kitz demanding the scientists ask armed personnel to leave and Drumlin taking over the project lead despite Arroway's discovery. The president and his advisors also dictate the narrative, controlling information and access.

title: Tomorrow Never Dies
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Carver instructing his staff ('Mr. Wallace, call the President'), M directing Bond ('I'm sending you to Hamburg, 007'), and Stamper's interactions with subordinates ('Herr Stamper, we have made contact').

title: The Full Monty
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Dave commands Little Lomper to find Auntie Jean, and Gaz pressures Dave to participate in the stripping act, highlighting a struggle for control and influence within their relationships. The dialogue between Gary and his ex-wife also showcases a power struggle over custody and financial responsibilities.

title: Metro
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include the initial SWAT training scene ('You're a wiseass. And I got a special little test for first-day wiseasses here.') and the interactions between Mike and Clarence ('I'll just stick around and take care of you for the rest of my fuckin' life.').

title: Shine
justification: The dialogue contains instances of command and control, particularly in the relationship between David and his father. Examples include the father demanding, "Say it. I'm a very lucky boy," and dictating David's musical choices, "David, always... win! Always... win!" There are also instances of characters asserting dominance, such as "Shut up, Sam."

title: Grosse Pointe Blank
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Marcella telling someone to "Find out where my mother is," and Grocer's controlling interactions with Martin, such as "Meet the new boss."

title: Fire Down Below
justification: Several characters exert authority: Lloyd gives orders to his crew ('Hold her there. Let her down.'), Hanner's son seeks his father's approval ('See, I know exactly what my daddy wants.'), and threats of violence are used to intimidate ('I ought to put a bullet in your head.'). The dialogue reveals a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Mulan
justification: The film revolves around Mulan defying societal expectations and imperial law by impersonating a male soldier. Dialogue like "You would do well to teach your daughter to hold her tongue in a man's presence" and the emphasis on obedience and fulfilling duties highlight the strict hierarchical structure and gender roles.

title: Antz
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of ants giving orders and expecting obedience. For example, soldiers constantly order workers around, and General Mandible exerts absolute authority. The princess also expects to be obeyed, highlighting the hierarchical structure of the ant colony.

title: The X Files: Fight the Future
justification: The dialogue includes numerous instances of characters giving orders and demanding information, such as "Toss it up here!", "Give me a 14-footer!", "Move 'em back!", and "Get everybody outta here!". There are also scenes of interrogation and blame assignment, indicating a struggle for control and accountability.

title: The Wedding Singer
justification: There are instances of power dynamics, such as Glenn making decisions for Julia without her input ('I know you wanted to set a date...so I went to the travel agent and set it') and Andy bossing Robbie around ('Come on, Andy, move your ass!'). There are also instances of Robbie's boss being rude and demeaning ('You are the worst wedding singer in the world, buddy!').

title: City of Angels
justification: Several scenes depict doctors giving orders to nurses and other staff ('Get her pressure. Let's give her O2. Ten liters.'). There are also instances of characters trying to exert control over each other, such as the bank robber demanding money ('Do it! Do it!').

title: The Horse Whisperer
justification: Annie is clearly in charge of Grace, dictating their actions and future. There are also power struggles between Annie and Tom, as well as Annie and her work colleagues, as she tries to maintain control from afar. The ranch hands also exert authority over Annie and Grace.

title: Six Days, Seven Nights
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. For example, the boss pressures Marjorie to abandon her engagement, saying, "This is the perfect opportunity to establish parameters." Also, Quinn initially tries to dominate Marjorie after the crash, ordering her around with phrases like "Keep your seat belt tight and let me fly this thing."

title: Blade
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and threatening each other. Examples include Frost's control over his vampire subordinates ('Send in Frost.','Deacon, there's someone here to see you.') and Blade's interactions with vampires ('Quinn... I'm getting a little tired of chopping you up.').

title: Lost In Space
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's decisions. Examples include Dr. Smith's demands regarding the cryo-sleep systems, Major West's interactions with Dr. Robinson, and the constant struggle for control between John and Maureen.

title: A Perfect Murder
justification: Characters exert control through financial leverage and manipulation. Steven hires David to kill Emily, showcasing extreme power imbalance. Dialogue like "You're in business" and threats of exposure highlight the struggle for dominance.

title: The Parent Trap
justification: Meredith exerts control over Nick, demonstrated by her directing him to wear his shirt a certain way. Hallie and Annie's switch also shows a manipulation of their parents' authority, and Meredith's threats to send Hallie to boarding school highlight her desire for control.
