title: Ever After: A Cinderella Story
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and maneuvering for social advantage. Examples include the Baroness's controlling behavior towards Danielle, Prince Henry's exercise of royal authority, and the constant jockeying for position among the courtiers.

title: You’ve Got Mail
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power dynamic between Joe Fox and Kathleen Kelly, as Joe's company threatens to put Kathleen's store out of business. Joe's interactions with his employees also show a clear hierarchy, as he gives orders and they obey. Kathleen also has power over her employees, as she is the owner of the store.

title: Hope Floats
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Mama exerts control over Birdee, telling her what to do and how to feel. Bernice also challenges Birdee's authority, creating tension and conflict.

title: U.S. Marshals
justification: Throughout the subtitles, characters give orders and instructions, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include 'Make the announcement,' 'Get the state police director on the phone,' and 'Get on the radio, move that perimeter 20 miles south of the river.' The interactions between Gerard and his deputies, as well as the agents from the Diplomatic Security Service, highlight the struggle for control and authority in the investigation.

title: The Man in the Iron Mask
justification: The King's commands are frequent and absolute, such as "I command you all!" and his expectation of obedience is clear. D'Artagnan's role as a loyal servant and Athos's struggle against the King's abuse of power also highlight the theme.

title: Everest
justification: There are some elements of power dynamics, but they are not a central focus. Ed Viesturs leads the expedition and gives instructions, and the Sherpas are tasked with carrying loads, indicating a hierarchy. Jamling also mentions feeling a 'hunger' to live up to his father's legend, suggesting a desire for status.

title: Snake Eyes
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and jockeying for position. Examples include the detective taking control of the crime scene ('This is mine about six different ways!') and various characters ordering others around ('Hey, you, get outta here.').

title: What Dreams May Come
justification: The dialogue shows some power dynamics, primarily in familial relationships. For example, a father tells his child, "Your mother and I talked. We always listen to each other," indicating parental authority. Also, the doctor-patient relationship has inherent power dynamics.

title: The Prince of Egypt
justification: The movie revolves around Rameses's authority as Pharaoh and Moses's challenge to that authority on behalf of the enslaved Hebrews. Dialogue like "Faster, you beasts! You run like mules" and Rameses's insistence on maintaining "ancient traditions" highlight the power imbalance and his determination to control his kingdom.

title: Halloween: H2O
justification: Several characters exert authority: the headmistress over students ("And that means no musical sleeping bags. No booze."), the counselor over Ronny ("I'm not lettin' you out of here."), and Laurie/Keri over John ("Do as I say, now!"). There are also instances of defiance, like John's repeated disobedience of his mother's rules.

title: Small Soldiers
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the Commando Elite's military commands ('Commando Elite! Fall in!') and Alan's father's attempts to control situations ('Obviously, you can't. Go home.'). There are also instances of characters struggling for control, such as the neighbor Phil cutting down Stu's tree.

title: Star Trek: Insurrection
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and directives, such as "Send the Admiral Data's schematics," "Report to the galley," and "Take us into a high orbit." Characters are constantly giving orders and asserting authority, indicating a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Practical Magic
justification: Several instances show attempts to control or influence others, such as Gillian's aunts meddling in her love life and casting spells. The investigator, Gary Hallet, exerts authority through questioning and investigation, while characters like Jimmy Angelov display dominance through violence and manipulation. The dialogue reveals a constant negotiation of control and influence.

title: Patch Adams
justification: The Dean exerts authority, expelling Patch and dictating rules. Patch challenges this authority through his actions and defiance, creating a power struggle. There are also instances of dominance and submission in the interactions with patients and fellow students.

title: The Negotiator
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding information, and asserting authority. Examples include, "Get him locked down first!" and "I want status reports now." Danny Roman's interactions with Farley and the hostages also highlight his attempts to control the situation and assert dominance, such as dictating what Farley can and cannot say.

title: Meet Joe Black
justification: The dialogue is filled with power plays, especially in the business context. Bill's authority as chairman is challenged, and Joe's mysterious influence creates tension. Examples include the board meetings, the discussion of Bontecou's offer, and the power struggle between Bill and Joe regarding Susan.

title: Wag the Dog
justification: The film depicts characters giving orders and exerting control over others. Examples include Stanley directing Tracy on set ('Tracy, stand against that wall, and on my signal "action"...I want you running toward me, screaming.') and Conrad manipulating the media and government officials ('We're going to war.').

title: Ronin
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, negotiating terms, and asserting dominance. Deirdre controls the team with instructions like "Tell Vincent what you need" and "For you, there's no one but myself." There are also power struggles, such as the interrogation scene and the constant questioning of Deirdre's plans.

title: The Siege
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and demanding information, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include "Tell me about the money!", "I want a list of the next 10 targets.", and "Call INS, Frank."

title: I Still Know What You Did Last Summer
justification: The priest/confessor dynamic establishes a clear power imbalance. Ty's aggressive flirting and insistence on dancing, despite Julie's reluctance, shows a struggle for control. Estes's secretive and manipulative behavior also indicates a desire for control.

title: Pleasantville
justification: The dialogue shows adults ordering children around, like the father insisting Jennifer eats breakfast: "Nonsense, young lady. You're gonna start your day off with a nice, big breakfast. HERE WE GO. SIT DOWN." Also, Bud's interactions at the soda shop show a clear hierarchy, with him directing the other employee.

title: Urban Legend
justification: The Dean attempts to control Paul's reporting, saying "Don't contact anyone without my permission." Damon's interactions with Natalie also show a power imbalance, as he tries to manipulate her emotions and actions, culminating in an attempted assault. Brenda's actions are driven by a desire for revenge and control over Natalie's life.

title: Sphere
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or expressing authority: "Come here," "Press it," and "Turn this thing over." Also, the military personnel, Edmunds, asserts his authority: "I'm just following my orders."

title: Stepmom
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting control, giving orders, and reacting to perceived slights. Examples include Jackie's controlling behavior towards Luke and Isabel, such as dictating who can see the children and threatening legal action. Also, the children are often told what to do.

title: Mercury Rising
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding answers, and asserting authority. Kudrow's interactions with his subordinates are particularly telling, as he demands absolute obedience and silence. The power dynamic is also evident in the interactions between Art and his superiors, as well as in the attempts to control and manipulate Simon.

title: A Night at the Roxbury
justification: The film depicts a constant struggle for status, particularly in the club scene. Characters like the bouncers and club owners wield authority, deciding who gets in and who doesn't. The Butabi brothers also try to assert dominance in their relationships and business dealings, often unsuccessfully.

title: Spice World
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Clifford gives orders to the Spice Girls and his assistant, like "Next up, publicity party...Have fun. That is all." and "Dennis, pull over." There's also a power struggle between Clifford and the girls, as they try to assert their independence, like when they say, "It's up to us whether we turn up to this gig or not tomorrow."

title: The Object of my Affection
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others, such as Vince's possessive behavior towards Nina and his attempts to dictate her choices. The dance instructor, Madame Reynolds, also demonstrates authority through her commands and corrections during the tango lesson. Additionally, Sidney's attempts to control Vince's legal career and Constance's unsolicited advice highlight power dynamics within relationships.

title: Grease
justification: The T-Birds exert dominance through insults and exclusion, like when they tell Putzie and Doody to "hit the pavement." Rizzo's sarcastic remarks and sexual innuendo also establish her as a figure of control within the group. Danny's attempts to change his image to win Sandy back also highlight the power dynamics at play.

title: Jack Frost
justification: The father-son relationship shows a clear hierarchy, with the father often giving instructions and the son sometimes resisting or seeking approval. Examples include the father teaching the son hockey moves ("Bring it back on the toe of the stick") and the father's disappointment when the son calls him "Butt Dad."

title: The Big Hit
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding respect, and threatening each other. Examples include Paris's speech about loyalty and discipline, Cisco's constant demands and threats, and the general hierarchical structure of the criminal organization.

title: Paulie
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting control. Examples include the father telling Marie to get the bird off the table, and Benny instructing Paulie to steal jewelry. Also, Dr. Manning asserts his authority over Paulie, declaring him property of the institute.

title: Bulworth
justification: Several instances show characters asserting dominance. Examples include threats like "I'll whoop your ass up, motherfucker!" and commands such as "Leave." The senator's staff also attempts to control his behavior, indicating a power struggle.

title: Great Expectations
justification: Several characters exert authority: Joe gives Finn instructions on how to behave, Nora Dinsmoor demands Finn dance for her, and Estella seems to manipulate Finn and Walter. Dialogue like "Shut up and get in the boat" and "Dance, dance, dance!" demonstrates a clear imbalance of power and attempts to control others.

title: Can't Hardly Wait
justification: Several instances of characters attempting to exert control or assert dominance are present. For example, Preston is accosted to sign a yearbook, and a character is told, "You can go upstairs, but just you." There are also instances of characters being mocked or belittled, such as "Bitch, get a life!"

title: Fallen
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Look for a syringe'), questioning authority ('Am I a suspect?'), and struggling to maintain control ('If somebody dies because you kept your mouth shut, you're holding the bag.'). The police hierarchy is evident, and characters are constantly trying to assert dominance.

title: The Avengers
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and establishing dominance. Examples include Mother's instructions to Steed and Peel, Sir August's control over his organization, and the Prime Minister's directives.

title: One True Thing
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Ellie and her parents. Her mother directs her in the kitchen ("Ellie made the lunch."), and her father dismisses her concerns about her mother's health ("Ellen, enough. Midterms."). There are also instances of characters giving orders or making demands, such as when the mother asks for a pill or when the father asks Ellie to wash his shirts.

title: The Players Club
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and demanding respect. Examples include Miron controlling the dancers ("No, thank you."), Dollar Bill's crew threatening Keys ("Today, you going to die."), and the police officers' interactions with the club patrons ("Watch your tone...and keep your hands on your head.").

title: Rounders
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and maneuvering for status. Examples include Grama's debt collection tactics ("Instead of you owing 15 grand spread out to five guys, you owe 25 to me.") and Mike's attempts to control Worm's behavior ("You gotta stop listening to that guy, man.").

title: Beloved
justification: The dialogue showcases power dynamics through Sethe's fierce protectiveness of her daughter, Denver, and her determination to control their environment. Paul D's attempts to assert his influence and challenge Sethe's decisions also highlight the struggle for dominance within their relationship. Examples include Sethe's declaration, "I will never run from another thing on this Earth," and her interactions with Paul D regarding Beloved.

title: Quest for Camelot
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles, especially Ruber's attempts to seize control of Camelot. Examples include Ruber's constant demands and threats: "Then it's time for the new king... and I vote for me," and "One day that sword will be in my hand... and all will be mine!"

title: The Borrowers
justification: Several characters exert authority: Potter demands the house be demolished, Arrietty's dad enforces borrower rules, and the mom bosses around the little brother. Examples include: "You have until Saturday to move out," "The first rule of borrowing: A borrower must never, ever be seen," and "Peagreen, put that marshmallow down and drink your milk."

title: He Got Game
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Jesus's father, Jake, exerts control through manipulation and guilt, while Uncle Bubba attempts to profit from Jesus's potential success. Sweetness physically abuses Dakota to maintain control over her.

title: The Apostle
justification: The preacher, Apostle EF, often takes charge, directing others in prayer and church activities. Examples include telling people to say "Jesus will save me" and directing the congregation during services. There are also instances of people seeking permission or approval from him, such as when he asks to be accepted as an apostle.

title: Psycho
justification: Several characters exert authority: the police officer interrogates Marion, the car salesman manipulates customers, and Norman's mother dominates him with verbal abuse and commands ('Shut up! Shut up! Shut up!'). Arbogast also uses his authority as a private investigator to question people.

title: Mighty Joe Young
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority are present. Examples include: "Hey, I said into bed," and "Everybody spread out. Get the baby." Also, O'Hara directs Pindi and his men, indicating a clear hierarchy.

title: Vampires
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, such as "Ready, boss," "Ill do it, boss," and "Sorry, boss." Jack Crow's leadership is unquestioned, and he frequently gives orders. Even the Cardinal is shown to have power over Jack, ordering him to rebuild his team.

title: Jane Austen's Mafia
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Don Cortino's control over judges and politicians is evident when Bonifacio seeks justice for his daughter. The dialogue between Don Cortino and Sal Gorgoni showcases the Don's authority and rejection of Gorgoni's partnership offer, reinforced by Joey's aggressive outburst.

title: Hard Rain
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and attempting to control situations. Examples include the sheriff directing people during the flood, the looters threatening each other, and various characters trying to dominate conversations or actions.

title: Species 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and directives, especially from mission control to the astronauts ('Excursion, Houston. You are go to reconfigure nominal DAP, B-1.') and between military personnel ('Colonel, you're welcome to replace me anytime you like.'). There are also instances of direct commands and assertions of authority within personal relationships ('You keep your dick in your pants and your eyes on the prize.').

title: The Replacement Killers
justification: Characters frequently give orders and make demands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Kogan directing actions ('Bring in professionals'), Wei's control over John ('Mr. Wei used my mother and sister to persuade me to do three jobs'), and Zedkov's authority as a detective ('Put a tail on her').

title: The Odd Couple II
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance over each other. Oscar constantly berates Felix, giving him orders and criticizing his actions. For example, Oscar says, "Make out a timetable, when you're going to eat, pee, fart, cry and sleep," and later threatens Felix with physical violence if he doesn't retrieve his suitcase.

title: The Faculty
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to exert control over others, such as the coach pressuring Stan to play football, Zeke trying to sell drugs and intimidate others, and the teachers, who are revealed to be aliens, ordering students around. The power struggle is evident in the interactions between students and authority figures, as well as among the students themselves.

title: Simon Birch
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the grandmother's controlling behavior and the children's interactions. For example, the grandmother says, "Slow down" and "That creature" referring to Simon. Also, Miss Leavey scolds Simon for his behavior in church.

title: The Big Lebowski
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, give orders, and intimidate others. Examples include Walter's aggressive outbursts and attempts to control situations, Lebowski's demands and threats, and the nihilists' menacing behavior towards Lebowski.

title: Disturbing Behavior
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy within the high school, with distinct social groups vying for status and control. Dialogue like "It's a class system here at C.B. High" and "Sluts need not apply" highlights the power struggles and social stratification. The Blue Ribbons, led by characters like Trent and Andy, exert dominance through manipulation and control, as evidenced by their recruitment and manipulation of other students.

title: Half Baked
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include: "Kenny, stop crying," "Show me your mean face, Kenny," and Samson demanding a cut of Mr. Nice Guy's profits, "I want half, $20,000 a week, or you're dead!"

The dialogue is filled with examples of Steve Rubell exerting his authority over employees (e.g., firing the busboy, manipulating the list, demanding favors). There are also instances of characters like Billie Austin wielding influence to advance others' careers, and the constant jockeying for status and access within the club.

title: Dance With Me
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. John's control over the studio and Rafael's job is evident in lines like, "I'm gonna take the rent out of your salary" and "You don't have to hang around." Stefano asserts authority by declaring, "In John's absence here and in Las Vegas, I am in charge."

title: The Sixth Sense
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Vincent's interactions with Malcolm showcase a power imbalance stemming from past treatment, with Vincent seeking retribution. Cole's interactions with ghosts also highlight a power dynamic, as they demand his help and evoke fear.

title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
justification: The dialogue is filled with Dr. Evil giving orders to Number Two, Mini-Me, and Scott. There are also power struggles between Dr. Evil and Scott, as well as Austin Powers's attempts to assert dominance over his enemies and allies alike. Examples include "Send in the clone!", "Down, Mini-Me", and "Zip it!"

title: Toy Story 2
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include Buzz ordering the other toys around, Al demanding things from others, and the Prospector manipulating Jessie and Woody.

title: The Matrix
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for control. Agent Smith interrogates Neo, asserting authority through threats and manipulation. Morpheus guides Neo, dictating actions and revealing truths, establishing a mentor-student dynamic.

title: Tarzan
justification: Kerchak's role as leader is emphasized through commands like "We will nest here for the night" and his disapproval of Tarzan. Kala challenges Kerchak's authority, but ultimately Kerchak makes the final decision about Tarzan staying. Clayton exerts control over the expedition, giving orders and dismissing Jane's opinions.

title: Big Daddy
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and attempts to control Julian's behavior ('Sleep, all right? Just try to sleep. Stay asleep. Sit still! Lay!'). Sonny frequently directs Julian, and there are instances of other characters asserting authority ('Customers only.').

title: The Mummy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and vying for control. Examples include the museum director berating Jonathan, Imhotep commanding his followers, and O'Connell taking charge in dangerous situations.

title: Runaway Bride
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. Examples include Maggie telling Sam to get back on the bike, and Coach Carpenter directing the athletes ('Run your laps! Go. Go, go.'). There are also instances of characters trying to exert influence over Maggie's choices, such as the discussion about who she should marry.

title: Notting Hill
justification: There are several instances of power dynamics at play. Anna Scott, a famous actress, holds a higher status, influencing interactions and creating awkwardness, as seen when Bernie is starstruck. The press also wields power, intruding on Anna's privacy and dictating her public image.

title: The World is Not Enough
justification: Several characters exert authority: M gives Bond orders ('M says you're off the active duty list'), Elektra commands her staff ('Send the pipe around. Do it.'). There are also instances of insubordination and power struggles ('I will not tolerate insubordination, 007').

title: Double Jeopardy
justification: The parole officer, Lehman, exerts control over Libby through strict rules and threats of re-incarceration: "Any violation of these conditions...and your 'get out of jail free' card will be revoked by me." Nick manipulates Libby with promises about their son, and later, with money. The auction scene displays Devereaux's (Nick's) status and control over the bidders.

title: Wild Wild West
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include General McGrath's demands, Loveless's manipulation of McGrath, and West's interactions with Gordon and others, where he often tries to take charge.

title: Analyze This
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, orders, and displays of dominance, especially from Vitti. Examples include: "I'm going to see a lot of you," "Get rid of the shrink," and the constant demands and intimidation tactics used by Vitti and his associates.

title: American Pie
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, like Stifler's constant need to dominate conversations and situations. Jim's father tries to awkwardly guide his son's sexual education, creating an uncomfortable power imbalance. The 'Bible' being passed down signifies a hierarchy of sexual knowledge and experience.

title: Inspector Gadget
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority. Examples include: "Sikes, release the remote-control van," "Concentrate, you twit!," "Pull over, you!," and "You're not on duty, Brown! I'm always on duty!". There are also instances of characters trying to assert dominance or status, such as the Gadget mobile's constant need to be in charge.

title: Shakespeare in Love
justification: The play director barks orders at the actors, like "Take off your hat!" and "Wait there!". Lord Wessex treats Viola as property, stating, "He has bought me for you." and demanding obedience: "Is she obedient? As any mule in Christendom."

title: Sleepy Hollow
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include the magistrate instructing Crane ('There are two courses open to me...') and the frequent commands given to subordinates ('Burn it', 'Stand down!'). The control of the Headless Horseman is a central plot point, demonstrating a supernatural power dynamic.

title: The Haunting
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dr. Marrow directs the experiment and its participants ("You are not in competition"), Mrs. Dudley lays down the house rules ("I don't wait on people"), and Luke attempts to dominate conversations ("Wow, you're so dominant").

title: Entrapment
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include Mac's instructions to Gin during the heist ("I am your eyes. So you keep yours closed, because you can't see.") and Hector's controlling behavior towards Gin ("Didn't I say something about checking in every day?").

title: Pokemon: The First Movie
justification: Mewtwo's dialogue is filled with assertions of power and superiority: "I will set my own rules," and "I was born stronger than every other Pokémon on this planet." The humans also exert control, stating, "Pokémon live for humans, to be used by humans," highlighting a hierarchical relationship.

title: Payback
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to exert control over each other, from Porter demanding his money back to Val Resnick's interactions with the Outfit. Examples include: "Give me my goddamn money, please." and "On your knees, bitch."

title: Deep Blue Sea
justification: Several characters give orders or assert authority. Franklin demands results from the doctor, saying "Give me till Monday morning. 48 hours. I'll give you results that'll skyrocket your stock price...or I'll help you pack the lab myself. It's your call." Carter also asserts his dominance, telling the bird, "Don't make me drown your feathery ass."

title: American Beauty
justification: Several characters exert dominance through verbal commands and assertions of authority. Carolyn frequently directs Lester, and Colonel Fitts uses his military rank to intimidate Ricky. The dialogue between Lester and his boss also highlights a power struggle, with Lester ultimately blackmailing his superior.

title: The Thomas Crown Affair
justification: Catherine Banning, the insurance investigator, frequently challenges Detective Paretti's authority and methods, often acting independently. Examples include her direct confrontation with Thomas Crown and her disregard for police procedure, leading to conflicts and assertions of control from both sides, such as when Paretti confronts her: "YOU COMPROMISED THE INVESTIGATION."

title: Stuart Little
justification: The cat, Snowbell, constantly asserts dominance over Stuart, a mouse adopted into the family, by threatening to eat him and reminding him of his place in the food chain. The parents also exert authority over George and Stuart, telling them what to do and how to behave, especially regarding their relationship.

title: Blue Streak
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and attempting to dominate conversations. Examples include the police officers ordering people to the ground, the FBI agent dismissing the LAPD, and the constant power plays between partners and criminals.

title: The Green Mile
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Guards give orders to inmates ('YOU PUT ON THESE CLOTHES NOW, YOU HEAR?'), and inmates jockey for position ('I WANT BRUTAL'S SPOT FOR THE NEXT EXECUTION.'). There are also instances of abuse of power, such as Percy stepping on Del's mouse.

title: Bowfinger
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, with Bowfinger giving orders to his crew and actors. Kit Ramsey's behavior, though eccentric, also reflects a position of power, with others catering to his demands and eccentricities. Examples include Bowfinger telling Afrim what to do, and the clothing store offering Ramsey clothes for a photo.

title: Life
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening violence. Examples include the sheriff's interactions with the protagonists, the prison warden's speech about owning the prisoners, and the constant power plays among inmates for respect and resources (e.g., the corn bread incident).

title: The Bone Collector
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Rhyme exerting his authority over others, particularly Donaghy and Thelma. Examples include Rhyme ordering Donaghy to work the case despite her reluctance and dictating her actions at the crime scene, and Thelma being subject to Rhyme's demands and temper.

title: She's All That
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Taylor's dominance is evident in her interactions with her friends, and Zack's father pressures him about college choices. Dean and his friends also try to exert power over Simon, bullying him until Zack intervenes.

title: End of Days
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority, such as "Sky Two, get the fuck down here, now!" and "Get down on the ground and put your hands behind your head." The dialogue also reveals struggles for control, as seen in the interactions between Jericho and the possessed individuals, and the attempts to control Christine.

title: Three Kings
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include: "Halt! Freeze, motherfucker!", "Get this reporter off my back", and "Get down on the ground!". There are also instances of characters questioning authority, but the overall tone suggests a clear hierarchy.

title: A Civil Action
justification: The deposition scenes highlight the power dynamics between the lawyers and the witnesses, with lawyers attempting to control the narrative and extract information, while witnesses resist or evade questions. For example, the lawyer says "Well, then sit down and shut up!" to an opposing lawyer. Also, the scene with Riley shows a clear power struggle, with the lawyer using a court order to access his property and interrogate him, while Riley attempts to assert his authority and control the situation.

title: Eyes Wide Shut
justification: Several interactions show power dynamics. Ziegler's control over Bill is evident when he demands Bill's presence to attend to Mandy, emphasizing secrecy: "I PROBABLY...OH, I KNOW I DON'T HAVE TO MENTION THIS, BUT THIS IS JUST BETWEEN US, OK?". Marion's declaration of love and desire to change her life plans for Dr. Harford also highlights a power imbalance.

title: Never Been Kissed
justification: Several characters exert authority or dominance. The coach yells orders during gym, and Gus pressures Josie to get a story, threatening her job. Guy and his friends also display dominance by bullying others.

title: Forces of Nature
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. For example, Vic tells the kids, "You got it, Vic," and later a police officer demands, "What part of quiet didn't you understand?"

title: Varsity Blues
justification: The coach's control over the team is a central conflict. He constantly gives orders ('Get out there and win this ball game') and threatens players ('You disobey me, and I will bury you'). The players struggle with his authority, especially Moxon, who challenges his methods.

title: Message in a Bottle
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or directions, such as Charlie telling Theresa what to do at the newspaper and Garret's father, Dodge, telling him what to do. There are also instances of characters asserting authority, such as when Chet threatens to call the police if the men in the diner don't stop fighting.

title: South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut
justification: Adults exert authority over children, as seen when Kyle and Stan are grounded and Cartman is punished with a V-chip. The U.S. government dominates Canada, arresting Terrance and Phillip and declaring war. Satan also dominates Saddam Hussein, showcasing a clear hierarchy in Hell.

title: Stigmata
justification: The dialogue between Andrew and Daniel shows a clear hierarchy, with Daniel giving orders and controlling Andrew's movements and investigations. Daniel states, "I'm not going to allow you to go back to Brazil," demonstrating his authority. The Church's internal structure and control over information are also highlighted, with phrases like, "The truth of any document is only known to a very powerful few."

title: Life Is Beautiful
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include "Don't move your hands," "Wake up," "Slow down!" and the school principal's instructions to the children to obey the inspector.

title: Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo
justification: Several scenes depict power imbalances. T.J. attempts to control Deuce's actions as a 'male madam,' and Detective Fowler uses his authority to pressure Deuce for information. The scene where Deuce is forced to pay the bartender or face violence also highlights a power dynamic.

title: House on Haunted Hill
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a struggle for control. Examples include Price's interactions with Pritchett ("Tell them I'm right there") and Evelyn's controlling behavior towards Stephen ("I got your guest list right here, princess. Shredded."). The premise of the million-dollar prize also creates a competitive dynamic.

title: Cruel Intentions
justification: The dialogue is filled with manipulation, control, and dominance. Kathryn gives Sebastian a 'mission' to seduce Cecile, showcasing her control. The wager between Kathryn and Sebastian is a constant power struggle, with sexual favors and a car on the line.

title: 10 Things I Hate About You
justification: The father exerts strong control over his daughters, setting strict rules about dating: "What are the two house rules? Number one, no dating till you graduate. Number two, no dating till you graduate." Characters also manipulate each other for social status, as seen with Joey paying Patrick to date Kat so he can date Bianca.

title: My Favorite Martian
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience, such as the government agent demanding silence about the alien incident: "Keep your mouth shut, you idiot...you got it? Yes, sir." The alien also asserts dominance over Tim, stating: "Warning, Tim O'Hara. Any attempt to expose me will be useless. Martians use 100 % of their brain capacity, humans less than 10."

title: Fight Club
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Tyler exerting control, giving orders, and establishing a hierarchy within Fight Club and Project Mayhem. Examples include Tyler's rules for Fight Club ("The first rule of Fight Club is you do not talk about Fight Club") and his manipulation of Raymond K. Hessel ("If you're not working to be a veterinarian in six weeks, you will be dead").

title: Any Given Sunday
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include the coach's interactions with Willie Beamen, the power struggles between players, and the mayor's demands regarding the stadium deal. The coach's statement, 'This game has got to be about more than winning,' highlights the conflict between individual ambition and team hierarchy.

title: 8MM
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, with characters giving orders and demanding information. Examples include Welles' interactions with Max, where he offers money for information and directs Max's actions, and the power dynamic between Dino Velvet and his associates, where he commands them and they obey.

title: The Thin Red Line
justification: The film depicts a clear military hierarchy with officers giving orders and soldiers obeying. Examples include the Colonel repeatedly ordering Captain Staros to attack, despite Staros's reservations, and Staros himself giving orders to his men, sometimes met with resistance or questioning.

title: For Love of the Game
justification: Several instances show characters asserting dominance or reacting to authority. Examples include the mechanic demanding payment ("That's $100 to me") and Billy Chapel's interactions with the team trainer, where he asserts his authority and dictates the terms of their relationship ("You get me back. I'll figure out how to win.").

title: Instinct
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include the warden dictating terms to Dr. Caulder ('I'm gonna have to ask you to try to fit in with our scheme of things…') and inmates fighting over a card ('Give me the card!').

title: Mickey Blue Eyes
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and trying to control situations. Vito and his associates exert power through intimidation and violence, as seen in lines like, "You're one of the guys now" and the constant references to killings and criminal activities.

title: Bicentennial Man
justification: The robot Andrew is initially subservient, always asking 'sir' and seeking permission ('May one speak frankly with you?'). Later, he seeks freedom and challenges his status, leading to negotiations and legal actions ('To purchase one's freedom. One wants to be free.').

title: The Best Man
justification: Several characters exert dominance through direct commands and controlling behavior. Lance's friends pressure Harper to be unfaithful, showing a disregard for his relationship. Shelby attempts to control Quentin's career choices and social interactions, highlighting her desire for control.

title: The 13th Warrior
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the Viking society, with kings, heirs, and warriors. Orders are given and followed, such as when Buliwyf is summoned to help King Hrothgar and when warriors are assigned tasks during battles. The dialogue also shows status struggles, such as the initial tension and insults exchanged between the Arab ambassador and the Northmen.

title: Random Hearts
justification: Several scenes show characters exerting authority: a police officer pressures a witness ('I gotta have that shotgun. Now.') and later threatens a congresswoman ('Don't you fuck with me!'). There are also instances of characters being ordered around ('Get him downtown. Take real good care of him, okay?').

title: Superstar
justification: There are many instances of bullying and social hierarchy. Evian's mean-girl behavior and the constant put-downs directed at Mary show a struggle for status. The grandmother's control over Mary's life also highlights a power imbalance.

title: Mystery Men
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Casanova Frankenstein's threats to Lance Hunt and the constant commands given to the 'sucker' regarding the jeep. The Sphinx also attempts to assert authority through cryptic pronouncements and training exercises.

title: Dogma
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance. For example, Bartleby orders Loki to "Kill the girl," and Rufus threatens to "yank your sac off like a paper towel." There are also power struggles, such as the argument between Bartleby and Loki about their mission.

title: The Out-of-Towners
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the hotel manager Mersault controlling staff and guests ('I'll speak to housekeeping') and Henry's controlling behavior towards Nancy and Susan ('Don't try and protect me'). There are also instances of characters being subservient, like the hotel staff to wealthy guests ('And that's the kind of service you shall receive').

title: The Other Sister
justification: The mother exerts control over Carla's life, dictating her living situation and relationships: "Carla's not ready for an apartment. And really, she may never be ready for an apartment." The mother also attempts to control Carla's sexuality: "Anyway, with this apartment, I just don't think that you should have, um, any boyfriends over for a while, all right?"

title: Baby Geniuses
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, manipulation, and power plays, especially between Dr. Kinder and the babies. Examples include: "Don't tell me how well we're doing," "Every great mind will be ours to mold," and "You are in my power. You will obey my commands."

title: The Story of Us
justification: The dialogue reveals a power struggle between Ben and Katie, with accusations of infidelity and neglect. Katie asserts control by criticizing Ben's behavior and decisions, while Ben attempts to deflect and minimize his actions. The line, "You gave me that role!" indicates a power imbalance in their relationship.

title: Blast from the Past
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Helen telling Calvin, "Do as I say!" and Adam's father instructing him on what to do and not do in the outside world, ending with "Yes, sir."

title: The Wood
justification: The dialogue shows characters asserting dominance through insults and challenges ('Why you wearing it like that, man? Like a poindexter.') and displays of status ('Whoever got the most numbers at the end of the night get $1.'). The robbery scene highlights a stark power imbalance, with the robbers controlling the situation through threats and violence ('Hey, motherfucker, give me the money! Shut the fuck up and move!').

title: T-Rex: Back to the Cretaceous
justification: Biff Tannen exerts dominance over George McFly, demanding homework completion and threatening physical violence ('You got my homework finished, McFly?'). Later, Biff attempts to force himself on Lorraine, showcasing his power through physical intimidation ('Let me go!').

title: The Iron Giant
justification: Several instances show adults exerting authority over Hogarth, such as his mother setting strict rules ("no scary movies, no late snacks, in bed by 8:00") and Kent Mansley's manipulative interrogation and threats to take him away from his mother. The General also has clear authority, giving orders to the army.

title: EDtv
justification: The show's premise creates a power dynamic where Ed is constantly being manipulated by producers and the audience. Examples include Cynthia telling Ed what to do and the audience's influence on Ed's relationships, such as the poll about Shari.

title: At First Sight
justification: Several scenes involve characters giving orders or expressing control. Examples include Jennie's controlling behavior towards Virgil, and Amy's attempts to direct Virgil's medical decisions despite his reservations. The dialogue also reveals power imbalances in relationships, such as Duncan's professional dominance over Amy.

title: The Bachelor
justification: The dialogue shows some power dynamics, primarily in the context of the grandfather's will and the conditions attached to the inheritance. The grandfather exerts control from beyond the grave, dictating the terms of Jimmie's marriage. Jimmie's friends also try to influence his decisions, but ultimately, he makes his own choices.

title: A Stir of Echoes
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. For example, one character says, "Drink, motherfucker, drink. Drink." There are also instances of characters trying to control situations, such as when Tom repeatedly demands that Jake use a certain voice.

title: Anna and the King
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles. The King demands obedience ('You do not set conditions of your employment. And you shall obey!'), while Anna asserts her independence ('May i respectfully remind his majesty That i am not his servant, but his guest!'). There are also power dynamics in the classroom, with the prince asserting his royal status.

title: Man on the Moon
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people trying to exert control over Andy Kaufman, his career, and his performances. Examples include arguments over creative control on his special ("It's my special! I have creative control. Now, roll it!" "No!") and the firing of Tony Clifton from Taxi ("I have to ask your permission to fire Tony."). There are also instances of Andy trying to control situations, such as his wrestling persona and his demands for silence from the audience.

title: Galaxy Quest
justification: The movie features a clear hierarchy, with Jason Nesmith's character, Commander Taggart, initially perceived as the leader and giving orders. Dialogue such as "Laredo, take us out" and "Would you sit your ass down? Sit!" demonstrates his assumed authority, even though it's based on a fictional role. Sarris also exerts power through threats and demands, such as "Deliver the device to me, or I will destroy your ship!"

title: Waking Ned Devine
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. For example, Jackie directs Michael in the scheme to claim the lottery winnings, and Annie scolds Dennis for jumping the queue. There are also instances of characters trying to assert themselves, such as when Pat tries to woo Maggie despite Finn's presence.

title: Doug's 1st Movie
justification: The episode features several power dynamics. Guy, an upperclassman, takes over the school dance committee, demonstrating authority over younger students. Bill Bluff, a wealthy figure, uses his influence to control the narrative around the monster, showcasing his power over the town and media.

title: Summer of Sam
justification: Characters frequently assert dominance through insults, threats, and demands. Examples include "Put your fucking clothes on. Clothes I put on your back," and "Beg me for it." There are also instances of characters being subservient, such as apologizing to "the princess" and following orders within the criminal underworld.

title: An Ideal Husband
justification: Characters like Mrs. Cheveley exert control through blackmail and manipulation, demanding specific actions from Sir Robert. Dialogue such as "I hold your husband in the hollow of my hand...and if you are wise you'll make him do what I tell him" and the constant negotiation for information highlight the power struggles.

title: Being John Malkovich
justification: Dr. Lester clearly holds power over Craig, expecting him to listen to his sexual fantasies at work. Maxine's manipulation of Craig and Lotte, and her control over the Malkovich portal for profit, also highlight power dynamics.

title: Anywhere But Here
justification: The mother-daughter relationship is fraught with power imbalances. The mother frequently manipulates and controls Ann, evident in lines like, "Do you want me to go?" and "You should definitely go." The mother also exerts financial control, as seen in the argument about the car scratch and the mother's job.

title: How the Grinch Stole Christmas
justification: The Mayor of Whoville exerts his authority, dismissing the Grinch as a non-issue and expecting obedience from Lou. Cindy Lou challenges the Mayor's authority by nominating the Grinch for cheermeister, defying his expectations and sparking debate.

title: Mission: Impossible 2
justification: Characters give orders and make demands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "I beg you, Dimitri, come to Sydney and accompany me to Atlanta. Immediately." and "Wallace, hold on to this. Ulrich, remember to dump the... Remember to dump the NO2 tank."

title: Gladiator
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for power. Commodus murders his father to become Emperor, and numerous scenes show him asserting his dominance through threats and executions. Maximus is constantly struggling against Commodus's power, seeking to overthrow him and restore the Republic.

title: The Perfect Storm
justification: Captain Billy Tyne exerts considerable authority over his crew, giving orders and making decisions that they often question but ultimately obey. Examples include Tyne deciding to head to the Flemish Cap despite the crew's reservations and his command to Sully to 'Take the goddamn wheel! That's an order!'

title: Meet the Parents
justification: Jack Byrnes exerts control through interrogation, lie detector tests, and strict rules ('Keep your snake in its cage for 72 hours.'). Greg is constantly trying to appease Jack and navigate the Byrnes family's expectations, highlighting a clear imbalance of power.

title: X-Men
justification: Several characters assert dominance, give orders, or express fear of others' power. Examples include Magneto's manipulation and threats (e.g., "Don't get in my way") and Xavier's attempts to control and guide others (e.g., "Give me 48 hours"). The film also explores the power dynamics between mutants and humans, with humans fearing mutants' abilities.

title: Scary Movie
justification: Several characters exert authority through commands and threats. Examples include: "Shut up, Bobby!", "Put him in the trunk.", and Greg's repeated demands for Cindy to say "We take this to our grave". The Sheriff also uses his position to intimidate Cindy during questioning.

title: What Lies Beneath
justification: Several scenes depict Norman's controlling behavior towards Claire, such as when he dismisses her concerns about the neighbors ("Honey, people argue. People fight. It's not our business.") and later manipulates her into questioning her sanity. The revelation of his affair and subsequent actions to cover it up further highlight his dominance and manipulation.

title: Dinosaur
justification: Kron's dominance is evident in his orders: "Move it!" and "We stop for nothing and no one." Aladar challenges this authority, questioning Kron's decisions and ultimately leading a group away from him. The herd dynamic is largely dictated by Kron's control and the challenges to it.

title: Erin Brockovich
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of people asserting authority, giving orders, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Masry's control over Erin's job, Erin's interactions with Scott at the water board, and the power plays between PG&E representatives and the residents of Hinkley.

title: Nutty Professor II: The Klumps
justification: Several characters exert dominance through orders and threats. For example, the Dean pressures Sherman about the money, and Buddy Love uses intimidation and threats against Sherman. Clesius also tries to force his wife to take the youth formula.

title: Charlie's Angels
justification: Several characters give orders or assert authority. Examples include: "This cabin is restricted to first class," "Eduardo, move me," and Charlie's instructions to the Angels. The villain, Knox, also exerts control by kidnapping and manipulating others.

title: Big Momma's House
justification: Big Momma exerts control through commands and questions, such as "Sit back, watch and learn" and "So what about it, child? You in trouble?" Ben's submissive "Yes, ma'am! My mouth is closed!" after being scolded highlights her dominance. The FBI agents also exert authority.

title: Remember the Titans
justification: The film showcases a clear power dynamic through the coach's authoritative commands ('You will report back to me,' 'We are going to do up-downs until Blue is no longer tired and thirsty') and the players' struggles for recognition and respect within the team ('Hold your man down. Don't you single me out like that.'). The racial tensions and integration issues further highlight the power imbalances and the fight for equality and dominance.

title: The Patriot
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the British officers commanding soldiers ('Lieutenant, have your attachment take our wounded...') and Benjamin Martin directing his sons in combat ('I want you two to start with the officers...'). There are also instances of defiance and negotiation, such as the discussion about the treatment of prisoners.

title: What Women Want
justification: The dialogue includes instances of characters asserting dominance, such as the boss-employee dynamic where the female boss challenges Nick's ideas and the father-daughter relationship where the father tries to control his daughter's dating life. Also, there are power plays in romantic relationships, with characters trying to manipulate or understand each other's desires.

title: Chicken Run
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy on Tweedy's farm, with Mr. and Mrs. Tweedy exerting control over the chickens. Dialogue like "Just deal with it. Now!" and "No chicken escapes from Tweedy's farm!" demonstrates their dominance. The chickens also have a hierarchy, with Ginger leading escape attempts and Fowler, a former RAF officer, attempting to enforce discipline.

title: Gone in 60 Seconds
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "DON'T LOOK AT ME ! LOOK AT THE PEOPLE NEXT TO YOU ! THAT'S-- TURN THE WHEEL ! PULL OVER ! PULL HER THE HELL OVER !" and "ALL RIGHT, ALL RIGHT. WE DO THIS, WE DO IT MY WAY. I RUN THE SHOW. YOU TAKE YOUR ORDERS FROM ME."

title: Cast Away
justification: The FedEx manager, Chuck, exerts considerable authority over his employees, emphasizing the importance of time and delivery efficiency. He reprimands workers for delays and praises those who go the extra mile, creating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "Eighty-seven hours is a shameful outrage" and "Crunch time! Crunch time!"

title: Space Cowboys
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting authority or challenging it. For example, Frank manipulates NASA by demanding his team be included, and Gene initially resists but eventually concedes. Also, there are constant arguments and one-upmanship between Frank and Hawk.

title: Hollow Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Lab's prepped,' 'Ready in 40,' 'Roll and record') and asserting dominance ('Well, your objections are duly noted and summarily overruled,' 'It's still my project'). Sebastian's descent into madness is marked by his abuse of power and control over others.

title: Shaft
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include: "Come here! Come here! Don't make me chase you!", "Disperse, motherfuckers! Disperse now!", and "Shut up, cornbread."

title: The Kid
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in professional and personal relationships. Russ's assistant, Janet, is often berated and given orders: "Do it, Janet!" and "Figure it out, okay?". Also, Russ's professional life involves telling people what to do: "You tell other people what to do. That's the fun of it. You boss people around."

title: Road Trip
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters jockey for control in conversations and situations. Examples include Rubin manipulating Kyle into a road trip ('You're 19 years old, and you're a fucking sissy.') and the constant one-upmanship between Josh and El. The interactions are frequently driven by attempts to assert dominance or influence.

title: Mission to Mars
justification: The dialogue contains elements of hierarchy and command, such as 'Take us 20 minutes to get there, Chief' and 'Okay, we're gonna send a packet to Micker. We're going out there. Keep working.' There are also instances of direct orders and reporting to superiors.

title: Coyote Ugly
justification: The bar owner, Lil, exerts considerable control over her employees, dictating their behavior and appearance. Examples include: "Don't date the customers," "Break my rules, I fire you on the spot," and the constant pressure to earn money for the bar.

title: Snow Day
justification: Several characters exert authority: the father telling Randal how to eat soup, the mom ordering Randy around, and the bossy weather woman, Laura, pushing her employee Nona to work despite the snow day.  There are also instances of characters defying authority, like Randy ignoring his mother's orders.

title: 102 Dalmatians
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Cruella's interactions with Alonzo and LePelt showcase her dominance, while Chloe's role as a probation officer puts her in a position of authority over Cruella. Examples include: "Lock them away! Bury them beyond sight and memory!", "You're five minutes late.", and "Am I being clear?"

title: Fantasia 2000
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the hosts directing the camera operators ('Camera back on me') and Mickey Mouse being congratulated by Stokowski. However, these are relatively minor and infrequent, not dominating the dialogue.

title: The Whole Nine Yards
justification: Several characters exert dominance through threats and commands. Sophie manipulates Oz with the promise of divorce: "You do this for me...and I give you your divorce." Janni Gogolak uses intimidation and violence to control others, as seen in his interactions with Oz and Frankie.

title: Next Friday
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and engaging in conflicts over status. Examples include Debo's constant bullying and demands, Willie's pronouncements of being the 'king' because he owns his house, and Pinky's abusive treatment of his employees.

title: Shanghai Noon
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders, such as "Give me the dynamite," "Get him!" and "Stop! Turn around!" There are also instances of characters asserting dominance, such as "Reach for the sky, O'Bannon! It's my gang now!" and "You stay here."

title: Dolphins
justification: The documentary touches on dominance briefly, such as mentioning adult males sometimes killing porpoises and young dolphins, and dolphins biting each other. There's also a mention of dolphins approaching aggressively, indicating a potential power struggle.

title: The Cider House Rules
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Mr. Rose is consistently portrayed as the boss, and he uses threats to maintain control: "Just tell him you're in the apple business!" Dr. Larch also displays authority, as others seek his approval and follow his instructions.

title: Final Destination
justification: Several instances show authority: the FBI agents questioning the survivors, teachers directing students ('Sit down, Carter'), and general social dominance ('Fuck off'). The dialogue also includes instances of giving orders and asserting control ('Alex, could you trade seats with Blake').

title: The Road to El Dorado
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Cortes orders his crew, "To the brig." Tzekel-Kan attempts to control the city through fear and sacrifice, demanding, "There will be no sacrifices! Not now, not ever! Get out!"

title: The Hurricane
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy within the prison system, with the warden exerting authority over inmates like Rubin Carter. Carter's defiance of the warden's orders to wear the prison uniform highlights a struggle for control and self-respect within a system designed to strip him of both. Additionally, there are power dynamics between inmates, with some attempting to dominate or intimidate others.

title: Vertical Limit
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority, especially during the rescue attempts. Examples include, "Peter, check your sister's belay," and "Cut the damn rope!" as well as Vaughn's insistence on reaching the summit despite warnings.

title: Men of Honor
justification: The diving school scenes are rife with power dynamics, particularly between Master Chief Sunday and the trainees. Sunday constantly asserts his dominance through verbal abuse and physical challenges, such as when he tells Brashear, "Maybe you'll remember that next time you imply we got anything in common!" and when he forces Snowhill to hold a weight underwater until he collapses. The racial element further exacerbates these power imbalances, as seen in Sunday's discriminatory remarks and actions towards Brashear.

title: The Emperor's New Groove
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Kuzco abusing his power as emperor, ordering people around, threatening to destroy Pacha's village, and generally acting entitled. Yzma also vies for power, plotting to overthrow Kuzco and issuing commands to Kronk, highlighting a constant struggle for dominance.

title: The Tigger Movie
justification: Rabbit attempts to direct the others in a rock-moving project, giving orders like "Pooh Bear! Release the counterweight!" and "Piglet, start pulling your own weight over there." Tigger disregards Rabbit's instructions and uses his own method, leading to conflict and demonstrating a struggle for control.

title: Frequency
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or instructions, such as Frank telling Proby to adjust the antenna: "Point the antenna out from under the house a little bit." The police detective also exerts authority, questioning Daryl Simpson and directing other officers.

title: The Replacements
justification: The coach gives orders and expects obedience: "Go suit up," "Wherever you want me!" There are also instances of players challenging each other's authority, like the fight over the huddle spot: "That's my spot in the huddle." "It's my spot now!"

title: Pokemon 2000
justification: There are a few instances of implied authority, such as "You have to come with us, Takeshi" and "All of you gather here. Got it? Is that clear?" which suggest a mild power dynamic. However, the overall focus is on friendship and celebration, minimizing the theme's salience.

title: Miss Congeniality
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people giving orders and others obeying. Victor is constantly telling Gracie what to do, and Morningside is shown to be a demanding and controlling figure. Frank is treated like a servant.

title: The Beach
justification: Sal exerts control over the community, dictating rules and punishing transgressions, as seen when she forces Richard to stand watch and confronts Francoise about the map. Bugs also demonstrates a disturbing power over Gregorio, inflicting pain to maintain the community's secret. The dialogue highlights a clear hierarchy and the consequences of disobedience.

title: Pitch Black
justification: The film is driven by the power struggle between Riddick and Johns, as well as the shifting dynamics within the group of survivors.  Johns attempts to control Riddick with promises of freedom, while Riddick manipulates and challenges Johns' authority. Carolyn's struggle to assert her authority as captain is also evident.

title: The Family Man
justification: Several characters exert authority over Jack, highlighting a clear hierarchy. Examples include the initial mysterious figure giving orders and controlling Jack's experiences, and Kate's frustration and scolding of Jack for his behavior, indicating her dominance in their relationship.

title: Little Nicky
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Examples include: "So go get them, Dad," "Calm down. Get off your knees," and the constant struggle for control between Nicky and his brothers.

title: The Original Kings of Comedy
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the comedian's jokes about relationships ('Why you always make me sleep in the wet spot?' 'Cause that's your side.') and societal observations ('I'ma drive past the police and try not to get my ass whooped.'). However, these are brief and not a central focus.

title: Autumn in New York
justification: Will Keane's wealth and influence are evident in his interactions, such as when he comps Cristal to Charlotte. The dialogue also shows him giving orders and making demands, like when he tells Charlotte, "I'll give you till Thursday, 4:00."

title: Bedazzled
justification: The Devil is clearly in a position of power, granting wishes but also manipulating the outcomes. Elliot is constantly trying to gain power and status through his wishes, showing a desire to climb the social ladder and control his relationships, but the Devil always has the upper hand.

title: The Exorcist
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, defiance, and struggles for control. Regan's possessed state leads to obscene and aggressive outbursts, challenging authority figures, while the doctors and priests attempt to assert their control through medical procedures and religious rituals. Examples include: "LAY PERFECTLY STILL, BREATHE NORMALLY," and Regan's vulgar retorts.

title: Keeping the Faith
justification: The rabbi's struggle to modernize his congregation shows a power dynamic between him and the traditionalists. Anna's professional success and assertiveness create a dynamic with Jake, who seems less decisive. The mother's constant advice and opinions also create a power dynamic within the family.

title: 28 Days
justification: Several characters exert authority, like the staff telling patients what to do ('Pack your bags by morning') and patients challenging each other ('No way should you be here!'). There are also instances of characters trying to control each other's behavior ('If that'll make you happy, I will stop drinking.').

title: Bounce
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Buddy and Jim, where Jim asserts his authority after Buddy's absence. Examples include Jim telling Buddy to "Sit down" and stating, "Since about a week after they shipped you to Palm Springs."

title: Hanging Up
justification: The dialogue reveals a constant struggle for control, especially within the family. The father's erratic behavior and demands, like insisting on Chinese food in the hospital and demanding Eve call their mother, highlight his attempts to exert control. Georgia's fame and Eve's subservience to her also show a power imbalance.

title: The Flintstones in Viva Rock Vegas
justification: The Great Gazoo frequently insults Fred and Barney, asserting his superior intellect and alien status. Wilma's mother attempts to control Wilma's life, dictating who she should marry and how she should live. Chip Rockefeller uses his wealth and status to manipulate situations and exert control over others.

title: The Skulls
justification: The Skulls organization exerts significant control over its members, demanding obedience and secrecy. Examples include: "Get up and shut up, Mandrake," and "Our rules supersede those of the outside world."

title: The 6th Day
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Drucker's constant demands ('Get me the Speaker') and the security team's responses ('Yes, sir'). There's also a clear hierarchy within RePet, with Drucker at the top and others scrambling to obey.

title: Dude, Where’s My Car?
justification: The movie contains many instances of characters trying to assert dominance over others. Examples include Tommy bullying Jesse and Chester, the twins bossing Jesse and Chester around, and the Chinese food worker repeatedly asking "And then?" to frustrate the customer.

title: My Dog Skip
justification: The father is stern and overbearing, demanding Will fill out invitations and taking away his dog. The bullies also exert power through intimidation and physical violence, demanding Will hand over Dink's belongings.

title: Where the Heart Is
justification: Willy exerts control over Novalee, demonstrated by his impatience and demands: "Novalee, you plan on leaving today?" and "All right, hurry up." Lil also displays some authority, telling Novalee "You should try to call whoever is coming."

title: Pay it Forward
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, often through aggression or manipulation. Examples include the man demanding the nurse attend to his daughter ("YOU'RE THE SUPERVISOR OF THE DAY. HUH?") and Arlene threatening the man in her truck with a gun ("I WANT YOU TO COME OUT, OR I WILL FIND YOU AND SHOOT YOU, I SWEAR--").

title: Return to Me
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority. Bob's construction site visit involves him dictating terms and threatening to leave if his demands aren't met. Also, Joe is told to change the baby's diaper by his wife.

title: Almost Famous
justification: Several characters exert authority: Ben Fong-Torres gives William assignments and deadlines ("Let's do 3,000 words"). Dennis Hope tries to take over as Stillwater's manager, outlining how he can improve their financial situation ("Your manager here needs a manager."). Elaine, William's mother, attempts to control his actions and whereabouts ("You told me you would call me twice a day").

title: The Legend of Bagger Vance
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the interactions between Hardy and Captain Junuh, where Hardy seeks Junuh's help and Junuh initially dismisses him. Later, Bagger Vance takes on a mentor role, guiding Junuh and offering advice, which establishes a power dynamic based on knowledge and experience. Adele also attempts to manipulate Junuh into playing, highlighting a struggle for control.

title: The Art of War
justification: Characters frequently give orders and make demands, such as "Call Amnesty. See if they can trace these to the ones that disappeared last month" and "Transfer the call. We're both here now." There are also instances of characters asserting dominance through threats and intimidation, like "Considering your, fragile condition... I think I can kick your ass."

title: Bless the Child
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Eric Stark manipulates Jenna and attempts to control Cody through psychological manipulation and threats. Agent Travis, despite his supposed authority, is undermined by his colleagues and struggles to maintain control of the investigation.

title: Proof of Life
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power assertions. Examples include: "Get inside, NOW!", "Bitch, when I give an order, you follow it!", "Chain him up! I give you an order, you do it!", and "You're being demoted...to work with the animals."

title: The Watcher
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance. The killer manipulates Joel with photos and threats ('I'll send you a picture, and you can have a day to try to find her.'). Detectives also use their authority to interrogate and direct others ('Welcome to my crime scene.').

title: Girl, Interrupted
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance and control over others. Examples include Lisa's manipulative behavior and verbal abuse, Valerie's role as an authority figure enforcing rules, and the power imbalance between patients and staff, as seen in the administration of medication and restrictions.

title: Love and Basketball
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. For example, the coach constantly berates Monica, demonstrating authority: "Monica, get up on her," and "While you were so busy posing, your man just scored." Also, Zeke's infidelity and lies create a power imbalance in his marriage, as he prioritizes his desires over his wife's feelings.

title: High Fidelity
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to assert dominance. For example, Rob manipulates the record sale to Louis, and Barry and Dick's behavior towards customers and each other indicates a hierarchy within the record store. Also, Rob's interactions with his exes reveal power struggles in relationships.

title: The Adventures of Rocky & Bullwinkle
justification: Fearless Leader constantly barks orders at Boris and Natasha, such as "So, Badenov, these shows had better be terrible!" and "Now catch moose and squirrel and next time use the C.D.I. On them!" Karen, as an FBI agent, attempts to exert authority, but often fails, highlighting a struggle for control.

title: Nurse Betty
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Wesley frequently berates his partner, such as, "Turn off that goddamn music!" and "Do I deserve this?". Also, the show producer Lyla is clearly in charge on set, directing David and Betty.

title: Reindeer Games
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, commands, and attempts to control others. Gabriel and his crew exert dominance through violence and intimidation, demanding information and compliance. Ashley and Nick also engage in power struggles, manipulating each other for their own goals.

title: Titan A.E.
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Eat this.', 'Humans wait.', 'Next! Keep the line moving.'). There are also instances of characters asserting dominance or complaining about being treated poorly ('You've been a little uppity.', 'I'm not askin' that much.').

title: Magnolia
justification: Several characters exert dominance through direct commands and manipulation. Frank T.J. Mackey's seminar explicitly teaches dominance over women: "Respect the cock and tame the cunt!" and "I am the one who's in charge! I am the one who says yes!". Solomon berates and fires Donnie, showcasing economic power: "Your sales suck, Don! I give! I give!".

title: Urban Legends: Final Cut
justification: The film school environment is rife with power struggles.  Dialogue like "Get me a coffee" and "I'll kill you!" showcases abusive director behavior. The Hitchcock award is a source of intense competition, leading to theft and murder.

title: Boys and Girls
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Amy asks, "Amy, are you breaking up with your boyfriend, or am I breaking up with your boyfriend?" Hunter tries to dictate Ryan's behavior, saying, "You've gotta weep... openly."

title: Monsters, Inc.
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and jockeying for position. Examples include Waternoose directing Sulley, Roz's control over paperwork, and Randall's aggressive pursuit of status.

title: Rush Hour 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include: "GET UP, DOG. LET'S GO," "NOW I SAID, GET UP," and the repeated demands for obedience. The interactions between Lee and Carter also highlight a struggle for control and understanding.

title: The Mummy Returns
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority, such as when Rick tells Alex to "Stay here and protect the car." Imhotep's control over his followers is evident in lines like "Get out of the way or I'm gonna shoot you in the face."

title: Pearl Harbor
justification: The film depicts a clear military hierarchy with characters giving and receiving orders. Examples include Colonel Doolittle's command over the pilots and the medical staff's triage decisions during the Pearl Harbor attack: "Only those that can be saved, you bring in here. You got that?"

title: Jurassic Park 3
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or making demands. Paul Kirby repeatedly directs Udesky and Nash, such as "Udesky? Nash? How about up front? You guys see anything?" and "Get on the plane!". Also, the pilot is told "Make sure you get us as close as you can! I'll give you something extra if you make it a good trip."

title: Hannibal
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, manipulate, or control others. Examples include Lecter's psychological games with Starling ('Quid pro quo, Clarice.') and Krendler's threats to her career ('If you don't, then all I have to do is draw a line through your name rather than under it, and it's over.'). Verger's control over Cordell and his plans for Lecter also highlight the theme.

title: Ocean's Eleven
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Terry Benedict who is a casino owner and is used to being in control. There are also scenes where characters give orders and expect obedience, such as when Danny Ocean directs his crew. The dialogue highlights the hierarchical structure within the casino and the team.

title: Traffic
justification: Several characters exert authority: Arnie directs Helena on how to behave after her husband's arrest, General Salazar displays dominance over subordinates, and Robert demands action from his staff regarding drug cartels. Dialogue such as "Now, do not discuss anything...over the telephone" and "Guard! Are you responsible for this? We are not savages!" exemplifies this dynamic.

title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
justification: Characters frequently give orders or instructions, such as "JOIN ME ONCE YOU HAVE FINISHED" and "TELL ME IF LI MU BAI IS NOT MORE OPEN THE NEXT TIME YOU SEE HIM.
