I'LL GIVE HIM AN EARFUL!". There are also instances of characters asserting authority or questioning others' actions, like "DON'T INVITE DANGER INTO YOUR FATHER'S HOUSE" and "WHERE IS YOUR MASTER?".

title: Dr Dolittle 2
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Dolittle gives orders to Archie ('You need to watch this, Archie, to learn how to feed yourself') and tries to manipulate Ava's romantic choices ('At least let me call him over. Please?'). The logging company attempts to intimidate Dolittle ('If I don't meet my quota, you'll be in danger.')

title: Spy Kids
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority. For example, "Carmen, leave your brother alone," and "Juni, stop talking like your sister." Also, the villains exert control over others, such as Floop's manipulation of his creations and Minion's command over Floop and the robot army.

title: The Princess Diaries
justification: The grandmother figure exerts considerable control over Mia, dictating her behavior, appearance, and future. Examples include the etiquette lessons ("Princesses never cross their legs in public") and the makeover scene where Paolo and his assistants aggressively transform Mia's appearance against her initial wishes ("You broke my glasses!").

title: The Others
justification: The governess exerts control over the children through strict rules and punishments ("I want to see those plates empty in less than a minute. Is that clear?"). The staff also show deference to the lady of the house ("Yes, ma'am."). The lady of the house also tries to control the staff and children through fear and intimidation.

title: Legally Blonde
justification: The professor, Stromwell, asserts authority by questioning students intensely and threatening expulsion: "Would you be willing to stake your life on it?" Callahan's internship is presented as a highly competitive opportunity, creating a power dynamic among the students.

title: America's Sweethearts
justification: Characters frequently give orders and express frustration when their authority is challenged. For example, Gwen demands, "You need to go to this junket," and later argues about who arrives first at the hotel. The publicist, Lee, also tries to control the narrative and manage the talent, showing a clear hierarchy.

title: Cats & Dogs
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and hierarchical language, especially within the dog agency. Examples include "Front and center, agents! Hup, hup, hup!", "Don't make me muzzle you!", and "Freeze, cat. I'm an agent."

title: Save the Last Dance
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance. Chenille gives orders to Sara about her clothing and appearance. Nikki's confrontational behavior and verbal attacks establish a clear hierarchy and struggle for status within the social group.

title: Atlantis: The Lost Empire
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and directives, such as "Attention. All hands to the launch bay," "Rig ship for dive! Aye, sir!" and "Lieutenant, take her down." Commander Rourke's interactions with his crew and Milo demonstrate a clear hierarchy and control.

title: Artificial Intelligence: AI
justification: The dialogue includes commands and obedience, such as Monica telling David, "David, when we leave, all the doors and windows will go smart. So you can't leave your room." There are also instances of Martin ordering David around, highlighting a hierarchical dynamic between the two.

title: Along Came a Spider
justification: The dialogue includes instances of authority and control, such as Mr. Soneji's interactions with Megan, where he manipulates and commands her. Agent McArthur's interactions with other agents also show a clear hierarchy. Soneji's phone calls to Cross are also about establishing control.

title: Bridget Jones's Diary
justification: Daniel Cleaver exerts control over Bridget at work and in their relationship, demonstrated by his comments on her appearance and his expectations. Mark Darcy and Daniel Cleaver's physical fight over Bridget shows a struggle for dominance. The mother's interactions with the Home Shopping Channel presenter also show a power dynamic.

title: The Score
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include "Just get the fuck out of my house," "I see you again, I break your fucking knees," and "You will tell me everything you know, then I will design the plan."

title: Swordfish
justification: The film is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include: "Move. I won't say it again," and "All shooters, you are holding for command." Gabriel's manipulation of Stanley and the Senator's threats further highlight the power struggles.

title: Vanilla Sky
justification: Several instances of characters attempting to exert control or influence over others are present. Examples include the discussion of controlling people's lives, the power dynamics within David's company, and the controlling and manipulative behavior exhibited in relationships.

title: Shallow Hal
justification: Hal's boss, Rosemary's father, exerts authority by offering Hal a promotion and candidly assessing his daughter's attractiveness. The friends also engage in status competition by criticizing Hal's choice of partner, implying a hierarchy of attractiveness.

title: Chocolat
justification: Several characters exert authority: the Comte over the townspeople, Reynaud over Pere Henri, and Serge over Josephine. Examples include Reynaud telling Pere Henri he's made 'one or two notes' on his sermon and Serge yelling at Josephine, 'YOU STUPID WOMAN! YOU'RE NOTHING WITHOUT ME.'

title: The Mexican
justification: Characters are constantly giving orders and threatening each other. Examples include: "Don't even move, ok? I'll call the office. We'll get me on a plane. I'll get down and help you shit out." and "This is what you're gonna do. You're gonna stop crying. And you're gonna walk out of here with me."

title: Down to Earth
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Wellington exerting his wealth and influence, such as offering raises to staff ('Startin' next week, both of you get a 200% raise') and trying to control Sontee ('Would you guys give us some privacy?'). There are also instances of others attempting to manipulate or control him, like the initial attempt to poison him and the board members trying to reign him in.

title: Spy Game
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, like when Duncan tells Harry, "I'll give you 25 minutes...before I transmit." Muir also exerts authority, telling Bishop, "Don't ever question me again. Ever." and later, "I gave you an order, you take it."

title: The Wedding Planner
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, Penny tries to set Mary up with Steve, saying, "We won't take no for an answer." Massimo also tries to orchestrate Mary's life, leading to conflict.

title: Moulin Rouge
justification: The Duke exerts financial power, demanding Satine's exclusive contract and the Moulin Rouge deeds. Zidler is subservient to the Duke's demands, while Satine struggles against the Duke's control, highlighted by the line, "Satine will be mine."

title: Rat Race
justification: The film is driven by Donald Sinclair's manipulation of others for his own amusement. He sets up a race with 'no rules' and enjoys watching the chaos unfold, stating 'I can do anything I like, Owen. I'm eccentric.' The characters also struggle for dominance within their groups, such as the family arguing about the vacation and the couple fighting over the truck.

title: A Knight’s Tale
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and jockeying for status. Examples include Ulrich's rise from commoner to knight, Adhemar's aristocratic arrogance, and the constant need to prove oneself in tournaments. Lines like "Hold your tongue, sir, or lose it" and "Each drop of this sweat has a price on it" highlight the power struggles.

title: The Animal
justification: The film features several characters vying for dominance. Marvin struggles to gain respect as a police officer, facing ridicule from kids and his sergeant. The police chief exerts authority over his officers, and the townspeople form a mob mentality, attempting to control the situation with the 'beast'.

title: Don’t Say a Word
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include the kidnapper dictating terms to Nathan ('YOU DO NOT MAKE DEMANDS. YOU LISTEN TO WHAT I TELL YOU.') and Cassidy asserting authority over Syd ('I'M GONNA NEED PRELIMINARY FINDINGS BY TONIGHT.').

title: Blow
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the courtroom scene where the judge asserts authority ("YOU'RE GOING TO HAVE TO STOP SLOUCHING AND STAND UP TO ADDRESS THIS COURT, SIR."). Later, Escobar's control is evident when he dictates terms and expects obedience ("EL SENOR ESCOBAR QUIERE VER SOLAMENTE AL SENOR JUNG.").

title: Exit Wounds
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include T.K. ordering his employees around ("Now, get my drink, bitch!") and the constant power plays between Boyd and other officers, like Mulcahy and Montini ("Answer the question, Boyd."). The interactions between criminals and law enforcement also highlight the struggle for control.

title: Enemy at the Gates
justification: The film is filled with characters giving orders and others obeying. Examples include Kruschev's demands of the political officers ('I want them to stop shitting their pants! That's your job.') and the constant military commands ('Fire!', 'Get back!', 'Keep back!'). The film also shows the power of propaganda and the creation of heroes to inspire obedience and sacrifice.

title: Behind Enemy Lines
justification: The film features numerous instances of characters asserting authority and navigating hierarchical structures. Admiral Reigart's interactions with subordinates, such as Lieutenant Burnett, demonstrate a clear power dynamic through reprimands and control over career decisions. The conflict between Reigart and Donnelly over the search and rescue mission further highlights the struggle for control and decision-making authority within the military.

title: K-PAX
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between doctor and patient, with the doctor giving instructions and the patient sometimes resisting. Prot's interactions with other patients also show him attempting to exert influence, as when he tells Howie to find the bluebird of happiness. The family dynamic also shows power struggles, such as the father's frustration with his son and the mother's attempts to mediate.

title: Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the classroom scenes where Miss Fowl struggles to maintain control over the students. Nick's rebellious attitude and Cindy's constant need to challenge Jimmy's intelligence also highlight the struggle for status.

title: Finding Forrester
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance or challenging authority. Examples include the professor's condescending remarks to Jamal about his academic abilities and Forrester's controlling instructions and criticisms of Jamal's writing and behavior. The basketball court scenes also highlight power struggles through trash talk and competition for a spot on the team.

title: Zoolander
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting dominance. Mugatu frequently barks orders, such as "Do me a favor and lose five pounds immediately, or get out of my building like now! Get out!" and "The center has to be at least three times bigger than this." Maury also tries to control Derek's career, saying "Sit down!" and attempting to manipulate him into modeling again.

title: Domestic Disturbance
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Rick's controlling behavior towards Danny during baseball practice ("Turn it! Turn it! Take it easy!") and Frank's physical altercation with Mike Patterson to defend Danny's honor demonstrate struggles for dominance and control.

title: The One
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Hold your fire!', 'Cease fire!', 'Hands high!'), threats ('I will kill you.', 'You're dead, Lawless!'), and assertions of dominance ('You are mine.'). The MVA agents also exert authority through procedure and control over travel between universes.

title: O Brother, Where Art Thou?
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance. Everett often takes charge and gives orders, such as "Pull over, Everett. Let's give that coloured boy a lift." Big Dan Teague also tries to intimidate and control others, as seen when he robs Everett and Delmar.

title: Thir13en Ghosts
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and attempts to control others, especially Arthur trying to manage his children ('Bobby, put away the damn tape recorder. Can you do that for me?'). Cyrus's will dictates the family's future, and the ghosts exert a terrifying power over the living.

title: Bandits
justification: The subtitles contain several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control. For example, Lieutenant McCormick demands, "Put down your weapons and come out of the bank with your hands in the air." Later, Joe tells Kate, "You have to choose."

title: Heartbreakers
justification: Characters are constantly trying to one-up each other, like when Page and her mother compete to seduce the man at the bar. There are also many instances of characters giving orders and expecting obedience, such as when the mother tells Page to remove the spikes from the road and Page is clearly annoyed by it.

title: Hardball
justification: Several characters exert authority: Pearla threatens Conor with 'hell will be paid with your ass' if he doesn't help the boys. Conor struggles to maintain control over the team, as seen when he yells 'Hey! That's enough!' to stop a fight. Fink, the bookie, holds power over Conor due to his gambling debt.

title: Evolution
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the professor directing students ("Don't move anything. Don't even breathe unless we tell you to.") and military personnel controlling access to the site ("You're not on the list."). The conflict between the scientists and the military further emphasizes the struggle for control over the situation.

title: Jeepers Creepers
justification: The siblings, Darry and Trish, engage in frequent power struggles, marked by insults and attempts to control each other's actions. Examples include Trish telling Darry to "Just drive, brat" and Darry's repeated attempts to dictate their course of action, such as "Get out to the road and find somebody who can help."

title: Kiss of the Dragon
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threatening each other, and asserting dominance. Examples include Richard's control over Jessica and other women, his orders to subordinates, and the general's instructions to Inspector Richard. The power struggles are evident in the interactions between characters, especially in the context of crime and law enforcement.

title: Recess: School's Out
justification: The adults, Principal Prickly and the rogue teacher Benedict, exert authority over the children. Benedict's desire to control summer vacation and Prickly's initial dismissal of T.J.'s concerns highlight the power imbalance. Becky's control over T.J. with his diary is another example.

title: Ali
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include Herbert directing Ali's career, Elijah Muhammad's dictates, and Ali's own demands and pronouncements of dominance, such as "You don't marry that girl" and "What's my name?".

title: Thirteen Days
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding information, and asserting authority. Examples include Kennedy directing actions during the crisis, military personnel reporting to superiors, and tense exchanges where individuals challenge or undermine each other's decisions.

title: See Spot Run
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the police officer telling people to leave, Gordon bossing James around, and the FBI agents giving orders to each other. Dialogue like "Out. Now. Go." and "You must come down now." demonstrates this dynamic. The mob boss Sonny also uses threats to maintain control.

title: Driven
justification: Several characters exert authority: Carl gives Jimmy driving instructions ('Don't overdrive the car') and later fires Joe. Beau attempts to intimidate Jimmy ('Block me again and I'll put you into the wall').

title: What's the Worst That Could Happen?
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, give orders, or manipulate others. Max frequently barks orders at Earl ('Move your fat ass') and others, while Lutetia controls Max through threats of divorce and financial ruin ('Scandal and disease, Max. These are the deal-breakers.'). Even the thief, Kevin, struggles to maintain control over his partner, Berger.

title: Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within
justification: The dialogue is filled with military rank and orders. Examples include: "Welcome back, captain," "Yes, sir," and "Lower your weapons. That's an order!"

title: Not Another Teen Movie
justification: The film revolves around Jake's bet to transform Janey into the prom queen, showcasing his control and manipulation. Dialogue like "I'll pick the most hopeless girl at this school...and I'll bet that you can't turn her into prom queen" and Priscilla's cheerleading dominance ("This isn't a cheerocracy. I am the cheertator.") further emphasizes the theme.

title: Black Knight
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance and others submitting. The King gives orders and expects obedience, as seen in lines like, "Silence, moor!" and "Phillip, have the servants ply this messenger with much food and drink." Jamal's interactions also show his attempts to assert himself, such as when he confronts the robot knight and later when he becomes a lord and gives orders.

title: From Hell
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority and others submitting. Examples include the sergeant's reprimands ("PIPE DOWN, WITHERS. WHEN THE INSPECTOR IS TALKING, YOU ARE LISTENING.") and the inspector's interactions with his superiors, where he must carefully navigate their expectations and prejudices.

title: Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, especially by Jay. Examples include Jay's constant swearing and insults, his attempts to impress Justice, and his interactions with Silent Bob, where he often gives orders or belittles him. The interactions between the animal rights activists also show a clear hierarchy, with Justice seemingly in charge.

title: Snatch
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threatening each other, and trying to assert dominance. Examples include Brick Top's constant demands and threats, and the various characters trying to intimidate each other during negotiations and confrontations: "Make sure your man goes down in the fourth. You understand me now, don't you, Turkish?", "Get back down and fucking stay down."

title: Double Take
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Daryl telling people what to do, Freddy's constant attempts to assert dominance, and the interactions with law enforcement and authority figures.

title: Baby Boy
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to exert control, accusations of infidelity, and power plays. Examples include Yvette's anger over Jody's cheating and her stealing his car, and Jody's attempts to manipulate and control Yvette through guilt and promises.

title: The Brothers
justification: Several characters exert authority: Mama dictates to her sons and grandson ("Tyrel, just go outside. Just watch my car."), Sheila controls Derrick by changing the locks and threatening him with the police, and Carla confronts Jesse and Brian with aggressive demands and physical violence. The dialogue reveals a constant negotiation and struggle for control within relationships.

title: Joe Dirt
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to assert dominance or control over others. Examples include the oil rig workers' confrontational banter, Buffalo Bob's disturbing control over his captive, and the school children's taunting behavior towards Joe Dirt.

title: Crocodile Dundee in Los Angeles
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include the director instructing the background actors ('Back to one, please!'), Sue's boss assigning her Tom's story, and the mugger demanding money ('Hand me over your money, man!').

title: Memento
justification: The dialogue shows characters trying to manipulate Leonard due to his memory condition. Natalie uses Leonard for her own purposes, and Teddy attempts to control his actions by providing misleading information. Burt also exploits Leonard's condition by renting him multiple rooms.

title: Captain Corelli's Mandolin
justification: The film depicts the power dynamics of military occupation, with Italian and German forces exerting control over the Greek island. Characters give orders and express resistance, such as the Italian captain demanding surrender and the islanders defying curfew. Pelagia's father dictates who she can marry, highlighting patriarchal power.

title: 15 Minutes
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and jockeying for position. Examples include the border agent demanding documents, the news director berating staff for ratings, and detectives controlling crime scenes.

title: Hearts in Atlantis
justification: Ted exerts control by giving Bobby tasks and information selectively, creating a hierarchy. He says, "your real job will simply be to...walk around the area...and if you see them...you will alert me immediately, ok?" and "run like hell was after you and tell me what you've seen."

title: Angel Eyes
justification: Several characters exert authority through commands and threats. Examples include police officers ordering suspects ('Shut up', 'Get down!'), and aggressive confrontations ('Get off of me! I'll kill you!'). There are also instances of verbal dominance and attempts to control conversations ('Shut the fuck up.').

title: Corky Romano
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Russo directing Pissant, Shuster berating agents, and the Romano family members vying for control. The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays.

title: Two Can Play That Game
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control and manipulate each other, especially in relationships. Examples include Shanté's 'rules' for handling men, Keith's friend advising him on how to regain control, and the constant back-and-forth of who has the 'upper hand'.

title: Joy Ride
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, manipulate, and control others. Examples include the constant pranks and put-downs between the brothers, the power plays in the CB radio conversations, and Rusty Nail's twisted control over the group, dictating their actions and movements.

title: Valentine
justification: Several exchanges highlight power dynamics. For example, Dorothy's interactions with Kim, her stepmother, show a clear struggle for dominance, with Dorothy asserting her independence and dismissing Kim's attempts to exert authority. Also, the detective's inappropriate behavior towards Paige demonstrates an abuse of power.

title: Spider-Man
justification: The film features several characters vying for power. Norman Osborn's struggle to maintain control of OSCORP is a central conflict, as is his alter ego, the Green Goblin, who seeks to dominate Spider-Man. Examples include: "The board expects your resignation in 30 days." and "Join me. Imagine what we could accomplish together."

title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of authority and obedience. Snape and Lockhart compete for dominance in the Dueling Club, and Dumbledore's authority is challenged by Lucius Malfoy and the other governors, who try to suspend him.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. Gandalf's interactions with Théoden and Wormtongue are prime examples of power struggles, as is Denethor's treatment of Faramir. The dialogue highlights the hierarchical structure and the attempts to control or influence others.

title: Austin Powers in Goldmember
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Dr. Evil's commands to his henchmen and Goldmember's control over his club and captives. The constant one-upmanship and attempts to assert authority contribute to a strong sense of power dynamics.

title: Men in Black 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Zed ordering agents around ("I GAVE THE ORDER, MY BEST AGENT CARRIED IT OUT.") and Kay's interactions with Jay, where he often takes charge and gives instructions ("GET A MOP AND ESCORT ALL NONESSENTIAL CIVILIAN PERSONNEL FROM THIS SITE IMMEDIATELY."). There are also instances of characters vying for control, such as Serleena's attempts to dominate and manipulate others.

title: Ice Age
justification: Several characters assert dominance through threats and insults. Examples include the rhinos bullying Sid ('We'll break your neck so you don't feel a thing') and Soto's pack's interactions with Diego ('I want that baby, Diego. I'll get it. You'd better, unless you want to serve as a replacement.').

title: A Beautiful Mind
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting dominance. Examples include the General directing Dr. Nash's actions ('Accompany Dr. Nash') and the professor dictating classroom rules ('Your comfort comes second to my ability to hear my own voice.'). The interactions with Parcher also highlight a power dynamic, with Parcher directing Nash's actions and emphasizing the importance of his work.

title: Scooby-Doo
justification: Throughout the show, Fred is often seen as the leader, dictating the plan and what everyone should do. Daphne is often portrayed as the 'damsel in distress,' needing to be saved, which creates a power dynamic. Scrappy-Doo attempts to assert dominance, demanding to be the leader and using force.

title: Die Another Day
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Turn around. Start walking. Keep walking, please.') and asserting dominance ('Your people have abandoned you.'). There are also power struggles evident in the betrayals and interrogations ('Who made him betray his country and his name?').

title: Lilo & Stitch
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Jumba tells Pleakley to "Keep quiet." The Grand Councilwoman intimidates Jumba into going to Earth to redeem his reputation.

title: xXx
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and control. Gibbons manipulates Xander with threats and promises, while Milan Sova attempts to exert authority over Xander, stating, "Here, you are under my jurisdiction. You take my orders, you do what I say."

title: The Santa Clause 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Santa commanding Bernard and the elves, Principal Newman's interactions with students, and the toy Santa's attempts to enforce stricter rules.

title: Minority Report
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders and asserting authority. For example, Chief Anderton directs his team, and Witwer takes control of the team from Fletcher. There are also instances of defiance, such as when Anderton refuses to comply with orders and runs from Precrime.

title: The Ring
justification: Several characters exert authority or try to dominate conversations. Rachel pressures people for information, and the video tape itself holds power over its viewers, dictating their fate. The dialogue between Rachel and Noah also shows a power struggle, with Rachel accusing Noah of being unreliable.

title: Mr. Deeds
justification: Several instances of hierarchical language are present. Examples include Emilio being told to 'Keep an eye on him, or it's your ass,' and Reuben addressing Deeds as 'sir.' Additionally, Cedar and Anderson exert control over Deeds's company affairs, stating, 'The officers of the company, like me...run the show.'

title: Sweet Home Alabama
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in several relationships. Wade, as sheriff, exerts authority ('I'm gonna have to escort you out') and Jake's mother controls him ('HELL, BOY, I THOUGHT YOU SAID YOU TOOK CARE OF THIS'). Melanie's mother also tries to control her ('YOU NEED TO STAY AS FAR AWAY FROM HERE AS YOU CAN').

title: The Bourne Identity
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding information, and asserting control. Examples include the director's interactions with his staff ('The director wants to know...'), Bourne's interrogations ('Who are you?'), and the constant struggle for dominance in conversations.

title: The Sum of All Fears
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Cabot directing Ryan ('When I asked for your advice, I didn't mean that you should actually speak') and Nemerov's interactions with his staff, demonstrating a clear hierarchy ('Just disappear them').

title: 8 Mile
justification: The movie features constant battles for dominance, both verbally in rap battles and physically through fights. Characters like Papa Doc and Future assert their authority, while Jimmy struggles to gain respect and control his own life, highlighted by lines like, "Me and Papa Doc will battle any motherfuckers here."

title: Black Hawk Down
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and directives, such as "Remember the rules of engagement," "Tell him to turn his damn radio off," and "We're Rangers, not some sorry-ass JROTC. We're elite. Let's act like it out there." There are also instances of insubordination and questioning of authority, but the overall tone is one of command and obedience.

title: The Road to Perdition
justification: The film revolves around John Rooney's control over his criminal empire and the people within it, including Michael Sullivan. Dialogue such as "You rule this town...as God rules the earth. You give, and you take away..." and Rooney's orders to Sullivan highlight the hierarchical structure and the characters' struggle for power and loyalty.

title: Panic Room
justification: Several characters give orders and assert dominance. Examples include the real estate agent pushing for an immediate offer ('You should make an offer immediately'), the criminals directing each other ('Kill the phones. Top floor, little girl.') and the tense negotiations between the criminals ('I'm in charge here.').

title: Red Dragon
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance or negotiate for power. Examples include Will Graham's interactions with Lecter, where they trade information and favors, and the Tooth Fairy's manipulation and control over Lounds, culminating in his gruesome transformation and forced confession.

title: The Scorpion King
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and displays of authority. Examples include Memnon's orders to his generals, the power struggles between tribal leaders, and the constant threat of violence to enforce obedience: "Silence! My father has called for silence!", "You'll scream in five different languages.", "Rivers of blood can never bring peace. But they can bring obedience."

title: Spy Kids 2: The Island of Lost Dreams
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the O.S.S. spy organization, with characters giving and receiving orders. For example, Donnagon directs Gary and Gerti, and Carmen and Juni hack to reinstate their level 2 status. Also, the parents show up and try to take over the mission.

title: Blade 2
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for power. Blade gives orders to Whistler and Scud, and the vampires have a clear hierarchy, with Damaskinos at the top, giving orders to Nyssa and others. The Bloodpack initially challenges Blade's authority, but he quickly establishes dominance through threats and violence: "From now on, we work as a unit. You'll be taking orders from me."

title: Snow Dogs
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as George the pilot yelling at Ted to move it, and Thunder Jack trying to intimidate Ted into selling the dogs cheaply. There are also instances of characters defying authority, like Ted refusing to leave Tolketna despite James's (Thunder Jack's) insistence.

title: We Were Soldiers
justification: The film depicts a clear military hierarchy with characters giving and receiving orders constantly. Examples include: "YOU NEED TO GET A COMPANY OVER TO REINFORCE THE LEFT FLANK" and "SIMPLE ORDERS, HAL. FIND THE ENEMY AND KILL HIM."

title: The Rookie
justification: The coach exerts authority over the team, demanding effort and berating them for quitting. There's also a subtle power play between Jimmy and his father, and Jimmy and his wife, regarding his baseball dreams and family responsibilities. Dialogue like "YOU QUIT OUT THERE. YOU QUIT ON ME, AND WORSE, YOU QUIT ON YOURSELVES" and "I'M NOT GONNA SAY THAT I DO NOT CARE ABOUT TOMORROW'S GAME, 'CAUSE I DO" demonstrates the coach's control.

title: Barbershop
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Mr. Wallace exerts financial power over Calvin, attempting to manipulate him. Eddie, the elder barber, frequently asserts his authority over the younger barbers, criticizing their skills and knowledge.

title: Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron
justification: The film depicts the struggle between humans and the wild horse, Spirit. Humans attempt to capture, tame, and control Spirit, as evidenced by dialogue like "Get him, boys!" and "He's ours now." The Colonel's determination to break Spirit's spirit further emphasizes this theme: "It's time to break that horse."

title: John Q
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power dynamic with one character begging for help from another, addressing him as "Sir" and saying "I beg you." This indicates a significant imbalance of power and a desperate plea for assistance.

title: The Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include "Listen up this minute," "Girls, get yourselves on upstairs now," and "Don't you dare tell her we have it."

title: Insomnia
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between detectives and suspects, with detectives interrogating and controlling the narrative. For example, Dormer pressures Randy, using intimidation and accusations to extract information. Also, Dormer manipulates Ellie, directing her actions and controlling the investigation.

title: Changing Lanes
justification: The film is driven by power struggles. Gavin uses his legal power to manipulate Doyle's life, while Doyle desperately tries to regain control, highlighted by his repeated demands for his 'time back'. The courtroom scenes also showcase the judge's authority and the lawyers' attempts to influence decisions.

title: Stuart Little 2
justification: Several characters give orders or express authority. Examples include the father coaching soccer ("You guys, spread out!"), Snowbell bossing Margalo around ("Get rid of her."), and Falcon threatening Margalo ("Now, get me that ring! Or the mouse is lunch.").

title: Jackass: The Movie
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics. Knoxville directs the stunts and gives instructions ('We're gonna be doing a hell of a lot of work here today. Trust us.'). The rental car employees hold power over Knoxville due to the contract ('Well, you are gonna get stuck with the entire thing.').

title: Catch Me if You Can
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting authority or seeking approval. Examples include John Modiger managing the bank branch, Captain Oliver giving Frank Taylor a 'lift,' and Roger questioning Frank's credentials and intentions towards Brenda.

title: Maid in Manhattan
justification: Several interactions highlight power dynamics. For example, the hotel manager instructs Marisa to end her association with Chris Marshall, demonstrating his authority over her employment. Also, Chris Marshall tells Jerry to get Caroline to go to the benefit, showing his power over Jerry.

title: The Time Machine
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. The professor's condescending attitude toward his colleagues ("They're dinosaurs") and Mrs. Watchit's controlling behavior towards the professor ("Now, go in there and change") demonstrate a struggle for dominance and control.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and manipulating others. Examples include Villefort's control over his father, Dorleac's sadistic treatment of prisoners, and the power struggles between Edmond, Danglars, and Mondego.

title: Unfaithful
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or expressing dominance are present. Examples include Connie's mother telling her son to brush his teeth and lift the seat, and Bill firing Ed. Also, Ed's controlling behavior towards Connie, such as telling her where to stand for a photo, demonstrates a power imbalance.

title: Like Mike
justification: The coach exerts authority over players ('Henderson, you're out. Tracy, you take Henderson's slot.') and Calvin's contract gives Bittleman control over his living situation ('your contract forbids it'). Tracy initially resists mentoring Calvin ('No. No. No. There is no way in the world I'm gonna be roomin' with that kid.') but eventually relents.

title: The Tuxedo
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Devlin ordering Jimmy around ("Get the car.") and Banning controlling his employees through threats and manipulation ("You're helping me out by being a guinea pig").

title: Two Weeks Notice
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of George's dominance over Lucy, from dictating her schedule ('I need you there.') to threatening her job ('or I will fire you'). Lucy's attempts to quit and assert her own boundaries are consistently undermined by George's control and manipulation.

title: Peter Pan: Return to Neverland
justification: Captain Hook constantly gives orders to Smee and his pirate crew (e.g., "Hurry, Smee!"). Jane initially disobeys her mother's wishes and later commands the Lost Boys, showing a shift in her power dynamic: "Lost Boys, fall in!".

title: Big Fat Liar
justification: Marty Wolf constantly asserts his dominance through verbal abuse and control over his employees. Examples include his demeaning remarks to the actor Jaleel White ('Watch yourself, Wolf.') and his dismissive attitude towards his assistant Monty ('Draw a line of chalk around me, baby, because I am dead!'). He also uses his position to exploit and manipulate others, such as stealing Jason's story.

title: Reign of Fire
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, with Quinn often giving orders and being deferred to, such as when he stops Eddie from harvesting unripe crops: "YOU'RE NOT GOING ANYWHERE. GIVE ME THE KEYS." Van Zan's arrival introduces a new power dynamic, with him attempting to assert dominance: "TURN AROUND, VAN ZAN. DON'T BE A FOOL."

title: The Royal Tenenbaums
justification: Royal manipulates situations to his advantage, such as faking an illness to reunite with his family and get money. Chas exerts control over his children, demonstrated by strict rules and training regimens. There are also instances of characters giving orders, such as Ethel telling Royal to sit down.

title: High Crimes
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of military hierarchy ('Yes, sir'), legal maneuvering, and attempts to intimidate or control witnesses. Characters like Colonel Farrell and Major Waldron exert authority, while others like Embry are expected to obey.

title: A Walk to Remember
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Landon is initially portrayed as someone who exerts control over his peers, demonstrated by his disregard for rules and his involvement in pressuring Clay to jump. Later, Principal Kelly uses his authority to impose disciplinary actions on Landon, forcing him to participate in activities he dislikes.

title: Orange County
justification: Several scenes depict authority figures exerting control, such as the principal dictating the terms of the fundraiser and the father attempting to control Shaun's career path. There are also instances of characters trying to manipulate or influence others, like Tanya leveraging her grandfather's position at Stanford.

title: Windtalkers
justification: The film depicts a clear military hierarchy with characters giving and receiving orders. Examples include: "Get up, marine! Hold the goddamn position!" and "Enders, we didn't pick your name out of a hat. We need good marines. That's why you're standing here."

title: About a Boy
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Marcus manipulates Will into a relationship with his mother, saying, "I won't tell anyone you don't have a kid if you go out with my mum." Later, Ali threatens Marcus, demonstrating a struggle for dominance among the children.

title: Gosford Park
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and expectations based on social standing. Examples include "Her Ladyship asked if you would join her...", "I need all the knives there", and "You have your hands in your pockets."

title: The Master of Disguise
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Examples include: "PUT A CLAMP ON YOUR PASTRY HOLE," "I'M BEGGING YOU, CURB YOUR YAMMERING SKULL CAVE," and "THIS IS WHAT I WANT YOU TO DO."

title: I Am Sam
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in professional and personal relationships. For example, Patricia is constantly ordered around by her boss, and Sam is often talked down to and underestimated due to his intellectual disability. There are also power struggles in the courtroom scenes.

title: Blue Crush
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the hotel scenes where Anne Marie is fired for 'scolding' a VIP customer. There are also instances of dominance in personal relationships, such as when Eden pressures Anne Marie about the surf contest and her personal life: 'You're not a quitter. You're just scared.'

title: Collateral Damage
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as "Get your ass over here and steady that ladder!" and "ETA on those units! Get Gilly, Perry, Copeland up here now." The agent in charge demands "paperwork in 10 minutes," illustrating a clear hierarchy.

title: Resident Evil
justification: Characters frequently give orders ('Get the computers covered! Move it!'), and there are clear hierarchical structures within the Umbrella Corporation ('All Umbrella staff must wear their identity tags...at all times.'). The Red Queen also exerts control, sealing the Hive and killing everyone.

title: Enough
justification: The dialogue contains instances of dominance and control, such as the aggressive house purchase offer ('Sure you are. That's the price.') and Mitch's controlling behavior in his marriage ('I make the money here, so I set the rules, right? It's my rules.'). Slim's struggle to escape Mitch's control and protect her daughter further emphasizes the power dynamics at play.

title: Drumline
justification: The dialogue is filled with hierarchical commands and challenges to authority. Examples include the constant giving of orders ('Give me 30 push-ups. Make it 32.') and the intense competition for status within the drumline ('I own the drumline. You wanna get down, you come through me.').

title: Undercover Brother
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include the Chief berating Undercover Brother ("Where the hell have you been?! This is a job, not some kind of damn summer camp!") and The Man issuing commands to Feather ("And they won't be a problem, will they, Feather? No, sir. Good.").

title: Showtime
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include the police chief ordering Mitch to do the show, Chase Renzi directing the detectives, and the detectives trying to assert authority over criminals and each other. The struggle for control is a constant theme.

title: 40 Days and 40 Nights
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in the workplace, with Matt's boss assigning him tasks and expressing dissatisfaction with his performance ('You are way ahead of schedule. If I were you, I'd give me something else to do, quick.'). There's also a betting pool centered around Matt's vow of celibacy, indicating a power dynamic where others are trying to control or influence his behavior.

title: Crossroads
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. For example, Lucy's father commands her to return home, and Ben initially refuses to let anyone else drive his car. There are also instances of characters manipulating or pressuring each other, such as when Kit tries to convince Lucy to stay on the trip.

title: Clockstoppers
justification: The father-son relationship is fraught with power struggles, as the father tries to control the son's choices ('Now, I want you to do your homework on this, Zak.'). Gates exerts authority over Dopler ('I want this fixed in 48 hours!'). The NSA's demands on Gates also highlight a clear power dynamic ('We're taking it whether you're ready or not.')

title: The Mothman Prophecies
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Cy telling John what to do, and Brian showing the house and pressuring the couple to buy it. There is also the dynamic between the police and John, where the police have authority.

title: K-19: The Widowmaker
justification: The captain constantly gives orders and demands obedience ('Report to the reactor control room. Yes, sir.'). There are frequent challenges to authority ('You're still the captain, as far as we're concerned.'). The crew's fate rests on the captain's decisions, highlighting his absolute power.

title: Gangs of New York
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and jockeying for status. Examples include Bill Cutting's control over the Five Points, his interactions with Amsterdam, and the constant threats and displays of violence to maintain order. The film depicts a society where power is enforced through fear and intimidation.

title: In the Bedroom
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Richard tries to intimidate Nat, Frank's mother tries to control his relationship, and Matt's boss seems to hold power over him. Dialogue like "No, you have to leave now" and "Come fall, you're on a plane" demonstrates this.

title: Treasure Planet
justification: Captain Amelia constantly gives orders and expects obedience, establishing a clear hierarchy. Silver manipulates Jim with false kindness, then threatens him to get the map back, showing his dominance. Scroop's insubordination is met with threats of punishment, reinforcing the captain's authority.

title: Monster's Ball
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance. Buck's racist remarks and demands for Sonny to relay orders highlight racial and familial power. Hank's outburst at Phil, asserting his authority as a superior officer, and the constant giving and taking of orders in the prison scenes further exemplify this theme.

title: Queen of the Damned
justification: Lestat frequently asserts his dominance, referring to his band as "my friends, my children, my band" and declaring himself a "new god." He gives orders to Roger ("Do you want me to take the girls home later?") and Akasha demands obedience ("You will address my king first.").

title: The Banger Sisters
justification: Lavinia exerts control over her daughters, demanding obedience and setting rules. Suzette and Lavinia's interactions are filled with power plays, from Lavinia offering money to Suzette to leave, to Suzette exposing Lavinia's past. Harry is manipulated by both women.

title: Halloween: Resurrection
justification: Several characters give orders or try to exert control. Freddie attempts to control the narrative and the participants' actions, saying, "Y'all need to do me a favor, all right? Go along with this shit. Don't blow it. Not now." Harris also tries to control the situation, directing Charley: "Take your ass in the back of the garage with Nora."

title: Bad Company
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Oakes directing Parish and McCain ('Parish, McCain, cover the exits. We need him alive. Yes, sir.') and the general tone of authority when dealing with Jake ('Don't be dramatic. He's got plenty of protection. I'll tell you when to pull him.').

title: Dragonfly
justification: Several characters exert authority: Joe's boss orders him to take time off, demonstrating professional hierarchy. Later, Joe demands information and access at the hospital, reflecting his position as a doctor. The dialogue between doctors in the operating room also shows a clear chain of command.

title: Space Station
justification: There are some instances of command and control, particularly between ground control and the astronauts ('Roger, I see you.'). Also, there are instances of astronauts directing each other ('Let's get some tethers on.'). However, the dialogue is mostly collaborative and focused on problem-solving.

title: Ghost Ship
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters give orders and assert authority. Examples include Murphy's repeated commands to Epps ('Get back here!') and his crew ('Come on! You heard the man!'). The negotiation over the finder's fee also highlights a power struggle, with Murphy dictating the terms.

title: The New Guy
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to assert dominance, give orders, and establish their status. Examples include Luther teaching Dizzy how to fight and act tough ('Man, I'm gonna take you from bitch...to bull.') and Conner Maguire's bullying behavior ('Wrong level, bitch.').

title: Swimfan
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the coach dictating Ben's training regimen ('For the next 8 days, I want you living in that pool') and Ben's mother telling him to see Mr. Tillman ('Better get started with Mr. Tillman. He's been asking for you.'). Madison also attempts to control Ben through manipulation and threats ('Tell me you love me.').

title: Analyze That
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and jockeying for position. Examples include Patti LoPresti's control over her crew, Paul Vitti's attempts to maintain authority, and the constant threats and intimidation between rival factions.

title: Kate and Leopold
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. J.J. exerts control over Kate at work, demonstrated by his comments on her performance and the dinner invitation. Leopold's old-fashioned manners, like standing when a lady leaves the table, also indicate a hierarchical understanding of social interactions.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, particularly between Barbossa and his crew ("You will speak when spoken to!") and Norrington giving orders to his men ("Return fire!"). Elizabeth attempts to negotiate with Barbossa, but he constantly asserts his dominance.

title: The Matrix Reloaded
justification: Several characters give orders or express authority. Examples include: "Let's go, kid," "Out the door! Both of you, march!", and Commander Lock's interactions with the Council, demonstrating a clear hierarchy and chain of command.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, oaths of service, and characters vying for authority. Examples include Denethor's control over Gondor, Gandalf's influence, and Aragorn's claim to kingship, as well as the power struggles between Frodo, Sam, and Gollum.

title: Bruce Almighty
justification: The newsroom environment is highly competitive, with individuals vying for recognition and advancement. Jack, the boss, clearly holds authority, making decisions about which stories to air and manipulating Bruce's career. Bruce's desperation for the anchor position and his subsequent outburst on live television highlight the power imbalances and the struggle for status.

title: X2: X-Men United
justification: Several characters exert authority, give orders, and challenge each other's status. Examples include Stryker's control over his subordinates ("Seal the room. Shoot it.") and Magneto's manipulation of Pyro ("You are a god among insects. Never let anyone tell you different."). There are also instances of direct conflict and dominance displays, such as the initial confrontation in the food court.

title: Chicago
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control and status. Mama Morton controls access and information ('all the calls have gotta go through me'), while Billy Flynn dictates the narrative and demands payment ('You call me when you got $5,000'). Roxie and Velma compete for attention and dominance in the jail and media.

title: Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines
justification: Several characters give orders and assert authority. Examples include the police officer demanding license and registration, the Terminator giving commands like "Take off your clothes," and General Brewster directing military personnel. The T-X also exerts control by manipulating other machines.

title: Bad Boys II
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats and insults. Examples include: "Talk polite in front of my little bonbon...or I'm gonna chop your balls off," and "You're in my country, though. Fuck you, how's that?"

title: The Matrix Revolutions
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the Merovingian who states, "Down here, I make the rules. Down here, I make the threats. Down here, I'm God." Also, Captain Mifune gives orders to his crew, demonstrating a clear hierarchy.

title: Anger Management
justification: Dr. Rydell exerts control over Dave through therapy mandates, dictating his actions and manipulating situations. Examples include forcing Dave to confront his childhood bully and orchestrating the encounter with Kendra. Dave initially resists but gradually complies, highlighting the power imbalance.

title: Bringing Down the House
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance and others submitting. Examples include Peter ordering Charlene to act as the nanny, Charlene's interactions with Mrs. Arness, and various characters giving orders or making demands of others, such as the constant need to control Charlene.

title: Hulk
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, giving orders, and asserting dominance. Examples include General Ross's control over the military and his daughter, Glen's attempts to recruit Bruce, and David Banner's manipulation of Bruce.

title: 2 Fast 2 Furious
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, with Carter Verone at the top, giving orders and expecting obedience. Examples include his treatment of Detective Whitworth ('I've got one last job for you') and his instructions to Brian and Roman ('Just put it in the car, drive it to me...and don't let anybody stop you'). The FBI also exerts authority over Brian and Roman, forcing them to cooperate or face legal consequences ('We can make this all go away in the interest of justice...if you're willing to play ball').

title: Seabiscuit
justification: Several scenes involve jockey rivalries and dominance on the track, such as the intentional fouling during a race. The dialogue also shows the power dynamic between the horse owners/trainers and the jockeys, with the owners ultimately making the decisions ('Red Pollard will remain Seabiscuit's jockey, now and forever.').

title: S.W.A.T.
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and displays of authority. Examples include: "Let me get your M-4," "Shooters, on the line! Stand by! Ready! Put them on safe and holster," and "That's why you're the marksman and I'm the guy who tells you who to shoot."

title: Spy Kids 3-D: Game Over
justification: Several characters exert authority: The President orders Juni to rejoin the OSS, Donnagon is shown to be controlled by Mrs. Giggles, and the Toymaker seeks to enslave the world's youth. Juni is given orders throughout the game to shut it down and not release the Toymaker.

title: Freaky Friday
justification: The mother-daughter relationship is fraught with power struggles, evident in lines like "Because I said so" and "No, you're not!" The mother attempts to exert control over Anna's life, while Anna rebels, creating a constant battle for autonomy.

title: Scary Movie 3
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or expressing dominance. For example, Brenda tells Cindy, "Pay my way, okay?" and the rap battle is inherently a competition for status and dominance.

title: The Italian Job
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. For example, Charlie directs the team, and Steve Frazelli asserts his authority over others, such as when he confronts Stella and his henchman.

title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
justification: Ben and Andie's relationship is a constant push and pull for control. Andie manipulates Ben to write her article, while Ben tries to maintain control by setting boundaries, like when he says, "You can't name my member Princess Sophia."

title: American Wedding
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Stifler frequently gives orders and insults others, while Jim's father attempts to offer guidance and advice, indicating a generational power dynamic. Michelle's parents also evaluate Jim's suitability as a husband, showcasing their authority.

title: Daddy Day Care
justification: The adults are clearly in charge of the children, giving instructions and setting rules. Examples include 'Get your shoes off the couch!' and 'Stop climbing the drapes.' There's also a power dynamic between the day care owners and the child services inspector.

title: Daredevil
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Fisk's control over Wesley, Daredevil's vigilante justice, and the power dynamics within the courtroom.

title: Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Charlie giving missions to the Angels, the Angels giving commands to Bosley, and the villainous Madison Lee declaring she doesn't take orders from a 'speaker box anymore'.

title: Dr. Seuss’ The Cat in the Hat
justification: The Cat in the Hat exerts control over the children, dictating activities and disregarding their mother's rules. Sally's initial obedience contrasts with Conrad's rule-breaking, creating a dynamic where the Cat exploits these differences.  The Fish character constantly tries to exert authority and control over the situation, but is ignored.

title: Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in the workplace, with Grace, the chief of staff, often asserting her authority over Elle and other staff members. For example, Grace sarcastically dismisses Elle's wedding plans and tells Reena to alphabetize, highlighting her position of power.

title: Brother Bear
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between the older and younger brothers, with the older brothers giving orders and teasing Kenai. Examples include "Get down! Get down!" and "Hey, I said knock it off." There's also a power dynamic between Kenai and the bear he hunts, and later, between Kenai and Koda, where Kenai initially tries to assert dominance.

title: Freddy vs. Jason
justification: Several characters give orders or express dominance. Freddy controls Jason, saying "You disobeyed me." The sheriff barks orders at Stubbs: "Contain the son of a bitch before he spreads any further."

title: Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World
justification: The film is replete with examples of naval hierarchy. Officers give orders ('KILLICK, AN EXTRA RATION OF RUM FOR THESE MEN') and expect immediate obedience ('AYE, SIR'). There are also instances of insubordination and the consequences thereof ('MASTER-AT-ARMS, TAKE THAT MAN BELOW AND CLAP HIM IN IRONS').

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as the sheriff who abuses his power and intimidates the group. Dialogue like "Get on your faces, all 3 of you! Get on the ground!" and "Take the gun and show me how she did it." demonstrates this. Also, the Hewitt family displays a clear hierarchy, with the grandmother giving orders and Leatherface obeying.

title: School of Rock
justification: The dialogue includes direct commands like "Turn this up! Now!" and "Step off! Step off!" indicating a clear power dynamic. The lyrics "You think you can kick me out of the band? Well, there's just one problem there, the band is mine" also highlight a struggle for control.

title: The Last Samurai
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between the Emperor and his advisors, as well as the military structure with officers giving orders to soldiers. Algren is hired to train the Japanese army, establishing a power dynamic where he instructs and they obey. There are also power struggles, such as Omura's manipulation of the Emperor and Algren's defiance of Bagley's orders.

title: Old School
justification: The Dean's dialogue demonstrates authority, as he informs the house occupants they have a week to vacate. Mitch's interactions with his father also show a power dynamic, as his father pressures him about work and his personal life. The fraternity initiation scene, with orders and tests, highlights a clear hierarchy.

title: Kill Bill: Volume 1
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, commands, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "What you gonna do now, huh?! What you got?! I got your ass!", "I'm not going to murder you in front of your child, okay?", and "The price you pay...for bringing up either my Chinese or American heritage as a negative is: I collect your fucking head."

title: The Haunted Mansion
justification: Ramsley exerts control through orders ('Carry on.') and manipulation, while Gracey's status dictates the Evers' actions ('Master Gracey wishes to discuss his affairs over dinner.'). Sara and Jim's marital conflict also reveals a power struggle, with Jim prioritizing work and Sara feeling neglected.

title: Holes
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance and others submitting. Examples include the Warden's control over the boys, Mr. Sir's abuse of authority, and the social hierarchy among the boys themselves, with bullying and the establishment of 'Caveman' as a new pecking order.

title: Kangaroo Jack
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. For example, Frankie instructs Louis and Charlie on their mission, emphasizing obedience: "You will not look in that envelope under any circumstances, understood?" Later, Mr. Smith threatens violence if they don't return his package.

title: The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for control and dominance. M (Moriarty) controls scientists by holding their families hostage, and characters like Quatermain and Nemo exert authority within the League. Dialogue such as "Kill any who resist" and "My underlings call me sir. My superiors call me M." highlights the hierarchical power structures.

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life
justification: The film features several characters vying for power and control. Reiss commands his subordinates, Chen Lo attempts to control Lara, and Lara asserts her authority over Terry. Examples include Reiss ordering Chen Lo to bring him the orb and Lara telling Terry, "You need to take me to the Shay Ling."

title: Something's Gotta Give
justification: There are several instances of power dynamics at play. Harry's assistants cater to his every need, and Erica initially resists his attempts to charm her, setting up a power struggle. Later, Erica dictates terms to Harry, such as forbidding him from smoking in her house.

title: About Schmidt
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence. Warren tries to dissuade Jeannie from marrying Randall, saying, "I think you should consider postponing it." Saundra's overbearing personality and control over Randall are evident when she says, "Randall, bring that into the kitchen."

title: Shanghai Knights
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and jockeying for position. Examples include Rathbone's manipulation of Wu Chow, Roy's attempts to control Chon, and the general hierarchical structure of British society as portrayed.

title: Open Range
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance and control. Baxter's men are giving orders and enforcing Baxter's will, while Boss and Charley are constantly strategizing about how to maintain control of their herd and their lives in the face of this threat. The marshal is also trying to assert his authority.

title: Gothika
justification: The film depicts power dynamics through professional hierarchies (doctors vs. patients, doctors vs. other doctors, law enforcement vs. suspects) and the abuse of authority. Examples include the psychiatrist's control over Miranda's treatment and the sheriff's interrogation tactics, as well as the sexual abuse and manipulation of women.

title: Love Actually
justification: The Prime Minister's interactions with the US President show a clear power struggle, culminating in the PM's defiant stance. Also, the PM's staff member is being reassigned based on his whim, indicating his authority. The school bully scene also shows power dynamics.

title: Once Upon a Time in Mexico
justification: Characters are constantly giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Sands directing EI to kill Marquez, and the President commanding his forces. The dialogue is filled with threats and displays of authority, such as the cartel members' interactions and Sands' manipulation of others.

title: Just Married
justification: The father's disapproval and financial control over Sarah and Tom creates tension. Examples include: "Park at service entrance!" and "I expect you to pay me back in full just as soon as that silly-ass radio show of yours yields any kind of reasonable income."

title: Cheaper by the Dozen
justification: The parents, especially the father, exert authority through commands like "Gunner, to the car!" and "Everybody out." There are also instances of children challenging or negotiating parental decisions, such as Charlie's initial resistance to moving and the kids' later rebellion against being grounded.

title: Mystic River
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the police detectives questioning suspects and Jimmy Markum's controlling behavior towards his daughter's relationships. Examples include: "We'll get the guy, sir." and "Eve, just tell them what they want to know."

title: The Recruit
justification: The dialogue is filled with instructors giving orders and trainees following them. Examples include Slayne and Burke instructing the trainees, and the constant testing and evaluation of the trainees' skills, such as in the lie detector scene and the surveillance exercise. Burke's manipulation of James and Layla also highlights the power dynamics at play.

title: Identity
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a struggle for control. Examples include Suzanne's abusive directions to the driver and Rhodes's attempts to control the situation at the motel, 'Everybody just stay here. Stay in this room.'

title: Underworld
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, betrayals, and characters vying for control. Viktor's dominance is evident in his orders and the fear he inspires, while Kraven's ambition leads him to manipulate events for his own gain. Selene's defiance and eventual confrontation with Viktor highlight a struggle against established authority.

title: Radio
justification: Several scenes depict Coach Jones asserting his authority, such as when he confronts Johnny Clay about his behavior and benches him despite the importance of the game. The school board also exerts its power, questioning Jones's judgment and considering removing Radio from the school.

title: Bad Santa
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance through insults, threats, and explicit commands. Examples include Santa's constant berating of the child and the store manager's abusive treatment of the shoplifter. The power struggles are also evident in the negotiations between Willie and the detective.

title: Runaway Jury
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people trying to exert control over others. Examples include the jury foreman election, where people vie for the position, and Fitch's attempts to manipulate the jury through intimidation and bribery. The lawyers also try to control the narrative and influence the jury's decision.

title: The Jungle Book 2
justification: The village elder confines Mowgli to his room as punishment, demonstrating authority. Shere Khan's threats and pursuit of Mowgli highlight a predator-prey dynamic, where he asserts dominance through fear. Hathi commands the elephant patrol, giving orders and expecting obedience.

title: The Rundown
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include Billy's control over his employees ('It is gonna be 10 off your vig') and Hatcher's exploitation of the miners ('That'll cost you $10,000'). Beck also uses threats and ultimatums to get what he wants ('Option A, you give me the ring. Option B, I make you give me the ring').

title: Final Destination 2
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Kimberly and her father, who gives her instructions and expresses concern over her safety. The police officer also exerts authority, questioning and directing the group after the accident. There are also instances of characters giving orders to each other, such as when the driver tells others to put out the weed.

title: Phone Booth
justification: The entire plot revolves around a sniper exerting complete control over Stu through threats and manipulation. Dialogue like "Stu, if you hang up, I will kill you" and "Just say the word, Stu" demonstrates the sniper's dominance. Stu's desperate attempts to regain control, such as offering money and pleading, further highlight the power imbalance.

title: 28 Days Later…
justification: The dialogue contains minimal power dynamics. There is a brief mention of being a 'creative executive' which implies some level of authority. However, the primary focus is on creativity, collaboration, and guest experience.

title: Tears of the Sun
justification: The film is filled with characters giving and receiving orders, often in high-stakes situations. Examples include the Captain directing Lt. Waters' mission ('Priority tasking. We need to extract a critical personality ASAP.') and Lt. Waters' interactions with Dr. Kendricks, where he initially tries to impose his orders ('I need you to get your things packed, and let's get out of here now.') but eventually concedes to her demands.

title: Under the Tuscan Sun
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Patti's somewhat controlling behavior towards Frances, offering unsolicited advice and pushing her to take the Tuscany trip. Also, the contessa's manipulation of the house price based on perceived wealth and desperation shows a power play.

title: Out of Time
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others through direct commands or manipulation. Examples include Chris's aggressive interrogation of Ann, Chief Whitlock's interactions with his subordinates, and the DEA agent's demanding tone with Whitlock.

title: Mona Lisa Smile
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of authority and control. For example, a character is told "Amanda needs to start minding her p's and q's" and another is told "You'll need to-- Whatever you do...don't put the boss's wife next to your husband."

title: Head of State
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include: "Just do what we say," and "If the party needs to get started, l'll handle it." Also, Debra's control over Mays' campaign and speeches indicates a power imbalance.

title: Good Boy!
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and status seeking. For example, the Greater Dane demands obedience and expresses disappointment in the Earth dogs' lack of dominance, and characters like Baker exert control over their dogs and others.

title: Uptown Girls
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Ray frequently gives orders and criticizes Molly's actions ('Shoes!', 'You missed a spot.'). Molly also tries to control Ray ('Take it back.').

title: Matchstick Men
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Roy manipulates Angela into participating in his cons, and Frank gives Roy orders related to their criminal activities. Roy also attempts to control Angela's behavior, telling her what to do and how to act.

title: National Security
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy within the police force, with detectives and lieutenants giving orders to officers. There are also scenes of dominance and control, such as when Hank, as a security guard, confronts Lola and attempts to exert his authority over her. The courtroom scenes also highlight the power of the judge and the legal system.

title: What a Girl Wants
justification: Several characters, especially Glynnis and Clarissa, try to control Henry's actions and Daphne's behavior to protect Henry's political career and their social standing. Examples include Glynnis dictating how to handle the press and Clarissa attempting to intimidate Daphne. Henry himself exerts authority, albeit sometimes awkwardly, as he tries to manage Daphne's integration into his life.

title: Jeepers Creepers II
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the initial instructions given to Billy and Jacky, the coach's commands to the basketball team, and Scotty's attempts to control the situation on the bus, culminating in his divisive actions and power plays.

title: Cradle 2 the Grave
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include: "Get this train out of here. You got it." and "Wait to hear from me." Also, there are scenes of torture and interrogation to get information.

title: Malibu's Most Wanted
justification: Characters are constantly trying to assert dominance, whether through threats ('Give me your ride, or I'm a dust your ass, beyotch!'), insults ('Your mama so fat...'), or displays of supposed street credibility. B-Rad's attempts to emulate gang culture and gain respect also highlight a struggle for status.

title: The Hunted
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the military and law enforcement, with characters giving and receiving orders (e.g., "Move!", "Copy that.", "We are to identify and neutralize him."). There's also a power struggle between the protagonist and antagonist, demonstrated through their dialogue and actions, as well as the government's attempts to control and eliminate Hallam.

title: Bend it Like Beckham
justification: The mother and father exert strong control over Jess, dictating her future and forbidding her from playing football: "I don't want you running around half naked in front of men." Jess is constantly trying to negotiate her desires against their traditional expectations, creating a power struggle.

title: Darkness Falls
justification: The townspeople's actions against Matilda, including hanging her and tearing off her mask, demonstrate a clear power imbalance and abuse of authority. Later, the police detective's aggressive interrogation of Kyle, marked by disbelief and accusations, highlights a power dynamic where law enforcement exerts control and suspicion.

title: The Pianist
justification: The subtitles contain numerous examples of power dynamics, particularly between Jews and Germans, and within the Jewish community itself. Examples include the enforcement of discriminatory decrees ("You're forbidden to walk on the pavement. Walk in the gutter!") and the exploitation of power within the Jewish police force ("Oh! More Jewish police! You mean you want me to beat up Jews with my truncheon and catch the Gestapo spirit.").

title: The Core
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include: "Major Childs, they're ready for you," and "All right. Get this ship in the ground. Now."

title: Lost in Translation
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. The director's demanding instructions during the Suntory commercial shoot, and the hotel staff's subservient behavior towards Mr. Harris, demonstrate clear hierarchical relationships.
