Also, the masseuse scene shows an attempt to exert control and dominance.

title: The Fighting Temptations
justification: Several instances of characters asserting authority or challenging it are present. For example, Darrin attempts to take control of the choir, and Paulina frequently challenges his decisions and asserts her own authority within the church. The dialogue also shows Dean's possessiveness and attempts to control Lilly.

title: Hollywood Homicide
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and jockeying for position. Examples include the lieutenant berating the detective trainee ('Don't call me sir. I work for a living.') and the detectives interrogating suspects ('Just sit down there and shut up.').

title: Cold Mountain
justification: The Home Guard asserts authority, demanding information and compliance: "Get back there!" and "We think you've got 'em hid up somewhere." Captain Teague's presence and interrogation also highlight the power imbalance and the threat of violence.

title: Johnny English
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within MI7, with Johnny English receiving orders from Pegasus. Sauvage's plan to become King and control England also highlights a strong desire for power. Dialogue such as "Now, English, I want you at the Tower tonight, monitoring this unveiling" and "The Queen has more power in her tiny white gloves than any other head of state" demonstrates the importance of authority and control.

title: Honey
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Michael directs Honey's career, demonstrated by dialogue like, "I thought I was making him look good, but, you know." B.B. exerts control through threats, stating, "So you tell him I'm looking for him."

title: Stuck On You
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Morty O'Reilly demands a $200 up-front service fee, establishing his control over aspiring actors. Cher asserts her authority on set, berating Howard and ultimately hiring Walt over his objections.

title: Basic
justification: The entire narrative revolves around Sergeant West's abuse of power and the recruits' struggle against his authority. Dialogue like "Pike, surrender your sidearm for inspection" and West's constant berating and humiliation of Pike exemplify this dynamic. The recruits are forced to obey West's orders, even when they are illogical or dangerous, highlighting the extreme power imbalance.

title: Shrek 2
justification: The dialogue contains instances of command and obedience, such as "All right, hit it!" and "Hey, waiter! How about a bowl for the steed?" There are also power struggles between Shrek and Fiona's father, with the father disapproving of Shrek's 'type' and trying to control Fiona's choice of partner.

title: Spider-Man 2
justification: Several characters exert authority: Harry over Peter and Otto, Aunt May over Peter, and Mr. Ditkovitch over Peter regarding rent. Doc Ock's control over his arms and his demands for tritium also highlight power struggles.

title: The Passion of the Christ
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, requests for help, and assertions of authority. Examples include Jesus's disciples calling him 'Master' and asking if they should flee, the High Priest interrogating Jesus and demanding answers, and Pilate asserting his power to crucify or free Jesus.

title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Snape deducting points from Gryffindor and Malfoy ordering his cronies around. Dumbledore and other professors also give instructions and enforce rules, demonstrating their positions of authority. Hagrid's lesson on hippogriffs emphasizes the importance of respecting the creature's pride and avoiding insults, highlighting a power dynamic between humans and magical creatures.

title: The Incredibles
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting authority, giving orders, and challenging each other's decisions. Examples include Helen directing the children, Bob's interactions with Mr. Huph, and Syndrome's controlling behavior towards Mirage and Mr. Incredible. The family dynamic also showcases power struggles, especially between parents and children.

title: The Day After Tomorrow
justification: Several scenes depict authority figures giving orders, such as the president and scientists. For example, the president gives the order for the National Guard to evacuate the southern states. Also, Jack is constantly trying to convince authorities to listen to his warnings.

title: The Bourne Supremacy
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and commands, especially within the CIA and Treadstone. Examples include "This is not a drill, soldier," "Get some men in there right now," and "Find Jason Bourne," indicating a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Shark Tale
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to exert control over others. Sykes demands money with threats, Don Lino commands his sons and enforces strict rules, and Oscar initially embraces the 'Sharkslayer' persona for fame and status.

title: The Polar Express
justification: The conductor exerts authority over the children, enforcing rules and schedules: "In case you didn't know, that cord is for emergency purposes only." Santa Claus is presented as the ultimate authority figure, deciding who receives the first gift of Christmas and embodying the spirit of the holiday.

title: National Treasure
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, such as Ben telling Riley what to do during the heist: "You want to go around to the front and present your invitation." The FBI agent also exerts authority, directing subordinates: "Get positive IDs. Search everyone, including the security staff."

title: I, Robot
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, particularly between humans and robots. Examples include 'Deactivate!' and 'Command confirmed,' showcasing a clear hierarchy. The robots' programmed obedience and the humans' attempts to control them highlight the struggle for dominance.

title: Troy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and maneuvering for control. Agamemnon demands allegiance from other kings ('I want all the kings of Greece and their armies.') and Achilles's mother warns him about the choice between glory and a peaceful life ('If you go to Troy...glory will be yours.').

title: Meet the Fockers
justification: Jack's controlling behavior is evident in lines like "Don't drink. I wanna make a toast. Now." and his surveillance activities. Bernie's attempts to dominate the conversation and Roz's attempts to control Bernie also contribute to the power dynamics.

title: 50 First Dates
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Examples include the father telling Keanu "Not now" and later ordering Doug to "Try not to sweat in the sauce." Also, Henry manipulates tourists with non-alcoholic drinks to "loosen up" for sex.

title: Van Helsing
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Dracula commanding his brides and Igor, Van Helsing directing Carl, and various characters threatening each other with violence to achieve their goals: 'Burn it! Burn it down!' 'My superiors would like for me to take you alive...' 'I'm here to help you. I don't need any help.'

title: Fahrenheit 9/11
justification: The dialogue shows Bush directing officials to find a link between Iraq and 9/11, demonstrating his authority. Rumsfeld's dismissive attitude towards bombing Afghanistan in favor of Iraq also highlights a power dynamic. The narrative also shows the Bush administration's control over the media and the American people through fear-mongering.

title: Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to assert dominance over others. Mr. Goodman tries to establish himself as Kate's boss, and later fires her to manipulate her into dating him. Patches O'Houlihan uses harsh training methods and demeaning language to assert his authority as coach.

title: The Village
justification: The community is run by elders who make decisions for everyone, such as whether Lucius can go to the towns.  There is also a clear hierarchy within families, as seen when Kitty asks her father for permission to marry.  The elders also use fear and manipulation to maintain control, such as fabricating stories about creatures in the woods.

title: The Grudge
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Alex instructing Karen on her care duties ('Just make sure she has what she needs and help out around the house') and Matthew telling Jennifer what to do ('Maybe you should say something to the helper').

title: Ocean's Twelve
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and asserting dominance. Examples include Danny's management of the heist team, the Night Fox's manipulation of Ocean, and the detectives' attempts to control the investigation.

title: Collateral
justification: The dialogue is dominated by Vincent's control over Max. Vincent gives constant orders like "Pop the trunk," "Get in the fucking car," and threatens Max's mother to ensure compliance, highlighting a stark power imbalance. Max is forced to obey due to fear and intimidation.

title: The Princess Diaries 2: Royal Engagement
justification: The Queen gives orders to Joseph, her head of security, and others. Mia is constantly being told what a princess should and shouldn't do. There are also power struggles between Nicholas and Mia for control of the throne.

title: Starsky & Hutch
justification: Several scenes show characters trying to assert dominance. Starsky and Hutch often use their authority as police officers to intimidate or manipulate people, such as when questioning Heather or Big Earl. The captain also holds power over Starsky and Hutch, suspending them from duty.

title: Along Came Polly
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Sandy giving Reuben unsolicited advice on how to behave with women, including the 'Hey, I'm your daddy' line. Leland also tries to manipulate Reuben into giving him insurance. However, these moments are not pervasive.

title: Mean Girls
justification: Regina exerts control over her friends, dictating their actions and appearance ('You can't sit with us!'). Cady and her friends plot to overthrow Regina's power by cutting off her resources and manipulating her relationships ('Regina George is an evil dictator. Now, how do you overthrow a dictator?'). The Plastics enforce strict social rules and hierarchies.

title: Lemony Snicket’s A Series of Unfortunate Events
justification: Count Olaf constantly orders the children around and threatens them. He manipulates adults like Mr. Poe and Aunt Josephine to gain control over the Baudelaire orphans and their fortune, highlighted by lines like, "All I ask in return is that you do every thing that pops into my head." and his manipulation of Josephine to write a false will.

title: Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed
justification: Fred often takes charge, giving orders like "Shaggy, use the ropes to tie him up!" and "Come on, gang. Let's get to the lab." There's also a clear hierarchy within the gang, with Fred often making decisions and the others following.

title: Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics. Mr. Harken asserts his authority over Miss Corningstone, assigning her stories and dismissing her journalistic aspirations: "Miss Corningstone, ma'am, you will do the stories to which you are assigned." Ron also tries to assert dominance over Veronica, but she challenges him.

title: SpongeBob SquarePants
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control and status. Plankton's constant attempts to steal the Krabby Patty formula and rule the world, Neptune's absolute authority and quickness to punish, and Krabs's hierarchical management style all contribute to this theme. Examples include: "Then everyone will eat at the Chum Bucket, and I will rule the world!" and "I am the king. I must enforce the laws of the sea."

title: The Notebook
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Allie's parents exert control over her relationships, demonstrated by their disapproval of Noah and attempts to dictate her future. Noah also displays dominance in his interactions with Allie, such as when he pressures her to jump into the water and say she's a bird.

title: Sex, Lies, and Videotape
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. John frequently gives orders to his secretary Janet ('Reschedule Kirkland...Family crisis.'). Cynthia manipulates John ('Then get those balls in the air and get your butt over here.').

title: Next of Kin
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Lenny, grab him," and "You do your job and I'll do mine."

title: Men At Work
justification: Several characters exert authority: Jack tells his campaign manager what to do, the police officer intimidates the garbage men, and Maxwell Potterdam orders his henchmen around. Examples include: "If you like 'em, use 'em. I trust your judgment." and "I've got my eye on you both."

title: Q & A
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include the Lieutenant's abusive interrogation of Sophia/Sylvester ('Don't you come in my hand, you cocksucker, or l'll rip it off') and Mike Brennan's racist rant where he declares himself 'the baddest motherfucker on the block'. There are also power struggles within the police force and between criminals, with constant jockeying for position and control.

title: Henry & June
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as June manipulating Henry's book deal and Henry's often demeaning and demanding behavior towards Anaïs. The dialogue includes instances of dominance, manipulation, and attempts to assert authority, like June saying "I'll get it published. The right way. Just like I always have." and Henry telling Anaïs "I'm going to demand everything of you."

title: Sleeping with the Enemy
justification: Several characters exert authority: Len manages his community with a mix of sweat and 'tricks', while Sam attempts to control the narrative and influence decisions. Charles, as a leader, sets rules and rebukes those who challenge his authority, as seen when he tells the newcomers, 'Look, we'll feed and board you, all right? But don't push it, that's all.'

title: School Ties
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between students and teachers, as well as between social classes. Cleary asserts his authority as housemaster by demanding the music be turned off, and Gierasch uses a sink-or-swim teaching style. There are also instances of social dominance, such as Dillon's family connections and the pressure on McGivern to attend Princeton.

title: Whispers in the Dark
justification: The dialogue between the psychiatrist and her patient, Eve, reveals a power imbalance. Eve's provocative behavior and statements like "May I get undressed?" and "I fantasized that I would masturbate in front of you" challenge the traditional doctor-patient dynamic, suggesting a struggle for control or influence within the therapeutic relationship.

title: Sommersby
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of men asserting dominance, particularly Jack. Examples include his interactions with Orin ('You calling me a nigger?') and his attempts to control Laurel ('Did he kiss you?'). The scene with the Knights of the White Camellia also highlights racial power dynamics.

title: Hard Target
justification: The film revolves around a clandestine organization that hunts homeless veterans for sport, highlighting a stark power imbalance. Dialogue such as "It has always been the privilege of the few to hunt the many" and the constant giving of orders ("Finish him!") underscores the theme.

title: Beverly Hills Cop III
justification: Several characters exert authority: Billy Rosewood as DDO-JSIOC controls the 'green lines,' and DeWald, as head of security, commands his staff. Axel's defiance of these figures and his attempts to expose DeWald's corruption also highlight power struggles.

title: Ri¢hie Ri¢h
justification: Several characters exert authority: Van Dough gives orders to Fergie ('Not now, moron. We'll talk later.') and later dismisses employees. Cadbury manages Richie's schedule ('Rise and shine, Master Richie.'). Richie eventually takes charge of Rich Industries ('And by the way, United Tool stays open.')

title: Bad Girls
justification: The film depicts a society where men exert control over women, particularly sex workers, as seen in the colonel's aggressive pursuit of a kiss and the preacher's condemnation of the harlot. Characters like Kid Jarrett demonstrate dominance through violence and manipulation, while law enforcement figures like the marshal wield authority, though sometimes ineffectively.

title: Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls
justification: The movie features several instances of power dynamics. Fulton Greenwall hires Ace Ventura and attempts to direct his actions, but Ace often disregards his instructions. Additionally, the consulate general attempts to exert authority over Ace, but Ace's eccentric behavior undermines their control.

title: Crimson Tide
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, commands, and challenges to authority. Examples include: "You're relieved of your position," "I do not concur and I do not recognise your authority," and constant reporting to superiors (e.g., "Aye, sir"). The conflict between the Captain and X.O. escalates into a full-blown mutiny, highlighting the struggle for control.

title: Legends of the Fall
justification: Several characters exert authority: the father figure (Colonel Ludlow) gives orders and expects obedience ('ALFRED! STOP MOONING OVER MISS FINNCANNON AND COME IN HERE'), and characters like Tristan often defy authority ('TRISTAN, GET BACK TO YOUR UNIT!'). There are also instances of social hierarchy, such as the sheriff deferring to Colonel Ludlow ('WHAT EXACTLY IS HE WANTED FOR, SHERIFF? WELL, UH-- THAT WOULD BE OF A PRIVATE NATURE, SIR.').

title: Jumanji
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting authority or struggling for dominance. Alan's father pressures him to attend Cliffside and demands obedience: "Get your coat! We're taking you there next Sunday! I don't wanna hear another word about it!" Van Pelt, the hunter, also exerts power through threats and violence.

title: Babe
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance. Fly instructs Babe on how sheepdogs control sheep: "They just have to know who's boss." Farmer Hoggett also gives Babe commands, such as "Get them up, Pig."

title: Heat
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and asserting dominance. Examples include "Be there," "Don't waste my motherfucking time!", "You're on," and "Have Harry bring me the spreadsheets."

title: Forget Paris
justification: The dialogue showcases power dynamics through arguments and attempts to control situations. For example, the referee's interactions with players and coaches, and the couple's arguments about their careers and living arrangements, reveal a struggle for dominance and control.

title: Powder
justification: The sheriff and deputies exert authority over Powder, questioning and detaining him. John and his friends bully and assault Powder, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. The dialogue includes commands like "Get back there," "Give me your hand," and threats like "Get out of here."

title: Major Payne
justification: Major Payne constantly asserts his authority through demeaning language, physical demands, and direct orders. Examples include: "Drop down, give me 25 pushups now! Count 'em out!", "Go change your Huggies, boy, and be back here pronto!", and his general treatment of the cadets as "turds" and "maggots."

title: Primary Colors
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding information, and asserting dominance. Examples include Libby's abrasive instructions ('Call Becky Raymond. 673-4982. Tell her it's for the governor. She'll know what you mean.') and the overall focus on controlling the narrative and suppressing damaging information.

title: How Stella Got Her Groove Back
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. Stella's mother's disapproval of Winston is a power play, and Stella's firing from her job shows corporate power. The dialogue between Stella and Winston also shows a power imbalance due to their age difference and life experiences.

title: Out of Sight
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance. Examples include the prison scenes with Maurice shaking down Ripley for money, and the interactions between Foley and Ripley where Foley often takes charge. There are also power plays in the professional setting, such as the interactions between Karen and her superiors.

title: Bride of Chucky
justification: The dolls, Chucky and Tiffany, exert control over the humans, ordering them around and threatening them. Examples include Tiffany telling Damien to 'crawl' and Chucky's general violent and bossy demeanor. The Chief of Police also uses his authority to intimidate David.

title: Madeline
justification: Lord Covington's interactions with Miss Clavel are driven by his authority and intention to close the school, demonstrated by his commands: "Paint them over" and his overall dismissive attitude. Miss Clavel's role is to obey and manage the girls, as seen when she directs them: "Downstairs, girls. In an orderly fashion."

title: Wild Things
justification: The film is driven by the power and influence of the wealthy Van Ryan family, who manipulate the police and legal system. Dialogue such as "My daughter does not get raped in Blue Bay!" and "End of discussion" demonstrates their control. Characters are constantly trying to gain leverage over each other, whether through blackmail, manipulation, or legal maneuvering.

title: Star Wars Ep. I: The Phantom Menace
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and hierarchical language, such as "kill her," "Your Highness," and "Halt." Characters like the Queen and Jedi Masters issue orders, while others are expected to obey, indicating a clear power structure.

title: The Blair Witch Project
justification: Throughout the film, Heather, as the director, attempts to maintain control, but her authority is constantly challenged, especially when they get lost. Examples include: "Give me the map. Heather, give me the map." and "Turn the camera off and get us home."

title: The General's Daughter
justification: The dialogue is filled with military rank and the associated power. Characters like Colonel Moore and Captain Goodson exert authority, while others like Sunhill and Brenner navigate the hierarchy. The interrogation scenes, especially those involving Colonel Moore, highlight the struggle for control and information.

title: October Sky
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between Homer and his father, especially concerning work and expectations. The mine foreman also exerts authority, and there are instances of characters giving orders and asserting dominance, such as 'Roy Lee, drive me to my house' and the father's reprimands.

title: Lake Placid
justification: Several characters attempt to assert authority, such as the Fish and Game warden superseding the sheriff's orders ('Unfortunately, Fish and Game supersedes the sheriff.') and Hector Cyr barking orders ('You don't just fly in here and start barking orders.'). There are also instances of resistance to authority, like Kelly Scott's sarcastic remarks and Mrs. Bickerman's defiance of the sheriff's questions.

title: The Talented Mr. Ripley
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Dickie manipulates Tom's emotions and later dismisses him, saying, "You can be a leech!" and "You can be quite boring." Inspector Roverini interrogates Tom, attempting to assert authority and uncover the truth about Freddie's death.

title: Mysteries of Egypt
justification: The narrative emphasizes the absolute power of the Pharaohs, who commanded vast resources and labor to build monumental structures. Dialogue such as 'the Egyptians accorded their rulers absolute power' and descriptions of the pharaoh's role as a living god on earth highlight the hierarchical structure of ancient Egyptian society.

title: The Insider
justification: The dialogue reveals a clear power imbalance, particularly between Bergman and Wigand, and between corporate entities and individuals. Bergman pressures Wigand to go public, emphasizing the 'power you have,' while corporate lawyers threaten CBS with lawsuits, demonstrating their control over media content.

title: Arlington Road
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence. Michael's intrusive investigation of Oliver's past demonstrates a power imbalance and a desire to uncover hidden information. The FBI agents' aggressive approach to Seaver Parsons' home highlights the government's authority and potential for abuse.

title: Me, Myself & Irene
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Examples include the police officer escorting Irene, Dickie's control over his associates, and the Colonel ordering Charlie to take a vacation. Also, Hank's aggressive and manipulative behavior demonstrates a constant struggle for dominance.

title: Unbreakable
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or dominance. For example, Elijah manipulates David with his theories, and David uses his physical strength to subdue criminals. Also, Joseph disobeys his father's instructions, leading to a dangerous situation.

title: Scream 3
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dewey as a (former) cop gives orders ('Stop following me,' 'I'm on duty'). The director, Roman, is shown to be in charge on set ('Roman, that's not the line'). There are also power struggles, such as the celebrity guard asserting his superiority over Dewey ('So how about you take suggestions from me?').

title: U-571
justification: The dialogue is replete with orders given and obeyed, establishing a clear military hierarchy. Examples include: "Mr. Tyler, call the crew to quarters. Aye, Captain. Quarters! Everybody fall in!" and "Lieutenant, prepare the boat to get underway. Aye, sir. Admiral."

title: Rugrats in Paris
justification: Madame LaBouche constantly gives orders and demands obedience from her employees, such as Jean-Claude and Kira. Examples include: "I want that nincompoop inventor here within 24 hours, or another head will roll" and "Kira! Madame LaBouche wants her Pickles. Now!"

title: Bring it On
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Torrance struggles to maintain control as captain, issuing orders and being challenged ('Courtney, I'm the captain. I'm pulling rank'). There are also instances of hierarchy and competition, such as the cheerleaders vying for spots on the squad and the rivalry between the Toros and the Clovers.

title: Rules of Engagement
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and asserting dominance. Examples include the NSC advisor demanding the trial be moved quickly, Colonel Childers issuing commands to his troops, and the intense questioning and pressure applied to witnesses and officials during the trial.

title: The Cell
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Baines pressures Dr. Kent for results, stating, "There's no proof, Catherine." Agent Ramsey barks orders, "Give me a coroner's report right away."

title: Romeo Must Die
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and vying for control. Examples include: "Get them out," "You work for me, Kai," and "Don't respect me, but respect your father and let us protect you."

title: Book of Shadows: Blair Witch 2
justification: Several characters attempt to assert authority, such as Jeff with his tour group and Cravens with his investigation. Dialogue like "We have jurisdiction here" and "Open the goddamn door!" demonstrates the struggle for control and dominance.

title: Battlefield Earth: A Saga of the Year 3000
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threatening each other, and jockeying for position. Examples include Terl's constant threats and demands, the Planetship's condescending treatment of Terl, and Jonnie's struggle to gain control over the humans.

title: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone
justification: Several instances show characters in positions of authority. McGonagall and Snape exert control through point deductions and detentions: 'Therefore, as punishment for your actions, 50 points will be taken. Each.' Dumbledore's reputation and influence are also highlighted: 'As long as Dumbledore is around, Harry, you're safe.'

title: Shrek
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Lord Farquaad gives orders to his knights and demands obedience, while Shrek initially tries to force Donkey to leave him alone. The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority, such as "All right, get out of here!" and "Silence! I will make this Princess Fiona my queen."

title: Planet of the Apes
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, orders, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "Captain Davidson, report to the bridge," "Get the humans!," "Rise when your master enters," and "Give me absolute power...to rid this planet of humans once and for all."

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
justification: Gandalf frequently gives orders and commands, such as "You must take it!" and "You must leave. And leave quickly." Saruman also commands Sauron, stating, "The power of Isengard is at your command...Sauron, lord of the earth."

title: American Pie 2
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to assert dominance, such as Stifler's crude behavior and attempts to control situations. The dialogue includes explicit power plays, like "I make the rules," indicating a struggle for control.

title: The Fast and the Furious
justification: Dominic Toretto exerts considerable control over his 'team,' dictating their actions and demanding respect. Examples include his interactions with Brian ('Get over there!'), Jesse ('Jesse, give me the wallet'), and the general expectation of obedience from the group.

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as Powell demanding explanations from Mr. Wilson and Lara commanding Bryce. There are also power struggles, like Lara defying Powell's attempts to control her and Alex's initial subservience to Powell before betraying him.

title: Training Day
justification: The dialogue is filled with explicit commands, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include "STAND UP, YOU. STAND THE FUCK UP!", "TURN AROUND, SUCKER.", and numerous instances of demeaning language and threats of violence, showcasing a clear power imbalance and struggle for control.

title: Scary Movie 2
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to assert dominance. For example, the caretaker's creepy, invasive behavior towards Cindy, and the professor's manipulation of the students for his experiment. Also, Shorty's aggressive, confrontational behavior with the bird and others.

title: Serendipity
justification:
There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the boss/employee relationship between Nick and Artie ("	Yeah. Whatever you say, boss."). There is also a hint of control in the relationship between Lars and Sara, where Lars pressures Sara to extend their tour, despite her existing commitments ("	Well, baby, your patients can do
without you for a couple weeks.").

title: Riding in Cars with Boys
justification: Several instances of parental control and hierarchical relationships are evident, such as "You won't see that girl again. You can't be trusted" and "Button your blouse." The dialogue also reveals struggles for control within relationships, like the argument between Bev and Ray, and Fay's confrontational wedding speech.

title: Someone Like You
justification: Diane, as the boss, exerts control through direct orders like "I need the ungettable get, got it?" and interrogative demands such as "Tell me, do you think we have a shot here?" Jane's submissive responses, like "Got it" and hesitant replies, highlight the hierarchical dynamic.

title: The Musketeer
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include: "I order you to stop!" and "You will not last the day."

title: Sweet November
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to assert dominance. For example, the hot dog company executive berates the advertising team, ultimately firing Nelson: "You're fired!". Sara also exerts control over Nelson, dictating the terms of their arrangement and his behavior: "Because I make the rules, Nelson. Rules you must submit to, utterly and completely."

title: Heist
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threatening each other, and vying for control. Examples include: "I want you to do the other thing!", "Get the fuck back in the car!", "You're the help.", and numerous instances of characters demanding information or compliance.

title: Kingdom Come
justification: Several characters exert control over others, like Lucille's domineering attitude towards Ray and her family, demanding specific actions and berating their choices. Junior's attempts to assert himself with Charisse often end in her shutting him down, highlighting a power imbalance in their relationship. Mama Ray also dictates terms, such as the tombstone inscription, showcasing her authority within the family.

title: Star Wars Ep. II: Attack of the Clones
justification: The dialogue is filled with master-apprentice relationships (Obi-Wan/Anakin, Dooku/Qui-Gon), political maneuvering (senators, chancellor), and characters giving/receiving orders. Examples include Obi-Wan constantly correcting Anakin, Palpatine issuing orders to senators, and Dooku commanding the Separatists.

title: Signs
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include: "TIE ISABEL UP TO THE BACK OF THE SHED, PLEASE, AND MAKE SURE THE KNOT'S VERY TIGHT," and "YOU TAKE A GLASS OF WATER, AND YOU FINISH IT."

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding
justification: The father, Gus, exerts control over his daughter Toula's life, dictating her future and potential husband. Maria, the mother, subtly manipulates situations to get her way, as seen in her orchestrating Toula's job at the travel agency. There are also constant arguments and nagging between family members, indicating a struggle for dominance within the family structure.

title: Star Trek: Nemesis
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within Starfleet, with characters giving and receiving orders (e.g., "That is the regulation, sir," "Shut up," "Yes, sir."). Shinzon's rise to power and his interactions with the Romulan commanders also highlight a struggle for dominance and control within the Romulan Empire (e.g., "Allegiance. It's something I demand from those who serve me.").

title: I Spy
justification: Throughout the subtitles, characters are constantly giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include T.J. demanding the most expensive suite and threatening consequences, and the BNS agents controlling Kelly Robinson during the mission ('Cut off his penis!').

title: Friday After Next
justification: Several characters assert dominance through threats and insults. Elroy is ordered around and belittled, while Day-Day abuses his security position, highlighting a struggle for authority and respect. Moly, the strip mall owner, exerts control over his employees, further emphasizing the hierarchical structure.

title: Brown Sugar
justification: There are several instances of power dynamics at play. Dre's struggle to assert control over his new artists, Ren and Ten, and his wife Reese's disapproval of his career change and reliance on Sidney, highlight the theme. Kelby Dawson also uses his fame to command attention and orchestrate romantic gestures.

title: The Lizzie McGuire Movie
justification: Miss Ungermeyer constantly asserts her authority over the students, issuing commands and punishments: "All right, moving on, people. Let's go." and "Ah, Gordon, you are on the list, and the list is not a place you want to be." Paolo also exhibits control, especially over Sergei, his bodyguard: "Paolo, go! Go!"

title: Intolerable Cruelty
justification: The dialogue is filled with legal maneuvering and strategic positioning, particularly in the divorce proceedings. Characters like Miles Massey and Freddy Bender are constantly trying to outwit each other, demonstrating a clear power struggle. Marylin's calculated actions to secure financial independence also highlight the theme.

title: AVP: Alien Vs. Predator
justification: Weyland exerts control over the expedition, demanding immediate action despite warnings: "He said he didn't have a week." Lex initially refuses to guide, but Weyland uses money and pressure to force her compliance: "Money's been wired to your account." Later, Lex takes charge of the team, issuing orders and expecting obedience: "No one goes anywhere alone. Ever."

title: Man on Fire
justification: Creasy is hired to protect Pita, establishing a clear hierarchical relationship. Dialogue like "I'm being paid to protect you, okay? No, no, no. I'm being paid to be your bodyguard. Look at me. I'm not being paid to be your friend" highlights this dynamic. Other characters, like the Madre at the school, also exert authority over Creasy, indicating a complex web of power relationships.

title: The Terminal
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the airport official who controls Navorski's fate ('As acting field commissioner, I've created a new position here at JFK.') and the construction foreman ('You give me job? Oh... 6:30, yes. Yes, boss.'). There are also instances of characters trying to manipulate or control others, like Enrique attempting to get information from Navorski.

title: Garfield The Movie
justification: Several characters exert authority: Garfield bosses around Odie, Jon gives commands to Garfield, and Happy Chapman controls Odie with a shock collar. Examples include Garfield saying, "That's my chair," and Chapman stating, "This collar...is the dog's future."

title: Ladder 49
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and orders, especially during the fire scenes. Examples include "Move it in!", "Get your asses in there and find him. Go, go, go.", and "Hit it high!". There are also instances of deference to authority, such as when the rookie is hazed and when subordinates address superiors as "Cap" or "Chief."

title: Christmas with the Kranks
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Nora and Luther argue about Christmas traditions, with Luther often dismissing Nora's concerns. The neighbors pressure the Kranks to conform to their Christmas traditions, using social pressure and even threats: 'AND FROSTY BETTER BE HERE.'

title: Ray
justification: The dialogue shows Ray asserting control over his bandmates and singers, dictating their roles and even their personal lives. Examples include Ray telling Bea what she will do on the road and his interactions with the Raelettes, where he dictates their singing parts and dismisses Mary Ann.

title: White Chicks
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to assert dominance through insults and social maneuvering. For example, the Vandergeld sisters try to assert their social status over others, and there are instances of characters giving orders and expecting obedience, such as when Tori directs the 'Wilson sisters' activities.

title: Hidalgo
justification: Throughout the film, characters give orders and assert dominance. Examples include, "If they choose to fight, subdue them," and "Get back behind the tent line." The race itself is a power struggle, with characters vying for status and control.

title: The Forgotton
justification: The film revolves around a conspiracy where an organization has the power to erase memories and manipulate reality. Characters are constantly struggling against this force, trying to regain control of their memories and lives, as evidenced by Telly's repeated defiance and attempts to remember her son despite the organization's efforts.

title: Kill Bill: Volume 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, insults, and demonstrations of dominance. Examples include 'You are not to speak unless spoken to,' 'Rise, and let me look at your ridiculous face,' and 'It's my arm now. I can do what I please.'

title: The Manchurian Candidate
justification: The dialogue contains numerous instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority, such as "Suffocate Private Baker. Kill him." and "That is an order.". There are also instances of deference to authority, such as characters addressing each other by rank (Captain, Sergeant, Congressman) and following orders.

title: Barbershop 2: Back in Business
justification: Several characters assert dominance through threats and insults. For example, one character says, "l keep my stuff with me, okay? l cut you." Alderman Brown also exerts his authority by dismissing concerns and demanding reports, stating, "This boy is gonna be the governor of the state of lllinois one day if he learns to do what l say when l say it."

title: Miracle
justification: The coach, Herb, exerts significant control over the team through demanding drills and strategic decisions ('Again!', 'You want to go home early?'). He also uses psychological tactics to motivate and manipulate the players ('How about it, Silky? You gonna be the first one to quit on me?').

title: Friday Night Lights
justification: The coach exerts authority over players ('Go sit on the bench', 'Find your helmet, son'). There are also instances of players questioning the coach's decisions ('You don't want me to go in, Coach?'). The community also exerts pressure on the coach to win.

title: Big Fish
justification: The giant Karl initially holds power through size and intimidation, demanding Edward 'Go away!' Edward attempts to negotiate and even offers himself as a 'human sacrifice,' shifting the dynamic. Ultimately, Edward persuades Karl to leave, establishing a form of leadership.

title: The Stepford Wives
justification: The film explores the power dynamics between men and women, particularly the men's desire to control their wives. The director states, "The men, really, are idiots. They're twits. They are frightened to death of strong women...the men could not handle strong women. That's the only way the men could actually feel superior and feel good about themselves is to feel superior to women."

title: Hellboy
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include: "Move it!" and "Hold the line." Also, Kroenen is described as "Hitler's top assassin," indicating a clear hierarchy.

title: Dawn of the Dead
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include C.J. assigning tasks and threatening violence to maintain control: "I'm gonna give everybody a job to do, and I expect you to do all of it." and "I'll kill each and every one of you to stay alive."

title: Without a Paddle
justification: There are several instances of power dynamics. Tom often takes charge, giving directions like "Follow my lead!" and "Same stroke, same stroke!". The pot farmers exert dominance through threats and violence: "Come with me, or I'll shoot your testicles off."

title: The Butterfly Effect
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Examples include: "Drop it or I'll slit your mother's throat in her sleep," and "Get the fuck out of my bar."

title: The Chronicles of Riddick
justification: The Lord Marshal commands the Necromongers, demanding obedience and threatening destruction. Riddick's interactions with Toombs and other characters also highlight power struggles, as he consistently asserts dominance and control over situations. Vaako's ambition and maneuvering within the Necromonger hierarchy further emphasize the theme.

title: Shall We Dance?
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to assert dominance or control. For example, the dance instructor says, "Slide that hand one inch south of the equator...and I will bust you on your ass, twinkle-toes." Also, there are instances of characters giving orders or instructions, such as when the boss tells Carolyn, "Look, Carolyn, I'm gonna need you to go to New York and sweet-talk them. Can you leave tomorrow?"

title: 13 Going On 30
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in the workplace, with Richard acting as the boss and giving orders to Jenna and Lucy. Examples include "Richard, you're my boss" and "I'll tell you what to do. Repeat after me: I am Jenna Rink, bigtime magazine editor. I'm a tough bitch."

title: Saw
justification: The entire plot revolves around Jigsaw's control over the characters, dictating their actions and fates. Dialogue like "Your aim in this game is to kill Adam" and "If you do not kill Adam by 6:00...then Alison and Diana will die" exemplifies the extreme power imbalance and the life-or-death stakes imposed by Jigsaw.

title: Jet Li’s Hero
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, decrees, and discussions of rank. Examples include: 'By order of the King,' 'Declare my decree,' and 'You have to be a hundred paces away from the palace to see the King. Or else you're dead. Remember that, strong man.' The entire plot revolves around assassination attempts on the King of Qin and the power he wields.

title: A Cinderella Story
justification: Fiona's treatment of Sam is a clear example of power dynamics, as she forces Sam to work long hours and belittles her dreams. Austin's father also exerts control over his son's future, dictating his college and career path. Shelby's dismissive and demeaning behavior towards Carter also highlights a power imbalance.

title: Resident Evil: Apocalypse
justification: The movie features a clear hierarchy within the Umbrella Corporation, with characters giving and receiving orders (e.g., "Take her to the Raccoon City facility," "Seal the gates," "Just do it."). There are also power struggles between characters, such as the Umbrella Corporation's attempts to control Alice and the S.T.A.R.S. team.

title: Home on the Range
justification: Several characters give orders or assert authority. Examples include the banker demanding payment ('They'll get their money soon enough') and Mrs. Caloway telling Sam to leave ('Stop right there, Sam'). Buck also displays a desire for recognition and status ('I'm wearing Rico's saddle!').

title: Blade: Trinity
justification: Characters give orders and assert dominance, such as Blade's interactions with the Nightstalkers ("You amateurs are supposed to be helping me?") and the vampires' hierarchical structure with Drake at the top. The FBI agents attempt to assert authority over Blade, and Dr. Vance tries to control the psychiatric evaluation.

title: Secret Window
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats and intimidation, particularly from Shooter towards Mort. Examples include Shooter demanding Mort fix his story and threatening Amy's safety: "You want to wake up from one of your stupid naps and find Amy nailed to your garbage bin?"

title: Walking Tall
justification: The sheriff initially asserts his authority over Chris, but Chris later becomes sheriff and exerts his power by firing the deputies. Jay Hamilton also displays dominance through his casino and attempts to control Chris, leading to a power struggle.

title: Napoleon Dynamite
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or demonstrate superiority. For example, Uncle Rico's sales tactics and Rex Kwon Do's self-defense demonstrations showcase attempts to impress and dominate, while Napoleon's interactions with Kip often involve insults and attempts to assert dominance.

title: Exorcist: The Beginning
justification: The film features multiple power dynamics. The British military asserts control over the dig site and the local population, as seen in Major Granville's interactions with Merrin and the Turkana. Additionally, the demon attempts to dominate Merrin and Sarah through psychological manipulation and physical threats, highlighting a struggle for control over their minds and bodies.

title: Catwoman
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. George Hedare's interactions with Patience are demeaning and controlling: "I do not reward incompetence." Laurel and George also have a power struggle: "Did I steal your moment?".

title: You Got Served
justification: There are several instances of power dynamics at play. Elgin and D exert control over their crew, dictating practice schedules and financial splits: "I'm talking practice every day, even on the weekend. Y'all gotta be on point. If y'all ain't down with us that night... You don't get none of that money." Mr. Rad also holds authority, demonstrated by his control over the battle events and his association with law enforcement.

title: Bridget Jones: The Edge Of Reason
justification: The film depicts power dynamics through Mark Darcy's professional status and influence, which allows him to get Bridget out of a Thai prison. Also, Daniel Cleaver's manipulative behavior and attempts to control Bridget highlight power imbalances in their relationship. Dialogue such as "The order came from above" and Cleaver's general demeanor showcase these dynamics.

title: The Ladykillers
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance and control. Examples include the Professor directing the heist, Gudge firing MacSam, and the constant bickering and attempts to establish hierarchy within the group, such as the argument over Mountain Girl's presence and Garth's injury compensation.

title: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as Paley telling Polly to "get the hell out of there" and Sky Captain barking orders to Dex. The villain, Totenkopf, exerts absolute control over his creations and followers, demonstrated by his doomsday device and Unit 11.

title: Raising Helen
justification: There are multiple instances of power dynamics. Helen is now in charge of the kids and tells them what to do: "Don't chew on the windowsills, all right?" and "Audrey's in charge, though, so listen to her, OK?". Also, Dominique is clearly the boss at work, giving Helen orders: "Helen will tell you what to bring."

title: Taxi
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and resisting control. Examples include the police commandeering vehicles ("I'm gonna need your car for official..."), characters threatening each other ("Hey! See this? This is a badge, okay? That means you're not allowed to scream at me."), and the lieutenant's reprimands ("Washburn... you took a cab to a bank robbery? You thought that was okay?").

title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
justification: Several characters are in positions of authority, such as doctors and technicians, who give instructions and orders to others. For example, the technician Patrick tells Joel, "Just please try to focus on the memories," and Dr. Mierzwiak instructs Mary, "If you'd take care of Mrs. Woo."

title: Monster
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of band members asserting control, expressing feelings of disrespect, and navigating the hierarchy within the group. James' need for 'complete control of the situation' and Lars' concerns about decisions being made without him highlight the ongoing power struggles.

title: Alexander
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Alexander gives orders to his generals ('Ptolemy, administer this'), and there are constant references to who is in charge and who must obey, especially in the context of Alexander's growing empire and his relationships with conquered peoples ('As I am... a princess. Then so be it.').

title: The Punisher
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, orders, and displays of dominance. Howard Saint's interactions with Micky, the Toro brothers, and his own family showcase a constant struggle for control and respect, highlighted by lines like "You're gonna help me" and the violent interrogation scenes.

title: Team America: World Police
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('cover his back', 'take super-secret hiding positions'), asserting dominance ('I'll rip your fucking balls off'), and struggling for control ('You wanna go?'). Even the team leader, Spottswoode, is shown to exert control and make demands.

title: Taking Lives
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between the FBI agents and local police, with the FBI agent taking charge of the investigation. There are also instances of characters trying to assert dominance, such as when the director confronts Agent Scott about making herself comfortable and when Costa manipulates and threatens others.

title: Cellular
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and struggling for control. Examples include the kidnappers' demands, the cop's aggressive interactions, and the powerlessness of the kidnapped woman.

title: Anacondas: The Hunt for the Blood Orchid
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance. Johnson sets a high price for his boat, saying "50 grand's my price. Take it or leave it." Later, Jack pressures Sam to continue the expedition, stating, "I'm the one with the authority here."

title: Johnson Family Vacation
justification: The father, Nate, exerts control over his family, dictating their travel plans and activities. Examples include forcing them to continue driving despite their tiredness and grounding his daughter for disobedience. There are also instances of Nate's mother, Glorietta, asserting her authority within the extended family, particularly during the prayer scene where she silences Nate and Mack.

title: Open Water
justification: The dive instructor, Davis, gives explicit instructions and expects compliance ("Ok, guys. I need to have your attention for just a few minutes."). There's also a brief power struggle when a diver insists he doesn't need a buddy, but Davis insists on the boat's rules ("I don't need a buddy...Unfortunately you do if you're on our boat, sir.").

title: Confessions of a Teenage Drama Queen
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for roles, attention, and status. Miss Baggoli controls casting, Carla asserts dominance through insults, and Lola manipulates situations to gain an advantage, such as stealing the dress and lying to the police. Examples: "I've already got the part," "Well, look what the wind blew in," and the constant competition for Stu Wolff's attention.

title: Paycheck
justification: Several characters exert authority: Rethrick gives orders to his staff ("lsaac, disable fire protection, please."), and the federal agents interrogate and attempt to control Jennings ("You need to tell us everything you did for Rethrick."). Jimmy also tries to manipulate Michael into taking a job, promising great wealth but withholding information.

title: Calendar Girls
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the W.I. committee needing to approve the calendar idea and Chris bossing people around during the photoshoot. Marie attempts to exert control by disapproving of the calendar and trying to stop it.

title: The Prince & Me
justification: The dialogue is filled with assertions of authority, manipulation, and strategic maneuvering for control. Albert attempts to use an archaic law to force Edvard's hand, while the Queen Mother exerts influence over Edvard's decisions. Characters like Kirsten also try to manipulate situations to their advantage, highlighting a constant struggle for dominance.

title: After the Sunset
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Lloyd's initial confrontation with Max, Mooré's manipulation of Burdett, and the constant power plays between Lloyd and Max.

title: Garden State
justification: Several interactions involve characters giving orders or directions, such as Samantha's mother telling her to put clothes in the dryer and bury Jelly. Mark's controlling behavior and directives to Andrew also highlight power dynamics. The doctor's professional authority over Andrew is evident in their conversation about medication.

title: Spanglish
justification: Several characters exert control over others, such as Deborah's attempts to influence Flor's daughter and John's dominance in the kitchen. Examples include Deborah's line, "You must learn English," and John's instructions to his staff, "Do this for me."

title: Jersey Girl
justification: The dialogue shows Ollie's struggle to regain his former status and authority in the PR world, contrasted with his current subservient role to his father and daughter. Examples include Ollie's attempts to impress potential employers and his father's blunt criticisms, as well as Gertie's demands and Ollie's eventual capitulation to her wishes regarding the school show.

title: Star Wars Ep. III: Revenge of the Sith
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, power plays, and status seeking. Examples include: "R2, do you copy?", "Activate ray shields", "Crush them! Make them suffer!", and Palpatine's manipulation of Anakin to gain power.

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe
justification: The dialogue includes direct orders ('Come on, hup!'), rules being laid down ('There will no shoutin'. Or runnin'.'), and characters asserting authority ('How dare you address the Queen of Narnia?'). The White Witch's interactions with Edmund also highlight a power imbalance, as she manipulates him with promises of power and treats.

title: Wedding Crashers
justification: Several characters exert dominance through orders and manipulation. John is pressured into activities he dislikes, and Gloria attempts to control Jeremy's behavior. The Cleary family traditions and expectations also create a hierarchical environment.

title: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance or control. Veruca Salt constantly demands things from her father ('Daddy, I want another pony,' 'I want a squirrel!'), and Violet Beauregarde declares her intention to win ('I'm gonna win the special prize at the end'). Willy Wonka also exerts authority, setting rules and dismissing others' opinions ('Can't imagine how it would matter. Come quickly. Far too much to see.').

title: Batman Begins
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, issuing threats, and vying for control. Falcone's interactions with the police and Crane, and Ra's al Ghul's manipulation of Bruce Wayne, exemplify this struggle for power.

title: Madagascar
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Alex and Marty, where Alex often tries to control Marty's actions and opinions. Examples include Alex telling Marty to "Shut up, shut up, shut up!" and trying to dismiss Marty's desire to explore life outside the zoo. King Julien also exerts authority over the lemurs.

title: King Kong
justification: Carl Denham constantly orders Preston around ("Give me that, quick.", "That's why I have you, Preston."). He also manipulates and pressures Ann into joining his film, showcasing his control over the situation ("Ann, I'm telling you... you're perfect. Look at you."). The Captain also asserts his authority over Denham, ultimately arresting him.

title: The Longest Yard
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the coach yelling "Move it! Hustle, hustle, hustle!" and the warden's control over the inmates, demonstrated by his ability to manipulate their activities and the sharpshooters being present to prevent escape.

title: Fantastic Four
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and jockeying for status. Victor's controlling behavior towards Susan and his employees, Reed's attempts to lead the team, and Ben's resentment of his situation all contribute to this theme. Examples: 'If you're good, maybe next time Daddy'll let you drive,' 'Get a grip, Reed,' 'So reel him in,' 'Don't wander off now, boy,' 'Just find him.'

title: Chicken Little
justification: The movie revolves around Chicken Little's struggle to regain his father's respect and the town's trust after his initial 'sky is falling' incident. Dialogue like 'Quiet, son. This is embarrassing enough already' and the town's general ridicule highlight the power imbalance and Chicken Little's low status.

title: Million Dollar Baby
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority, especially between Frankie and Maggie. Examples include: "If I take you on, you don't say anything, you don't question me," and "I'm listening, boss," showing a clear trainer-trainee hierarchy.

title: Walk the Line
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Vivian lays down 'rules' for John when he's home, indicating her attempt to control his behavior. Also, the interactions with the band members and Jerry Lee Lewis show John's status as the headliner, with others seeking his approval or trying to impress him.

title: Saw II
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('All right, fellas. Listen up.') and asserting authority ('Don't ever pull some shit like that again on me at a crime scene.'). The Jigsaw character exerts control through his games and manipulation ('The decisions are up to them.').

title: Monster-in-Law
justification: The mother, Viola, constantly tries to control the wedding plans and Charlie's life, showcasing a power struggle. Dialogue like "Ruby, give me the key" and Viola's attempts to manipulate Charlie into specific wedding choices demonstrate her desire for control.

title: Are We There Yet?
justification: There are several instances of power dynamics at play. Nick is often bossed around by the kids, and Suzanne expects Nick to take care of her kids. The kids also try to assert dominance over each other, as seen in the line, "That's my seat."

title: March of the Penguins
justification: There are some power dynamics present, primarily in the mating rituals. The narration mentions "hostilities among the ladies are inevitable" because "there are fewer males than females here." Also, "Every year some bereft mother will respond to her agony...in an unimaginable way...she will attempt to steal another's."

title: The Ring Two
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. For example, Jake pressures Emily to watch the video, culminating in him yelling, "Emily, play the goddamn tape!" Later, the doctor restricts Rachel's access to her son, stating, "Until we can talk further, I cannot let you be alone with him."

title: Constantine
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority. Examples include Constantine ordering Chas around ("Move the car!", "Lift it up over the bed.") and the angel Gabriel's condescending interactions with Constantine, highlighting a hierarchical relationship and struggle for control.

title: Four Brothers
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, commands, and displays of dominance. Examples include: "Shut up," "Get your ass over there on the couch," and "You better start saying what the fuck I wanna hear. Speak."

title: Sin City
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Marv telling Wendy what she can and cannot do, Gail giving orders to Becky and Miho, and the mercenaries bossing around the prostitutes.

title: The Interpreter
justification: Characters frequently give orders and make demands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Keller directing his team ('Dot, wake up Roy, have him dust her locker') and Woods instructing Keller ('So, State wants you to know: NSA, CIA, FBI, whatever you need...it's yours.'). Zuwanie's head of security also asserts authority ('He's gotta wait a couple hours, when we get back from Washington.')

title: Sahara
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and negotiating for control. Examples include the Admiral directing Dirk, Yves Massarde's controlling interactions with General Kazim, and the power struggles between Kazim and the Tuaregs.

title: Guess Who
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters attempting to exert control over others, such as Percy's overbearing behavior towards Simon, Marilyn's attempts to control Percy, and the general struggle for dominance within the family. Examples include: "You'll obey Mr. Jones now... but when you're up at 3:00 in the morning... all hot and horny, you'll obey Mr. Johnson." and "Sit down and take your call."

title: Coach Carter
justification: The coach exerts considerable control over the team, setting strict academic standards and punishing disobedience with intense physical drills ('2,500 push-ups...and 1,000 suicides'). There are also instances of dominance within relationships, such as Kenyon's controlling behavior towards Kyra regarding her pregnancy and lifestyle choices ('You ain't doing it right. You gotta soothe him, Kenyon.').

title: Herbie: Fully Loaded
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the Peyton racing family, with the father figure dictating who races and how. Trip Murphy's arrogance and dominance on the track also highlight power dynamics, as he seeks to maintain his status as a champion. Dialogue such as "My house, my rules" and Trip's demands for a rematch showcase the struggle for control and status.

title: The Amityville Horror
justification: George frequently asserts dominance over his family, especially the children, using commands and threats: "Get your feet off the chair," "Wipe that stupid look off your face...and go to bed," and "From now on, I'm doing the disciplining around here, end of story." He also tries to control Kathy, telling her to "shut up" and that he's "not going anywhere, neither are you."

title: Sky High
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of hierarchy and status seeking. Characters are labeled as 'heroes' and 'sidekicks,' creating a clear power differential. There are also instances of direct commands and assertions of authority, such as 'On demands it' and 'You're not supposed to use your powers outside of the gym.'

title: Jarhead
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and displays of authority, such as "Attention on deck! Take your seats." and "You stay ready, you ain't got to get ready!" The Colonel's speech is a clear display of dominance, and the gas mask drill showcases the Staff Sergeant's control over the Marines.

title: Bewitched
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Jack, the male lead, tries to control Isabel's performance and image, saying things like "Just stand there" and "Now do that thing that you do." Isabel eventually rebels against this control, telling Jack "Everything is about you" and quitting the show.

title: Cinderella Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority, especially from Joe towards Jimmy ('Sharpen up,' 'You're meat, Jimmy'). There's also a clear hierarchy in the boxing world, with managers, promoters, and fighters jockeying for position and control ('I got you a fight,' 'You're gonna fight John Henry Lewis again.').

title: Red-Eye
justification: The primary conflict revolves around Jack's manipulation and control over Lisa, using her father's life as leverage. Dialogue such as "You call, I call, Dad wakes up, puts on coffee, never suspects a thing, you go back to work, life goes on" and "One simple phone call saves your dad's life" highlights this dynamic.

title: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit
justification: The dialogue contains instances of command and obedience, such as Wallace instructing Gromit ('Pile it up, lad') and Victor ordering Phillip ('Attack!'). Lady Tottington's social status is evident in how others address her ('Your Ladyship. This is an honor.').

title: White Noise
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or instructions, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include John's interactions with Karen ('Hey, Karen, order me a bouquet of flowers') and the general dynamic of Raymond seemingly controlling the EVP sessions.

title: Be Cool
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, give orders, and manipulate situations to their advantage. Examples include Sin LaSalle's aggressive demands for money from Edie, Nicky Carr's control over his associates, and Chili Palmer's strategic maneuvering to protect Linda Moon and resolve conflicts.

title: Crash
justification: The film is filled with examples of power dynamics. Police officers exert authority over civilians ('Step outta the car, please, sir.') and superiors over subordinates ('Write a full report.'). There are also power struggles within relationships ('And you just stood there! And then you apologized to him?').

title: Fun with Dick & Jane
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. For example, Dick's boss McAllister displays authority by firing him and later flaunting his wealth. Other examples include the INS agents abusing their authority and the couple resorting to robbery to regain control of their lives.

title: Corpse Bride
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to control others, especially regarding marriage and social status. For example, the Van Dorts are desperate to elevate their status, while the Everglots are concerned with maintaining theirs, leading to controlling statements like "Everything must go according to plan" and "You shall marry Lord Barkis tomorrow."

title: Kicking and Screaming
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or seeking approval, such as Chet being asked to get pitchers of beer ("Chet. Two pitchers, please. Sir.") and Max's condescending attitude towards Skippy's academic pursuits. The dynamic between the older characters and the younger college students at the bar also highlights a power imbalance.

title: Hide and Seek
justification: The father-daughter relationship shows a clear power dynamic, with the father trying to guide and control Emily's behavior, especially concerning her imaginary friend Charlie. Examples include: "Emily, stop it." and "Go to your room."

title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands of others, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include "Throw them off the ship," "Freeze," and "Bring me the request to pursue fugitive forms."

title: Yours, Mine and Ours
justification: There are instances of command and obedience, such as when Frank tells Mike to handle the bar and Susan to help. Helen also gives instructions to the children, like telling Phillip to stop dawdling. The dialogue also shows Frank's attempts to control the situation with his 'system' for managing the children.

title: Diary of a Mad Black Woman
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of Charles exerting control over Helen, such as when he demands she leave his car ('Get the hell out of my car.') and orchestrates her eviction from their home. Additionally, Madea's forceful personality and actions, like confronting Charles and taking matters into her own hands, highlight a struggle for dominance and justice.

title: Racing Stripes
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, issuing threats, and jockeying for position. Examples include "Only room for one wise guy on this farm," and threats like "someday somebody's gonna wake up with your head in their bed."

title: Sideways
justification: Jack exerts dominance over Miles, dictating their trip's purpose and berating Miles for his negativity: "I'M GOING TO GET MY NUT ON THIS TRIP, MILES, AND YOU ARE NOT GONNA FUCK IT UP FOR ME." Later, Jack manipulates Miles into lying to Maya about his upcoming wedding, showcasing his control over the situation.

title: Miss Congeniality 2: Armed and Fabulous
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Collins ordering Hart and Fuller off the case, Hart and Fuller arguing about who is in charge, and the kidnappers dictating terms for the ransom.

title: Just Like Heaven
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. For example, the real estate agent tells David to "grow up," and Elizabeth frequently tells David what to do, such as "Open his shirt" and "Get the knife."

title: The Skeleton Key
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and instructions, such as Violet telling Caroline how to care for Ben and manage the house ('Don't bother with the housework. I'm the only one that knows how.'). There's also a clear hierarchy established between employer and employee, and later, a struggle for control between Caroline and Violet as Caroline tries to protect Ben.

title: Kingdom of Heaven
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Godfrey claiming Balian as his son and ordering him to Jerusalem, Reynald's blatant disregard for the King's peace, and various characters asserting dominance through threats and challenges.

title: Boogeyman
justification: There are instances of characters giving orders or expressing control, such as "Don't go to sleep" and "Shut up. It's their house, not mine." However, these moments are infrequent and do not dominate the dialogue.

title: Cheaper by the Dozen 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, especially between Tom and Jimmy. Examples include Jimmy buying properties to keep Tom out, boasting about his children's achievements, and the competitive nature of the family activities. Tom also tries to assert control over his children, particularly Sarah, and there are moments of parental authority being challenged.

title: The Legend of Zorro
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Elena's frustration with Alejandro's Zorro persona, Armand's manipulation and threats, and the power struggles between landowners and peasants.

title: In Good Company
justification: The film showcases a clear power dynamic between Carter, the young executive, and Dan, the older sales manager. Carter fires Dan, then offers him a demoted position as a 'wingman.' Carter also demands that Dan fire two of his long-time employees, demonstrating his authority.

title: The Transporter 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include: "STEP OUT OF THE CAR," "GET OUT OF THE CAR, NIGGER!", and "HANDS UP! STOP MOVING, OR I WILL SHOOT YOU!"

title: Fever Pitch
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Ben's friends pressure him to abandon his promise to wait for him, and Ben's control over Red Sox tickets is used to manipulate others, like making a man dance for tickets. Lindsey's career ambitions also create a power dynamic in her relationship.

title: The Family Stone
justification: The provided subtitles consist almost entirely of song lyrics. There is only one line of dialogue, "Um, I'm not comfortable," which does not indicate any power dynamics.

title: The Adventures of Sharkboy and Lavagirl in 3-D
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy between teachers and students, as evidenced by Mr. Electricidad's control over the class and his use of 'minuses' as punishment. Linus's bullying of Max and attempts to dominate him also highlight power struggles. Sharkboy and Lavagirl also have a hierarchy, with Sharkboy often giving orders.

title: The Phantom of the Opera
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of authority. Examples include the Phantom's demands regarding box five and Carlotta's role, as well as the managers' attempts to control the situation and each other: "And commands that you continue to leave box five empty...for his use," and "Until you stop these things from happening, this thing does not happen!"

title: The Brothers Grimm
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and jockeying for position. Examples include the General's commands to his soldiers, Cavaldi's attempts to manipulate situations, and the power struggles between Will and Jake.

title: Beauty Shop
justification: The dialogue shows Gina asserting authority as the new owner, firing stylists and setting rules. There are also instances of customers demanding specific services and belittling the staff, indicating a power imbalance. Finally, Darnelle is being bailed out and forced to work off her debt, showing Gina's control over her.

title: The Island
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Cut the O2', 'Sever the umbilical', 'Tag him and ship him to Foundation'), demanding information ('Where do you get that stuff, anyway?'), and exerting control ('You two. Watch your proximity.'). There's also a clear hierarchy within the facility, with supervisors and doctors holding authority over others.

title: Derailed
justification: Several characters exert control through threats and manipulation. LaRoche demands money and threatens Charles's family: "I'm gonna kill all your women, do you understand?" Winston also leverages his knowledge of Charles's situation for financial gain.

title: Hostage
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Shut up, Kevin', 'Get out of the truck', 'Check the car, Mars'), asserting dominance ('I'm talking', 'I'm ordering'), and struggling for control ('Fuck you.
