I'm running this shit'). The Chief's interactions with Mikey also highlight a clear hierarchical structure and the importance of obedience.

title: Pride and Prejudice
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance or navigating social hierarchies. Mr. Collins's constant name-dropping of Lady Catherine and his condescending remarks about the Bennet family's social standing highlight his attempts to assert superiority. Darcy's initial disdain for the Bennet family and his interference in Bingley's relationship also demonstrate his exercise of power based on social status and wealth.

title: The Constant Gardener
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Sandy, a High Commission official, promises to act on Tessa's information 'within reason,' indicating his control. Justin is often told what to do by other characters, such as when he is told to leave matters to the police and is later detained by them.

title: The Bad News Bears
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Buttermaker asserting his authority over the team, such as when he forces them to practice despite their desire to quit: "Nobody's vote counts around here but mine!" There are also instances of characters like Kelly Leak displaying dominance through gambling and manipulation, and Amanda's negotiation for ballet lessons in exchange for pitching.

title: In Her Shoes
justification: Several instances of characters asserting dominance are present. Jim's controlling behavior towards Rose is evident in lines like, "if you say you're gonna be in Chicago, you should be in Chicago." Ella also displays authority over Maggie, setting conditions for financial assistance: "You get that job, stop loafing around here like some princess... and I will match what you earn, penny for penny."

title: Dreamer: Inspired by a True Story
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and directives, highlighting a clear hierarchy. Examples include: 'Take your money,' 'Sedate her, Dan,' 'Hook up a trailer,' and 'Manny, take her out to the truck,' demonstrating a constant giving and taking of orders.

title: Because of Winn-Dixie
justification: Several characters exert authority: the preacher over Opal, Mr. Alfred over the preacher regarding rent and the dog, and the police officer over Otis. Dialogue includes commands like "You're supposed to be in bed," "Call the pound," and the threat of arrest, indicating a clear hierarchy.

title: House of Wax
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. Examples include: "Sit still. Stop it!", "Be quiet!", "Shut up!", and "Dalton, put down that damn camera.". There are also instances of characters trying to exert dominance through verbal sparring and intimidation.

title: Stealth
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and defiance. Examples include: "You either do what I tell you or you can crash and burn," and "I'm placing you under arrest." There are also instances of characters questioning or outright disobeying orders, indicating a struggle for control.

title: The Wedding Date
justification: Several characters exert control over others, like Kat dictating Nick's attire and behavior. Amy's mother also displays dominance through her controlling behavior. The dialogue reveals a constant negotiation of status and influence.

title: Just Friends
justification: Samantha's status as a celebrity is leveraged for Chris's benefit, and he attempts to control her actions. Chris manipulates Mike into detaining Samantha, showing his control over Mike. The dialogue also reveals a past dynamic where Chris was subservient to Jamie, which he now tries to overturn.

title: A History of Violence
justification: Several characters exert authority, like Tom telling Charlotte, "You can go home now." The mobsters display dominance through threats and violence, demanding, "Coffee!" and later, "Don't fucking move."

title: Get Rich or Die Tryin'
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include "Give me the damn fucking weed," "Don't you speak to me like that!," and the numerous rules laid down for the drug crew, such as "Rule number one, never leave this product in the house" and "Rule number five, don't show no love."

title: The Fog
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include: "Clear us now, Williams," and "Let's weigh the anchor, call it a day." The dialogue also shows Nick asserting his role as 'Skipper'.

title: Rent
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the landlord offering free rent in exchange for stopping a protest, indicating a power imbalance. Also, Mimi's flirtatious behavior and the doorman's wink suggest a transactional dynamic.

title: Zathura
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between the father and his children, as well as between the older and younger brother. The father gives instructions and sets rules ('You're gonna be at Mom's house. She's coming to get you at 3.'). Walter asserts his dominance over Danny ('Those belong to me. Put them back.').

title: Doom
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and insubordination. Examples include: "Listen up, men. Leave is canceled." and "Got a problem with that, Duke? Me, Sarge? Hell, no, I love my job."

title: Finding Neverland
justification: The grandmother exerts control over Sylvia and the children, dictating their activities and disapproving of Barrie's influence. Mary, James' wife, expresses her frustration at his emotional distance and perceived neglect. There are also instances of Barrie directing the children in their games and the play, showcasing a subtle power dynamic.

title: Elizabethtown
justification: Phil, the shoe company head, clearly holds power over Drew, dictating how he should present himself to the press after the shoe launch failure. Examples include: "We need to make him understand...we hired you from our National Scholarship Program" and "I think you should stand up...for your incredible work."

title: XXX: State of the Union
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include: "You work for us now. So you're gonna do-- What I want when I want," and "I run the chop shop now," and "You still work for me, whether you know it or not."

title: Dark Water
justification: Several characters exert authority: the mother over Ceci ('Don't you ever run away from me'), the superintendent over the tenants ('I check it. Hour ago, it was locked. Someone else open it'), and the father threatening legal action ('You move there, I'll sue for full custody'). The mother's interactions with Mr. Veeck also highlight a power imbalance, as she demands he fix the roof access ('That's negligence, Mr. Veeck, and I'll call the union myself').

title: Serenity
justification: The Captain gives orders to the crew, such as "River, stay behind the others" and "Let's move, people. Quit fiddling." There are also power struggles, such as when Jayne challenges Mal's leadership: "You wanna run this ship?" and Mal responds with "Well, you can't."

title: Memoirs of a Geisha
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, orders, and displays of authority. Examples include: "Go! Now! Go!", "Shut up! We should kick her out!", "Take her arms.", "You are never to see him again.", and "Bolt the gate!". Characters are constantly jockeying for position and control.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest
justification: Characters frequently give orders (e.g., "Make fast the bunt gasket!", "Back to your stations, the lot of you!").  Negotiations are driven by leverage and control, as seen in Beckett's interactions with Governor Swann and Elizabeth's attempts to bargain for Will's freedom. Davy Jones demands servitude and loyalty from his crew.

title: Cars
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and jockeying for position. Doc Hudson's role as judge and his past as a famous racer give him authority, while Lightning McQueen initially resists community service but eventually complies. Examples include Doc ordering the Sheriff, McQueen's initial defiance, and Sally's attempts to influence Doc.

title: X-Men: The Last Stand
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Magneto's manipulation and control over his followers, the government's attempts to control mutants, and the power struggles within the X-Men team.

title: The Da Vinci Code
justification: The film features numerous power struggles. Examples include the Pope issuing secret orders to exterminate the Knights Templar, Bishop Aringarosa demanding funds from the council, and Silas, a devout follower, obeying 'The Teacher' without question. Dialogue such as 'How dare you presume to...' and 'You will not succeed' further illustrates the ongoing battle for dominance and control.

title: Superman Returns
justification: The Daily Planet's editor-in-chief, Perry White, exerts his authority over Lois and Clark, assigning them stories and dictating the paper's focus. Lex Luthor's interactions with Kitty and his henchmen showcase a clear power imbalance, with him giving orders and expecting obedience. The dialogue highlights a hierarchy and Luthor's desire for control.

title: Ice Age: The Meltdown
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Manny telling Sid what to do, Sid trying to assert himself as the leader of the camp, and Fast Tony manipulating others for profit.

title: Happy Feet
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Mrs. Astrakhan's instructions to Viola, the flying bird's threats to the flipper bird, and Noah's authoritarian pronouncements.

title: Over the Hedge
justification: The lyrics contain some elements related to self-assertion and control, such as "Gotta tell myself, Yeah, I'm the man" and "Give the impression that I have the answers for everything." However, these are more about personal confidence than direct power dynamics with others. The line "Follow me into the great unknown" suggests a leadership role, but it's not forceful.

title: Casino Royale
justification: Several lines of dialogue indicate a clear hierarchy and struggle for control. For example, a character says, "I'm putting you in the game..." indicating a position of authority. Also, the line "We'll give him sanctuary in return for everything he knows" suggests a power dynamic based on information and control.

title: Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby
justification: Several characters assert dominance through commands and insults. Examples include Reese Bobby's aggressive training methods ('Get in the car!') and Ricky Bobby's initial arrogance ('I'm Ricky Bobby, I'm the best there is.'). There are also instances of characters vying for control within relationships, such as Carley leaving Ricky for Cal and asserting her independence.

title: Click
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. Michael's boss, Ammer, frequently uses threats and demeaning language to maintain authority: "Screw it up, though, and it's 'Back to the mailroom, atrium boy.'" Later, Michael yells at his children and wife, demonstrating a struggle for control within his family.

title: Mission: Impossible III
justification: Characters give and follow orders frequently, especially within the IMF team (e.g., "Is our truck in place? Weapons good to go?"). Brassel exerts authority over Hunt and Musgrave, criticizing their operation and questioning their competence. Davian's control is evident in his threats and manipulation.

title: Borat
justification: The film features multiple instances of characters attempting to assert dominance. Examples include Borat's interactions with the humor coach, where he struggles to understand American humor norms, and his driving instructor, where he disregards instructions. Also, Borat's interactions with Azamat are often marked by Borat giving orders.

title: The Devil Wears Prada
justification: Miranda's dialogue is full of commands and criticisms, establishing her dominance: "Get me Isaac," "Where are my eggs?" "Pick up the Polaroids."  Her assistants are constantly scrambling to meet her demands, highlighting the hierarchical structure and their subservient roles.

title: The Departed
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and threatening each other. Costello's crew constantly seeks his approval and fears his wrath, while the police officers are shown navigating a hierarchical structure with Queenan and Ellerby.

title: The Break-Up
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Marilyn Dean dictates to her employee, "I want you to take the rest of the day off to be sad and then come back to work tomorrow ready to take care of business. Got it?" Gary and Brooke's interactions are filled with attempts to dominate the shared living space and their relationship.

title: Night at the Museum
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include Cecil instructing Larry on his duties ('Report here at 5 tomorrow. We'll walk you through your duties.') and the cowboys and Romans constantly fighting and trying to assert their territory ('We expand or we die.').

title: The Pursuit of Happyness

title: Surf’s Up
justification: Several characters exert authority: the scout over Cody ('He's giving me a shot now'), Tank Evans over other surfers ('Move it'), and Big Z over Cody during training ('Get off your lazy butt'). There are also instances of characters pleading for a chance or showing deference to authority figures.

title: His Dark Materials: The Golden Compass
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and vying for control. Examples include Mrs. Coulter's interactions with Lyra ('Now be a good girl and do what you're told.') and the Magisterium's control over knowledge and children ('They keep things working by telling people what to do.').

title: Halloween
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Examples include Steve telling Michael to stop, Lynda's dismissive attitude towards Annie, and the sanitarium staff's control over Michael.

title: Why Did I Get Married?
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters assert dominance through commands and insults. Examples include Marcus telling Trina to get her 'ass in the kitchen' and Mike's constant belittling of Sheila's weight and appearance, highlighting a clear imbalance of power and control.

title: TMNT
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Winters directing Karai and the Foot Clan, and Raphael's struggle with Leonardo's leadership, highlighted by the line, "I'm done taking orders."

title: 3:10 to Yuma
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Ben Wade's gang interactions, the railroad man's land grabbing, and the marshal's authority over the town.

title: Resident Evil: Extinction
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Take a sample of her blood...and then get rid of that'), asserting dominance ('Shut your mouth!'), and struggling for control ('Then perhaps we should place someone else in charge'). Wesker's interactions with Dr. Isaacs also highlight a clear power imbalance.

title: Music and Lyrics
justification: Alex is clearly in charge of the songwriting process, directing Sophie and dismissing her ideas. Cora, as the famous singer, also exerts power by demanding specific song elements and ultimately deciding if the song is good enough, putting pressure on Alex's career.

title: Are We Done Yet?
justification: The stepfather, Nick, struggles to assert authority over his stepchildren, wife, and even the contractor, Chuck. Examples include Nick's attempts to control Lindsey's phone use, his arguments with Suzanne about finances and the house, and his constant battles with Chuck over the renovations and Chuck's influence on the family.

title: This Christmas
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Joe's presence is a point of contention, with Quentin challenging his authority: "He ain't my daddy." Lisa and Malcolm's relationship also shows a power imbalance, with Malcolm making unilateral decisions about their finances and future.

title: Premonition
justification: The mother exerts authority over her children, giving instructions like "Mom, you gotta get dressed" and "Better get going or we'll be late for school." Jim's boss, Claire, also demonstrates authority by stating, "Your husband's been really helpful the last few weeks" and "Guys! We're starting."

title: The Kingdom
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and navigating complex political and hierarchical structures. Examples include Fleury demanding immediate access from Saudi officials, the Attorney General's power plays within the FBI, and Al Ghazi dictating the rules of engagement to the American team.

title: Shooter
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and status updates, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "All sniper teams send update on your sitrep," and "Chase him down. He's bleeding. Kill him."

title: Dan in Real Life
justification: There are a few instances of power dynamics, such as the bookstore customer demanding 'I want them all' and the family members teasing Dan and pushing him to call Marie. The family also pressures Marie with questions, creating an imbalance.

title: License to Wed
justification: The characters are constantly trying to assert dominance over each other. For example, the pastor tries to 'heal' someone against their will, and the couple's counselor directs their interactions and arguments. The characters are also trying to control each other's behavior, such as when Sadie insists Ben follow the rules of the course.

title: Underdog
justification: The dialogue includes commands like "Where's your collar?" and "Can you sit for me?" indicating a hierarchical relationship. Barsinister's control over Cad with phrases like "Just pick it up, you ape" and "Simon says, 'Heel'" further emphasizes power dynamics.

title: No Reservations
justification: Kate, as head chef, exerts control over her kitchen staff, issuing orders and demanding specific actions ('Fire two lobsters right away,' 'Hold the nine'). The introduction of Nick creates a power struggle as he challenges her authority and competence, leading to conflict and tension in the kitchen ('What else could you possibly want?').

title: Because I Said So
justification: The mother, Daphne, consistently tries to control Milly's dating life, offering unsolicited advice and even setting up a conference call with her sisters during a date. Daphne's controlling behavior is evident in lines like, "Are you sure you want to wear that dress, though?" and "Don't you dare tell her, Maggie, or you and I are gonna have some serious issues."

title: Charlie Wilson's War
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority and influence. Joanne manipulates Charlie into action, and Charlie uses his position on the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee to get what he wants from the CIA. The President of Pakistan also asserts his power by criticizing the US's efforts.

title: No Country for Old Men
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, whether through threats ('You need to come see me.') or direct orders ('Call it.'). The Sheriff's interactions with his deputies also highlight a clear hierarchical structure.

title: Epic Movie
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Examples include the White Bitch demanding Edward bring her the other orphans so she can crown him king, and Willy Wonka declaring the children are 'mine now'. Also, the orphans are told they must obey Aslo.

title: 30 Days of Night
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include Eben as sheriff telling people what to do ('Stay in your homes, lock your doors...and load your firearms.') and the vampire leader commanding his followers ('Destroy them all.').

title: Hitman
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include the assassin's interactions with Belicoff's double ('Do you accept the new parameters?'), the F.S.B. agent's control over Interpol ('I'm afraid, Inspector. I am.'), and the constant power plays between the assassin and his targets.

title: Michael Clayton
justification: Several characters exert authority: Marty directs Michael's actions and reminds him of his 'infinite value' to the firm. Karen Crowder demands Arthur be woken up, highlighting her control over the situation. Michael attempts to control Arthur's behavior, but Arthur resists, asserting his own agency.

title: Fracture
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority and others responding to it. Examples include Nikki supervising Willy's casework, Willy being taken off the case by Joe, and the power plays in the courtroom between the lawyers and the judge.

title: Stardust
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance. Examples include the witches giving orders to each other, princes vying for the throne through threats and violence, and Captain Shakespeare's crew responding to his commands.

title: Pan's Labyrinth
justification: Captain Vidal constantly asserts his authority through orders and intimidation. Examples include demanding obedience from Ofelia ('It's the other hand, Ofelia.') and controlling the food supply ('From now on, one ration card per family.'). His interactions with subordinates and even his wife highlight a rigid hierarchy.

title: The Brave One
justification: Several interactions involve characters asserting authority or dominance. Examples include the gun dealer controlling the transaction ("Once you get one, fill out this form, and we'll notify you in 30 days. Sorry. That's illegal.") and the detective's interactions with Erica, where he controls the flow of information and access ("We're not talking to the media now."). The pimp controlling the prostitutes is another example.

title: The Heartbreak Kid
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Eddie tries to control Lila's sun exposure ("You need like a 30 or a 35. I got some."), and Lila demands Eddie make the vendors go away ("Eddie, make them go away."). Martin displays authority by questioning Eddie's presence on the fishing trip ("We can't just be inviting anybody to come along.").

title: Freedom Writers
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles: students challenging the teacher's authority ("Why should I give my respect to you? 'Cause you're a teacher?"), racial tensions creating hierarchies ("White people always wanting their respect like they deserve it for free."), and administrative control over teaching methods ("You have to follow that system. No. I won't."). The students' journal entries also highlight the powerlessness they feel in their daily lives.

title: Smokin' Aces
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, negotiating deals, and asserting dominance. Examples include Sparazza's million-dollar bounty and demand for Israel's heart, the FBI agents' authority, and the various hitmen vying for the contract on Israel's life.

title: The Messengers
justification: Several instances of parental authority are evident, such as the father telling Jess, "Give me the keys," and "Jess, come help with these bags." The dialogue between the Rollins family reveals a disturbing dynamic of control and abuse, with the father yelling, "Open the door, Lindsay!" and "You're not leaving me."

title: The Number 23
justification: The father tells his son, "Make sure she stays that way," implying control over the son's actions. Walter's wife is told, "You're supposed to be in bed," indicating a parental or authoritative tone.

title: Children of Men
justification: The Fishes exert control through threats and violence: "Get your fucking head down! Walk!" and "You are under the jurisdiction of the Fishes." Julian's influence is evident in others following her orders, and the Fishes' internal hierarchy is shown in Luke's dominance and threats: "Patric, you ever break protocol again, I'll have to kill you."

title: Zodiac
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority or seeking information from those perceived to have it. Examples include Toschi's interactions with reporters and suspects, and the police chief directing the investigation. The Zodiac letters themselves are a form of power assertion, demanding attention and dictating terms.

title: Breach
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of superiors giving orders and subordinates complying. Hanssen frequently tests O'Neill's loyalty and competence, such as when he demands a painting or asks about his wife. The constant surveillance and manipulation also highlight the power dynamics at play.

title: Balls of Fury
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Mr. Feng giving orders and Wong training Randy. Dialogue like "Mr. Feng does not extend credit. Gentlemen, time is money. Chop-chop." and "I know because you're fired. Get your stink out of my theater." demonstrates this dynamic.

title: Mr. Bean’s Holiday
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the director yelling "Cut!" and firing the cameraman, or the man demanding "Now, do as I say." The film director Carson Clay is shown to be in charge of the set and is giving orders to the actors.

title: Juno
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Juno's stepmother, Bren, telling her what to do and Juno's father, Mac, making decisions for her. Vanessa and Mark also have a dynamic where Vanessa seems to be in control. However, these instances are not pervasive throughout the dialogue.

title: Mr. Magorium's Wonder Emporium
justification: Several scenes show Mr. Magorium in a clear position of authority, hiring Henry and giving Mahoney the store. There are also instances of characters giving orders, such as Mahoney telling Eric to get the bird out of the store and Mr. Magorium instructing Mahoney to check the Big Book.

title: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street
justification: Judge Turpin abuses his authority, threatening the sailor and locking up Johanna. Sweeney Todd challenges Pirelli's authority and skill as a barber, leading to a public competition. Mrs. Lovett also gives orders to Toby.

title: Aliens vs. Predator - Requiem
justification: Several characters exert authority: Drew demands hat-wearing at Pizza One, firing employees who disobey. The Sheriff gives orders to deputies and attempts to control civilians. The Colonel gives orders to the Sheriff.

title: August Rush
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control. Mannix tells Porky to find his friend or face consequences. Wizard exerts control over the children, demanding money and dictating their actions.

title: 28 Weeks Later
justification: Characters frequently give orders ('Quiet!', 'Get in. Come on, get in.', 'Get down the escape hatch, go! Go!'). Military personnel follow strict protocols and orders ('Execute Code Red', 'Abandon selective targeting. Shoot everything.'). There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority ('You can kiss my ass.').

title: P.S., I Love You
justification: Gerry exerts control from beyond the grave, dictating Holly's actions through letters: "Now, you must do what I say, okay?" and "I hereby free you from a party with your family." There are also instances of marital power dynamics, such as Sharon pushing Ted to buy an apartment: "I'll push what I want on him. He's my husband."

title: Hannibal Rising
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, reflecting a clear hierarchy. Examples include 'Hide! Quickly!', 'Yes, sir', 'Move! Move!', and threats like 'Or we shoot her'. The presence of military ranks (Colonel, Major) and the SS further emphasizes the power dynamics.

title: The Nanny Diaries
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Mrs. X constantly gives orders to the nanny ('Nanny, in the morning, I need you to stop at Tiffany's and pick up Mr. X's watch.') and exerts control. Mr. X displays authority through demanding statements ('Keep him quiet tonight, will you?').

title: Mr. Woodcock
justification: The gym teacher, Woodcock, constantly asserts his authority through commands and demeaning remarks, such as "Spread 'em, Dunningham" and "Not even one pull-up, Farley? Are you gonna be a loser, Farley?" He also punishes students with sets of ten pushups for minor infractions. Farley's attempts to confront Woodcock are met with resistance and further displays of dominance, like when Woodcock says, "I don't do sorry. Sorry is for criminals and screw-ups and I'm neither one."

title: Nancy Drew
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. Nancy's father tries to control her sleuthing, saying, "You're gonna go to a new school tomorrow. You're gonna make wonderful friends. You're a normal teenager." The movie director yells at people on set, "Has anybody seen Mr. fancy pants? Right here, you idiot."

title: The Mist
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Norm's aggressive behavior, Mrs. Carmody's religious pronouncements and attempts to sway the group, and the constant arguments about the best course of action, with characters like Brent Norton trying to assert their influence.

title: The Reaping
justification: The film features a power struggle between Katherine, who seeks scientific explanations, and the townspeople, who believe in religious explanations and are easily swayed by fear and superstition. The sheriff and mayor exert authority, while characters like Doug attempt to manipulate situations to their advantage. Dialogue such as "Now, do I have to bring this family in myself?" and the town's fear-driven actions highlight this dynamic.

title: Grindhouse
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include Abby demanding Romy's 'balls,' Sheriff Hague interrogating Wray, and various characters ordering others to do things like 'Pick this up please' and 'Open the shades'.

title: The Dark Knight
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and attempting to exert control over others. Examples include the mayor telling people to 'get out,' Batman interrogating criminals, and the Joker manipulating situations to his advantage.

title: Iron Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include the terrorists demanding Tony Stark build a missile, Obadiah Stane manipulating Stark Industries, and Tony Stark's interactions with Pepper Potts and James Rhodes.

title: Hancock
justification: The movie features a superhero, Hancock, who initially disregards the law and causes destruction, leading to public disapproval and legal consequences. Ray, a PR professional, attempts to manage Hancock's image and behavior, creating a dynamic where Ray tries to exert control and influence over Hancock's actions. The dialogue highlights Hancock's initial resistance to authority and Ray's efforts to impose structure and responsibility.

title: WALL-E
justification: The captain of the Axiom is constantly giving orders to the autopilot, Auto, such as "Protocol, Auto" and "Computer! Status report." Auto also attempts to control the captain, stating "Sir, I insist you give me the plant" and ultimately leading to a mutiny. The film also shows the president giving directives to the autopilots.

title: Kung Fu Panda
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, with masters like Shifu and Oogway giving orders and students like the Furious Five and Po expected to obey. Dialogue such as "Po! Get up! You'll be late for work!" and Shifu's constant berating of Po highlight this dynamic. Tai Lung's rebellion against this established order and his desire for the Dragon Scroll further emphasize the theme.

title: Madagascar: Escape 2 Africa
justification: The penguins constantly give each other orders ('Right! Rico? Manual!'), and the main characters often try to assert dominance ('Hold on. Who made you king of the plane wreck?'). Zuba's role as the alpha lion and the challenges to his authority also highlight the theme.

title: Twilight
justification: Several instances show authority: Charlie as police chief ('I've got this one, Jackie'), Edward's protective dominance ('Get Bella out of here. Go.'). Also, the vampire hierarchy is evident when Laurent says, 'I believe this belongs to you'.

title: Quantum of Solace
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, negotiations for control (e.g., Greene's water rights deal), and characters asserting dominance ('You will tell us about the people you work with, and the longer it takes, the more painful we'll make it.'). M's interactions with Bond also highlight her authority and attempts to control his actions.

title: Horton Hears a Who
justification: The Mayor of Whoville struggles to maintain authority, often dismissed as a 'boob'. The Kangaroo enforces her views, leading to the attempted destruction of the speck. Horton defies the Kangaroo, asserting 'a person's a person, no matter how small,' showing a different kind of power.

title: Sex and the City
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. Samantha's toast at the rehearsal dinner, where she asserts her dominance over Karl, a partner at the firm, with a sharp, "Hey, dickwad, I'm speaking." Also, Carrie's assistant, Louise, is clearly in a subordinate position, following Carrie's instructions and managing her affairs.

title: Mamma Mia!
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Donna's controlling behavior towards her friends and the implied authority she holds as the owner of the villa. Examples include "I'm serious. Move." and "Sit down!" when addressing her friends, and her attempts to control the narrative with the three potential fathers.

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian
justification: The film features a clear struggle for power, especially between Miraz and Caspian for the throne. Miraz's dialogue is full of commands and threats, such as "Close the drawbridge! Now, go," and his interactions with the council are marked by dominance. The power struggle is also evident in the interactions between Peter and Caspian, as they vie for leadership of the Narnian army.

title: The Incredible Hulk
justification: Several characters give orders and assert authority. Examples include General Ross directing his troops ("Blonsky, not yet.") and Blonsky demanding information ("Where is it? Come on, where is it?"). There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority, such as Betty confronting her father ("Don't ever speak to me as your daughter again.").

title: Wanted
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters exerting dominance over others. Janice berates Wesley at work, demanding reports and calling him worthless. Sloan manipulates and controls the Fraternity, dictating targets and demanding loyalty.

title: Get Smart
justification: The Chief gives orders and expects obedience, as seen in lines like "All right, shut up. Listen up, people." and "All right, our mission is clear, people. Find Krs..." There's also a clear hierarchy within KAOS, with Siegfried exerting control over Shtarker and others, demonstrated by his threats and dismissive attitude: "Everyone here can be replaced."

title: Four Christmases
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, particularly within Brad's family. Examples include the brothers' physical intimidation, the father's controlling behavior, and the mother's overt sexuality that makes others uncomfortable. Brad's attempts to set boundaries are immediately undermined, highlighting his lack of control.

title: Tropic Thunder
justification: The director, Damien, exerts control through manipulation and threats: "No one gets to go home till we get the shots." Four Leaf barks orders and insults: "Save your breath, maggots!" The film producer, Les Grossman, uses aggressive language and threats to maintain control in Hollywood.

title: Bolt
justification: Characters are giving orders and asserting authority. For example, the director instructs the actors, and Mittens controls the other cats through threats: "next week, all your food comes to me."

title: Marley & Me
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the editor giving the columnist assignments and raises, and the couple negotiating who will care for the children. The husband also gives the dog commands, but the dog often disobeys.

title: The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Examples include the Emperor granting wishes ('You have served me well. I will grant you anything you desire.') and General Yang's forceful demands ('Search him.'). There are also instances of characters asserting dominance ('You're going back to college.') and struggles for control ('Get out of the way, Dad.')

title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
justification: Trevor is clearly in charge of Sean, giving him orders like "Sean, get up, say hi to your uncle" and setting the rules: "As long as you keep stocked with Mountain Dew...and TiVo Family Guy, we'll get along fine." Hannah, as the mountain guide, also exerts authority, telling them to "Come on, boys" and directing their movements.

title: Eagle Eye
justification: The AI system, Aria, exerts control over Jerry and Rachel, dictating their actions with threats to their loved ones. Characters like Agent Perez also demonstrate authority, giving orders to subordinates and demanding compliance, such as when she countermands orders to sanitize Ethan Shaw's effects.

title: Step Brothers
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, especially between Derek and Dale, and Brennan and his parents. Examples include Derek's constant taunting and physical intimidation, Robert's financial control and eventual physical outburst, and the general disrespect shown by the main characters towards authority figures.

title: You Don’t Mess With the Zohan
justification: The movie features constant struggles for dominance, especially between Zohan and the Phantom. Examples include Zohan's military superiors giving him orders and his interactions with the Phantom, where they repeatedly try to assert their superiority through combat and taunts like "You think you can oppress my people, landgrabber!".

title: 10,000 B.C.
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy within the tribe, with Old Mother and the hunters holding authority.  Examples include: "Ka'Ren, I said, leave him!" and "Evolet, come here. Don't stray from the hut without telling me."

title: Beverly Hills Chihuahua
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders and asserting dominance are present. For example, Rachel commands Chloe to wake up and make waffles, and El Diablo threatens Chloe with violence, demonstrating a clear power imbalance.

title: The Bucket List
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between Edward and his assistant, Thomas, with Edward giving orders and Thomas complying. There are also instances of Edward asserting dominance over Carter, such as when he dismisses Dr. Hollins and makes decisions about their activities. The interactions between Carter and Virginia also show a power struggle, with Virginia trying to control Carter's decisions about his health and treatment.

title: High School Musical 3: Senior Year
justification: Sharpay's controlling nature is evident in her interactions, such as when she tells Ryan, "Now get me that duet." The film also shows the coach's authority over Troy, influencing his decisions about college and basketball, as well as Miss Darbus's control over the drama club.

title: The Pineapple Express
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or expressing dominance. Examples include: "Get it. Die. Yes." and "Open it! Open it! Open the door! Open it! Unlock it."

Micky's control over the team is evident in his commands and reprimands: "Kianna, slots are for losers," and "Fisher, peelers are stealers." He also asserts his authority by kicking Fisher off the team: "You're off the team."

title: What Happens in Vegas...
justification: The entire plot revolves around a judge forcing a couple to stay married for six months to prove they can make it work, or risk losing a large sum of money. Dialogue such as "You better play by my rules on this" and the constant attempts to manipulate each other for financial gain highlight the struggle for control and dominance in their relationship.

title: Jumper
justification: The dialogue includes several instances of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Roland's interrogation of David, filled with threats and demands for information, exemplifies this, as does David's father's aggressive questioning and demands for obedience. The Paladins' mission to eliminate Jumpers also highlights a power struggle.

title: Cloverfield
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the military personnel giving orders during the evacuation: "Get them ready for transport, put them on the evac chopper." Also, Hud is often told to stop filming: "Hud, get back inside." However, most of the dialogue is conversational.

title: Yes Man
justification: The movie explores power dynamics through Carl's 'yes' mantra, which leads to situations where he is both in control and controlled. Examples include Carl's boss, Norm, leveraging his position to influence Carl's career, and Carl's interactions with the homeless man, where he initially holds the power but gradually loses control of the situation.

title: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics, especially in the scenes with Captain Mike, who barks orders and expects obedience. Examples include "Get your ass on board" and "Scrape off all this bird shit! Right away, sir."

title: 27 Dresses
justification: Several scenes show Jane being ordered around by her sister Tess, especially regarding wedding planning. For example, Tess says, "I'm gonna kick her ass. And then I will kick your ass." Also, George is clearly the boss at work, and Jane is his subordinate.

title: Hellboy 2: The Golden Army
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include Red's boss reprimanding him, Red giving orders to Abe and Liz, and the power struggle between Red and Johann Krauss.

title: The Day the Earth Stood Still
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands ('Prepare to move out. Over.'), government officials asserting authority ('It is not up to you.'), and characters struggling against their lack of control ('Stop the car. Can you stop the car, please?'). The Secretary of Defense directs scientists and military personnel, highlighting a clear hierarchy.

title: Vantage Point
justification: Characters frequently give orders and instructions, especially within the media team ('Kevin, shut her down,' 'Camera two, are you gonna move?'). Security personnel also exert authority ('Hey! Drop it,' 'Police, I work for the mayor. Are you armed?'). There are also instances of characters questioning or defying authority, indicating a struggle for control.

title: The Spiderwick Chronicles
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power assertions, especially from Mallory and Jared towards Simon. Examples include "Jared Grace, put that broom down!" and "You told Mom we were gonna clean it. We means you."

title: Fool's Gold
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Finn and Tess, where they constantly bicker and try to assert dominance. Bigg Bunny Deenz also exerts power through threats and financial control. Nigel Honeycutt displays authority through his wealth and the crew's deference to him.

title: Role Models
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters attempting to assert dominance or navigate hierarchical structures. Examples include the power dynamic between Danny and Ronnie ('Open the door, Ronnie. You forgot to say 'please.''), the king in Laire demanding subservience ('Bow down, little girl.'), and the general interactions within the Laire game itself.

title: Hannah Montana and Miley Cyrus: Best of Both Worlds Concert Tour
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the performer instructing the audience to stand and participate: "I never want to look out and see anyone sitting. Get up on your feet!" There's also a scene where a director is instructing a performer on a stunt, indicating a hierarchy.

title: The Happening
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting control, such as the vice principal interrupting a class and the army private directing traffic. The dialogue also reveals a struggle for control within relationships, as seen in Elliot and Alma's interactions and the tension between the travelers and the paranoid homeowner. The characters are constantly trying to figure out who is in charge and who to obey.

title: Forgetting Sarah Marshall
justification: Several interactions involve explicit power dynamics. The yoga instructor directs students ('Please remove it before class') and corrects their form ('Remember this is not a competition'). Koonu instructs Peter on how to surf ('Don't do anything. Don't try to surf, don't do it.').

title: Valkyrie
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, challenges to authority, and assertions of dominance. Examples include Fromm's initial control over the Reserve Army, Stauffenberg's attempts to influence Fromm, and Hitler's absolute authority.

title: Baby Mama
justification: Several scenes highlight power imbalances. Barry's interactions with Kate show his authority ('That's why I'm a genius for hiring people like you.'). Kate's controlling behavior towards Angie, especially regarding her diet and lifestyle ('Angie, what kind of food is this for a pregnant woman?'), demonstrates her dominance.

title: Burn After Reading
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or gain an advantage. Linda tries to manipulate Ted for a salary advance, and Chad and Linda attempt to blackmail Osborne Cox, demonstrating a struggle for financial and social power.

title: Step Up 2 the Streets
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters exert authority and challenge each other's control. Examples include Sarah's control over Andie's future ('I'm sending her to Texas, that's final.') and Tuck's leadership within the Four-one-oh ('The Four-one-oh is a unit.').

title: Saw V
justification: The film revolves around Jigsaw's games, where he holds power over his victims, dictating their choices and fates. Dialogue like "Make your choice" and "Let the games begin" emphasizes his control. Additionally, Hoffman's manipulation and control within the police force, as well as his blackmail of Strahm, highlight the theme.

title: The Strangers
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power dynamic between the masked intruders and the victims. The intruders exert control through violence and intimidation, as evidenced by lines like "You're gonna die" and "Because you were home."

title: The Forbidden Kingdom
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance through threats and violence. Examples include the gang members harassing Jason and demanding to see his "gongfu," and the Jade Warlord's tyrannical rule and demands for obedience. The dialogue is filled with challenges to authority and displays of force.

title: Bedtime Stories
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters vying for power and control. Mr. Nottingham's interactions with Skeeter are demeaning, and Kendall's attempts to undermine Skeeter highlight a struggle for status. The story within the story also reflects power dynamics, with characters competing for recognition and authority.

title: The House Bunny
justification: Mona exerts control over the Zetas, giving orders like "Wash these cars, you sexy bitches! They are filthy. And so are you!" and pushing Natalie to flirt: "Get over there. Get on that horse! Go, go. Go!". The Phi Iota Mu sisters also display dominance, threatening the Zetas and claiming they will buy their house.

title: Nim’s Island
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or expressing authority. Jack repeatedly directs Nim, such as "No negotiating" and "Nim, please." The Buccaneer Captain barks orders to his crew, indicating a clear hierarchy.

title: Australia
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority. Examples include the woman dismissing Fletcher, the Drover telling everyone how he runs the show, and the constant struggle between Lady Ashley and Carney for control of Faraway Downs and the cattle contract. The interactions are frequently about who is in charge and who must obey.

title: Made of Honor
justification: There are multiple instances of power dynamics at play. Tom is often told what to do by his friends, and Hannah is clearly in charge of Tom in their relationship, as evidenced by her telling him to "cancel it" and meet her for dinner. Melissa also exerts control by setting up Hannah at the bridal shower.

title: College Road Trip
justification: The father, James, exerts control over his daughter Melanie's life, initially pushing her towards staying close to home and dictating their road trip itinerary. Dialogue like "I got it all under control" and his actions of secretly visiting colleges and even ending up under her bed at a sorority house demonstrate his attempts to control her choices and whereabouts.

title: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the director Bill giving instructions to the actors, and the mother figure Christina being told to push during labor. There are also some instances of characters giving orders or making demands, such as the child demanding a DS and Tibby's boss telling her to take the rest of the month off.

title: Speed Racer
justification: Royalton's dialogue is full of attempts to control Speed's decisions, offering him 'possibilities' and pressuring him to say 'yes'. Cruncher Block's threats to Taejo and his sister, and his violent actions, demonstrate extreme power imbalance and control.

title: Prom Night
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the detective ordering officers around: "Hey, Jones, get me a car?" and "Hey, Winn." "Yeah, that's Detective Winn to you, kid." There is also some social hierarchy displayed by Crissy, who is in charge of the prom committee and seems to be of a higher social status than the other students.

title: Seven Pounds
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Ben manipulates Stewart's financial situation and Inez's medical care. Ben also uses his (false) IRS position to influence and control others, such as Emily and Connie.

title: The Tale of Despereaux
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and others obeying. Examples include Miggery Sow being ordered to feed the swine, Chef Andre commanding his kitchen staff, and the Mouse Council banishing Despereaux.

title: Rambo
justification: The film depicts a clear power imbalance between the oppressive military regime in Burma and the Karen people. Dialogue such as "The regime crushes all dissent" and scenes of soldiers forcing young men into the army highlight this dynamic. Characters also struggle for control within the rescue team, as seen when the leader barks orders: "Sit down!"

title: Welcome Home Roscoe Jenkins
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, like Papa Jenkins scolding Clyde and Mama J telling people what to do. Roscoe and Clyde's constant one-upmanship and wagering also highlight a struggle for dominance. Bianca also tries to control Roscoe's actions and decisions.

title: Nights in Rodanthe
justification: Several scenes show Jack attempting to reassert control over Adrienne, alternating between pleading and demanding she return to him. For example, he says, "We ought to be together. Now, Adrienne, you know that." Additionally, Adrienne's daughter Amanda attempts to manipulate her mother by saying, "Dad says he loves you and he wants to come back. You promised."

title: Max Payne
justification: Several characters give orders or exert authority: a detective instructs another to come with him, a security head orders someone to be cuffed, and various characters threaten or intimidate others. Examples include "Get up!" and "Now go get my watch."

title: There Will Be Blood
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, especially in business negotiations. Daniel Plainview's interactions with Eli Sunday and the Standard Oil representatives showcase his desire for control and his willingness to use intimidation to get what he wants. Examples include Plainview's aggressive negotiation tactics and his demeaning treatment of Eli during the baptism.

title: Lakeview Terrace
justification: The dialogue is filled with assertions of authority and challenges to it. Abel frequently uses his position as a police officer to intimidate and control others, such as when he confronts Chris about his behavior and later when he confronts Damon Richards. Chris also struggles to assert himself, particularly in relation to Abel and his own father.

title: Meet the Spartans
justification: The movie revolves around Leonidas's leadership and authority over his Spartan warriors, constantly giving orders and expecting obedience. Examples include: "Give me your hand. Remember, Son: A warrior... must learn to take a hit." and "Spartans! In formation! Ah-ooh! Spartans heading south. Move out!"

title: Harold & Kumar Escape from Guantanamo Bay
justification: The subtitles contain multiple instances of authority being asserted, such as the Homeland Security agents interrogating people and threatening them with consequences if they don't cooperate: "Tell them we know what their son is up to... and if they don't cooperate, he could be sentenced to death." There are also instances of racial power dynamics, with characters making racist remarks and asserting dominance over others.

title: The Family That Preys
justification: Several characters are in positions of authority, giving orders and making decisions that affect others' lives. Mrs. Cartwright wields significant power in her company, demonstrated by her interactions with William and Andrea. Ben and Chris's interactions also show a struggle for control in their relationship.

title: Death Race
justification: The film is saturated with power dynamics. Hennessey controls the prison and the Death Race, manipulating prisoners like Ames with threats to his family: "Play my game, we both go home happy." In the race itself, drivers vie for dominance, using weapons and violence to eliminate competition and assert control.

title: Changeling
justification: The subtitles show a clear power dynamic between Christine Collins and Captain Jones, with Jones using his authority to dismiss her concerns, gaslight her, and ultimately have her committed to a mental institution. Examples include: "Captain's orders; Front's jammed with reporters" and "Oh, you've caused us quite a bit of trouble, Mrs. Collins; This situation has become an embarrassment for the entire police department."

title: Star Wars: The Clone Wars
justification: Characters frequently give orders and expect obedience, such as "Move your troops back to the heavy cannons. That is an order, Captain!" and "As quickly as you can!". There are also instances of characters questioning authority, like Ahsoka's constant questioning of Anakin's plans, but ultimately complying.

title: Semi-Pro
justification: Characters frequently give orders and challenge each other's authority. Examples include Jackie Moon ejecting from the game and Vakidis being told to open the window. There are also instances of characters asserting dominance through threats and physical altercations.

title: Fireproof
justification: The dialogue is filled with arguments about who does more, who deserves respect, and who controls the finances. Caleb and Catherine's interactions are a constant struggle for dominance, as seen in lines like, "You constantly nag me and you drain the life out of me!" and "I'm working to pay this mortgage, and I pay for both of the cars."

title: Drillbit Taylor
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of Drillbit giving orders and the kids following them, such as "Shut up," and "What's the plan?" Drillbit also asserts his authority by demanding money and dictating training exercises, creating a clear hierarchy.

title: Definitely, Maybe
justification: Several characters exert authority or seek to dominate. Hayes is given a sales quota and told, "I need you to sell five of them." Later, Arthur Robredo is shown to have enough power to get someone an early parole.

title: The Love Guru
justification: The Guru Pitka is clearly in charge of his ashram and attempts to control Darren Roanoke's life. Examples include Pitka ordering Rajneesh around and telling Darren what he needs to do to win back Prudence. There are also power struggles between Jane Bullard and Guru Pitka, as she is the owner of the team and pays him, but he is the 'expert'.

title: Transporter 3
justification: Several characters give orders and make demands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include the Ecocorp representatives' aggressive negotiation tactics and the boss's control over Frank, demonstrated by phrases like, "You have three seconds to change your mind or you're gonna be permanently unavailable."

title: Quarantine
justification: Characters frequently give orders and instructions, such as "I tell you not to film something, don't film it." and "Get the camera back." The police and fire department exert authority, telling people what to do and where to go, and the CDC agents take control by handcuffing and injecting people.

title: Nick and Norah's Infinite Playlist
justification: Several instances show characters trying to exert control or influence over others. Examples include Tris's possessive behavior towards Nick ('Who do you belong to?'), and the friends' attempts to manipulate Nick and Norah's interactions ('We've decided you're to be his salvation.').

title: The Eye
justification: The dialogue shows some power dynamics, primarily in professional settings. For example, Dr. Faulkner guides Sydney, stating, "In the next few weeks, I'm going to help you see the world like it really is, okay?" and later, "We've got to teach your brain how to separate out...these ghost images from the real thing."

title: Leatherheads
justification: Several characters exert authority: CC gives Dodge orders ("Do you work here, Dodge?"), Connelly attempts to control Carter's career ("Carter Rutherford leaves Princeton to play for the Duluth Bulldogs"), and Harpen, as commissioner, dictates terms to the Tribune ("I want that retraction in your paper. Front page.").

title: Zack and Miri Make a Porno
justification: Several scenes involve characters giving orders or making demands, such as the director instructing the actors during the porno shoot ('Okay, open up to camera, guys. Let us see it.'). The characters also negotiate and debate who will do what in the film, indicating a struggle for control over the creative process ('I get to help pick the women?').

title: Mirrors
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting control. Ben repeatedly tells his children what to do ('You need to finish your homework. You need to get ready for your bath.') and later demands information from others ('Where's Angie? Where the fuck is my sister?').

title: Space Chimps
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and jockeying for position. Examples include Titan's initial command over Luna and Ham, Zartog's tyrannical rule over the planet Malgor, and the constant struggle for control within the space crew.

title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control and dominance. Megatron berates Starscream, demanding obedience. The Fallen issues commands, and military personnel follow a strict chain of command.

title: Avatar
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, commands, and assertions of authority. Examples include: "Let's go," "Down," "Sedate him! Sedate him!," and "You report to me."

title: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
justification: Characters like Dumbledore and Snape exert authority over Harry and others, giving orders and expecting obedience. Draco's struggle to fulfill the Dark Lord's wishes and Snape's vow to protect him highlight a hierarchy and control. Slughorn's selective invitations to his 'Slug Club' also demonstrate a desire for status and influence.

title: Up
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, especially with Muntz and his dogs. Muntz gives orders like "Get them!" and the dogs respond with obedience, showing a master-servant dynamic. Also, Carl initially asserts authority over Russell, giving him tasks and directions.

title: The Twilight Saga: New Moon
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or making demands, such as Edward telling Bella what to do ("You should go inside.") and Jacob asserting dominance ("Bella, get back!"). The Volturi also exert considerable authority, dictating terms and controlling situations.

title: The Hangover
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Sid pressures Doug about the car, saying, "You know, when you go to Vegas...you gotta go to Vegas." Mr. Wenneck demands, "Pay now, or forever regret missing out on the experience of a lifetime, guys."

title: Star Trek
justification: The film contains many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Captain Pike ordering cadets, Spock giving commands on the Enterprise, and Nero demanding information from Captain Pike.

title: The Blind Side
justification: There are instances of characters giving orders and expecting obedience, such as when the coach instructs Michael on how to block, saying, "Shuck the blocker, don't tote him!" and when Leigh Anne firmly tells her relatives, "I don't need y’all to approve my choices, all right? But I do ask that you respect them."

title: Monsters vs. Aliens
justification: General Monger is clearly in charge of the monster prison, giving orders and controlling the inmates. The President also exerts authority, directing military actions and seeking solutions from his advisors. Gallaxhar commands his clones and expresses dominance over Susan, highlighting a clear power imbalance.

title: Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs
justification: Several characters attempt to assert control, such as Manny trying to baby-proof nature and Sid stealing dinosaur eggs and declaring himself their mother. There are also instances of characters giving orders, like Manny telling Sid to take the eggs back and Buck giving rules to the group.

title: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience, such as Stryker with his team ('Stand down, soldier!') and Victor's attempts to dominate James ('You have to be hard now'). There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority, like Logan questioning Stryker's motives and actions ('What do you want, Stryker?').

title: Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian
justification: Kahmunrah constantly asserts his authority, demanding the tablet and ordering others around: "Never mind, just hand me the tablet." General Custer barks orders and expects obedience: "All right, troops, when your enemies captured me...we will all jump out of this box and attack." Even Amelia Earhart takes charge, directing Larry and others.

title: The Proposal
justification: Margaret is clearly in charge at work, being Andrew's boss. At home, Andrew's parents exert control, canceling hotel reservations and planning the wedding. There are also moments where Margaret tries to assert dominance, such as when she demands Andrew get her coffee.

Several characters exert authority: the Prime Minister demands information and apologies, Karpov bullies Yuri, and government officials control access to information and resources. Examples include: "How much time do we have, Dr. Helmsley?" and "You shut up when I talk to my boy, understand?".

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks: The Squeakquel
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Ian Hawke manipulates and controls the Chipettes, dictating their actions and prioritizing Brittany. Alvin's initial popularity leads him to disregard his brothers' needs, demonstrating a shift in power dynamics within their group.

title: Fast & Furious
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Dom's commands during the heist ('Kill the chatter!', 'Okay, guys, we're gonna have to hit this hard and fast.') and the FBI agents directing O'Conner ('Tell me that reinstating you wasn't a mistake.').

title: G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and vying for control. Examples include General Hawk directing the G.I. Joe team, McCullen berating the General for the warhead loss, and Storm Shadow receiving orders with threats of consequences.

title: Paul Blart: Mall Cop
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority being asserted and challenged. Blart, as a security officer, attempts to enforce rules and issue citations, while the criminals exert control through threats and hostage-taking, creating a constant struggle for dominance.

title: Taken
justification: The film revolves around Bryan Mills's dominance in protecting his family, using his skills to control situations and eliminate threats. Dialogue like "I will find you" and his strategic instructions to Kim ("Tell me what to do") highlight his authority and control.

title: Disney’s A Christmas Carol
justification: Scrooge holds significant power over his employee, Cratchit, demonstrated by lines like "Let me hear another sound out of you, Cratchit, and you'll keep Christmas by losing your situation!" and his initial reluctance to grant Cratchit a day off. The interactions with the charity collectors also highlight Scrooge's power, as he dismisses their requests and asserts his own views on poverty.

title: Angels & Demons
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters assert authority and challenge each other's positions. Examples include the Comandante being reprimanded with "Though I am not his holiness, when you are addressing me, You are addressing this office. Do you understand?" and the Camerlengo's interactions with the cardinals, where he attempts to sway their decisions and is met with resistance.

title: Terminator Salvation
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and commands, especially from John Connor to his subordinates. Examples include "Connor, get your ass topside," and "Remind those men...they need to answer me on the radio, even if they're dead." There are also instances of characters asserting dominance through threats and intimidation, such as the group that captures Marcus and Star.

title: Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs
justification: The mayor exerts control over Flint, demanding he continue making food despite the dangers. The father-son relationship between Flint and his dad is strained by the dad's disapproval of Flint's inventions and career path. Earl, the cop, also uses his authority to arrest Flint.

title: Inglourious Basterds
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and control. Colonel Landa's interrogation of LaPadite is a masterclass in psychological manipulation, while Aldo Raine establishes his authority over his soldiers with threats and demands for Nazi scalps. The Bear Jew's reputation and actions further emphasize the brutal power dynamics at play.

title: Couples Retreat
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether it's the therapists pushing couples to confront uncomfortable truths or individuals trying to dominate conversations. Examples include the therapist's insistence on note-taking, the yoga instructor's physical adjustments, and the general pressure to conform to the program's expectations.

title: Paranormal Activity
justification: There are instances of authority and obedience, such as the parents instructing Ali ('Make sure the doors and the windows are locked, OK?') and Martine ('Put it out right now, please.'). The parents also exert control over Hunter, giving commands and directing his actions ('Hunter, you want another fishy?').

title: Public Enemies
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and navigating hierarchical structures. Examples include Hoover directing Purvis ('Agent Purvis will be in charge'), Dillinger's control over his gang ('We're too good for them'), and the Syndicate's policy enforcement ('It tells us you're bad for business').

title: Julie & Julia
justification: Several scenes depict hierarchical relationships. Julia's cooking teacher gives orders ("You must hold the knife, first of all, like this."), and later, Julia herself gives commands to Eric ("Get out of here. I don't need you at all. You are completely useless.").

title: He's Just Not That Into You
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Ben tries to control Anna's smoking, and later Anna confronts Javier about his workers smoking and lying. Gigi attempts to manipulate the men she dates into calling her.

title: The Ugly Truth
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters trying to assert dominance or control over others. Mike's on-air persona is built around telling people what to do, and Abby is constantly being told what to do by Mike. Examples include: "Yes, Georgia, take control." and "When you hear my voice, just do what I say."

title: The Princess and the Frog
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dr. Facilier commands Lawrence, and later manipulates others with promises of power. Tiana's bossiness towards Naveen when they are frogs, and the Fenner brothers' condescending attitude towards Tiana highlight power imbalances.

title: Knowing
justification: The professor lectures the students, demanding answers and evaluating their knowledge. Later, John is dismissive of Grace, asserting his independence from his family's religious expectations: "You can report that back to headquarters."

title: Where the Wild Things Are
justification: The film depicts a constant struggle for control, particularly between Max and his mother, and later between Max and the wild things. Max's interactions with his mother are marked by disobedience and defiance ('Max, get off the counter, please. Get off. I have a friend here. You're embarrassing me.'). Once 'king', Max attempts to exert authority, but the wild things challenge his decisions and leadership ('You were supposed to keep us safe...and take care of us, and you didn't.').

title: Zombieland
justification: Tallahassee often dictates actions, such as telling Columbus to buckle up or deciding where they go. Wichita and Little Rock steal weapons and a vehicle, asserting dominance through force and deception: "Better you make the mistake of trusting us...than us make the mistake of trusting you."

title: Coraline
justification: Several characters exert authority: The Other Mother manipulates and controls Coraline with promises and threats ('There's one tiny little thing we need to do.','You may come out when you've learned to be a loving daughter!'). Coraline's real mother also displays control, limiting Coraline's activities and choices ('No, Coraline. Rain makes mud. Mud makes a mess.').

title: Hotel for Dogs
justification: Several characters exert authority: Bernie threatens to separate Andi and Bruce if they misbehave, highlighting his control over their living situation. Lois enforces strict rules and schedules, demonstrating her dominance within the foster home. Dave at the pet store uses his position to pressure Andi into taking more dogs.

title: Law Abiding Citizen
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the detectives interrogating suspects ('Freeze! Get down!'), the warden managing the prison ('Turn around.'), and Clyde manipulating the legal system and law enforcement ('Release me and drop all charges by 6:00 AM. Or what? Or I kill everyone.').

title: Michael Jackson's This Is It
justification: There are instances of Michael Jackson directing the musical director and dancers, indicating a hierarchy. For example, Jackson says, "I'm not feeling that part enough," and "So you gotta watch me for that growl, okay?"

title: Obsessed
justification: The dialogue shows a constant struggle for control, especially in Derek's relationships. Lisa attempts to assert dominance by manipulating situations and declaring, "One of us has to take charge, and I guess that's gonna be me." Derek also tries to control the narrative and his relationships, but ultimately loses control as the situation escalates.

title: Race to Witch Mountain
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience, such as the government agents ('I want access to every single surveillance camera Vegas has turned on.') and the crime boss Wolfe ('And yOu better get me an ETA! Capisce?'). Jack is also told what to do by the kids ('Return to your vehicle. Your services are no longer required.').

title: The Final Destination
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Examples include 'Move, move, move,' and 'Sir. I need you to move your foot. Thank you.' There are also instances of characters attempting to control situations, such as when Nick tries to force others to leave the racetrack.

title: The Taking of Pelham 123
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and asserting authority. Examples include Ryder's constant threats and ultimatums ('Put Garber on the fucking line or I kill the motorman') and the police officers barking orders at each other ('Shoot any motherfucker that moves. That's an order!').

title: Friday the 13th
justification: Several characters give orders or assert dominance. Examples include the killer's commands like "Kill for Mother" and "You need to be punished," as well as Trent's bossy behavior and attempts to control situations with phrases like "My house, my rules."

title: 17 Again
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the high school scenes. Stan bullies others, and there are instances of parents trying to control their children's lives ('I forbid you to see him anymore'). The principal also exerts authority over students and parents.

title: The Time Traveler’s Wife
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or dominance. For example, the younger Henry is told what to do by the older Clare, and Gomez confronts Henry about his relationship with Clare, displaying a protective stance. Philip's questioning of Henry before the wedding also highlights a power dynamic.

title: Brüno
justification: The film depicts power dynamics through various scenarios. For example, Brüno gives orders to his assistant Lutz, and the military training scenes involve instructors yelling orders at recruits. Also, the talk show segment shows the host attempting to control Brüno's behavior and narrative.

title: Bride Wars
justification: The movie revolves around two friends vying for the same wedding date and venue, leading to constant one-upmanship and sabotage. Examples include Liv grabbing the first date without consulting Emma and Emma sending out save-the-dates to assert her claim.

title: The Haunting in Connecticut
justification: Wendy is put in charge of the children while the parents are away, indicating a temporary authority. Peter's drunken behavior and subsequent reprimand by Sara highlight a struggle for control within the family, with Sara asserting her dominance through scolding and threats: "Wendy is in charge. Okay?" and "You get drunk again, don't come home."

title: Ghosts of Girlfriends Past
justification: Connor's uncle teaches him how to manipulate women by insulting them to "flip the power dynamic." Connor also frequently makes suggestive and demeaning comments to women, asserting dominance through sexual innuendo and objectification. For example, he tells Jenny to "scamper up to my room, boil some water...get the chicken claw out of my suitcase, do some light stretching...and I will be up in 5?"

title: Funny People
justification: George Simmons frequently barks orders and insults his assistant Ira, such as "You should have fucking called them!" and "Where the fuck were you last night?". There is also a clear power imbalance in George's interactions with his doctor, where he uses humor to deflect from his fear and discomfort, but the doctor clearly finds it annoying.

title: I Can Do Bad All By Myself
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats, commands, and manipulation. Examples include Madea's interactions with the children ('Sit down. You better stop rolling your eyes at me.') and Randy's controlling behavior towards April ('Hey, come here now. I said you ain't going, all right?').

title: My Bloody Valentine
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority or challenging it. For example, the mine foreman yells, "Damn kids! Everyone out now!" and there is a constant back and forth between characters like "I know my job, Harry." "Like fuck you do, Hanniger."

title: Land of the Lost
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters give orders and assert dominance.
