Examples include Marshall commanding Chaka ('Chaka, your master commands you to...') and later declaring himself Chaka's 'fair but very strict master'. The Zarn also threatens destruction, demonstrating a desire for control.

title: My Sister’s Keeper
justification: The mother, Sara, exerts significant control over her daughters, particularly Anna, demanding medical procedures despite Anna's reluctance. This is evident in dialogues like "I asked her to help her sister, and she agreed" followed by the revelation that nurses had to hold Anna down, and Sara's admission that she didn't ask Anna's permission for certain procedures.

title: Old Dogs
justification: Dan and Charlie's business relationship involves clear power dynamics, with Dan often giving orders and Charlie reluctantly complying. For example, Dan tells Charlie, "So, tomorrow morning, 7:30, I want you outside your apartment ready to go. Because if I'm going to be an old dad for two weeks, you're going to be 'Uncle Charlie.'" Also, Vicki exerts parental authority, setting rules and expectations for Dan's care of the children, such as "Promise me you will not leave them with strangers."

title: Underworld 3: Rise of the Lycans
justification: The subtitles are filled with examples of power dynamics. Viktor commands vampires and Lycans, demanding obedience and punishing disobedience: "Get in there," "Keep your eyes on the ground," "For removing the collar, 30 lashes." There's also a clear hierarchy among the vampires, with the nobles demanding respect and resources from humans.

title: Up in the Air
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of superiors giving orders ('Now, Ned, I need you to go back to your desk'), employees being fired ('Mr. Bingham, I regret to inform you that your position at this company is no longer available'), and characters asserting their dominance ('No, frankly, we're making you irrelevant'). There are also frequent challenges to authority and status ('Am I the only one that sees that by doing this we're making ourselves irrelevant?').

title: Confessions of a Shopaholic
justification: Several characters exert authority: Luke gives Rebecca work assignments and Edgar West pressures Luke regarding Rebecca's journalism. Alette dictates Rebecca's style choices, and Derek Smeath aggressively pursues debt collection.

title: Precious (Based on the Novel Push by Sapphire)
justification: The film depicts a clear power imbalance between Precious and her abusive mother, who controls her through verbal and physical abuse and manipulation of welfare benefits. Examples include the mother demanding Precious cook and clean, berating her appearance, and controlling her access to resources like food and money. The school environment also shows power dynamics, with teachers directing students and setting rules.

title: Year One
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders ('Tend to the slaves', 'Rub me with oil or die'), and others being subservient ('Yes, sir'). There are also power struggles, such as the king demanding sacrifices and the princess questioning his authority.

title: The Unborn
justification: Several characters give orders or try to exert control. Examples include: "Keep looking" (repeatedly), and Sofi's commanding Casey to "Get out!" when questioned. The exorcism scene is entirely driven by the need to control and expel the dybbuk.

title: Drag Me To Hell
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Christine is shamed and cursed by Mrs. Ganush after denying her a loan extension. Christine's boss, Mr. Jacks, holds power over her career advancement, and her mother pressures her about her choice of partner.

title: Orphan
justification: There are instances of characters giving orders and exerting control, such as when the mother tells the daughter, "Take a seat, please. Take a seat. Don't make me ask again, please." and when the father tells the son, "Apologize to your sister."

title: Duplicity
justification: Characters are constantly trying to one-up each other, extract information, or assert control. Examples include the constant questioning and suspicion between Claire and Ray, and the corporate power plays with phrases like "I own you."

title: It’s Complicated
justification: The rekindled affair between Janey and Jake is fraught with power imbalances. Jake attempts to manipulate Janey with nostalgia and guilt, while Janey struggles to maintain her independence and boundaries. Examples: Jake says, "Fate brought us together once, maybe it happened again," and Janey retorts, "You were so great, so loose and sexy. How often do you get to be like that?"

title: Planet 51
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the General commanding the army ("Captain, mobilize the army. Yes, sir!") and Lem's initial reluctance to help Chuck, fearing the consequences from authorities ("If they catch me helping you, who knows what they'll do to me?").

title: Surrogates
justification: The film explores power dynamics through the control humans exert over surrogates. Examples include commands like "Get lost, meatbag," and the hierarchical structure within the FBI, with agents taking orders from superiors. The conflict between humans and surrogates, and the debate over their rights, also highlights power struggles.

title: Ninja Assassin
justification: The film is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the tattoo artist's threats, Ozunu's training methods, and the Europol agents' hierarchical structure.

title: State of Play
justification: Characters frequently give orders and make demands, such as "Tell her to forget it. It's your gig." and "You want me to go and sit around in some hospital...while you clean up the rest of the story?". There are also instances of characters asserting authority, like when the detective says, "You slow us down, endanger the public any more than you already have, it won't be pretty."

title: Notorious
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. Puffy directs Biggie's career, dictating song choices ('Trust me, Big'). Biggie exerts control over Lil' Kim in the studio ('Do the fucking song').

title: The Pink Panther 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting authority, giving orders, and attempting to control situations. Clouseau's interactions with Ponton and Mrs. Berenger highlight his attempts to exert dominance, while the Dream Team detectives compete for recognition and control of the investigation.

title: All About Steve
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Steve's boss pressures him for better news footage, saying, "If you keep this up, you're leaving me no choice." Mary's behavior towards Steve is also a struggle for control, as she disregards his wishes and inserts herself into his life.

title: The Informant
justification: Several characters, particularly within ADM, exert authority and control over others. Examples include Mick Andreas directing Whitacre ('Whitacre, from now on we're doing things your way') and Terry Wilson's aggressive stance in negotiations ('Listen here, you mousy motherfucker'). The FBI agents also hold power, directing Whitacre's actions and pressing him for information.

title: The Last House on the Left
justification: Characters are frequently giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include: "Tell the or that the compound fracture to the left femur is on its way up," and "Get back here, you stupid cunt!"

title: (500) Days of Summer
justification: The lyrics contain some elements hinting at power dynamics, but they are not central. The line "Power to the people / We don't want it / We want pleasure" suggests a rejection of traditional power structures. The song "I'm the hero of the story / I don't need to be saved" implies a self-sufficient and independent stance, which can be interpreted as a form of personal power.

title: The Reader
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power imbalance, especially in the interactions between Hanna and Michael. Hanna gives orders like, "Wait in the hall while I change," and "You can fill them and bring them up," establishing her dominance. The trial scenes also highlight power dynamics, with the court holding authority over the defendants.

title: earth
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as Madame over Shanta ('What rubbish, Shanta.') and the Ice Candy Man's controlling behavior towards Shanta ('And you! Why are you smiling at him? Is he your hero?'). There are also instances of physical dominance and threats ('Put me down, you bastard! I'm going to drop you on your face!').

title: The Men Who Stare at Goats
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders, such as "Move out! Go! Go! Go!" and "Hold your fire!". The dialogue also reveals a military hierarchy, with characters like Bill Django holding positions of authority and giving instructions to subordinates.

The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between One and the others. Examples include: 'Go to the watch tower... and take our guest, with you,' and 'We have rules!' indicating a structured environment with enforced authority.

title: Invictus
justification: The film depicts Mandela's struggle to unite a divided nation through rugby. He exerts his authority to reinstate the Springboks, despite opposition: "In this instance, the people are wrong. And as their elected leader, it is my job to show them that." The rugby team also experiences internal power dynamics, with the captain trying to inspire his team.

title: The Stepfather
justification: David exerts control by offering opportunities (swim team, driver's license) and then subtly withholding them ('Maybe. I'll think about it.'). Susan also tries to control Michael's behavior ('I just need you to try and get along, okay?').

title: Defiance
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('I send you for food'), asserting dominance ('On your knees'), and negotiating status ('You know who I am? Sit.'). There are also power struggles within the group, such as the conflict between Tuvia and Zus, and the challenges to Tuvia's leadership.

title: Alice in Wonderland
justification: Throughout the movie, characters are constantly giving orders and asserting dominance. The Red Queen frequently shouts "Off with his head!" and demands obedience, while characters like Hamish and the aristocracy exert control through social expectations and arranged marriages, as seen when Alice is pressured to marry Hamish.

title: Iron Man 2
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance. Tony gives orders to Pepper ('Make it us'), and Hammer tries to control Vanko ('You don't just go and try and kill the guy'). There are also constant status battles, like Hammer trying to one-up Tony with Christine Everhart.

title: Inception
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and vying for control. Examples include Cobb directing the team, Saito asserting his presence, and Fischer's internal struggles with his father and godfather.

title: Despicable Me
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, particularly in Gru's interactions with his minions ('Minions, assemble!') and Dr. Nefario ('Assemble the minions!'). There are also power struggles, such as Gru's rivalry with Vector ('Now, maybe you'll think twice before you freeze someone's head!') and Miss Hattie's control over the orphans ('We wouldn't want to spend the weekend in the Box of Shame, would we?').

title: Shrek Forever After
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters are constantly trying to exert control over Shrek, demanding he 'do the roar'. Rumpelstiltskin manipulates Shrek into signing a contract, highlighting a power imbalance and exploitation.

title: How to Train Your Dragon
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Stoick, as chief, constantly directs the villagers and reprimands Hiccup, while Gobber instructs Hiccup in his apprenticeship. The dragon training scenes are also driven by hierarchy, with the teens competing for status and the instructor barking orders.

title: The Karate Kid
justification: The mother is constantly telling Dre what to do ('Dre, you're ready?', 'And don't forget to use the bathroom.'). Mr. Han also exerts authority over Dre, especially during training ('Jacket on!', 'Take it off.').

title: Clash of the Titans
justification: The movie revolves around the power struggle between gods and humans, with humans defying the gods and the gods punishing them. Dialogue like "Kneel" from Hades and Zeus's pronouncements about the order of things highlight the hierarchical conflict. The constant demand for worship and obedience from the gods further emphasizes this theme.

title: Grown Ups
justification: Several instances of power dynamics are present. Lenny often dictates activities and makes decisions for the group, like planning the trip to Milan and then changing plans. There are also instances of parents setting rules for their children, such as taking away video games and cell phones.

title: Sibling Rivalry
justification: Several interactions show characters trying to exert control. For example, Nick tries to persuade Donnie to show his blinds to Mr. Diamond, and Marjorie is told what to do by Harry, 'You've got a dinner to cook'.

title: Stop! Or My Mom Will Shoot
justification: The mother, Tutti, consistently disregards Joe's boundaries and professional life, cleaning his gun and interfering in his police work. Joe attempts to set boundaries with a list of rules, but Tutti continues to assert her influence, highlighting a struggle for control in their relationship. Dialogue like "Officer, secure the megaphone!" and "Mom, please, get rid of the pictures!" further illustrates the dynamic.

title: Rookie of the Year
justification: Several characters exert authority: the baseball manager over players ('Get dressed. I'm taking you home'), the team owner over staff ('FIND HIM!'), and even kids over each other ('Go get me a screwdriver'). There are also instances of defiance, like Henry refusing Jack's orders ('Get out of my face, Jack!').

title: Beethoven's 2nd
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Regina's interactions with Floyd are consistently demeaning, as she barks orders and insults him: "Brillo, shut up and pay up!" and "Didn't my trainer teach you how to stand?". Also, George's bossiness with his kids is evident when he says, "Not now, boy. We're late."

title: The Beverly Hillbillies
justification: The plot revolves around manipulating Jed Clampett for his money. Miss Hathaway and Mr. Drysdale exert control over Jethro, and Laurette attempts to manipulate Jed into marriage for financial gain, showcasing a constant struggle for dominance and control.

title: Murder by Numbers
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority. For example, Cassie tells Swanson to "SHUT UP" and later Sam tells Al, "DON'T TALK ABOUT HER LIKE THAT, PLEASE." Richard also manipulates Justin throughout the show.

title: One Hour Photo
justification: Several characters exert authority: Sy over Yoshi in the photo lab ('Mrs. Levitt has a problem, offer her a free roll of film.') and Will over Nina ('Get on the goddamn bed!'). The police also exert authority during the arrest ('Police! Freeze!').

title: Finding Nemo
justification: Several scenes involve characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Bruce the shark tries to control Marlin and Dory, and Gill attempts to control the tank gang.

title: Elf
justification: Several characters exert authority: the boss at Gimbel's yells at employees, Walter is dismissive of Buddy, and the fake Santa demands respect. Examples include: 'You're not supposed to be down here!' and 'Just do your job.'

title: Agent Cody Banks
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Ronica telling Cody, "You will speak only when spoken to, you will follow orders without question," and Brinkman commanding Connors to program the nanobots, stating, "You are going to program them to march in like a column of ants."

title: Secondhand Lions
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Hub and Garth frequently give orders to Walter and each other, like "Get out of the car" and "Pull." Walter's mother and Stan try to manipulate him into revealing the location of the money, demonstrating a clear power imbalance.

title: The Hours
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. Virginia's interactions with Leonard show her chafing under his control, while Clarissa's interactions with Richard reveal her attempts to manage his illness and public image. Nelly's subservient role to Virginia is also evident.

title: Rugrats Go Wild
justification: Charlotte's interactions with Dr. Lipschitz show her demanding a rescue, indicating a sense of entitlement and power. Angelica's bossy behavior towards the monkey and her attempts to control the other babies also highlight power dynamics. Betty's election as leader and her assignment of tasks further emphasize the theme.

title: Dreamcatcher
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the boys bullying Duddits ("Come on. Eat it. Eat it. Eat it and you can go.") and Colonel Curtis's absolute authority over Blue Unit, demanding obedience and punishing disobedience ("When a soldier disobeys a superior's orders, he puts everyone at risk.").

title: King Arthur
justification: The Bishop's orders to Arthur and his knights demonstrate Roman authority. Arthur's defiance and negotiation with the Bishop, as well as his interactions with Merlin and the Saxon leader, show a struggle for control and respect. The Saxon leader's dominance over his men and his challenge to Arthur further highlight the theme.

title: Closer
justification: Several interactions involve one character attempting to exert control or judgment over another. Examples include Dan telling Alice to "Sit up," Larry calling himself "The Sultan," and various characters making demands or issuing commands within their relationships.

title: Peter Pan
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy, especially between adults and children. Hook's interactions with his crew involve constant threats and displays of authority, such as when he threatens to plunge his hook into Smee. Also, George Darling's attempts to assert dominance over his family are evident when he declares he must become a man that children fear and adults respect.

title: Fat Albert
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Don't you guys make noise when you enter a room?", "You guys just stay put. Don't walk. Don't talk. Don't do anything.", and "Two more laps."

title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire
justification: The film features several power dynamics. Teachers like Moody exert authority over students ("Stand still!"), while authority figures like Dumbledore and Fudge clash over how to handle the crisis ("In times like these, the wizard world looks to its leaders for strength, Dumbledore!"). There are also instances of social hierarchy, such as Malfoy's attempts to intimidate Harry and Ron's jealousy over Harry's unexpected champion status ("You're being stupid.").

title: War of the Worlds
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Ray telling Robbie what to do and where to go, or the soldiers ordering people around during the evacuation. Ogilvy's increasingly erratic behavior and pronouncements also represent a struggle for control, albeit a desperate and misguided one.

title: Mr. And Mrs. Smith
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control situations and each other. Examples include the constant correction of details ('Five years ago.' 'Six.') and direct commands ('Miss, your passport please... your papers.'). The couple's professional lives as assassins also contribute to the power struggle, as they are constantly trying to outmaneuver each other.

title: Hitch
justification: The dialogue shows characters asserting dominance and control. Allegra Cole's interactions with Albert and Chip highlight her high status, while Hitch coaches Albert on how to exert control in his interactions with women. Vance's behavior towards Casey also demonstrates a power imbalance.

title: Robots
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include Mr. Gunk ordering Copperbottom to clean up the mess and Ratchet's controlling behavior at Bigweld Industries, such as dictating the new slogan and eliminating spare parts.

title: The Pacifier
justification: The Lieutenant barks orders at the children, establishing a clear hierarchy: "Whatever Lieutenant Wolfe asks you to do, do it." He later enforces strict rules and discipline, further solidifying his authority: "I tell you what to do and you do it! End of chain."

title: The 40 Year-old Virgin
justification: Several characters give unsolicited advice and try to control Andy's dating life. Dave pressures Andy to take a box of porn, saying "You need to. You're wound up." Joe and Sara set up a speed-dating event for Andy, ignoring his protests: "No, don't ignore me. I know what this is."

title: Flightplan
justification: Several characters exert authority: the flight attendants give orders to passengers ('Can you fasten that seat belt, please, ma'am?'), the captain controls the search ('Get the lights up. Get every passenger seated.'), and the air marshal enforces rules ('You're a threat to the safety of this aircraft.'). The protagonist also struggles against this authority, questioning and defying them in her desperate search.

title: The Dukes of Hazzard
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Boss Hogg frequently commands Roscoe and others, threatening them with consequences if they fail to comply. For example, Hogg says, "I want you to find the Dukes and lock 'em up! Oh, and bring me my damn safe back."

title: The Aviator
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, whether through wealth, social status, or professional achievement. Examples include the Hepburn family's condescending remarks towards Howard, Juan Trippe's competitive business tactics, and Howard's controlling behavior towards his employees and romantic interests. The constant one-upmanship and attempts to control situations highlight the power struggles at play.

title: Must Love Dogs
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or directions to others, such as "Stop that growling! Use your words," and "Stop, sit." There are also instances of characters asserting control in conversations, such as when Jake tells Sarah, "Too late. You're meeting her at 11. Bring a dog."

title: Syriana
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people giving orders, negotiating for status, and maneuvering for control. Examples include the discussions about promotions ('You get him an audition downtown'), directives within the CIA ('Easy on the memos'), and negotiations for oil rights ('We'd like to offer your firm the rights').

title: Miami Vice
justification: Characters are constantly giving orders and making demands, such as "Get Michael out of there" and "Alonzo, pull over! Pull over! Stay back!" There are also frequent negotiations and renegotiations of deals, highlighting the struggle for control and profit, like when Sonny and Rico propose a new partnership with Isabella, demanding 25% of the load in product.

title: The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift
justification: Several characters assert dominance through threats and challenges, such as DK's control over his territory and Takashi's Yakuza connections. The dialogue includes explicit power plays: "You're done. You understand me? You're done." and "I only race for pink slips."

title: Déjà Vu
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as "So, Agent Carlin, where do we look?" and "All right, dazzle me." There are also instances of characters asserting authority, like when the agent criticizes the crime scene investigation: "Man, when did you completely forget how to investigate a crime scene?"

title: The Shaggy Dog
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dave as a DA and father, Strictland as a wealthy boss, and Kozak giving orders in the lab. Examples include Dave telling his daughter, "If you don't get out of here now, I'm gonna ground you," and Strictland demanding, "Have you unlocked the dog's secret?"

title: Little Miss Sunshine
justification: Throughout the dialogue, Richard attempts to assert control over the family's decisions, often clashing with Sheryl. Grandpa's explicit and inappropriate advice to Dwayne, and his general disregard for others' boundaries, highlights his dominance within the family structure. The pageant organizers also exert power, setting strict rules and deadlines that the family struggles to meet.

title: United 93
justification: The dialogue includes numerous instances of air traffic controllers giving instructions and pilots complying, such as "United 93, wind 050 at 6. Runway four-left. Clear for take-off." and "Maintain flight level 220 and maintain a speed of 300 knots. Roger, you got it." The hijackers asserting control is also evident: "Just stay quiet and you'll be okay."

title: Good Luck Chuck
justification: Several instances of characters attempting to exert control or influence over others are present. For example, Reba pressures Dr. Charlie into sleeping with her, and Stu manipulates Charlie into going out with Eleanor Skepple. Also, there are instances of characters giving orders or making demands, such as when Eleanor demands peanut butter.

title: Daddy's Little Girls
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance. For example, the mother of Monty's children is verbally abusive and controlling, demonstrated by her command, "You're gonna stay right here with me. And you're going..." Also, Joe is shown to be a local drug dealer who controls the neighborhood and forces Sisi to sell drugs, threatening her family if she doesn't comply.

title: The Queen
justification: The Queen and Prime Minister Blair clash over how to respond to Diana's death, with the Queen initially resistant to public displays of grief and asserting her authority. Blair pressures her to change course, citing public opinion and his constitutional responsibility: "As your Prime Minister, I believe it is my constitutional responsibility to advise the following."

title: Sicko
justification: The documentary highlights the power dynamics between the healthcare industry, politicians, and the general public. It shows how lobbyists and campaign contributions influence legislation, giving the healthcare industry significant control. The film also contrasts the US system with those of Canada and the UK, where universal healthcare aims to reduce the power imbalance between patients and providers.

title: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull
justification: Several characters exert authority: General Ross interrogates Indy, demanding answers and accusing him of suspicious activities. Irina Spalko leads KGB teams, directing operations and seeking to control paranormal military applications. Mutt and Indy have a back and forth of dominance, with Mutt challenging Indy's age and authority.

title: Meet the Browns
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as Miss Mildred demanding money for childcare and threatening to stop caring for Lena. Brenda is often seen struggling to assert herself, while others like Calvin display dominance through material possessions and implied criminal activity. The scene where the plant shuts down and the supervisor dismisses the workers' concerns also highlights a significant power imbalance.

title: Righteous Kill
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting authority, such as the Lieutenant assigning the case and detectives arguing over seniority. The dialogue also reveals power imbalances in criminal relationships, like the pimp Rambo and the gun dealer Trager being 'knocked off'. The courtroom scene highlights the judge's authority and the frustration of the lawyer.

title: Atonement
justification: Several characters exert authority: Briony directs the play, Cecilia makes decisions for the younger children, and Paul Marshall's wealth gives him influence. Examples include: 'If you're going to be Arabella, then I'll be the director, thank you very much,' and 'Briony, you'll do as you're told, or you'll go straight to your room.'

title: Body of Lies
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, questioning each other's competence, and maneuvering for control. Examples include the CIA director's interactions with his field agent, Hani Pasha's interrogation and manipulation of potential informants, and the constant struggle for dominance between different intelligence agencies.

title: First Sunday
justification: The robbers exert control through threats and intimidation: "Take your two-ways, cell phones, beepers...put it in the basket. Drop it in the bucket. Save yourself a trip to the hospital." The deacon also attempts to control the church's direction, leading to conflict: "Maybe moving the church will inspire them to get a job...so that they can afford some transportation."

title: The Secret Life of Bees
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. For example, August directs Lily and Rosaleen to work in specific areas, and June initially resists Neil's advances, demonstrating a struggle for control in their relationship. The dialogue also reveals societal power dynamics, such as the prejudice Rosaleen faces and the authority figures like the police.

title: Sherlock Holmes
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and vying for control. Blackwood's pronouncements about a 'new future' and controlling the world, coupled with Irene's manipulation of Holmes and the Temple members' deference to authority, highlight a constant struggle for dominance.

title: Gran Torino
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and using derogatory language to demean others. Walt frequently barks orders and insults Thao, while gang members threaten and intimidate others in their neighborhood. Even casual interactions, like the barber shop scene, involve a constant exchange of insults and attempts to assert superiority.

title: G-Force
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Kendall shutting down G-Force ('I'm shutting you down. Yeah, I can.') and the FBI agents demanding information ('I'll need to inspect your goods. Let's go.'). Even among the animals, there's a clear hierarchy, with Darwin often taking charge and Bucky the ferret asserting dominance over his 'zone'.

title: District 9
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and displays of authority. Examples include MNU agents ordering aliens to "Get down on the ground or I'll shoot" and "Sign the fucking paper," as well as Obesandjo's control over his gang members: "Don't play with these boys. He'll cut you in four pieces."

title: Slumdog Millionaire
justification: The subtitles contain numerous instances of characters exerting authority and dominance over others. Examples include the police interrogating Jamal, the game show host controlling the contestants, and the gangster Javed giving orders and threatening violence. Dialogue such as "Motherfucker, name?" and "On your knees! Down!" clearly demonstrates the power imbalances and struggles for control.

title: Watchmen
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance or struggling for control. For example, Nixon gives orders to his staff regarding military actions, and Veidt intimidates business leaders to push his agenda. Rorschach's interactions with criminals and his prison confrontation also highlight a struggle for power and control.

title: Madea Goes To Jail
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in several relationships. For example, the pimp controls Candy, dictating her actions and claiming ownership: "You belong to me. You're my slave." Madea also exerts authority over Cora, scolding her and demanding obedience: "Where the hell you at?"

title: Hannah Montana: The Movie
justification: Robby Ray exerts parental control over Miley, setting boundaries and expectations: "This is absolutely, T-totally, without a doubt unacceptable." Vita, Hannah's publicist, dictates her image and actions: "It's all about the publicity." The mayor expects Hannah to perform at the concert.

title: I Love You, Man
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Tevin trying to get Peter to split the listing and Lou Ferrigno yelling at Peter for not selling his house. Sydney also exerts some influence over Peter, getting him to yell on the boardwalk and play golf, even though Peter is reluctant. However, most of the dialogue is friendly and conversational.

title: Halloween 2
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance. Lou, the strip club owner, barks orders at Howard and makes demeaning jokes. The father figure in the rural family violently assaults a transient, asserting his control over his property.

title: The Uninvited
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. For example, Matt repeatedly pressures Anna with "Come on, Anna" and Rachel directs Anna with "Take out the garbage, will you?". The father also exerts authority, telling Anna, "Wear something decent."

title: The Last Airbender
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and vying for status. Examples include Tus demanding homage from Dastan, the King scolding his sons, and Nizam manipulating situations to his advantage.

title: Shutter Island
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Marshal, continue your investigation'), questioning authority ('What the hell's going on?'), and struggling for control, especially concerning the experiments and the protagonist's mental state ('Marshal, take the pills'). The power dynamic is also evident in the doctor-patient relationships and the hierarchical structure of the institution.

title: The Other Guys
justification: The dialogue includes instances of characters giving orders ("Get over here."), asserting authority ("Police, shithead."), and displaying dominance through aggression and intimidation ("Now you listen to me, you piece of shit."). The good cop/bad cop routine also highlights a power dynamic.

title: Tron: Legacy
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. For example, Richard Mackey directs the ENCOM team, and CLU commands programs with phrases like "Greetings programs" and "Be loyal to me."

title: Valentine's Day
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. The phone sex operator is given orders by her boss. The florist is questioned about his discretion and understanding of the 'florist code' by a customer.

title: The Expendables
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include Gunner's insubordination ('This isn't how we work. Let him go.') and Barney's team's interactions with Mr. Church ('So if you take this money and you don't deliver, me and my people are gonna come get you and your people and chop you up into little fucking dog treats.').

title: Little Fockers
justification: Jack's constant testing and questioning of Greg's abilities, finances, and even sexual attraction to Pam highlight a struggle for dominance. Dialogue like "Do you have the money or not, Greg?" and "Are you still physically attracted to my daughter, Greg?" exemplify this dynamic.

title: Date Night
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and attempts to control situations. Examples include the criminals demanding the flash drive with threats like "I will blow a hole in your face" and "Move!", and Claire and Phil being forced to comply under duress.

title: The Book of Eli
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, commands, and displays of dominance. Characters like Carnegie exert control through violence and manipulation, while others struggle to resist or comply, exemplified by lines like "Take off the fucking pack and put it on the ground. Or die!" and "Stay on the path. It's not your concern."

title: The Social Network
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of people trying to assert dominance, whether it's Mark dismissing Eduardo's concerns about advertising, the Winklevoss twins seeking intervention from the Harvard president, or lawyers trying to intimidate Mark in depositions. Mark's flippant attitude and disregard for authority figures further highlight the power struggles at play.

title: The Town
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. For example, the interrogation by the FBI agent, where he asserts dominance and control over Doug. Also, Jem's aggressive behavior and attempts to control Doug's actions and relationships demonstrate a struggle for dominance within their group.

title: Prince of Persia: Sands of Time
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include Tus ordering the attack on Alamut despite his father's wishes, Dastan leading his company, and the power struggles between the brothers for recognition and control.

title: Red
justification: Several characters give orders or exert control. Examples include: "Get back. Get out!", "Listen to me. Right now. Out the back door.", and "Have Endercott intercept the girl at the Hotel Capri.". There are also instances of characters being held captive and forced to comply, indicating a clear power imbalance.

title: Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief
justification: Throughout the movie, characters are constantly giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Chiron commanding the demigods during training ('Heroes! Warriors! Fall in! Hustle, hustle!') and Hades demanding the lightning bolt ('Percy Jackson, bring me the bolt!'). There are also instances of characters struggling for dominance, such as Annabeth's competitive nature and desire to always win.

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader
justification: Throughout the movie, characters vie for authority and control. Caspian asserts his royal authority, giving orders like "Drinian, pick some men and come ashore." Edmund and Caspian also clash, questioning each other's leadership and bravery.

title: True Grit
justification: The dialogue is filled with assertions of authority, challenges to that authority, and negotiations for control. Examples include Mattie hiring Cogburn and dictating terms, LaBoeuf's attempts to assert his Ranger status, and the constant bickering and one-upmanship between Cogburn and LaBoeuf.

title: Paranormal Activity 2
justification: There are instances of authority and obedience, such as the parents instructing Ali ('Make sure the doors and the windows are locked, OK?') and the tense interactions with Martine where they demand she stop certain behaviors ('That's enough, Martine. Put it down.'). There are also moments where characters try to exert control over situations or others, like when the father dismisses Kristi's concerns ('You're Crabby McRumpelstein.')

title: Eat Pray Love
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the guru's followers obeying her instructions and the Italian family's matriarch setting rules for Liz. However, the overall focus is more on personal growth and relationships. Examples: "Ketut told me I would." and "I have one rule. No strange men spending the night."

title: Dear John
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, John's friends pressure him to drink ("Come on, you should drink. It'll make you feel better."), and John confronts a man harassing Savannah ("How about you get your hands off?").

title: Unstoppable
justification: Throughout the subtitles, characters give orders and instructions, demonstrating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Connie directing Ned and Dewey, Galvin reprimanding Hooper, and Frank and Will arguing over train operation procedures. The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority.

title: The A-Team
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and challenging each other's status. Examples include the General's initial reprimand of the Captain, Hannibal's strategic commands to his team, and the power plays between Lynch and Sosa.

title: Knight and Day
justification: Roy is constantly giving June orders, such as "Run," "Open the door, June," and "Stay down." The FBI agents also exert authority, telling June, "We're gonna take you to a secure location" and attempting to control her narrative.

title: Dinner for Schmucks
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over Tim, such as Darla and Julie.  Barry also tries to control situations, often with disastrous results, like when he gives Julie's address to Darla.  Therman's mind control also highlights power dynamics.

title: The Bounty Hunter
justification: The bounty hunter/bail jumper dynamic is inherently about power. Milo constantly gives Nicole orders ("Get in the car," "Stay here"), and she resists, but he ultimately controls her movements and fate. There are also scenes where Milo is threatened by Irene's crew, showing a different power dynamic.

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters trying to assert dominance or avoid being dominated. Greg constantly tries to control Rowley, telling him what to say and wear, and Rodrick bullies Greg. Patty Farrell threatens Greg, and characters jockey for position in the school's social hierarchy.

title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
justification: The film features a clear master-apprentice dynamic between Balthazar and Dave, with Balthazar giving orders and Dave initially resisting but eventually complying.  Horvath also exerts control over other characters, issuing commands and threatening violence to get what he wants: "Get him," and "Kill him."

title: A Nightmare on Elm Street
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. For example, Freddy taunts and manipulates Nancy in her dreams, saying, "You're in my world. And you can't ever leave." Also, the adults' decision to take the law into their own hands and burn Krueger alive demonstrates a forceful assertion of power.

title: The Wolf Man
justification: The dialogue shows Sir John Talbot in a clear position of authority, directing his son Larry and the local police. Examples include: "Run aIong. Get on with the good work." and the Chief Constable deferring to Sir John's wishes regarding questioning Larry.

title: Get Him to the Greek
justification: The film features a record executive, Sergio, who exerts control over his employees through intimidation and humiliation, such as forcing an employee to answer his phone and then ordering him to throw it away.  Aaron is tasked with managing the erratic rock star Aldous Snow, whose behavior constantly tests Aaron's authority and forces him to navigate Aldous's demands and whims.

title: Resident Evil: Afterlife
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Wesker's interactions with his subordinates ('And you waited 30 minutes to tell me?') and the Umbrella soldiers' obedience highlight a clear hierarchy. Alice's confrontations with Wesker also showcase a struggle for dominance ('Any more questions?').

title: Why Did I Get Married Too?
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to control each other, especially in relationships. Examples include Angela wanting Marcus to do what she says, and Sheila demanding Troy's phone password, highlighting a constant struggle for control and trust.

title: The Tooth Fairy
justification: Throughout the movie, Derek is constantly being ordered around by the head fairies and Tracy, his social worker. Examples include: "You're ordered to spend time as a tooth fairy." and "Slip inside and get the tooth."

title: Legend of the Guardians: The Owls of Ga’Hoole
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and displays of dominance. Examples include: "Keep your mouth shut, or I'll shut it for you," "Hey! No questions," and "Silence!" The owls are constantly struggling for control and status within the hierarchy of St. Aegolius and the Pure Ones.

title: The Tourist
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as 'Stay on his face. His face,' and 'All right, grab him. Take him. Let's get him.' Reginald Shaw's monologue about killing those who wrong him also highlights a ruthless assertion of power.

title: Letters to Juliet
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or expressing dominance. Victor prioritizes his work and tells Sophie she can join the letter writers, and Charlie often speaks condescendingly to Sophie, highlighting a power imbalance in their interactions. The grandmother, Claire, also exerts authority over Charlie, directing his actions and correcting his behavior.

title: Life as We Know It
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control Sophie's upbringing, arguments about childcare responsibilities, and social worker visits assessing their parenting abilities. Examples include: 'Mind watching her for another minute? I gotta talk to Messer,' and the social worker's interrogation about their living situation and plans for Sophie.

title: Wall Street 2: Money Never Sleeps
justification: Several characters exert authority, give orders, and manipulate others. Examples include Bretton James's control over financial deals and Gordon Gekko's attempts to influence his daughter and Jake. The dialogue reveals a constant struggle for control and influence in both professional and personal relationships.

title: Predators
justification: Characters are constantly testing each other, jockeying for position, and giving orders. Examples include Royce's leadership and the power struggles between the various mercenaries, such as when Nikolai demands a gun and Royce asserts control.

title: Hot Tub Time Machine
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. For example, Lou demands, "Let's get this party started! Who is carrying me home tonight?" and later directs, "Don't you dare fucking tell him. You'll screw the time thing up."

title: Kick-Ass
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening others. Examples include Frank's interactions with his son and subordinates, and the general tone of intimidation used by criminals and vigilantes alike, such as "Get the fuck out of here" and "I want Kick-Ass's fucking head on a stick, and I want it now."

title: Black Swan
justification: The ballet director, Thomas, exerts significant control over the dancers, demanding specific performances and manipulating their emotions. Nina's mother also tries to control her daughter's life. There are also power struggles between the dancers, especially between Nina and Lily, as they compete for the lead role.

title: Killers
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Holbrook ordering Annabell to do a job, and Jen's boss telling her to "dominate" a conference. Spencer's past as a hitman also implies a power dynamic where he was controlled by an organization.

title: The Fighter
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Alice telling Dicky to do things, Micky's mother managing his career and telling him what to do, and the general struggle for control over Micky's boxing career.

title: Saw 3D
justification: The film revolves around Jigsaw's games, where he dictates the rules and forces people to make life-or-death choices, asserting his dominance. Dialogue like "Live or die, make your choice" and characters giving orders such as "Do it!" highlight the power imbalances and struggles for control.

title: Cop Out
justification: Several characters exert authority, give orders, or try to dominate conversations. Examples include the detectives interrogating suspects ("Give it up."), the robbers demanding money ("Open up the register. Open it."), and the general tone of disrespect and threats throughout many interactions.

title: The Lovely Bones
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the parents setting rules for Susie's photography and film usage ("One roll a month?") and the general parental authority over the children ("Susie, You used up all the film?"). There is also a scene where the father confronts Mr. Harvey, displaying a protective and assertive stance.

title: Cats & Dogs: The Revenge of Kitty Galore
justification: Kitty Galore frequently gives orders to her henchmen, such as "Paws! What are you waiting for? I want this pigeon Seamus in your mouth...on my doorstep immediately. Out! I said out! Out! Out! Out!" and "We've been compromised. Unless you turn into a parrot, never talk in front of humans!"

title: Edge of Darkness
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and making threats. Examples include Jedburgh's control over situations ('And then I decide what happens next'), Bennett's authority at Northmoor ('Get Detective Craven a ginger ale, would you?'), and Craven's interrogations and threats ('I tell the police you opened the door with it, automatic year in jail').

title: Death at a Funeral
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Derek's interactions with Elaine and her father, and the constant bickering and one-upmanship between Aaron and Ryan, highlight a struggle for status and control. The blackmail plot adds another layer of power imbalance.

title: Step Up 3D
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Luke leading the Pirates and giving orders. Julien's attempts to buy the Vault and undermine Luke's crew also highlight power struggles. The Samurai's aggressive pursuit of Moose demonstrates a desire for dominance.

title: The Last Exorcism
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Examples include the father telling his son, "What's your problem, boy?" and later demanding, "Let's go ahead and just turn it off for right now." The Reverend also attempts to take charge during the exorcism, directing others and commanding the demon.

title: Legion
justification: Several characters give orders and assert authority. Examples include: "Stop! Drop the bag. Put your hands on your head," and "Take the shot, Burton." There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority, such as Michael saying, "I'm following my own orders now."

title: The Crazies
justification: The sheriff and his deputy are the main authority figures, giving orders and being obeyed. The military presence also establishes a clear hierarchy, with soldiers controlling civilians. Examples: "Deputy does what the sheriff tells him, right?" and "Get on the ground!"

title: Crazy Heart
justification: The dialogue shows Bad Blake's struggle for respect and control in the music industry, especially in his interactions with Tommy Sweet and his agent, Jack.  For example, Bad asserts himself during the sound check, stating, "You set the mix the way I want it, or I'm going to be up here rehearsing right through Tommy's set."

title: Burlesque
justification: Several characters exert dominance. Marcus tries to buy the club, saying, "I see something I like, I have to have it." Tess controls the dancers, telling Ali, "Stop. Take her and remove her."

title: For Colored Girls
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Examples include Beau demanding a drink from Crys and berating her, Carl controlling Jo's finances, and the mother's abusive and controlling behavior towards her daughters.

title: The Back-up Plan
justification: Several interactions involve attempts to assert dominance or control. For example, the dog trainer discusses 'leadership' and 'follower' roles, and Zoe jokes about showing her dog 'who's the pack leader.' There are also instances of characters trying to control conversations or situations, such as when Zoe tells Stan, 'Quiet,' or when someone says, 'Don't you have someplace...to be tonight?'

title: Vampires Suck
justification: The movie contains several instances of power dynamics. Frank, the sheriff, exerts authority over Becca, his daughter, and others in the town. Edward, as a vampire, holds a position of power over Becca, especially when he threatens to kill her.

title: The American
justification: Pavel gives Jack orders and sets the terms of their relationship: "You can't stay here. I've made arrangements for you to leave town while I sort this out. Stay there. Lay low, till you get my call. Don't talk to anyone. And above all, don't make any friends, Jack." Later, Jack is given orders to "Finish the job."

title: Green Zone
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include: "Your job's to execute them, not worry about how they're put together. Are we clear on that?" and "Get in the fucking car! Get the fuck back!". There are also scenes where characters are clearly subordinate, such as the soldier responding with "Yes, sir" after being given an order.

title: Devil
justification: Several characters exert authority: the security guard demands sign-in, detectives give orders to each other and the people in the elevator, and the building engineer directs the temp worker. The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy and attempts to control situations, such as 'Just get on the damn elevator' and 'You got to sign in'.

title: Marmaduke
justification: Bosco, the alpha male, dominates interactions with threats like, "This is my park, and these are my rules. You look at my girlfriend again, and you're dead." Marmaduke also tries to assert dominance, especially after his makeover, but often fails, highlighting a struggle for status.

title: Hereafter
justification: Several instances of power dynamics are present. A boss pressures an employee to take time off, hinting at job insecurity: "Take some time off to get over what happened. Just a couple of weeks." Also, a character is given instructions: "Down the end of the hall, on your left."

title: When in Rome
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Celeste's demanding tone with Beth regarding the art exhibit, and Nick's persistence in pursuing Beth despite her initial disinterest. The magician's unwanted advances and the model's self-aggrandizing behavior also contribute to a sense of social dominance.

title: She's Out of My League
justification: Several characters exert control over others, like Dylan bossing Kirk around and Molly's ex, Cam, displaying a sense of superiority. Examples include: "Let butt off!" and "You two stay here. Discuss."

title: Scott Pilgrim vs. The World
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, particularly through physical fights and verbal sparring. Examples include Scott fighting Ramona's exes to 'win' her, Envy's band being more successful, and characters like Todd using veganism as a status symbol.

title: Love and Other Drugs
justification: Several interactions involve characters attempting to exert control or gain an advantage. Jamie uses his charm and sales tactics to get what he wants from women and doctors, while other characters like Trey use threats and intimidation. The dialogue showcases a constant negotiation for dominance, whether in professional settings or personal relationships, such as when Jamie tries to persuade the receptionist to give him a patient's number.

title: Charlie St. Cloud
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Charlie being the 'boss man' at the graveyard and giving instructions to his employee. Also, the sailing coach, Tink, gives orders to Tess, demonstrating his authority in that domain. However, these instances are not pervasive.

title: Morning Glory
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles. For example, Jerry threatens to terminate Mike's contract if he doesn't take the co-host position, and Colleen and Mike constantly compete for on-air dominance, as seen in their arguments about who says goodbye and their contrasting approaches to news.

title: Daybreakers
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority, such as "Let's be clear about this," and "All the material in this meeting is classified, Commissioner." Characters like Bromley exert control through manipulation and threats: "How much do you think they'd be willing to pay for your daughter?"

title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part II
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Voldemort demands obedience and punishes those who fail him: "Give me Harry Potter and I shall leave Hogwarts untouched." Snape, as headmaster, also exerts authority: "should anyone...attempt to aid Mr. Potter...they will be punished." There are also power struggles, such as the conflict over the Elder Wand's allegiance.

title: The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the wolves following Sam's orders and Jacob eventually breaking away. Also, Edward is very protective of Bella and makes decisions for her, such as not wanting her to be in pain on their honeymoon: "l didn't really wanna spend my honeymoon writhing in pain."

title: The Hangover Part II
justification: The lyrics hint at a power dynamic through phrases like "the world is your oyster" and "the tough guy humble," suggesting a potential shift in control. The line "the bars are temples but their pearls are not free" implies a transactional dynamic.

title: Fast Five
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Hobbs' interactions with local police ('Stay the fuck out of my way'), Dom's leadership within his crew ('Get out'), and Reyes' control over the favelas ('I own them').

title: Cars 2
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as Finn commanding Mater: "Drive forward. Whatever you do, don't stop!" and Professor Z directing his subordinates: "Go 50% power." There are also instances of characters asserting dominance through threats and intimidation, like when the lemons capture Finn and declare, "Lightning McQueen must be killed!"

title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power assertions. Examples include, "Donnie, you get her ready?", "Open the cage! Open up!", and "Find the most cost effective way to put those apes down."

title: The Help
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of white employers dictating terms to black maids, such as Hilly's control over Yule Mae's job and Skeeter's newsletter content. Minny's instructions to Celia on how to behave around white people, and the constant fear of crossing racial boundaries, further highlight the power imbalance. The threat of violence and job loss underscores the maids' vulnerability.

title: X-Men: First Class
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Get in the car', 'Dispatch the fleet!'), asserting dominance ('Go ahead, pull it. No you won't.'), and vying for control ('Now you let me walk out of here with my money. Or I will pull this pin and we all die.'). Shaw's interactions especially highlight a desire for control and manipulation.

title: Puss in Boots
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Jack and Jill's interactions, Puss's commands to others, and Humpty's attempts to manipulate situations to his advantage. The constant struggle for control and status is evident throughout the subtitles.

title: Rio
justification: Several characters exert authority: Nico and Pedro give Blu unsolicited advice and physical direction, Nigel commands the monkeys, and Marcel bosses Fernando around. Examples: "Little word of advice, you make the first move." and "Shut up, kid."

title: Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, either through intellect (Sherlock and Mycroft's deductions), physical prowess (the fights), or social standing (Moriarty's manipulation of world leaders). Examples include Sherlock's constant need to be right, Moriarty's control over the arms trade, and the power plays between the various nations at the peace summit.

title: Super 8
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as the father telling the daughter what to wear and who to see ('No! You are not wearing that.'). The Air Force personnel also demonstrate control, ordering the deputy to drop his weapons ('Deputy, drop your weapons.').

title: The King’s Speech
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of power dynamics. The King's father demands obedience and berates him: "Show who's in command." Logue's methods also involve a power dynamic, pushing the King to confront his fears and insecurities, and the King struggles with his brother's dominance and the expectations placed upon him.

title: Horrible Bosses
justification: The characters are trying to hire a hitman to kill their bosses, indicating a desire to exert control and eliminate those in positions of authority over them. Dialogue such as "We want them...killed" and the negotiation with Motherfucker Jones over the price of the 'hits' further emphasizes this struggle for power.

title: Hop
justification: Several characters exert authority: Sam gives Fred strict instructions ('Do not touch anything. Do not break anything. Do not go upstairs!'). The head bunny gives orders to Carlos ('Assemble the Pink Berets at once!').

title: Paranormal Activity 3
justification: Dennis is constantly telling Randy what to do, and Randy is subservient. Dennis also tries to control Julie by filming her and manipulating situations. The parents also exert control over the children, telling them what to do and where to go.

title: Just Go With It
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to manipulate each other, especially the adults negotiating with the children. Examples include Michael's demands for a Playstation and unlimited tokens, and the adults' attempts to control the children's behavior and emotions.

title: Cowboys and Aliens
justification: Several characters exert authority through threats and violence. Percy Dolarhyde frequently abuses his power due to his father's influence, as seen when he demands respect and free drinks, stating, "'Cause if it wasn't for my pa's cattle, there'd be no money going through this town!" Colonel Dolarhyde also displays dominance, threatening Roy: "Nobody calls me 'Colonel.' Them that did are mostly dead."

title: Bad Teacher
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Examples include the principal reprimanding Arkady, Elizabeth manipulating students for test scores, and Amy's constant attempts to undermine Elizabeth's position.

title: Gnomeo and Juliet
justification: The dialogue is filled with conflict between the Red and Blue gardens, with leaders like Lord Redbrick and Lady Blueberry constantly asserting dominance. Examples include the garden race with strict rules enforced by force, and the constant one-upmanship and insults exchanged between the factions.

title: The Green Hornet
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, give orders, and establish hierarchy. Britt constantly tries to control Kato and Lenore, while Chudnofsky demands obedience from his underlings, threatening violence to maintain control. Examples include Britt telling Kato what to do and Chudnofsky's reaction to the Green Hornet's actions.

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks: Chipwrecked
justification: Dave is constantly trying to control Alvin's behavior, setting rules and punishments: "if you guys disobey me one more time, you will be off the ship." Ian also tries to assert authority, especially over Dave: "You're not gonna eat this. This was a gift from Theodore."

title: Real Steel
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters assert dominance and control. Charlie gives orders to Max ('Get in the truck!'), and fight promoters dictate terms ('I'll give you a 100 bucks'). The Zeus team's control over the sport is evident in their offer to buy Atom.

title: Crazy, Stupid, Love
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power dynamic, especially in the interactions between Jacob and Cal, where Jacob coaches Cal on how to pick up women, giving commands and advice. Examples include: "Be better than the Gap. Say it." and "You want something, you take it."

title: Battle: Los Angeles
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and orders, such as "All right, first squad, line it up," "Let's form it up, let's go!" and "Lockett, get me an exit down that alley!" Characters frequently address each other by rank, reinforcing the hierarchical structure and obedience expected within the military unit. The interactions between officers and subordinates, and the constant giving and receiving of orders, highlight a strong focus on power dynamics.

title: Immortals
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy with gods, titans, kings, and mortals. Hyperion's dialogue is full of commands and threats, such as "Give him to the beast. Make him tell you where the oracle is being kept." and "I will end the reign of gods."

title: The Muppets
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "We hired you, and we can fire you, so get your butt in here now!" and "Order 28,000 tons of plumber's putty from Beijing."

title: Limitless
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in Eddie's interactions with Vern initially, where he is desperate for the drug and willing to do anything. Later, Eddie gains power, demonstrated by his interactions with Liev and Carl Van Loon, where he asserts dominance and control over situations and people.

title: Tower Heist
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include Slide's dominance over the group, Shaw's manipulation and threats, and the power dynamics between employees and management at The Tower.

title: Contagion
justification: Several characters are in positions of authority, giving orders and expecting compliance. For example, Dr. Cheever directs his team, and Homeland Security officials make demands of medical personnel. There are also instances of resistance to authority, such as the nurses' strike and Krumwiede's accusations against the CDC.

title: Moneyball
justification: Billy Beane exerts control over his staff and players, dictating strategies and personnel decisions. Examples include ordering the head scout to be fired, trading players against the manager's wishes, and telling players how to play. The manager, Art Howe, also tries to assert his authority, but ultimately yields to Beane's decisions.

title: Justin Bieber: Never Say Never
justification: There's a minor element of power dynamics when Usher asks JB, "You think that you can hold the house till I get back?" and JB responds, "Yeah, I can do that."

title: Jack and Jill
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Jack manipulates Jill into dating Pacino for a commercial deal, and there are moments where characters try to dictate Jill's actions and choices, such as pressuring her about dating and her future.

title: Mr. Popper's Penguins
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. Mr. Popper is fired by his superiors, demonstrating workplace hierarchy. He also struggles to manage the penguins, giving commands like "Spread out!" and "Now shut up and go to sleep."

title: Unknown
justification: The film features several instances of characters asserting authority, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include hotel staff interacting with guests ('How may I help you, madam?'), security personnel questioning individuals ('Do you have any identification?'), and the protagonist being dismissed and manhandled by security ('Get your hands off me.').

title: The Adjustment Bureau
justification: The dialogue includes characters who are 'case officers' and 'the Chairman' who control events and people's lives. They make 'adjustments' and 'recalibrations' to keep people 'on plan,' demonstrating a clear hierarchy and control.

title: Happy Feet Two
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance, such as the Beachmaster who refuses to move for anyone, and Sven, who gains a following and is seen as a leader. Mumble is respected as a leader, but also has to persuade others to follow his plans, indicating a less absolute form of power.

title: Water for Elephants
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. August, the circus owner, constantly asserts his dominance through commands and threats: "You do right by me, Cornell, I'll show you a life most suckers can't even dream of." and "I tell you to fix a horse, you shoot it? That's breaking my law. The penalty is red-lighting." There is also a clear hierarchy within the circus, with bosses at the top and roustabouts at the bottom.

title: The Lincoln Lawyer
justification: The dialogue is filled with power plays. Haller manipulates Minton to get the discovery file, and later, he interrogates and directs his client, Louis, demanding obedience: "If you want to stay out of the shithouse, you do exactly as I tell you from now on. You got it?"

title: Friends with Benefits
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders or directions, such as "Stop it," "Hand on the iPad," "Keep your hand still," and "Little faster. More circular." The characters also negotiate and challenge each other's boundaries, indicating a struggle for control in their interactions.

title: Source Code
justification: Characters give and take orders frequently. Examples include: "Start with the bomb! Where is it, what does it look like." and "I need all of you turn off your personal electronic devices till we pull into the station, okay?"

title: Insidious
justification: Several instances of parental authority are evident, such as 'Foster, can you please get up off the floor?' and 'Share it with your brother.' The demon's desire to possess Dalton's body to 'cause pain to others' also highlights a struggle for control.

title: Madea's Big Happy Family
justification: Characters like Madea and Tammy exert dominance through verbal commands and threats: "Come wash these plates, H.J., and I'm not playing." and "You better shut up." There are also instances of characters like Byron being fired, highlighting employer authority: "You're fired."

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Rodrick Rules
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters attempting to exert control over others, such as Greg's mom telling him to tell Manny he loves his gift, Rodrick locking Greg in the basement, and the constant struggle between Greg and Rodrick. There are also instances of characters giving orders, like Malone telling the kids to kick the ball, and Greg's mom telling him to tell Mrs. Gillman she isn't home.

title: Footloose
justification: The film features multiple instances of authority figures exerting control, such as the Reverend's strict rules for his daughter and the town, and the school principal's disciplinary actions. Dialogue like "I will not tolerate it, Ren. Not in my school" and "Daddy, it's not a big deal. We were just messing around. I think it would be best if you came home with me. Right now" demonstrates this dynamic.

title: The Adventures of Tintin
justification: Sakharine gives orders to his crew: "I want you to go back down there and make him talk. Break every bone in his body if you have to!" Captain Haddock is also shown giving orders, but his authority is challenged, and he is often undermined, showing a struggle for control.

title: The Dilemma
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of people trying to exert control over others. Nick barks orders at his team ('Heat it up. Is the sub-amp active? Bring it up.'). Ronny attempts to manipulate and guilt-trip Nick into signing loan forms, threatening his contract ('Unless you just want to kiss that long-term contract goodbye.')

title: New Year’s Eve
justification: Several interactions involve power imbalances. Ingrid 'buys' a man for the day and dictates his actions ('I bought you for the day'). A mother restricts her daughter's freedom ('It's just my mom won't let me').

title: Arthur Christmas
justification: The dialogue is filled with hierarchical commands and status assertions. Steve's control over the S-1 and the elves, Grandsanta's insistence on his past authority, and Arthur's initial deference to authority all highlight power dynamics. Examples include: 'Let's pick this up, people!' and 'This is just the beginning, right, sir?'

title: Hall Pass
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Examples include the initial argument where one character demands another to 'Get out,' and later scenes where characters like Ed display authority through their possessions and social standing, and the discussion about the 'hall pass' reveals underlying power struggles within the marriages.

title: We Bought a Zoo
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Benjamin and his staff. Examples include Kelly being told to "go home" and MacCready's deference to Benjamin as "boss." There are also instances of Benjamin giving orders to his children, such as "Grab a box, man. Go, go get a box."

title: Soul Surfer
justification: The mother's strict homeschooling rules and the father's attempts to mediate create a clear hierarchy. The dialogue shows the mother's authority: "Just say the word and we can enroll you girls in Kapa'a..." and "Why didn't you just ask? Because she knew you'd say no."

title: Final Destination 5
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dennis correcting Sam, Candice's internship being mocked, and the general manager berating employees for wasted time. The dialogue shows clear hierarchical structures and attempts to assert dominance through insults and commands.

title: The Ides of March
justification: The dialogue is filled with power plays: characters giving orders ('Get me a hard copy'), negotiating for influence ('I want you to work for us'), and maneuvering for status ('We promised him secretary of state'). The constant back-and-forth about Thompson's endorsement highlights the struggle for control within the campaign.

title: The Descendants
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and control. Matt's father-daughter relationships are strained by his attempts to control their behavior ('You need to watch your language.') and Alex's defiance ('Fuck Mom.'). There are also instances of Matt giving orders to Sid ('Watch your sister.').

title: Hanna
justification: Several characters give orders and exert control. Erik trains Hanna with commands like "Think on your feet. Adapt... Or die." Marissa directs her team with phrases like "Just find him, Lewis." and "Do what you're told."

title: Scream 4
justification: Dewey, now sheriff, struggles to assert authority over Gale, who insists on being involved: "But I'm the sheriff now, Gale. Right." The killer taunts Sidney, asserting control over her fate: "You'll die when I want you to, Sidney, not a moment before."

title: Big Mommas: Like Father, Like Son
justification: Several characters assert dominance. Jasmine says, "l call the shots around here." Big Momma also declares, "Big Momma don't take orders from nobody."

title: Red Riding Hood
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. For example, the arranged marriage between Valerie and Henry highlights the power her parents exert over her future. Additionally, Father Solomon's arrival and subsequent control over the village demonstrate a clear power imbalance.

title: The Change-Up
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include the father instructing his daughter to "shank" anyone who wrongs her, the boss berating his employee for a deal gone wrong, and the constant demands and expectations placed on Dave by his wife and others.

title: In Time
justification: The film is filled with examples of power dynamics. Characters are constantly giving orders ('Move it', 'Get in here!'), negotiating for time ('Lend me an hour'), and struggling against a system designed to keep them oppressed ('The cost of living keeps rising to make sure people keep dying').

title: 30 Minutes or Less
justification: The entire plot revolves around characters forcing others to do their bidding through threats and violence. Examples include: "Stop. Escape is impossible," "Right now, you are wearing a highly explosive bomb vest," and "It's not my problem, it's yours. Get creative."

title: J. Edgar
justification: The dialogue is filled with hierarchical interactions, especially between Hoover and his subordinates. Examples include Hoover giving orders to Tolson and Gandy, and his interactions with Kennedy where he asserts his authority and experience. The constant need to control situations and people is evident throughout the script.

title: Sucker Punch
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and control. Blue constantly reminds the girls that they are his property, and Gorski's role involves manipulating them. Sweet Pea and Rocket are constantly being told what to do.

title: A Very Harold & Kumar 3D Christmas
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Latrell trying to intimidate Kumar at the tree lot ('You think you can buy the black man's soul') and Neil Patrick Harris's controlling behavior on set ('These talentless fuck butt-crackers...are ruining everything!').
