Harold also tries to take responsibility for the tree situation ('I take full responsibility. Please leave.').

title: The Avengers
justification: The dialogue is filled with power plays. Loki demands "Kneel before me!" and asserts that humans "crave subjugation."  There are also hierarchical exchanges like "Stow the captain's gear. Yes, sir."

title: The Dark Knight Rises
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Bane's takeover of Gotham, police officers directing each other, and Alfred's attempts to control Bruce's actions.

title: The Hunger Games
justification: The Hunger Games themselves are a blatant display of power, with the Capitol exerting control over the districts. Dialogue like "Happy Hunger Games. And may the odds be ever in your favor" and the film shown to the districts highlight the Capitol's dominance and the districts' subjugation. The tributes' struggle for survival within the arena further emphasizes the power dynamics at play.

title: The Amazing Spider-Man
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dr. Connors is pressured to 'save' Norman Osborn, with threats implied. Flash bullies Peter, demanding his belongings. Captain Stacy, as a police officer, asserts his authority and distrust of Spider-Man.

title: Brave
justification: The film features a clear power dynamic between Merida and her mother, Elinor, with Elinor dictating Merida's life and future. Dialogue such as "A princess does not chortle. Does not stuff her gob!" and "Merida, I forbid it" demonstrates Elinor's control. Merida's rebellion against these expectations and her attempts to change her fate also highlight the struggle for control.

title: Ted
justification: There are multiple instances of power dynamics at play. Lori is constantly trying to get John to change his behavior and get rid of Ted, showing her desire for control in the relationship. Rex, John's boss, also exerts power by making advances on Lori and flaunting his wealth.

title: Madagascar 3: Europe’s Most Wanted
justification: The penguins are constantly giving orders to each other, establishing a clear hierarchy. Captain Dubois commands her team with authority, and the animals struggle for leadership roles within their group, as evidenced by Marty and Alex's constant bickering.

title: Dr. Seuss' The Lorax
justification: O'Hare's control over Thneedville is evident in his surveillance and threats to Ted: "Don't go poking around in things you don't understand or I'll be your worst nightmare." The Once-ler's initial authority is shown through his business and family's dependence on him: "You're all here, you all work for me, and that's cool."

title: Men in Black 3
justification: The dialogue includes numerous instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. For example, Agent K instructs Agent J, and characters like the MIB chief issue commands related to containment and cleanup. The interactions between Boris and younger Boris also highlight a struggle for dominance and control over their shared destiny.

title: Wreck-It Ralph
justification: The movie features several characters vying for control. Sergeant Calhoun barks orders at her troops ("Now listen up, because I'm only going to say this once.") and King Candy rules Sugar Rush with an iron fist, manipulating events to maintain his power ("Sour Bill, that glitch cannot be allowed to race!").

title: Ice Age: Continental Drift
justification: The pirate Captain Gutt exerts strong control over his crew, demanding obedience and threatening violence. Manny is protective of his daughter, Peaches, grounding her and dictating her interactions with others. Granny also displays a domineering personality, bossing around Sid and others.

title: Snow White and the Huntsman
justification: The film features a clear power struggle between Snow White and Queen Ravenna, with Ravenna constantly seeking to maintain her dominance and control over the kingdom. Examples include Ravenna's commands to Finn ('Lock her up.') and her manipulation of the huntsman ('Bring me the girl and I will bring back your wife.').

title: Hotel Transylvania
justification: Dracula exerts control over Mavis, lying about humans and manipulating her experiences. He also commands the hotel staff and attempts to control Johnny's actions and memories. Examples: "I did what I had to do," and "You are never to return here."

title: Taken 2
justification: Bryan's interactions with Kim and Lennie are often about control and protection, demonstrated by his GPS tracking and interrogation of Kim's boyfriend. The film also shows the power dynamics of the villains, who kidnap and threaten the protagonists to get what they want, as seen when Marko threatens Lennie.

title: 21 Jump Street
justification: Several characters exert authority: the teacher giving a pop quiz, the drug dealer demanding immediate consumption, and the coach pressuring Doug to join the track team. Dialogue like "Take it now or get the fuck out" and "I need me some Doug McQuaid. Understand?" demonstrates this dynamic.

title: Prometheus
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and directives, such as "Let's go!", "Go faster!", and "Ellie, don't move!". Characters like the Captain and Vickers exert authority, giving commands and expecting obedience, as seen in "Vickers, that is an order! Get that goddamn door open!". There are also instances of insubordination and questioning of authority, but the overall tone suggests a hierarchical structure.

title: The Bourne Legacy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and demanding information, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Paulsen interrogating and directing others, Byer issuing orders to Aaron, and the constant need for clearance and authorization throughout the scenes.

title: Flight
justification: The pilot, Whip, is constantly trying to exert control, whether it's over his copilot, his lawyer, or Nicole. Examples include his demanding tone with Harling to get his smokes, his attempts to manipulate Margaret's testimony, and his insistence that Nicole come with him to Jamaica despite her reservations.

title: Think Like a Man
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to assert dominance or control in relationships. Examples include Lauren setting a 'five-date rule,' Michael's mother interfering in his relationships, and the basketball court scene where Cedric escalates a minor dispute into a challenge for dominance.

title: Rise of the Guardians
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging each other's authority. Examples include North commanding the Guardians, Bunny's constant challenges to North's leadership, and Pitch's attempts to instill fear and control.

title: The Campaign
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters attempting to assert dominance or control over others. Examples include Tim Wattley's controlling behavior towards Marty, Cam Brady's trash-talking and physical altercations, and the Motch brothers' influence through financial contributions.

title: Life of Pi
justification: The film depicts power dynamics through the father's strict lessons ('You have just ignored everything I've ever taught you.') and the cook's dominance on the lifeboat ('Haw dare you talk to my wife like that?'). Pi's struggle for survival against Richard Parker also highlights a constant negotiation for dominance.

title: The Expendables 2
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include: "Keep this sucker steady, Toll!", "Toll Road, get him up.", and "Cut me loose, Frankenstein.". There are also instances of characters challenging authority, such as when Lee says, "Go get it yourself."

title: Wrath of the Titans
justification: The film revolves around the power struggle between gods and humans, and within the god family itself. Zeus and Hades vie for control, while characters like Ares constantly seek to assert dominance. Dialogue like "You're in the underworld, Ares, where it's wise to obey me" and "I am my own master" highlights this theme.

title: Dark Shadows
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include Barnabas ordering Willie around ("You will cleanse me, miscreant."), Elizabeth asserting authority over Barnabas ("But whoever you are, you're not to look at those children again. Am I clear?"), and Angelique's control over Collinsport ("My Angelbay is Collinsport now.").

title: John Carter
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include Colonel Powell trying to recruit Carter ('I suggest you find the horse sense to accept my offer') and Tars Tarkas commanding the Tharks ('Sola, chain him'). There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority, such as Carter's initial refusal to cooperate with Powell and Tal Hajus challenging Tars Tarkas.

title: Les Misérables
justification: The subtitles contain many instances of characters asserting authority and others being subservient. Javert constantly asserts his power as a police officer, and Valjean struggles with his past as a convict, constantly being reminded of his place in society. The Thenardiers also exert power over Cosette, treating her as a servant.

title: Act of Valor
justification: The dialogue contains many instances of superiors giving orders to subordinates (e.g., "All right, man, lead the way," "Hey, Senior, you mind giving us a couple minutes, man?"). There are also scenes where characters assert dominance through threats and intimidation (e.g., the interrogation of Miss Morales, the conversation with Christo).

title: Django Unchained
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include the sheriff's interactions with John Ellis ('If you don't come out by three, we're gonna have to start shootin''), and the Colonel's commands to his men ('Stop right there. What regiment you in?'). The dialogue highlights a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Looper
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the looper organization, with Abe giving orders and expecting obedience. Joe's interactions with Abe highlight this dynamic, as Abe controls Joe's livelihood and future. The Rainmaker's rise to power in the future also suggests a struggle for dominance.

title: Tyler Perry’s Madea’s Witness Protection
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through orders, threats, and insults. Examples include Madea bossing around her houseguests, the daughter's disrespectful attitude and the grandmother's racist remarks, and the FBI agent giving orders to Brian.

title: Battleship
justification: The film features numerous instances of hierarchical interactions, particularly within the military. Examples include Hopper's repeated insubordination and the Admiral's stern reprimands, as well as the constant giving and receiving of orders during battle sequences. The dynamic between Hopper and the Admiral, and the formal interactions between officers and subordinates, highlight the importance of rank and obedience.

title: Mirror Mirror
justification: The Queen constantly orders Brighton around, and there are frequent power struggles, such as when the dwarfs initially capture the prince and Renbock and demand they obey. The Queen's control over the kingdom through taxation and fear also highlights her dominance.

title: Chronicle
justification: There are instances of characters giving orders and asserting dominance, such as "Matt, beam him. Beam him." and "Just do it." There's also a clear power imbalance in the relationship between Andrew and his father, demonstrated by the father's verbal and physical abuse: "Look at me when I'm talking to you!" and "Did you call me an idiot, you shit?".

title: Pitch Perfect
justification: Aubrey exerts control over the Bellas, dictating song choices and rehearsal schedules, as evidenced by her statement, "Our goal is to get back to the finals and these songs will get us there." Bumper, as the leader of the Treblemakers, displays dominance through competitive taunts and actions, such as throwing a burrito at Fat Amy during a performance. The riff-off scene also highlights the competitive struggle for status and vocal dominance between the groups.

title: Hope Springs
justification: The dialogue reveals a power struggle between Kay and Arnold, particularly regarding financial control and decision-making. Kay states, "I paid for it. With my own money, from savings," asserting her financial independence, while Arnold retorts, "Means we have a marriage license and I pay all the bills," highlighting his perceived dominance.

title: Underworld: Awakening
justification: The film features humans hunting vampires and lycans, with military personnel giving orders like "Spray her with silver!" and "Get back! No cameras!" There are also scenes of vampires giving orders to each other, such as "Lock the door" and "Everybody to the shelter. Now!"

title: Total Recall
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting authority, giving orders, and questioning each other's motives and loyalties. Examples include the Cohaagen administration questioning workers' loyalty, Lori's controlling behavior towards Quaid, and Cohaagen's manipulation of Hauser.

title: American Reunion
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Stifler's constant need to dominate situations and people, and Jim's father being manipulated into drinking and partying. There are also instances of direct orders and expectations of obedience, like Stifler's boss demanding he work on Sunday and the general disrespect shown towards Kara.

title: ParaNorman
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Perry tries to control his son Norman's behavior, and Mrs. Henscher dominates her classroom. Alvin bullies Norman, and Mitch tries to dictate Neil's friendships.

title: This Means War
justification: The film features a constant struggle for dominance between the two male leads as they compete for Lauren's affection. This is evident in their initial agreement with 'ground rules' and the repeated attempts to 'one-up' each other, such as Tuck revealing he slept with Lauren to Franklin.

title: Project X
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. Costa frequently gives orders and directions to Thomas and J.B. Rob, the neighbor, attempts to shut down the party, leading to a physical altercation and power struggle.

title: The Woman in Black
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Kipps is given a 'final warning' by his boss, showing his precarious position. He is also initially denied a room and faces resistance from locals, highlighting his outsider status and lack of authority.

title: Paranormal Activity 4
justification: The adults give orders to the children ('Wyatt, honey. Wyatt! You got to come upstairs and get dressed.') and set rules ('You know the rules. Be good.'). There are also instances of manipulation and control, such as Robbie's influence over Wyatt ('If you do what he says.').

title: Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance
justification: The film features constant power struggles, deals with the devil ('Are you willing to make a deal, John?'), and characters giving orders ('Go!', 'Shut up!'). Moreau's role as a leader within the Order also highlights hierarchical structures.

title: The Grey
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance through threats and insults. Ottway's knowledge of wolves gives him authority, while Diaz challenges him. The dialogue includes phrases like "Shut the fuck up," and "I'm gonna knock you the fuck out," indicating a struggle for control.

title: Red Tails
justification: The dialogue includes orders given to subordinates ('Decoy Squadron, move in', 'Concentrate on the stragglers!'), indicating a clear hierarchy. The line 'Show no mercy' also highlights a power dynamic through command.

title: The Possession
justification: Clyde's ex-wife, Stephanie, exerts control by boxing up his belongings and dictating terms in their shared space: "Clyde, it's not your office any more." Later, Stephanie's new partner, Brett, establishes dominance by setting house rules: "Careful, Brett. You are entering a shoe-free zone." Finally, Clyde's coaching position involves giving orders and demanding performance: "Move when you got the ball!"

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Dog Days
justification: The father-son relationship is a constant struggle for control. The father repeatedly takes away Greg's privileges, saying things like "No more video games for the rest of the summer!" and "I'm unplugging it!". Greg also tries to manipulate his father, such as when he pretends to enjoy the Wilderness Explorers.

title: Sinister
justification: The dialogue shows Ellison's struggle to maintain control over his family and his work. Tracy challenges his decisions, and the children express their anxieties, creating a power dynamic where Ellison tries to assert his authority but faces resistance. For example, Tracy says, "Is there anything you won't do for your goddamn book?"

title: Beauty and the Beast
justification: The Beast's dominance is clear in his commands and imprisonment of Maurice and Belle. Gaston's manipulation and threats to Belle and her father also highlight power imbalances. Examples: "You're not welcome here!", "Take him to the village.", "lf you marry me."

title: Savages
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making threats, and negotiating for dominance. Examples include Elena's control over her organization ('The next time we ask you to do something, I don't want to hear, Eat-shit-caviar. Am I clear?') and Miguel's attempts to control his wife and children ('One time, I tell you. You talk to a lawyer again, and I will take the three kids to Mexico and you will never see them again.').

title: The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Mrs. Donnelly demands an "English doctor," showcasing racial hierarchy. Sonny's mother exerts control over his life and business decisions, dismissing his girlfriend and dictating his marriage prospects.

title: Moonrise Kingdom
justification: The scout master gives orders to the scouts, emphasizing his authority: "You have your orders." and "Your mission is to find him, not to hurt him under any circumstances. Am I making myself understood?" The adults also exert control over Suzy and Sam, dictating their actions and future.

title: Here Comes the Boom
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Scott initially seeks Miguel's help, creating a student-teacher dynamic, but later asserts himself. There are also scenes where authority figures like the principal exert control over Scott, and instances where characters like Niko give Scott orders during fights.

title: Resident Evil: Retribution
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Examples include Jill's brainwashed orders, "Shoot to kill," and Wesker's manipulation, "Now, be a good girl. Put down the knife." The Red Queen also exerts control, stating, "You're all going to die down here."

title: The Cabin in the Woods
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('You guys better not be messing around in there'), asserting dominance ('We know what we're doing, Lin'), and struggling for control ('Does it really matter if we see her.. We're not the only ones watching, kid. Gotta keep the customer satisfied'). The facility workers are shown to have power over the victims.

title: End of Watch
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and control, particularly between police officers and civilians. Examples include officers demanding to see hands, ordering people to sit down, and threatening violence ('Shut the fuck up!', 'I'm gonna kill you!'). There are also instances of dominance in personal relationships, such as the discussion about marriage and controlling one's partner.

title: The Artist
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics, such as commands ('Speak!'), firings ('You're fired'), and blackmail ('Hey, I'm blackmailing you! Get it?'). The transition from silent films to talkies also creates a power shift, with some characters gaining and others losing status.

title: This is 40
justification: There are many instances of parents controlling children (e.g., "No computer. Listen to your mom."). There are also examples of marital power struggles (e.g., "Give me your iPhone, now."). Finally, there are boss/employee dynamics (e.g., "Here's the deal, I want you to meet me tomorrow morning at 8:00.").

title: Rock of Ages
justification: The dialogue shows some power dynamics, such as Dennis giving orders to Chico ('Dennis told me to tell you to come in early tomorrow.') and later to Drew ('Three songs. No covers. I need you guys to be amazing tonight so start drinking...now.'). There are also instances of Stacee Jaxx's manager, Paul, exerting control over him and others.

title: Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Barts demanding debt repayment with interest, and the vampire Adam controlling his subordinates and slaves. The dialogue highlights a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Lawless
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, commands, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "Give me your money, boy," "You do as I say or I'm gonna cut you," and constant power struggles between the Bondurants and law enforcement.

title: That’s My Boy
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, often through insults, dares, and challenges. Examples include the constant teasing and belittling of Todd, Donny's crude and aggressive behavior, and the Father's physical dominance and judgmental pronouncements. The characters are constantly trying to one-up each other or establish themselves as superior.

title: Trouble with the Curve
justification: There are several instances of characters asserting authority or challenging it. For example, the scoutmaster tells his players, "No room for bad play. Don't suck today." Also, Mickey's boss makes a decision about her case without consulting her, demonstrating a clear power imbalance.

title: Step Up Revolution
justification: The dialogue contains several instances of characters asserting authority and others responding. Examples include the new manager telling Sean, "I'm your boss, not your boyfriend!" and Bill Anderson's controlling behavior towards his daughter Emily, dictating her career path and expressing disapproval of her choices.

title: Tyler Perry's Good Deeds
justification: Several scenes depict power imbalances. Wesley, as the boss, has authority over Lindsey, the janitor, and offers her housing. John gives orders to Wesley, and Wesley's brother Walter seems to challenge his authority within the company.

title: Frankenweenie
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Uncle Bob asserts his authority over Victor, stating, "While your parents are away, I am in charge here." Mr. Rzykruski also displays a sense of superiority over the townspeople, calling them "ignorant" and asserting his intellectual dominance.

title: The Watch
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the police officers' interactions with the neighborhood watch, Bob's controlling behavior towards Franklin, and the general struggle for control within the group, especially when dealing with the alien.

title: Parental Guidance
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between the grandparents and grandchildren. Artie often gives orders or tries to exert control, such as when he tells Turner to stand up to the bully or when he manipulates Barker with money. Alice also attempts to control her parents' behavior and the children's activities.

title: 2016: Obama’s America
justification: The documentary explores the influence of colonialism and anti-colonialism on Obama's life and political views. There are discussions about the power dynamics between colonizers and the colonized, and how these historical power structures continue to affect contemporary society. For example, the documentary mentions how the British 'owned India' and set a 'low ceiling' above which no Indian could rise.

title: Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the mother telling Oskar to leave his cell phone on and check in every hour. Also, Oskar's mother is shown to be in charge when she tells him to open the door. However, these are relatively mild and infrequent.

title: Iron Man 3
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, such as Tony telling Jarvis what to do ('Jarvis, where's my flight power?') and Killian controlling his subordinates ('No talking and no eye contact. Unless you want to get shot in the face.'). Tony also asserts dominance in his relationship with Pepper ('And you're gonna join me.').

title: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire
justification: The Capitol exerts control through the Hunger Games, dictating the lives of the districts. President Snow manipulates Katniss and Peeta to quell rebellion, demonstrating his authority: "So he wants you to make them believe it? To calm things down." Peacekeepers enforce the Capitol's will with violence and curfews: "Anyone out after dark will be shot on sight."

title: Man of Steel
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include General Zod's ultimatum to Earth, Colonel Hardy's interactions with Lois Lane, and Jonathan Kent's instructions to Clark about hiding his powers.

title: Monsters University
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters trying to assert dominance or prove themselves. Sulley's lineage grants him immediate status ('He's a Sullivan! I should have known. I expect big things from you.'). Characters like Johnny Worthington and Dean Hardscrabble wield authority, while others like Mike Wazowski struggle to gain respect ('Slow down, squirt. This party is for Scare students only.').

title: Frozen
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics. Elsa is in charge as Queen, giving orders such as "Close the gates." Hans is left in charge of Arendelle and gives orders to his men.

title: Gravity
justification: Throughout the dialogue, Houston (mission control) gives orders and instructions to the astronauts, who generally comply. Examples include "Please verify that the P1 ATA removal...are complete," and "Dr. Stone, Houston. Medical is asking if you want to return to Explorer." There are also instances of astronauts questioning or pushing back against Houston's instructions, indicating a negotiation of power, such as when Dr. Stone initially refuses to return to Explorer despite medical concerns.

title: Oz the Great and Powerful
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, giving orders, and establishing hierarchies. Examples include Evanora's control over the Emerald City, Oz's attempts to manipulate Finley, and the power struggles between the witches.

title: Thor: The Dark World
justification: Odin's authority is constantly challenged, especially by Loki, who seeks to undermine his rule and sow discord. Odin gives orders and expects obedience, but characters like Thor and Loki frequently question or defy him: "I'm telling you this, not as the Allfather, but as your father. You are ready. The time has come for you to take the throne."

title: World War Z
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, especially in moments of crisis. Examples include 'Get back in your car right now!' and 'Everybody out of the car.' The military personnel also give orders to Gerry and his team, demonstrating their authority.

title: The Croods
justification: Grug's strict rules and overprotective nature create a clear hierarchy within the family, as evidenced by lines like, "You are supposed to wait for my signal. Eep?" and "Fear keeps us alive, Eep. Never not be afraid." Eep's rebellious nature and the family's eventual shift away from Grug's control also highlight the power struggle.

title: The Heat
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance over each other. For example, the DEA agent berates Ashburn and Mullins, saying, "I don't want to see you two anywhere near this case!" and later, Mullins's boss reprimands her for her actions: "I want you to stand down..."

title: We’re the Millers
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include David telling Kenny to 'grab the hats. Hurry,' and the border patrol officer demanding, 'Sir, pull forward to lane two.' Senior Chacon's interactions with his subordinates also highlight a clear power imbalance.

title: The Great Gatsby
justification: Gatsby's interactions with Nick are often transactional, offering business deals in exchange for favors. Tom asserts dominance through wealth and social status, questioning Gatsby's background and Oxford education. The dialogue reveals a constant struggle for control and validation.

title: The Conjuring
justification: There are instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority, such as "Honey, have April come in, okay?" and "Come on, April! Mom wants us inside!" There are also instances of characters trying to control each other, such as when Nancy and another girl fight over a wind chime, and when a father tells his daughters to go to bed.

title: Identity Thief
justification: The subtitles contain frequent instances of characters attempting to exert control over one another. Diana is initially in a position of power, manipulating and deceiving others, but later finds herself at the mercy of Sandy and other pursuers. Dialogue such as "Get out of the car!" and "You're not going anywhere" highlights the ongoing struggle for dominance.

title: Grown Ups 2
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to assert dominance, such as the bus driver yelling at the kids, the confrontation at the quarry where college kids try to assert their territory, and the ice cream shop scene where Higgins is mocked and humiliated. The dialogue reveals a constant struggle for status and control.

title: The Wolverine
justification: The film features constant struggles for control of Yashida Industries, with characters like Shingen vying for power. Dialogue such as "When I die, someone else will take my place as chairman" and "You have brought this company close to ruin" highlights the hierarchical structure and the stakes involved.

title: G.I. Joe: Retaliation
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and hierarchical exchanges. Examples include "All right, listen up!" and "Negative, Flint! Stick with the plan!" Also, there are instances of characters asserting dominance, such as the President's imposter's behavior and dialogue.

title: Now You See Me
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance through threats and manipulation. Bradley threatens Tressier, stating, "My bank account is much, much bigger than yours. And my lawyers are much stronger." Atlas also displays control, telling Dray, "You're dismissive enough about me when you're sober."

title: Lee Daniels' The Butler
justification: The provided text consists of error messages, indicating a server issue. There is no dialogue or interaction to analyze for power dynamics.

title: The Hangover 3
justification: Characters are constantly giving orders (e.g., "Get down! Get down!") and asserting dominance. Marshall's control over Doug and the wolfpack, and Chow's unpredictable behavior create a volatile power dynamic.

title: Epic
justification: Several characters exert authority: Boggan gives orders ("I don't think I saw a salute, Boggan!"), Ronin commands Nod ("Don't walk away from me. I'm your commanding officer!"), and Mandrake demands obedience ("If it dies, you die."). There are also instances of defiance, such as Nod quitting the Leafmen ("I quit!").

title: Captain Phillips
justification: The entire plot revolves around pirates seizing control of a ship and its crew. Dialogue like "I'm the captain now" and constant demands/threats highlight the struggle for dominance. The captain's attempts to regain control and protect his crew further emphasize this theme.

title: Silver Linings Playbook
justification: There are many instances of characters trying to exert control over others, such as Pat's father demanding he wear the jersey and stay for the game, or Pat's outbursts where he yells and refuses to calm down. Tiffany also attempts to manipulate Pat into doing the dance competition in exchange for delivering the letter to Nikki. The police intervention and restraining order also highlight the power dynamics at play.

title: Pacific Rim
justification: There are many examples of power dynamics. Pentecost gives orders to rangers, and rangers give orders to each other. For example, "Wait here" and "I have a plan. I need you ready. That's all."

title: This is the End
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control resources ('That's my Milky Way'), exert dominance ('I'm invading your little area'), and establish social hierarchy ('If anyone's gonna rape anyone here, it's probably gonna be Danny'). The constant bickering and voting on decisions also highlight the struggle for power within the group.

title: Jackass Presents: Bad Grandpa
justification: The grandfather exerts control over Billy through commands and dismissals, such as "Just get in the damn car" and "No!" to simple requests. The grandfather also manipulates and directs others, like when he instructs James to "get the head" of the corpse, demonstrating a clear hierarchy and expectation of obedience.

title: Olympus Has Fallen
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's positions. Examples include the President directing his staff, Banning defying orders, and the terrorists demanding compliance under threat of violence. The interactions highlight a constant struggle for control and dominance.

The dialogue is filled with instances of racial prejudice and attempts to assert dominance over Jackie Robinson. Examples include the Phillies manager's constant racial slurs and the threat of violence if Robinson doesn't leave the field, demonstrating a clear power imbalance and struggle for control.

title: Zero Dark Thirty
justification: The dialogue is filled with interrogation scenes where characters are trying to extract information from detainees, exerting power over them. Examples include: "You determine how you're treated. And your life is gonna be very uncomfortable until you give me the information I need." and "I'm gonna break you."

title: Elysium
justification: The subtitles are filled with examples of power dynamics. Max is constantly being ordered around by parole officers, bosses, and criminals. Delacourt exerts authority over Kruger and others, giving orders and threatening consequences.

title: Anchorman 2: The Legend Continues
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance through verbal sparring and intimidation. Jack's popularity is a source of jealousy, leading to a confrontation where he threatens physical violence: "I'm gonna rip this guy in half." Linda, as the boss, fires the entire news team for their on-air antics, demonstrating her authority.

title: Disney Planes
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Skipper training Dusty and giving orders: "0500, tomorrow. Don't be late." Ripslinger also displays dominance through insults and threats: "Well, first place is for losers."

title: Insidious Chapter 2
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Elise directing others in investigations ('Show her', 'May I meet him?'), and the mother of Parker Crane compelling him to kill ('You must! Or you'll waste away'). There are also instances of characters being ordered around, like when Josh is told to show the photos or when Lorraine is told to get Dalton out of the house.

title: 2 Guns
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and negotiating power. Examples include the Navy Commander directing Stigman ('Tick all the boxes, nothing left undone. You got it?'), Papi's control over his organization, and the constant back-and-forth between Bobby and Stigman regarding who is in charge.

title: White House Down
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and orders, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "all WFO, get as many men as you can to the Capitol," "Fred, open the gate," and "Stand back! Go out and do your job!"

title: Mama
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority: the father yelling "Shut up!" at his daughter, the police officer telling Lucas to "wait here," and Burnsie giving orders with "Yes, sir, yes, sir, yes, sir."

title: Safe Haven
justification: There are subtle power dynamics at play. The detective uses his authority to question a child, and Alex, as a father, exerts control over his children's activities and whereabouts. The interaction between Kevin and his wife also shows a clear imbalance of power, with Kevin displaying controlling behavior.

title: The Smurfs 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority, particularly from Papa Smurf ('All right, Smurfs, listen up') and Gargamel ('Alakaz-kneel. Bow. Kneel.'). There are also instances of characters vying for approval or recognition, such as the Smurfs wanting to be chosen for the mission.

title: The Best Man Holiday
justification: Several characters exert authority or seek to control situations. Examples include Mia directing others, Lance's status as a football legend influencing interactions, and power struggles within relationships, such as the tension between Harper and Robyn, and Julian's attempts to control Candace's past.

title: Percy Jackson: Sea of Monsters
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as Clarisse commanding the zombie sailors. Luke's manipulation and control over other half-bloods also highlights power dynamics, as does the Oracle's pronouncements about fate.

title: American Hustle
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, give orders, and manipulate others. Examples include Irving directing Rosalyn ('Go get ready') and DiMaso's controlling behavior ('Don't look at me...don't talk to me outside of these roles'). The interactions with the mob boss, Tellegio, also highlight the struggle for control and respect.

title: A Good Day to Die Hard
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Make the call', 'Seal the doors!'), threats ('I own everybody in that courtroom'), and power plays ('Just give me the file... and I'll hand your life back to you'). Characters are constantly trying to assert dominance and control over each other.

title: Warm Bodies
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between humans and zombies, with humans initially holding power through weapons and control of resources. However, this dynamic shifts as zombies begin to 'cure' themselves, challenging the established order, as seen when Julie's father initially threatens R, but later accepts him.

title: The Purge
justification: The dialogue is filled with hierarchical interactions, from Mr. Sandin's business dealings ("You're number one, Mr. Sandin.") to the Purge participants asserting dominance ("Just give us the homeless pig, you fuck!"). The film explores the power dynamics inherent in a society where violence is sanctioned, highlighting the vulnerability of the poor and the arrogance of the wealthy.

title: Last Vegas
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Sam's friends try to control his drinking, and there are constant arguments about who is in charge of reservations. The casino staff also exert authority, and the group encounters mobsters who demand subservience.

title: Ender’s Game
justification: The dialogue is filled with hierarchical interactions, from Ender's initial encounters with authority figures like Sergeant Dap ('Sir, yes, sir!') to Bonzo Madrid's strict control over his army ('When we go into battle, you will not pass through the gates until all my soldiers are through.'). Characters are constantly jockeying for position and respect, and the military structure reinforces a clear chain of command.

title: Prisoners
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert control, interrogate, and manipulate each other. Examples include detectives questioning suspects ('Where do you usually park your RV, Alex?'), parents demanding action ('He stays in custody until my daughter's found, right?'), and characters resorting to violence to extract information ('We hurt him until he talks, or they're gonna die.').

title: After Earth
justification: The film features a clear military hierarchy with characters giving and receiving orders ('Go! Go!', 'Dismissed.', 'Denied! Sit down!'). The relationship between Cypher Raige and his son Kitai is fraught with power imbalances, as Cypher constantly commands and criticizes Kitai ('This isn't a race, cadet!', 'You weren't ready.'). Kitai's struggle to earn his father's approval and become a Ranger also highlights the theme.

title: Escape From Planet Earth
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance. Scorch and Gary constantly bicker, with Scorch often belittling Gary. Shanker is also shown to be in control, giving orders and threatening others.

title: Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of authority. Examples include: "Take them into the forest now," "I said, stay here!", "Burn her!", "Let the girl go or I'm gonna blow your sheriff's brains all over these fucking hillbillies.", and various characters giving orders and asserting dominance.

title: Free Birds
justification: Several characters give orders or express authority. Examples include General Sagan's presence, Standish's commands to his men, and Broadbeak's leadership of the flock. Jake's initial attempts to command the turkeys also highlight a struggle for control.

title: Evil Dead
justification: The film revolves around a demonic entity seeking to possess and control the characters. This is evident in lines like "One by one we will take you! You are all going to die tonight" and the constant struggle for control over Mia's body and mind.

title: RED 2
justification: Characters give orders and make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Honey, you need to go to ground and it's best I don't know where," and "Nobody's going public." There are also instances of characters being controlled or manipulated, such as the Senior Director of Military Intelligence being "caramelizing his onions."

title: Tyler Perry’s Temptation
justification: Harley exerts control over Judith, offering her opportunities and dictating her actions ('If you were mine, you wouldn't have to work.'). Janice also displays dominance in her workplace, manipulating Judith and controlling her career ('This is your last day.'). Brice attempts to control Judith's actions and emotions, but ultimately fails.

title: The Call
justification: The 911 operators are clearly in positions of authority, directing callers and dispatching resources. The kidnapper exerts extreme control over Casey, silencing and threatening her. The police also give orders to each other.

title: Pain & Gain
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include: "You better fucking man up," "Okay, you're fired!", and "Wake him up! Get up!". The interactions are often aggressive and hierarchical.

title: Gangster Squad
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and jockeying for position. Examples include O'Mara recruiting a squad to wage 'guerilla war' against Cohen, Cohen's brutal treatment of those who fail him, and various characters threatening each other to get what they want.

title: Tyler Perry’s A Madea Christmas
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance or resisting authority. Madea's interactions with the children and her pronouncements on behavior showcase her attempts to control the situation. Additionally, the tension between Eileen and Lacey, and the parents' interactions, highlight struggles for control and differing opinions on how things should be done.

title: The Internship
justification: The new Googlers are immediately placed in a subordinate position to the existing Googlers, as evidenced by Lyle's attempts to assert his authority and the interns' competitive drive to win challenges. Dialogue such as "You'll mentor the leftovers" and "You have five minutes. Pick your teams" highlights the hierarchical structure and the pressure to perform.

title: Saving Mr. Banks
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of Mrs. Travers asserting her authority and control over the film's creative process, often clashing with Walt Disney and his team. Examples include her dictating changes to the script, characters, and even the color palette, demonstrating a constant struggle for dominance over the artistic direction.

title: Snitch
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others. Examples include the U.S. Attorney dictating terms to John Matthews ('We need your son to help us make arrests before we can help him reduce his sentence.') and Malik's dominance over John ('You gonna drive the first load.').

title: Riddick
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, issuing orders, and asserting dominance. Examples include Santana's constant need to be in charge, Johns's manipulation of the bounty hunters, and Riddick's strategic moves to outwit and control his opponents. The Necromonger scenes also highlight a rigid hierarchy.

title: The Wolf of Wall Street
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of dominance and submission. Jordan's interactions with his employees involve yelling, insults, and demands, establishing a clear hierarchy. His interactions with his wife also show a struggle for control, with arguments and attempts to manipulate each other.

title: A Haunted House
justification: Malcolm and Kisha's relationship is marked by attempts to exert control, especially when dealing with the paranormal activity. Malcolm often tries to dismiss Kisha's concerns ('That was just the house settling. No big thing.') and later tries to take charge of the situation ('You evil spirit! You leave this house alone!').

title: 12 Years a Slave
justification: The dialogue is dominated by masters giving orders to slaves, threats of violence, and displays of ownership. Examples include 'You are ordered to return that property immediately or be charged with thievery,' 'Strip your clothes,' and constant references to slaves as property.

title: The Family
justification: Several characters exert authority: Maggie bosses Giovanni around, Stan controls Fred through the Witness Protection Program, and various characters give orders or make demands of others. Examples include: "Maggie? Can you get me a coffee?", "Don't move for ten minutes, you understand?", and "You were supposed to be here at nine in the morning, you don't show up till about noon. What's that all about?".

title: Carrie
justification: The film showcases extreme power dynamics, particularly between Carrie and her abusive mother ('Go to your closet and pray') and the bullying she endures at school ('Plug it up!'). Ms. Desjardin attempts to exert authority over the students ('Everyone get out! Now! Out!'), and Chris manipulates Billy ('Pull it, Billy, pull it!').

title: Texas Chainsaw 3D
justification: The sheriff and mayor are constantly vying for control, with the mayor often undermining the sheriff's authority. Examples include the mayor ordering Marvin to ignore the sheriff's instructions and the sheriff's attempts to control the crowd versus the mayor's encouragement of violence. Jed's actions are driven by a need to protect his family, showcasing a different kind of power dynamic.

title: R.I.P.D.
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and jockeying for position. Examples include Roy's constant berating of Nick ('You ain't my partner, rook.') and Proctor's authoritative commands ('Get back out there.'). Even in death, characters like Hayes try to control situations.

title: Blue Jasmine
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. For example, Chili is told to "change the subject" and Jasmine is told to "go and start your cooldown." Hal also displays dominance by making decisions for others and expecting obedience.

title: Kevin Hart: Let Me Explain
justification: The comedian establishes a hierarchy in relationships, particularly friendships, where lying for a friend is expected: "If you're my best friend...that means that my bullshit is your bullshit." He also describes power dynamics in romantic relationships, highlighting the struggle for control and the potential for manipulation and insecurity: "Are you done? Are you done? Okay. Okay. I'm about to shit on this bitch right now."

title: Side Effects
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. The pharmaceutical reps attempt to influence doctors with perks ("buy you doctors lunch as long as we talk about business for at least five minutes"). Also, the legal system exerts power over Dr. Banks, threatening him with consequences if he doesn't cooperate ("Either she's a murderer or she's a victim of her medical treatment. In which case, you're the target of a big civil suit.").

title: Scary Movie 5
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or asserting authority. For example, Dan tells Jody, "Now, no more rock band, no more silly wig... And no more tattoos." Also, the ballet instructor directs the dancers, and the scientist bosses around his colleague.

title: The Secret Life of Walter Mitty
justification: Walter's boss, Ted, frequently belittles and berates him, demanding the missing photo and ultimately firing him. The interactions between Walter and his eHarmony advisor, Todd, also show a power dynamic, with Todd pushing Walter to change his profile and judging his experiences.

title: The Mortal Instruments: City of Bones
justification: Characters give orders and express authority: "Sit," "Run!", "You can't stay here.". There are also power struggles, such as Valentine's attempts to control Luke and Jace, and Isabelle's assertion of authority over Clary.

title: Delivery Man
justification: Several scenes depict power imbalances. For example, the barista is berated by a customer, and David is constantly being asked to do favors or being told what to do by his family and friends: "I'm begging you, man. I really, really need you to do this for me."

title: One Direction: This is Us
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Paul, the tour manager, giving orders: "We're on stage in 5 minutes!" and "Guys, come on, we gotta go!". There are also instances of the band members playfully bossing each other around, like when one says, "I said, sit down!"

title: Kick-Ass 2
justification: Several characters assert dominance through threats and commands. The Motherfucker frequently orders his crew, such as telling them to "Cut the old man's head off." Javier's initial subservience to Chris, followed by Chris's uncle's attempt to control him from prison, also highlights power struggles.

title: Rush
justification: Several instances show power dynamics. For example, Hesketh's team has a butler serving oysters, indicating wealth and status. Also, the dialogue between drivers reveals competition and attempts to assert dominance, such as when one driver says, "So says the nobody who had to pay for his own drive."

title: Guardians of the Galaxy
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Ronan's interactions with Thanos and Nebula, Yondu's control over Quill, and the general hierarchical structure within the prison all highlight power dynamics. Examples include 'Out of the way,' 'Lower your tone!' and 'Bring it to me.'

title: The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles, especially between Katniss and President Coin. Katniss makes demands to become the Mockingjay, stating, "But I have some conditions," and Coin responds with her own power plays, such as, "If Katniss Everdeen fails to fulfill her duties the deal will be off."

title: Captain America: The Winter Soldier
justification: The dialogue showcases a clear hierarchy, with characters giving and receiving orders. Examples include Fury's directives to Hill ('Give me four hours. You have three. Over.') and Pierce's authority within S.H.I.E.L.D. ('Operations Control. Confirmed. Keep all S.T.R.I.K.E. personnel on site.')

title: The Lego Movie
justification: Lord Business exerts control through commands and threats, as seen in his interactions with Bad Cop and his parents ('Would you cancel my 2:00?', 'I'll do it on your parents!'). The dialogue highlights a clear hierarchy and the consequences of disobedience.

title: Transformers: Age of Extinction
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include Savoy's command to "Use the girl," Lockdown's control over the Knights, and Cade's protective, often controlling, behavior towards Tessa, such as "You are so grounded!" and "You're gonna do what I say!".

title: Maleficent
justification: The film showcases power dynamics through Stefan's ambition to become king by betraying Maleficent, King Henry's desire to conquer the Moors, and Maleficent's initial dominance over Diaval. Dialogue such as "A king does not take orders from a winged elf" and "I am your servant. Whatever you need" highlight the hierarchical relationships and struggles for control.

title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
justification: Characters frequently give and receive orders, highlighting hierarchical structures. Examples include 'Stand aside, soldier. That's an order,' and Trask's manipulation of government officials to fund his Sentinel program. The film also explores the power dynamics between humans and mutants, with humans seeking to control or eliminate mutants.

title: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
justification: The film depicts a constant struggle for dominance between humans and apes, and within each group.  Examples include Dreyfus asserting authority over the human colony and Koba challenging Caesar's leadership among the apes: "Listen to me. Not a word of this back at the colony, you understand me?" and "Caesar love humans more than apes."

title: Big Hero 6
justification: The dialogue shows Hiro giving orders to Baymax ('Baymax, destroy') and his friends, trying to control the situation. There are also instances of characters like Callaghan asserting authority ('Give me the mask, Hiro').

title: The Amazing Spider-Man 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Harry asserts his authority at Oscorp, firing people and demanding information. Max Dillon is mistreated and ignored, highlighting his lack of power, while Spider-Man is seen as a figure of authority and control.

title: Godzilla
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience, highlighting a clear hierarchy. Examples include the plant supervisor ordering 'Take us offline. Now, Joe...Do it!' and military personnel directing subordinates, such as 'All right! Let's go!'

title: 22 Jump Street
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control or influence over others. Examples include the police captain's aggressive behavior, the fraternity's hazing rituals ('Drink, motherfucker!'), and the general's attempts to manipulate others ('You're gonna be all right, man.').

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Shredder commands his Foot Clan, demanding results and threatening consequences, while Leonardo often directs his brothers, sometimes leading to conflict as seen in Raphael's rebellious attitude.

title: The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies
justification: Several characters vie for authority. Alfrid attempts to assert power as the Master's deputy, but is challenged. Thorin's leadership and descent into 'dragon-sickness' create internal power struggles within the dwarves.

title: How to Train Your Dragon 2
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy between Vikings and dragons, initially with Vikings dominating and trapping dragons. Later, Drago seeks to control dragons to build an army, demonstrating a desire for power and control.

title: Gone Girl
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Nick's infidelity and Amy's manipulation showcase a struggle for dominance in their relationship, with Amy ultimately seeking to punish Nick. The police investigation also highlights power dynamics, with detectives questioning Nick and attempting to uncover the truth.

title: Neighbors
justification: The movie features constant struggles for dominance between the couple and the fraternity. Examples include the couple trying to control the fraternity's behavior by calling the cops and the fraternity retaliating with pranks and escalating actions. The Dean also exerts authority by placing the fraternity on probation.

title: Ride Along
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include the officer telling the bikers to leave, James constantly ordering Ben around, and the interrogation scenes where characters threaten each other to gain information.

title: Rio 2
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the father figure telling Blu what to do and how to act in the jungle. There is also a clear hierarchy in the soccer game, with Roberto being the star player and Blu being relegated to water boy. The line 'Understood?' also implies a power dynamic.

title: Lucy
justification: The film features constant power struggles. Richard manipulates Lucy into delivering a package, and Mr. Jang's gang uses violence and intimidation to control people. Lucy's transformation gives her immense power, which she uses to control others, like the police officer and the drug mules.

title: Lone Survivor
justification: The film depicts a clear military hierarchy, with characters giving and receiving orders. Examples include Murphy directing his team ('Axe, give us our route') and Kristensen briefing the team on their mission ('Leaving here at 1800. Two Chinooks and two Apaches.'). There's also a scene where new recruits are hazed, demonstrating a struggle for dominance.

title: The Fault in Our Stars
justification: There are instances of power dynamics, such as Augustus using his 'wish' to take Hazel to Amsterdam, demonstrating a degree of control and influence. Also, Hazel's mother has authority over whether Hazel can go to Amsterdam, and the doctor has authority over Hazel's health decisions. However, these are not the primary focus of the dialogue.

title: 300: Rise of an Empire
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for power, giving orders, and asserting dominance. Artemisia's manipulation of Xerxes and her control over her fleet, as well as Themistokles' leadership and strategic decisions, highlight the constant struggle for control. Dialogue such as "You will be a god-king" and "Silence for the hero of Marathon!" demonstrates the hierarchical relationships and the importance of authority.

title: Noah
justification: The film features multiple power struggles. Tubal-cain challenges Noah's authority, stating, "This all belongs to me. This land. This forest." Noah also asserts his dominance within his family, dictating their actions and beliefs, culminating in his near infanticide.

title: The Equalizer
justification: The film is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include Slavi's control over the prostitutes, Teddy's management of the corrupt cops, and McCall's interactions with Pushkin's organization, where he dictates terms and punishes disobedience.

title: Edge of Tomorrow
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and assertions of authority. Farell constantly berates and orders Cage, emphasizing Cage's low status: 'On your feet, maggot!' and 'Get in line before I bust your hole with my boot heel!'

title: Non-Stop
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include: "Agent Marks, I need you to take me through the events from the beginning," and "Go back to your seat." There are also instances of characters questioning authority and struggling against it, such as the passenger who asks, "Did you just call me 'ma'am'?"

title: Heaven is for Real
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the initial offer to the lion and his friends, "All you have to do is give up that lion." Also, the church board exerts some control over Todd's preaching, "If you're going to lead this church, you've got to make a decision."

title: Fury
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "First Platoon, mount up! Move out!", "Next German you see with a weapon, you rake the dog shit out of him.", and the constant berating and attempts to control Norman.

title: Dumb and Dumber To
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Penny, do you have the speech I wrote for you?" and "Honey, can you bring me some more Pepto?". Also, the plot revolves around controlling a billion-dollar invention.

title: Tammy
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. Tammy's grandma is bossy and manipulative, ordering Tammy around and taking her car. Earl is also shown ordering his son Bobby around, and the attempted robbery shows a clear power imbalance.

title: Annabelle
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or expressing dominance. John tells Mia to shut off the TV and later tells her to get out of the house. Pete's comment, 'You just make sure to take care of this wife and baby of yours,' implies a position of authority.

title: The Other Woman
justification: Several characters exert dominance through commands and manipulation. Kate frequently gives orders and sets boundaries, such as "You have one hour" and "Get down." Mark's infidelity and attempts to control the narrative also highlight power imbalances.

title: Let’s Be Cops
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters trying to assert dominance, give orders, and control situations. Examples include the initial argument between Chang and the sergeant ('Stand down! I'm the sergeant, Chang. I'm going first.') and the attempts to control the fighting women ('You need to stop! I'm controlling the situation!').

title: The Monuments Men
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the Colonel's interactions with subordinates ("I don't give a shit! Do not interrupt me!") and the German officer's interrogation tactics ("Take a goddamn cigarette.").

title: Penguins of Madagascar
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and hierarchical language, especially between Skipper and the other penguins (e.g., "Private, come on!", "Kowalski, analysis!"). There's also a clear power struggle between the penguins and Agent Classified, with both sides vying for control of the mission (e.g., "I give the orders around here.").

title: Hercules
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, with kings giving orders ('Finish him,' 'Bring me his head!'), generals commanding troops, and Hercules often being looked to for leadership and decision-making. There are also instances of defiance and challenges to authority, such as when characters question orders or plot against the king.

title: Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb
justification: The dialogue shows a clear struggle for control, especially between Larry and his son Nicky, with Larry trying to enforce rules and Nicky pushing back. Examples include the argument about NYU, taking a year off, and tracking Nicky's phone. Also, the Pharaoh demands respect and obedience, highlighting a hierarchical dynamic.

title: Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day
justification: Several instances show parents directing children ("Alexander, would you grab that and wash it off, please?") and children pushing back ("Dad, don't!"). There's also a clear hierarchy at work with the book publisher boss and employee, and the driving examiner and student.

title: Think Like a Man Too
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, Ced tries to control Dom's decisions about his relationship, and Miss Loretta attempts to dictate the bachelorette party activities. There are also instances of characters giving orders or directions, such as when Ced directs the bachelor party activities.

title: The Nut Job
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and vying for control. Raccoon's leadership and manipulation are evident in lines like, "Quiet. Quiet." and "Do what you will, do what is right." Surly's defiance and attempts to assert dominance are also present, as seen in his interactions with Andie and the other animals.

title: Into the Woods
justification: Characters frequently give orders (e.g., "Take the cow and go home," "Stay," "Let down your hair to me!"). There are also instances of characters being forced to obey (e.g., "Go on, get in there!"). Royalty also exert power, as seen when the Prince commands, "Quickly!" and "Onward!".

title: Unbroken
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority, especially the interactions with 'The Bird' (Corporal Watanabe). Examples include Watanabe's commands like 'Look at me!' and the general hierarchical structure of the POW camp.

title: God’s Not Dead
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. Examples include the professor's intimidation of the student, the girlfriend's demands regarding the boyfriend's studies, and the father's oppressive control over his daughter's religious beliefs.

title: Son of God
justification: The film depicts the power dynamics between the Roman Empire and the Jewish people, with the Romans exerting control through taxation and military presence. Religious leaders also vie for authority, challenging Jesus's teachings and ultimately orchestrating his crucifixion. Dialogue like "In the name of Rome, taxes are owed" and "Disorder will not be tolerated" exemplifies this struggle.

title: Planes: Fire and Rescue
justification: Several characters exert authority: Cad Spinner demands Dusty perform a flyover and generally bosses around the park staff. Blade Ranger gives orders to the firefighting team, and Dusty is initially subordinate to him as a trainee, with dialogue like "Pull up, that's an order!"

title: The Grand Budapest Hotel
justification: Gustave's interactions with Zero are often hierarchical, with Gustave giving orders and Zero obeying ("So keep your mouth shut, Zero. Yes, sir."). Gustave also exerts authority over hotel staff and even attempts to control situations with law enforcement ("Sit down, Zero.").

title: RoboCop
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Sellars directing Norton on how to manage Murphy, and the police chief issuing commands to her officers. The interactions between Murphy and criminals also highlight a power dynamic, with Murphy using his authority to extract information and enforce the law.

title: Annie
justification: The movie features a clear power dynamic between Will Stacks and Annie, where Stacks initially sees Annie as a political tool to boost his campaign. Dialogue like "Taking in a foster kid, that's an automatic 15 point jump in the polls. Guaranteed." and Stacks' staff dictating Annie's actions highlight this imbalance.

title: Dracula Untold
justification: The film revolves around Vlad's struggle against the Turkish Sultan, who demands 1,000 boys as tribute, showcasing a clear power imbalance. Vlad's transformation into a vampire is driven by his desire to protect his people and defy the Sultan's authority, leading to conflicts and negotiations based on power.

title: Exodus: Gods and Kings
justification: The movie is filled with examples of power dynamics. Pharaoh gives orders to generals ("Deploy Amun division to the north..."), and Ramses asserts his authority over Moses and the slaves ("Work quotas shall be doubled..."). There are also struggles for power, such as the viceroy trying to maintain his position and Moses challenging Ramses' rule.

title: The Hundred-Foot Journey
justification: The film features a clear power struggle between the Kadam family and Madame Mallory, owner of a Michelin-starred restaurant. Examples include Mallory buying all the ingredients to sabotage the Kadam's opening, and Kadam retaliating by stealing pigeons for a dish. The dialogue highlights their competitive and antagonistic relationship, with each trying to assert dominance.

title: No Good Deed
justification: The parole hearing scene shows the power of the board over Colin's fate. Later, Colin exerts control through threats and violence, demanding obedience from Terry: "Get in. Stay right there." and "I will kill you. Do you understand me?".

title: Horrible Bosses 2
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Rex berating his maid Kim, and Julia trying to manipulate Blanston. The power dynamic shifts when Rex proposes partnering in his own kidnapping, attempting to take charge of the situation.

title: Ouija
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or directions, such as "Debbie, cut it out!" and "Get out of here, Sarah!" show a struggle for control. Laine's attempts to control Sarah's behavior, like "You're not going anywhere," further highlight this dynamic.

title: Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and maneuvering for control. Examples include Cherevin's interactions with Jack Ryan, the Russian minister's directives, and the CIA's operational commands.

title: The Boxtrolls
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Acquire them!', 'Get them!'), demanding respect ('Give me that hat!'), and vying for status ('A white hat indicates privilege, prestige, position!'). Snatcher's relentless pursuit of a white hat and the boxtrolls' initial subservience highlight the hierarchical power struggles.

title: If I Stay
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Adam's bandmate telling him to kiss Mia and leave, indicating a subtle pressure or expectation. justification: Several characters exert authority or challenge it. Bucky's comments to Ruby are critical and controlling: "You love everybody at arm's length, keep it up and you'll end up alone, Ruby." Officer Williams' initial robotic behavior and Emma's attempts to break through his emotional barriers also highlight a power struggle.

title: Spotlight
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and obedience. For example, a reporter asks to interview victims, but the lawyer initially refuses, stating, "I spoke to my clients, and they don't want to be in the press. I'm sorry." Later, the editor pressures the team to get more information, saying, "You can't empty his pockets? I'll get to him. I just need more time. Oh, come on, Mike. You gotta get him."

title: The Lazarus Effect
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Clay, what did I say about smoking in here?" and "Eva, put the camera down. Put it down."

title: Ex Machina
justification: Nathan exerts control through non-disclosure agreements and manipulation, demonstrated by his control over Ava and Caleb. Ava's actions, like causing power cuts and manipulating Caleb, also show a struggle for control. Dialogue such as "You shouldn't trust him" and the constant surveillance highlight the power imbalances and attempts to subvert them.

title: The Big Short
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy in the financial world. Junior firms are dismissed ('B of A and Bear didn't even return our calls'), while established firms dictate terms ('If we don't give them the ratings, they'll go to Moody's'). There are also power struggles between investors and fund managers ('Give me my fucking money back').

title: In the Heart of the Sea
justification: The film is filled with examples of power dynamics. Captain Pollard's inexperience is constantly challenged by First Mate Chase, and the crew's survival depends on obedience to authority, even when those orders are questionable. Examples include: "To be a captain, you cannot be a friend. You are their superior. Never forget that. Never let them forget that."

title: Finding Dory
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Hank frequently bosses Dory around, telling her to be quiet and follow his plans. The sea lions also display dominance by yelling at Gerald and making him get off the rock.

title: Captain America: Civil War
justification: Characters give and receive orders ('Ready to comply', 'I have a mission for you', 'Sanction and extract'). There are clear superior/subordinate relationships, with one character referred to as 'Soldier' and another as 'Father'. The dialogue also shows a struggle for control ('It's okay, I can manage!').

title: The Secret Life of Pets
justification: The dialogue shows a clear struggle for dominance between Max and Duke, especially evident in their interactions about the bed and food bowl: "this bed is mine" and "That's my bowl." Snowball also exerts authority over the Flushed Pets, giving orders and expecting obedience: "From now on, you work for me."

title: Deadpool
justification: Characters give orders and assert dominance. Examples include Ajax controlling Wade in the workshop ('Shut the fuck up') and Deadpool bossing around Colossus and Negasonic Teenage Warhead ('Zip it, Sinéad!').

title: Zootopia
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between predators and prey, and within the police force. Judy faces prejudice and is assigned demeaning tasks, while Chief Bogo exerts his authority. The dialogue highlights these power imbalances, such as when Judy is told she'll 'never be a real cop' and when Mr. Big's power is displayed.

title: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether through direct orders ('Get out of here before dark'), threats ('Next time they shine your light in the sky, don't go to it'), or manipulation ('You're digging up snakes, Lo. It's kind of dangerous'). Lex Luthor's machinations are all about demonstrating his power over Superman and the world.

title: Suicide Squad
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Amanda Waller's control over Task Force X is a central element, as evidenced by lines like, "You disobey me, you die. You try to escape, you die." and "It's a 'need to know', and all you need to know is you work for me."

title: Doctor Strange
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and vying for control. Examples include Strange demanding procedures ('So, speed it up.') and challenging the Ancient One's methods ('You're just another tiny, momentary speck within an indifferent universe.').

title: Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include Madam President's interactions with Tina Goldstein ('I made your position here quite clear, Ms. Goldstein.') and Graves's manipulation of Credence ('Find the child and we'll all be free.').

title: Glengarry Glen Ross
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of dominance and submission. Shelly's desperation for leads and his past influence over Murray, Roma's aggressive sales tactics and verbal dominance over Williamson, and the constant threat of being 'on the board' all highlight a cutthroat environment where status and control are paramount.

title: Tombstone
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, challenges to authority, and displays of dominance. Examples include the constant verbal sparring and threats of violence, such as "I said throw down, boy" and the power plays in the card game, like "You're sitting in my chair."

title: Jurassic Park
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Hammond tries to control the scientists and his park, while Nedry sabotages the system for personal gain. Muldoon displays authority over the raptors, and various characters give orders or instructions, highlighting hierarchical relationships.

title: Dennis the Menace
justification: Adults are constantly telling Dennis what to do ('You go sit in the corner and think about what you've done.'). Mr. Wilson frequently asserts his authority and complains about Dennis's behavior ('Your kid is driving me nuts.'). There are also instances of children attempting to exert control over each other ('Do it! I can make you.').

title: Robin Hood: Men in Tights
justification: The Sheriff of Rottingham and Prince John exert authority through commands and threats, such as "Kill them!" and levying evil taxes. Robin challenges this authority, vowing to "put an end to the injustice" and leading a revolt. The dialogue is filled with orders, challenges, and assertions of dominance.

title: Little Man
justification: Several characters exert authority: Mr. W gives orders to Percy, demanding his diamond and threatening consequences. Darryl attempts to control Calvin's actions, and the parents at the park compete to show their children's dominance. The father of Calvin shows his authority by trying to take Calvin back.

title: The Guardian
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and displays of authority, particularly from Senior Chief Randall. Examples include 'Aye, aye, Senior Chief,' 'Permission to be dismissed, sir?
