Granted,' and constant orders during training exercises like 'Let's go. Let's go. Keep it together. Look tight!'

title: We Own the Night
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and maneuvering for status. Examples include Vadim's criminal activities and the police raid, where officers bark orders and exert control: "Everybody get your hands on your fucking heads," and "Get the fuck down!" Also, Buzhayev's influence over others is evident in his ability to dictate terms and make decisions.

title: The Soloist
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power dynamic between Lopez and Ayers, with Lopez often trying to guide and control Ayers' decisions, such as where he should live and whether he should take medication. Ayers resists this control, asserting his own preferences and beliefs, but Lopez persists in trying to influence him, indicating a struggle for dominance in their relationship. Examples include Lopez trying to get Ayers to go to Lamp and the apartment.

title: Push
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, threats, and asserting dominance. Examples include Division agents demanding information and compliance, and characters like Chen threatening violence over debts: "I'll have you beaten."

title: The Twilight Saga: Eclipse
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Sam leading the wolf pack and Edward being protective of Bella.  There are also power struggles, like Jacob challenging Edward's decisions regarding Bella's safety: "I decided this, not him." and "We don't need you to handle anything."

title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part I
justification: The film features several instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Hermione telling Ron to take off the Horcrux, Harry instructing Hermione to get the Dittany, and various characters being interrogated or held captive, highlighting power imbalances.

title: MegaMind
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles, especially between Megamind and Metro Man, and later Titan. Examples include Megamind giving orders to Minion ('Ready the death ray, Minion.') and Titan demanding control ('Drop 'em!').

title: Salt
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and directives, especially from superiors to subordinates. Examples include "Walk me out," "Please remove the hood," and numerous instances of characters giving orders to each other during the crisis, such as "Call Protective Services, find Mike" and "Get me Medford on a secure line."

title: Jackass 3D
justification: There are many instances of dominance and submission. Examples include Knoxville directing others in stunts ('Loomis, come retrieve the ball'), the electric avenue scene where people are forced to run through stun guns, and the 'Really Bad Grandpa' skit where Knoxville's character acts inappropriately and disregards social norms.

title: Robin Hood
justification: The Sheriff of Nottingham asserts his authority through threats and intimidation, demanding tax payments and dismissing Marion's concerns. The dialogue between Prince John and Marshal reveals a power struggle, with John asserting his dominance and ultimately dismissing Marshal from his position. Godfrey's orders to 'Take no prisoners' and 'Leave no stone un-scorched' highlight his ruthless pursuit of power.

title: Due Date
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Peter frequently bosses Ethan around, and Ethan manipulates Peter with money and transportation: "Guess who's got the Subaru Impreza. Me. Guess who's got all the money. Me." There are also instances of authority figures like the Western Union employee and the border patrol agent asserting their power.

title: Secretariat
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders or asserting authority. Penny's interactions with Lucien and Eddie demonstrate her authority as the owner, while her interactions with her husband and brother reveal a struggle for control over the family's finances and future.

title: Takers
justification: Characters give orders and make demands of each other, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include "Turn that off," "Relax," and "Do l look like l care what he says?". Ghost exerts control by setting the terms of the heist and questioning others' loyalty.

title: Transformers: Dark of the Moon
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include: "Ladies and gentlemen, I need some lunch time filing done, stat." and "Give me my jacket!" and "I'll do whatever you want me to do."

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of authority. Examples include Blackbeard's crew being zombified for compliance, Barbossa's control over his crew and his pursuit of revenge on Blackbeard, and Jack Sparrow's attempts to manipulate situations to his advantage.

title: Thor
justification: The dialogue is filled with assertions of authority, challenges to leadership, and characters vying for control. Examples include Odin's pronouncements, Thor's defiance, Loki's manipulations, and the power struggles within Asgardian society, such as 'As King of Asgard....But you're not king! Not yet.' and 'You are a vain, greedy, cruel boy! And you are an old man and a fool!'

title: Captain America: The First Avenger
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Colonel Phillips berating recruits ('Get your ass up out of that dirt') and Agent Carter supervising operations ('I supervise all operations for this division'). There's also a clear hierarchy within Hydra, with Schmidt demanding obedience and expressing dominance.

title: Bridesmaids
justification: Several scenes show characters vying for control, such as the shower planning where Annie's ideas are dismissed, and the dress-fitting scene where Helen manipulates the group towards her preferred choice. Lillian eventually takes control of the shower planning, indicating a shift in power.

title: Kung Fu Panda 2
justification: Lord Shen gives orders to his wolf army: "Search the farthest villages! Find more metal!" and "Find this panda and bring him to me!". The Masters' Council also asserts authority, stating Gongmen is under their stewardship and they will protect it, even from Shen.

title: The Smurfs
justification: The dialogue includes commands and power plays, such as "Henri, escort this lunatic out" and "Stop bleating like a sheep and let me hog-tie you, you wriggly numptie." Gargamel's interactions with Azrael also highlight a master-servant dynamic, with Gargamel issuing orders and expressing dissatisfaction.

title: Mission: Impossible—Ghost Protocol
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the IMF, with Ethan Hunt giving orders to his team. There are also scenes of interrogation and dominance, such as the scene where Ethan demands the codes from Brij Nath's associate, and Hendricks's overall goal is to exert control through nuclear threat.

title: Rango
justification: The Mayor's dialogue, such as "Control the water and you control everything," highlights his dominance. Rango's initial attempts to assert authority through fabricated stories and later as sheriff, giving orders like "I want my shoes shined every morning," further emphasize the theme.

title: Green Lantern
justification: Several characters exert authority: Ferris fires Hal, then grounds him. Sinestro commands the Green Lantern Corps, and the Guardians hold ultimate authority. Kilowog bullies Hal during training, highlighting a hierarchical structure.

title: Zookeeper
justification: Several characters give orders and advice, attempting to control Griffin's behavior and romantic prospects. Examples include the animals instructing Griffin on how to attract Stephanie ("You listen to us and we turn you into an Alpha male.") and Gale's aggressive behavior towards Griffin, demonstrating dominance.

title: Dolphin Tale
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include Clay directing others on how to care for Winter and Sawyer's aunt and uncle scolding him for skipping school and not following their rules: 'Come on, son. Let's go to bed.' and 'You are going to school tomorrow and that is it. Period.'

title: Midnight in Paris
justification: Several characters exert control over others. Hemingway critiques the protagonist's fear of death and writing style, while Inez dismisses Gil's artistic inclinations and insists on her preferences. Zelda's emotional instability also creates a dynamic where others try to manage her behavior.

title: I am Number Four
justification: Henri constantly gives John orders and dictates his actions, such as "This time, you stay out of sight, huh? No school, no teams, nothing." John also displays authority over Sam, demonstrated by his command, "You follow that guy and you text me if he comes back, OK?"

title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
justification: The dialogue between Lisbeth and her guardian, Bjurman, is a clear example of power dynamics. Bjurman controls Lisbeth's finances and uses this power to manipulate and abuse her: "Starting now, you will be given a monthly allowance. You'll provide me with receipts for your expenses. If the numbers don't balance, I assume the difference is going to drugs." Also, the Vanger family interactions show a clear hierarchy and struggle for control, especially regarding the biography and family secrets.

title: Hugo
justification: Several characters exert authority through commands and threats. Examples include the Station Inspector's aggressive pursuit of orphans and Georges's demanding behavior towards Hugo, such as when he says, "Fix it. I said, fix it."

title: Something Borrowed
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Darcy frequently manipulates Rachel's relationships, and Dex's father pressures him regarding his choices: "Now, whatever's going on between you and that girl, you stop it. Now."

title: Spy Kids: All the Time in the World
justification: The stepmother, Marissa, is revealed to be a spy, giving her authority and control. The Timekeeper's dialogue is filled with threats and demands, highlighting his dominance. The children also compete with each other, vying for dominance.

title: The Roommate
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Examples include Tracy ditching Sara for a guy with a Porsche, Professor Roberts's inappropriate behavior and subsequent abuse of power, and Rebecca's increasingly controlling and ultimately violent behavior towards Sara, culminating in her attempt to isolate Sara from everyone else.

title: Jumping the Broom
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles, especially between Jason's mother and Sabrina's mother. Examples include the fight over the wedding traditions ('You've got to jump the broom.') and Sabrina's mother's condescending remarks ('You black.'). There are also instances of Gregg's controlling behavior towards Claudine and Jason's friends trying to influence his decisions.

The therapist attempts to guide Adam's emotional state, but he resists, creating a power struggle. Examples include: "For this to work, you're gonna have to trust me" and "I don't need you to take care of me."

title: Drive
justification: Characters frequently give orders and make demands, such as "Go get them" and "Put out the fucking cigarette." The Driver sets strict terms for his services, stating, "You give me a time and a place...Anything happens in that five minutes and I'm yours."

title: The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2
justification: Several scenes involve characters giving orders or asserting dominance. Examples include Edward telling Bella to control her thirst, Jacob's possessive claim over Renesmee ('She's mine!'), and the Volturi's hierarchical structure and control over the vampire world.

title: The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey
justification: Throughout the dialogue, Thorin asserts his authority, especially over Bilbo and the other dwarves. Gandalf also wields considerable influence, directing the company and challenging Thorin's decisions. Elrond and Galadriel hold positions of power, offering advice and judgment, while Saruman dismisses Radagast.

title: Lincoln
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Lincoln's authority is evident in his interactions with Stanton and the congressmen, as he navigates political maneuvering and demands action. Stevens' forceful personality and influence are clear in his interactions with other congressmen, as he tries to sway votes and control the narrative.

title: Safe House
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, interrogating, and asserting dominance. Examples include Frost's manipulation and control over Weston, Kiefer's interrogation tactics, and Linklater and Whitford's command over their subordinates.

title: The Vow
justification: Several characters attempt to control Paige's decisions, especially regarding her living situation and medical care. Her father and husband, Leo, argue over what's best for her, with her father even offering Leo money to divorce her. Jeremy also tries to exert influence by reminding her of their past relationship.

title: Magic Mike
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of dominance and submission. Dallas gives orders to the dancers ('Just start taking your clothes off') and controls their earnings ('Every man keeps every dollar he makes on that stage'). There's also a clear hierarchy in the club, with Dallas at the top and the new recruits at the bottom ('We all had to do it, man. It's like the initiation').

title: The Lucky One
justification: Several characters exert authority: Sanders barks orders to secure a hallway, and Beth is clearly the boss at the pet motel, directing Oscar. Keith also attempts to exert control over Beth and Ben, culminating in a dangerous situation.

title: The Devil Inside
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy within the Catholic Church, with priests and exorcists holding authority. Characters like Father Ben and David struggle against this established power, performing exorcisms without permission and facing potential consequences. Dialogue such as "As I said, we must be sure to rule out mental illness" and "The Church will never pursue your mother's case because the last time someone did, people died" highlights the control and influence of the Church.

title: The Odd Life of Timothy Green
justification: The interview process with the adoption agency shows a clear power dynamic, with the interviewers holding authority. Jim's boss at the pencil factory also exerts power, assigning him the unpleasant task of delivering layoff notices, highlighting the hierarchical structure of the workplace.

title: The Three Stooges
justification: The Monsignor announces the orphanage will close, immediately establishing his authority. The nuns and children are subject to his decision. Later, Moe is clearly the leader of his group, bossing Larry and Curly around, and even physically hitting them.

title: Red Dawn
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, challenges to authority, and displays of dominance. Examples include military commands ('Come on, kid, now, execute!'), challenges to leadership ('Who the hell put you in charge, anyway?'), and assertions of control ('Just do what I say.').

title: House at the End of the Street
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Sarah tries to control Elissa's relationships, stating "I do not want the two of you to be alone in your house or this house if I am not here." Tyler displays dominance by assaulting Ryan and vandalizing his car. Ryan's internal struggle manifests as him trying to control Elissa by forcing her to be Carrie Anne.

title: The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience. Examples include Gandalf's instructions to the group, Thorin's commands to the dwarves, and the Elvenking's control over his realm. The dwarves also struggle against the authority of the Elvenking.

title: Oblivion
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy between Mission Control (Sally) and the field technicians (Jack and Vika), with Mission issuing directives and monitoring their performance. Examples include: "Your directive today is to rehabilitate 166 and find 172" and "Are you and Jack an effective team?". The Tet itself exerts ultimate control, wiping memories and assigning tasks.

title: Turbo
justification: Several characters give orders or express authority. Examples include Chet telling Theo to tuck and roll, Carl firing Chet, and Whiplash inviting Turbo to join his crew and asserting dominance.

title: Interstellar
justification: There are several instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. For example, Cooper instructs TARS to adjust its humor setting ("Let's bring it down to 75, please.") and later directs CASE during the landing sequence ("On, my cue, CASE. Fire!"). Also, the professor is seen as an authority figure, guiding Murph's work.

title: Divergent
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and maneuvering for control. Examples include Eric's harsh instructions to the Dauntless initiates, Jeanine's manipulation of Beatrice, and Four's disciplinary actions and training methods.

title: The Maze Runner
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Newt, do me a favor. Go find Chuck'), asserting dominance ('If you respect this place... you and I will get along just fine'), and enforcing rules ('We only have three rules'). There's also a clear hierarchy with Alby and Newt in positions of authority.

title: Muppets Most Wanted
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially between Constantine and Number Two, with Constantine giving orders and asserting his dominance: "Now that we control the Muppet tour, Number Two, phase one of our plan is complete." and "Dance, monkey, dance!". Also, the prison scenes show Nadya in charge, giving orders to Kermit: "You are going to help me."

title: August: Osage County
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Violet's pill addiction and the family's intervention showcase a power struggle. Barbara's line, "I'M RUNNING THINGS NOW!" when confronting her mother, exemplifies this theme.

title: Inside Out
justification: Several instances of parental authority are evident, such as the father telling Riley to go to her room: "Go to your room! Now!" and the mother's subtle manipulation: "if you and I can keep smiling, it would be a big help. We can do that for him. Right?". Also, Joy attempts to control Sadness and the other emotions.

title: Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Come on. Follow me.', 'Get your ass back in that chair.', 'Get them to their bunks.') and exerting control over others. There are also instances of characters questioning authority and rebelling, indicating a struggle for power ('Why won't you let me see her?', 'Back off!').

title: Sicario
justification: Throughout the subtitles, characters give orders and expect obedience, such as "Call DOJ, let 'em know what we have" and "Vickers! I need bolt cutters!". The dialogue also reveals a hierarchy within law enforcement and between agencies, with some characters deferring to others' authority and expertise, as seen in the interactions between Kate, Matt, and their superiors.

title: Chappie
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include the police commissioner dismissing the weapons platform, the gangsters threatening Deon to reprogram the robot, and Ninja's attempts to control and influence Chappie's behavior.

title: Ricki and the Flash
justification: There are many instances of characters asserting dominance or struggling for control. Maureen's passive-aggressive control over the household and her family is evident in her interactions with Pete and Linda. Julie's emotional outbursts and attempts to manipulate situations also highlight power struggles within the family.

title: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Krennic demands explanations and compliance, while Tarkin undermines Krennic's authority, stating, "I will be taking control over the weapon...effective immediately."

title: Moana
justification: Moana is constantly struggling against the authority of her father, who forbids going beyond the reef. Maui also asserts his dominance over Moana, initially refusing to help and constantly reminding her of his demigod status, singing "You're Welcome" to assert his importance.

title: The Revenant
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and assertions of authority. Examples include: "Listen up!", "Fitzgerald! Cap'n. Where are we with the haul?", and "That's an order!". There are also instances of insubordination and challenges to authority, indicating a struggle for dominance.

title: Jason Bourne
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, directives, and power plays. Examples include: "Drop everything you're doing, get on it right now!", "Kill the power to the building.", and Dewey's constant manipulation and control over Lee and Kalloor.

title: Star Trek Beyond
justification: The film features a clear command structure within Starfleet, with characters like Captain Kirk giving orders and subordinates like Uhura and Sulu following them ('Lieutenant Uhura, open a ship-wide channel. Yes, Captain.'). The antagonist, Krall, also exerts strong control over his forces, demanding obedience and displaying a clear hierarchy.

title: X-Men: Apocalypse
justification: Characters give orders and assert authority: "Get back! Get back!" and "Don't let any of the children come this way."  Apocalypse seeks to dominate and control mutants, stating, "I want to set you free" while actually manipulating them.

title: Sing
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the auditions and rehearsals. Mr. Moon is in charge, giving instructions and making decisions: "All right, call everyone back to stage, Miss Crawly" and "Okay, everybody, listen up! I gotta send you all home." There are also instances of dominance within families, like Johnny's father pushing him into criminal activity.

title: Trolls
justification: The Bergen King gives orders to Chef and Bridget ('You work for me now'), demonstrating a clear hierarchy. Poppy also takes charge, directing the trolls and even ordering Branch around ('Branch, you can't say no').

title: Kung Fu Panda 3
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for authority, giving orders, and asserting dominance. Kai's pronouncements of power and Shifu's role as a master teacher exemplify this dynamic, as well as Po's journey to become a master.

title: Ghostbusters
justification: The Ghostbusters give Kevin orders, such as 'Can you answer the phone that's ringing, please? Buddy.' There are also scenes where authority figures like the Mayor and Homeland Security agents attempt to control the Ghostbusters' actions, demanding they 'knock it off' and let the government handle the situation.

title: Central Intelligence
justification: Agent Harris exerts authority over Calvin, demanding information and dictating his actions: "I need you to tell me everything and anything about your contact with Agent Stone." Bob also manipulates Calvin, forcing him into dangerous situations: "Take my gun, Jet, we may have to kill some people."

title: The Legend of Tarzan
justification: The movie features multiple power struggles. Rom gives orders to his mercenaries and attempts to control Tarzan. Mbonga seeks revenge and dominance over Tarzan, while Leopold's control over the Congo and its resources is a central conflict.

title: Sully
justification: The NTSB investigation scenes highlight a clear power dynamic, with investigators questioning Sully's decisions and procedures. Dialogue such as "our job is to investigate how a plane ended up in the Hudson River" and the focus on whether Sully followed proper procedure (QRH) demonstrate the investigators' authority and Sully's need to defend his actions.

title: Bad Moms
justification: The film showcases a constant struggle for power, particularly among the mothers at the school. Gwendolyn's dialogue, such as "I run this school...and I can make life a living hell for you," exemplifies her desire for control. Amy's decision to run against her and the subsequent campaign further highlight the power struggle.

title: The Angry Birds Movie
justification: The pigs, led by Leonard, manipulate the birds with gifts and parties, masking their true intentions. Red challenges the established order and questions the pigs' motives, leading to conflict and ultimately a battle for control.

title: Independence Day: Resurgence
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and commands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "All personnel, report to your stations immediately," "Arm the primary," and "Get me the Security Council."

title: The Conjuring 2: The Enfield Poltergeist
justification: The dialogue shows a clear struggle for dominance, especially through the spirit's control over Janet and its interactions with the investigators. Examples include the spirit commanding "Get out now!" and threatening "I'll break her neck," demonstrating its desire to control the house and the people within it.

title: The Magnificent Seven
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Hands up', 'Get his guns, Dicky', 'Faraday, walk!'), asserting dominance ('Ain't no Wild Bill. They call me the Two Gun Kid'), and negotiating for control ('You tell Bogue if he wants his town, come see me'). The constant threat of violence and the clear hierarchy within groups contribute to the high salience.

title: Arrival
justification: The film displays a clear hierarchy between military personnel and scientists, with the military exerting control over the scientists' access to information and movement. For example, the Colonel orders Dr. Banks to 'pack your bags' and later states 'Takeoff in ten'. Also, the military personnel are constantly giving orders to each other.

title: Ride Along 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include the detectives telling AJ to "Stop!" and "Get your ass in there," and the Nigerian Consul's demeaning treatment of his bodyguard: "You are what I say you are!".

title: Don’t Breathe
justification: Characters are constantly giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include "Okay, then, open the door," "Yo, kill that already," and "Minus my 40 percent. Take it or leave it." The blind man also asserts his power, saying, "Stay right fucking there. Don't you fucking move."

title: The Accountant
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Lamar Blackburn giving orders to Chris, and the enforcer intimidating Simon Dewey. Dialogue like "Whatever you need to do your job, you let me know" and "Are we good? Yeah? Attaboy, Simon. Proud of you" demonstrates this dynamic.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Out of the Shadows
justification: The Krang dictates terms to Shredder, who then commands Stockman and the mutants. The police chief exerts authority over subordinates, and Leonardo struggles to maintain control over his brothers, highlighting a constant negotiation and assertion of dominance.

title: Alice Through the Looking Glass
justification: The initial scenes show Alice being dismissed from her captain position due to societal expectations and a power play by a male figure who bought her shares. Later, the Red Queen's tyrannical rule and Time's control over the Grand Clock of All Time highlight the theme.

title: Pete’s Dragon
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Gavin disregards Jack's authority at the logging site: "Don't worry about Jack. Just keep cutting." Later, Gavin captures Elliot and declares, "The dragon is mine."

title: The Girl on the Train
justification: Several characters exert control over others. Tom frequently dismisses Rachel's feelings and actions, telling her to "Relax!" and controlling the narrative around her behavior. Scott displays possessive behavior towards Megan, checking her passwords and exhibiting jealousy.

title: Tyler Perry’s Boo! A Madea Halloween
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance, especially the older women. Examples include: "Get that devilment out of here," "Go to bed," and "Sit down!"

title: Storks
justification: The dialogue includes multiple instances of characters giving orders ('Ninja force, attack!', 'Always deliver!'), firing employees ('You're fired!'), and vying for positions of authority ('I'm the alpha!'). Junior's desire to be the boss and Hunter's control over Cornerstore also highlight the theme.

title: 10 Cloverfield Lane
justification: Howard exerts control through threats and manipulation: "Don't even think about trying that again. You're lucky to be here at all." He dictates rules and punishes disobedience, culminating in violence and confinement: "Keep your hands to yourself! Understand? No touching." Michelle and Emmett are initially compliant but eventually resist, leading to a power struggle.

title: Now You See Me 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, issuing threats, and asserting dominance. Walter Mabry controls the Horsemen by threatening their lives, and Thaddeus Bradley manipulates Agent Rhodes with information and payback. The constant power struggles drive the plot and character interactions.

title: Hacksaw Ridge
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands and displays of authority, such as "Line up! Move it!" and "I am Sergeant Howell or Sarge. 'Sir' you save for useless people." There are also instances of hazing and attempts to assert dominance through insults and challenges, like "You marry your first cousin?" and "Are you contradicting me, you wagon-burning son of a bitch?"

title: Ice Age: Collision Course
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance. Manny tries to control Peaches's life choices, and Buck gives orders to the group. The dino-birds also try to assert dominance by kidnapping Granny.

title: London Has Fallen
justification: The film is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Barkawi directing his organization, the President being constantly advised and directed by his security team ('Sir, you need to take this now, sir'), and Banning taking charge in crisis situations ('Get down!').

title: Miracles from Heaven
justification: The dialogue shows a clear parent-child dynamic, with parents making decisions about medical care and daily routines. There are also instances of medical professionals holding authority, such as Dr. Nurko explaining Anna's condition and treatment options to her parents.

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding 2
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or give orders. For example, "Eh, come on, don't let them boss you around," and "My niece wants to come to your school, you're gonna say, 'Welcome.'"

title: Jack Reacher: Never Go Back
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, commands, and assertions of authority. Examples include "Do it now," "Open BA211," "Stand here. Don't move," and the constant questioning and interrogation scenes, highlighting the power imbalances between characters.

title: Me Before You
justification: Will exerts control over Louisa, ordering her to watch a film with him: "Sit down. Watch this with me. That's an order." He also displays dominance by criticizing her life choices and attempting to dictate her future: "You need to widen your horizons, Clark. You only get one life."

title: The BFG
justification: The BFG kidnaps Sophie and dictates her life, stating, "You're just gonna have to be stayin' here with me for the rest of our lives." The other giants bully the BFG, with Fleshlumpeater saying, "You is an insult to giant people." Sophie also challenges the BFG's authority, such as when she says, "You can't stop me."

title: Passengers
justification: The AI systems on the ship, like Arthur and the automated voices, exert control through rules and restrictions (e.g., "Bridge access requires special authorization," "Sorry. The Mocha Cappuccino Extreme is reserved for gold-class passengers."). Jim's initial isolation also creates a power imbalance, as he grapples with the ship's systems and his own loneliness, ultimately leading to his decision to wake Aurora.

title: The Shallows
justification: There are multiple instances of power dynamics. The local surfers display dominance by warning Nancy and using derogatory terms like "gringa." Nancy's father attempts to exert control by pressuring her to return to med school.

title: Barbershop: The Next Cut
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting dominance, such as Quis threatening violence and Calvin attempting to control the situation in his barbershop. Jalen's parents also exert authority over him, dictating his choices and associations. The dialogue highlights struggles for control and respect within the community.

title: 13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghazi
justification: Characters frequently give and receive orders, highlighting a clear hierarchy. Examples include "Dave, take right side," "Get back down!," and "You're not giving orders anymore, you're taking them."

title: Office Christmas Party
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of power dynamics. Carol's position allows her to threaten Clay's branch closure and offer Josh a job, while Clay struggles to maintain control over the party and his employees, often resorting to bossing them around.

title: Kubo and the Two Strings
justification: The Moon King and his daughters exert control through threats and violence ('We just need your other eye'). Kubo's mother and Monkey give him orders ('Promise me, Kubo!') and try to protect him from the Moon King's power.

title: The Huntsman: Winter’s War
justification: The film is driven by power struggles, particularly between Ravenna and Freya, and Freya's control over her Huntsmen. Examples include Ravenna taking kingdoms, Freya commanding her army with phrases like "Burn it down! Kill them all!", and Freya's Huntsmen being forced to obey her strict rules.

title: Warcraft
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, challenges to authority, and assertions of dominance. Examples include Gul'dan's control over the Horde, Blackhand's challenges to Durotan, and the human king's orders to his soldiers. The constant struggle for control and status is evident throughout the script.

title: Mike and Dave Need Wedding Dates
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Eric's father trying to control the wedding party's behavior after Jeanie's accident. There are also instances of characters giving orders or making demands, like when Mike insists Dave practice their speech or when Jeanie's father confronts the girls about Jeanie's face.

title: War Dogs
justification: Several characters exert authority: Efraim over David (e.g., "Pick up the fucking phone"), Captain Santos over Efraim and David ("I'm shutting you down"), and Henry Girard over Efraim ("I can't spend more than 48 hours in this dump"). There are also instances of negotiation and resistance, indicating a struggle for control.

title: Almost Christmas
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and control over others, particularly within the family. Examples include Aunt May ordering everyone around, Lonnie's disruptive behavior and attempts to assert himself, and the constant bickering and one-upmanship between siblings.

title: Money Monster
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters give orders and instructions, highlighting a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "Patch this line into the PA system, please. Right now," and "Cut the line, Charlie. Right now." Also, there are power struggles, such as the hostage-taker controlling the situation and demanding answers.

title: The Hateful Eight
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and challenging authority. John Ruth's control over Daisy and his interactions with others, such as disarming Joe Gage, highlight power dynamics. The General's past actions and Warren's confrontational story about his son further emphasize the struggle for dominance and status.

title: Allied
justification: Characters frequently give orders and instructions, such as "Keep going straight. I'll tell you when to turn" and "Don't slow down. This is how you drive in Casablanca." The film also explores the power dynamics within espionage, with characters questioning each other's trustworthiness and loyalty, like "But do they trust you?"

title: Nerve
justification: The game 'Nerve' is entirely based on power dynamics, where 'Watchers' dictate dares to 'Players'. Dialogue such as "Watchers decide your dares" and "Do you accept your dare, Vee? Say, 'Yes.'" exemplifies this dynamic.

title: Risen
justification: The film is driven by the power struggle between Rome and the Jewish people. Characters like Pilate and the Tribune exert authority through commands and military force: "Move forward! Now! Come on!", "Tribune, Pilate summons you.", and "Take control out there and finish things."

title: Assassin’s Creed
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and displays of authority. Examples include: "Hang his family and make him watch. Burn the whole village," and "Surrender the Apple." The Templars' goal is to establish "one Templar rule," demonstrating a clear power dynamic.

title: The Nice Guys
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Freeze!", "Drive the fucking car!", and "Sir, I was told to keep you here, so I'm keeping you here. Just following orders."

title: The Boy
justification: The Heelshires exert control through strict rules and expectations, demonstrated by their detailed schedule for Brahms and their insistence on Greta's adherence. Brahms himself displays dominance through violent actions and manipulation, demanding Greta's attention and obedience, as seen when he punishes her for not following his rules.

title: Dirty Grandpa
justification: Characters frequently assert dominance through insults, threats, and commands. Examples include the initial gun scene ('I thought you were gonna shit your pants, little guy.') and the lacrosse players' aggressive behavior ('We've been looking for you bitches all day. Where the fuck have you been?'). The grandfather's manipulative requests also highlight a power imbalance ('Please, Jason, just stay one more day so I can do this.')

title: Ouija: Origin of Evil
justification: The mother, Katie, exerts control over her daughters, especially Lina, demanding obedience and dictating their actions. The priest, Father Tom, attempts to exert moral authority, questioning Katie's practices and Lina's behavior. The spirits also exert power, manipulating Doris and influencing events in the house, leading to a struggle for control over Doris's actions.

title: The 5th Wave
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy within the military, with characters giving and receiving orders. Examples include Colonel Vosch commanding soldiers and the training regimen where recruits are expected to obey without question. The manipulation of children to fight a war they don't understand also highlights a significant power imbalance.

title: Inferno
justification: Characters are constantly giving and receiving orders. Examples include: "Stay in your room. We're sending someone now," and "Go! I want that pointer back! And I want Langdon. Whatever it takes."

title: Mother’s Day
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, Tina tries to set 'rules' for Sandy, and Lisa aggressively confronts the referee at the soccer game. Also, Miranda's assistant is clearly subservient, and Miranda herself holds power over potential employees.

title: Gods of Egypt
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and displays of dominance. Set demands worship and obedience, stating, "Gods... Bow before me or die. Mortals, worship me or be enslaved!" and later, "From now on, you have to buy your way in with riches earned."

title: La La Land
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, Bill fires Seb from the band, and the director on set tells Mia how to act. Also, Laura tries to give Sebastian life advice.

title: Why Him?
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to assert dominance, particularly between Laird and Ned, and Laird and Goose. Laird repeatedly tries to win Ned over, even calling him 'Dad' against his wishes ('I think it's gonna, Dad. Don't. Dad, come on.'). Goose trains Laird and gives him orders ('You have to find a way in. You have to do something for him that's truly special').

title: Hail, Caesar!
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters exerting authority and others complying. Mr. Laurentz directs Hobie's acting with precise instructions, and Mannix manages studio crises, directing employees and negotiating with powerful figures. The kidnapping plot itself is a power play, and the studio system's exploitation of writers is a central theme.

title: When the Bough Breaks
justification: Characters exert control through financial means ('We'll pay you whatever you were making'), manipulation ('You're just the uterus'), and direct orders ('Go in the house right now'). John uses his connections and resources to control Mike's future ('In 10 days, you're gonna be shipped off to the Middle East').

title: Zoolander 2
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Don Atari ordering around his 'collective' and Alexanya Atoz's demanding presence.  Mugatu's control over the fashion world and his manipulation of Zoolander also highlight power imbalances. The Interpol agent also tries to exert authority over Zoolander.

title: The Finest Hours
justification: Several characters give and receive orders, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include Cluff ordering Webber to tie up fishing boats and Bangs to take a boat out, and the captain of the Pendleton being addressed as 'sir' and giving orders to his crew. Sybert eventually takes command and directs the crew to run the ship aground.

title: Florence Foster Jenkins
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the music lessons. Florence gives commands like "Raise the soft palate" and "Use the air," while St. Clair manages and manipulates people around Florence, such as Mr. McMoon, and the ticket sales.

title: Manchester-by-the Sea
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. Examples include: "Lay down," and the coach yelling at Chandler, "One more time and you're out."

title: The Forest
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or expressing control. Rob tells Sara, "Why don't you just sleep on it, okay?" and later, the police officer instructs, "Do not leave the path."

title: Ben-Hur
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and displays of authority, such as "Follow us," "Open this door!" and "Confess your crime, or they all stand accused!" Messala's position as a Roman officer gives him power over Judah and his family, leading to their enslavement.

title: Fences
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Troy exerting his authority over Cory, such as demanding he get his job back and forbidding him from playing football: "I'm the boss around here. I do the only saying what counts." Troy also emphasizes his role as the provider and head of the household, expecting obedience and respect: "Nigger, as long as you in my house, you put a 'sir' on the end of it when you talk to me."

title: Star Wars Ep. VIII: The Last Jedi
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert authority. Examples include Poe's demotion and Holdo's command over the remaining Resistance forces: 'You're demoted. What? Wait!' and 'To your stations! Move, move, move!'

title: Beauty and the Beast
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Examples include the Beast's orders to Belle ('You'll join me for dinner. That's not a request.') and Gaston's manipulation and control over the villagers ('We're not safe until he's dead').

title: Wonder Woman
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially in the military context with orders given and expected to be followed. Diana's interactions with authority figures, like her mother and the generals, highlight her struggle against established power structures. Ludendorff's control over Dr. Maru and his manipulation of the German military also demonstrate a strong power dynamic.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, issuing orders, and asserting dominance. Yondu's Ravagers challenge his leadership ('Suppose it's time for a change in leadership'), while Ego manipulates Peter ('Give me your hands, son'). Even Mantis is presented as subservient to Ego ('I mostly use it to help my master sleep').

title: Spider-Man: Homecoming
justification: Tony Stark repeatedly asserts his authority over Peter, scolding him for his actions and ultimately taking away his suit: "Previously on Peter Screws the Pooch...I tell you to stay away from this." The villain, Toomes, also exerts control over his crew, firing one member for insubordination: "I can't afford your bullshit. Get out of here."

title: It
justification: There are multiple instances of bullying and intimidation, such as Henry Bowers's interactions with Bill and Ben, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. Adult figures like Beverly's father and Eddie's mother exert control over their children, highlighting hierarchical relationships. The clown, Pennywise, also uses fear and manipulation to dominate the children.

title: Thor: Ragnarok
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and vying for control. Hela demands "Kneel before your queen," and the Grandmaster establishes ownership by declaring, "You are the property of the Grandmaster." Thor also attempts to assert authority, stating, "I am Thor, son of Odin."

title: Despicable Me 3
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Valerie da Vinci firing Gru, Bratt's constant need to prove his villainy, and the minions' initial rebellion against Gru's reformed lifestyle.

title: Logan
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance or control. Logan barks orders like "Stay out of my shit" and "Go inside and keep Charles quiet." The villains also display power through threats and violence, such as "You need to turn around, asshole."

title: The Fate of the Furious
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders (e.g., "Move.", "Get back in your cell!"), asserting dominance (e.g., Hobbs and Shaw's constant bickering and threats), and struggling for control (e.g., Cipher manipulating Dom and others). Mr. Nobody's role also highlights a clear hierarchy.

title: Justice League
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance or questioning authority. Steppenwolf's dialogue is all about power and subjugation: "After the unity, you will join my legion and you will know the righteousness of power. You will love me. You all will." Even within the 'hero' group, Bruce Wayne is clearly in charge, giving orders and making decisions, though challenged by Diana.

title: Dunkirk
justification: The film depicts a clear military hierarchy with officers giving orders and soldiers obeying (e.g., "Ready on the stern! Yes, sir!"). There are also instances of civilians asserting authority, such as Mr. Dawson's interactions with the shell-shocked soldier and the men on the beach vying for space on the boats ("Get off! Get off!").

title: Coco
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, especially regarding Miguel's musical aspirations. His family, particularly his grandmother, exerts strong control: "You will listen to your family. No more music. End of argument." Miguel's defiance and attempts to seize control of his own life create conflict.

title: The Lego Batman Movie
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Batman directing Robin, Commissioner Gordon leading the police, and the Joker commanding villains.

title: Get Out
justification: The film establishes power dynamics through several interactions. The police officer's interrogation and the family's subtle control over Chris, such as the mother's unwanted hypnosis and the father's overbearing friendliness, highlight a struggle for dominance and manipulation. Georgina's statement, "I don't answer to anyone," also suggests a complex power dynamic.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and vying for control. Examples include Jack Sparrow's crew questioning his leadership ("We will no longer follow a captain without a ship.") and Captain Salazar commanding his ghostly crew ("Secure that woman!").

title: Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle
justification: Throughout the movie, characters give orders and express dominance. For example, Nigel repeatedly instructs the group, and Van Pelt commands his henchmen to retrieve the jewel at any cost. There are also instances of characters asserting themselves, like Fridge challenging Spencer's authority.

title: Kong: Skull Island
justification: The dialogue is filled with military commands ('Roger that', 'Move that gear', 'Form a perimeter') and shows a clear hierarchy. Packard's determination to pursue his mission despite the dangers and objections from others ('You don't like the way I'm running things? You know where the door is.') further emphasizes his authority and control.

title: Hidden Figures
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority or challenging it. For example, Mrs. Mitchell directs Dorothy's work, and Katherine confronts Mr. Johnson about his disrespectful comments, asserting her intellectual capabilities and demanding respect. Also, Al Harrison makes decisions about who attends briefings, demonstrating his authority within NASA.

title: Cars 3
justification: Sterling, as the sponsor, exerts control over Lightning's training and career, dictating his schedule and even threatening to end his racing days. Cruz, as the trainer, is initially presented as having authority over Lightning's training regimen, though this is challenged and evolves throughout their interactions. The dialogue highlights the shifting power dynamics as Lightning struggles to regain his former status.

title: War for the Planet of the Apes
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and obedience, such as "Yes, sir," and "Fall back! Fall back!" Caesar's leadership and the Colonel's command over their respective groups are central, with constant struggles for control and dominance evident in their interactions.

title: Split
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Sheldon telling people to 'make yourselves at home' and offering to take their coats, indicating a host-guest dynamic. Chris also gives Ollie an order to 'get out of this bowling alley'. These moments suggest a mild awareness of social hierarchy and control.

title: Transformers: The Last Knight
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and jockeying for position. Examples include Megatron's commands to the Decepticons, Lennox directing his team, and Cogman's controlling behavior towards others.

title: Wonder
justification: The dialogue shows adults directing children, such as the teacher saying, "Any questions for Julian?" and "Who wants to read this month's precept?" There are also instances of bullying and social hierarchy, like when kids make fun of Auggie's appearance and Jack Will is pressured to befriend him.

title: Girls Trip
justification: Several characters exert control over others, such as Ryan directing Stewart's behavior during the cooking segment ('There's nothing better than a tender sausage who knows who's in charge!') and Sasha's aggressive confrontation with Miss Vanzant ('If you think that you can trash my name and reputation...that is not gonna turn out well for you.'). There are also instances of dominance within relationships, like the dynamic between Ryan and Stewart, where Ryan often dictates the terms of their partnership.

title: Fifty Shades Darker
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Christian exerting control through wealth and influence ('I make that kind of money every 15 minutes. Keep it.'). There are also power plays in the relationship itself, with Christian dictating terms and Ana pushing back ('Okay, you can either walk or I can carry you. Your choice.').

title: Baby Driver
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include Doc's control over Baby, Bats' volatile behavior and attempts to intimidate others, and the general hierarchical structure within the criminal gang. Dialogue like "Move! Move! Move!" and Doc's ultimatum to Baby ("behind the wheel or in a wheelchair?") highlight the power imbalances.

title: Annabelle: Creation
justification: The nuns are clearly in charge of the orphans, giving them orders and expecting obedience. The demon also exerts power, manipulating the Mullins and later possessing Janice, forcing others to act against their will. Dialogue like "You absolutely cannot disobey the Mullins" and the demon's demand for souls highlight this struggle for control.

title: Daddy’s Home 2
justification: The movie features constant jockeying for position between Dusty and Brad as co-parents, and Don's old-fashioned views clash with modern parenting. Examples include arguments over the thermostat, Brad's advice to Dylan about girls, and the disastrous hunting trip where Megan shoots Don.

title: Murder on the Orient Express
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control or influence over others. Ratchett tries to hire Poirot, then resorts to intimidation with a gun when Poirot refuses. Bouc attempts to direct Poirot's investigation, and Poirot asserts his authority during interrogations.

title: Kingsman: The Golden Circle
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, interrogations, and assertions of dominance. For example, the antagonist demands, "So why don't you go on and get down on your knees... and tell me who you really work for," and later threatens to "set your balls on fire."

title: John Wick: Chapter Two
justification: The film is filled with power struggles. Santino uses a 'marker' to force John into a task, demonstrating control. Winston, the hotel manager, wields authority by enforcing rules and ultimately declaring John 'excommunicado'.

title: Blade Runner 2049
justification: There are many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Luv's interactions with subordinates ("Follow me."), Wallace's pronouncements and expectations of Luv, and the police chief's reprimands to K ("Drop your gun and keep your hands where I can see 'em.").

title: The Emoji Movie
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Smiler who commands the Anti-Virus Bots and other emojis. There are also clear hierarchies, like Alex being the 'user' who controls the emojis' fates, and the 'favorites' having higher status. Dialogue includes commands like 'Emojis to your cubes' and 'Abort! Abort! Shut it down!'

title: Power Rangers
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, with Jason often taking the lead and giving orders ('Okay, you drive,' 'Let's go'). There are also instances of characters challenging authority ('Why are you talking to us like you're the boss now?').

title: The Mummy
justification: Several characters give orders and assert authority. Examples include: "Clear them out, please," "Evacuate your men. We'll take it from here," and "You got two hours, then we're moving out. You're getting in the hole with her. Him? Me? Yep. Sir... You gear up. That's an order."

title: The Hitman’s Bodyguard
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and negotiating status. Examples include the initial exchange about payment for Kincaid, Bryce's constant instructions to Kincaid, and the power plays within Interpol.

title: Alien: Covenant
justification: The captain gives orders and is often questioned, creating tension. For example, Danny protests the decision to investigate the rogue transmission, saying, "As your second, I need to protest. Officially." Also, the androids David and Walter have a clear master-servant dynamic with humans, but also express their own desires for control and creation.

title: Captain Underpants: The First Epic Movie
justification: The primary conflict revolves around Principal Krupp's authority over George and Harold, and their attempts to subvert it, especially after hypnotizing him. Dialogue like "Put the pen down, Mr. Krupp...or we'll hypnotize you" and Krupp's attempts to separate them highlight this struggle.

title: The Lego Ninjago Movie
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and vying for control. Examples include Garmadon's commands to his generals, Master Wu's instructions to the ninjas, and the constant struggle between Garmadon and Lloyd.

title: Baywatch
justification: Mitch is clearly in charge of the Baywatch team, giving orders and expecting obedience: "Jonas Brother, listen to me. Get your beauty rest. We're starting bright and early tomorrow." Victoria Leeds exerts control through threats and violence: "Leon, would you show Mr. Rodriguez what we do to people who don't deliver?"

title: The Shack
justification: The father figure asserts his authority over the children, dictating their actions and dismissing their desires: "No stopping. We gotta get to the campground before dark." Later, Wisdom judges Mack, highlighting a power imbalance and moral hierarchy.

title: Happy Death Day
justification: Several scenes show characters attempting to exert control over others. Examples include the sorority house meeting where the leader dictates rules, and the doctor/student relationship where the doctor holds authority.

title: Ferdinand
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy among the bulls, with Valiente asserting dominance and Ferdinand initially resisting. Dialogue like "Now, you're either a fighter or you're meat" and Valiente's constant belittling of Ferdinand highlight the pressure to conform to a violent, competitive environment. El Primero's visit and selection of a bull further emphasize the power humans wield over the bulls' fate.

title: Atomic Blonde
justification: The film is filled with characters vying for control and dominance. Examples include Lorraine's debriefing where she resists control, Percival's manipulation of Spyglass, and the constant struggle for information and advantage between various intelligence agencies.

title: American Made
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and asserting control. Examples include the drug cartel dictating landing locations and cargo amounts, and Schafer directing Barry's actions for the CIA. The constant negotiation and manipulation highlight the struggle for dominance.

title: The Dark Tower
justification: The film features a clear power dynamic between the Gunslinger and the Man in Black, with constant struggles for dominance. The Man in Black uses his powers to control others ('Stop breathing. Breathe. Fight it. Fight it!') and manipulate situations, while the Gunslinger resists and fights back. There are also elements of control and manipulation in the scenes with Jake and the 'skin people' who try to take him.

title: The Greatest Showman
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Barnum gives orders to his staff ("That's good, but I need it five times bigger! And I want it everywhere!"), and there are instances of social hierarchy and prejudice ("Your master's calling!"). The interactions between Barnum and Carlyle also show a negotiation of power and influence.

title: Tyler Perry’s Boo 2! A Madea Halloween
justification: Several characters exert authority over others, such as Madea bossing around Mabel and Joe ("Come on, y'all, come on, let's go on in the kitchen.") and parents setting rules for their children ("But you have to promise to be responsible."). There are also instances of defiance and negotiation, like Tiffany convincing her mom to let her go to the party and the friends arguing about whether to leave the party or not.

title: Lion
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the adoptive parents instructing Saroo on table manners ("Serviette.", "Fork.", "Knife.") and the general dynamic of adults guiding children. However, the primary focus is on familial love and Saroo's journey, not power struggles.

title: Snatched
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. Emily's mother, Linda, frequently tries to control Emily's behavior, saying things like, "You're coming!" and manipulating her with the book. The kidnappers also exert extreme power over Linda and Emily, highlighted by the line, "Should you ever make me angry I will skin you alive while your mother watches."

title: The Great Wall
justification: The text emphasizes obedience to authority and the unquestioning execution of orders. Phrases like "We have only come to know ourselves... in the spelling out of the orders of the highest authorities" and "Ask the authority" highlight the absolute power dynamic. The text also explores the dangers of independent thought, suggesting that questioning authority can lead to ruin.

title: Smurfs: The Lost Village
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays, especially from Gargamel ('Monty, capture me some Smurfs') and Papa Smurf ('You're grounded'). There's also a clear hierarchy within the Smurf groups, with leaders giving orders and others following.

title: All Eyez on Me
justification: The dialogue is filled with displays of dominance, threats, and negotiations for control. Examples include Suge Knight's offer to protect Tupac, the prison interactions, and the constant struggle for respect and authority in various situations ('Turn around, nigger,' 'You heard him. Do it, nigga.').

title: xXx: Return of Xander Cage
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and challenging authority. Examples include the initial briefing where authority figures demand answers, Xander's interactions with the team where he establishes his leadership, and the constant power struggles between Xander and the antagonists.

title: The Big Sick
justification: The dialogue showcases power dynamics through familial expectations and cultural clashes. Kumail's family pressures him into an arranged marriage, while Emily's parents exhibit control over her medical decisions, dismissing Kumail's input: 'We're gonna handle things from here, okay?'. There are also instances of verbal dominance and attempts to assert control in arguments.

title: Ghost in the Shell
justification: The film is filled with characters giving and receiving orders, such as "Initiate Project 2571" and "Sedate her." Characters also struggle for control and dominance, as seen in the conflict between Cutter and Aramaki, and the power plays within Hanka Robotics.

title: Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets
justification: Characters give orders such as "Stay here," "Secure all people," and "Go back to your room," indicating a clear hierarchy. The urgency in commands like "Come on, quickly!" and "Faster!" further emphasizes the power dynamic.

title: The Star
justification: Several characters give orders, such as "Now, get going," "Get back here!" and "Follow me." Herod demands obedience with "Send the royal guard to round up every man and woman." There are also instances of characters resisting authority, like the donkey running away.

title: King Arthur: Legend of the Sword
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and negotiating their positions within a clear hierarchy. Examples include Vortigern's commands, Arthur's control over his crew, and the Blacklegs' enforcement of the king's law through threats and violence. Lines like "In the back room, now," "Tell me. Every detail," and "Off with his head!" highlight the constant struggle for control and the exercise of authority.

title: Jigsaw
justification: The film revolves around a series of deadly games orchestrated by a Jigsaw copycat, where individuals are forced to confess their sins and make life-or-death choices under duress. Dialogue like "Cut yourself!" and "Confess!" highlights the manipulative and controlling nature of the game master, while the victims' pleas for help and desperate attempts to survive showcase their powerlessness.

title: American Assassin
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include Hurley's constant commands to Rapp ("Eyes front and center," "Shut the door") and Kennedy's directives to Hurley and others regarding the mission and Rapp's involvement. There are also instances of characters challenging authority, like Rapp's frequent disobedience and questioning of orders.

title: The Foreigner
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, making demands, and asserting authority. Examples include Liam Hennessy's commands regarding the arms dumps and the police inspector's control over the investigation. The interactions between Hennessy and McGrath also highlight a power struggle, with threats and accusations flying.

title: Everything, Everything
justification: The mother's role as a doctor caring for her daughter creates a clear power dynamic. She makes decisions about Madeline's health and access to the outside world, as evidenced by the line, "You can't see him again."

title: Wind River
justification: Multiple characters exert authority: the sheriff giving orders to his deputy, the FBI agent directing the local law enforcement, and the hunter instructing the FBI agent on tracking. Examples include: "Uh, order a rape kit." and "Come here. I'll show you."

title: Geostorm
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and asserting dominance. Examples include Jake's interactions with his brother Max, his crew, and President Palma, showcasing a constant struggle for control and influence.

title: Monster Trucks
justification: Several characters exert authority: Dowd gives orders to scientists ("So we keep going, yes? Yeah. Punch through."), and Wade is clearly in charge of the junkyard ("Hey, lock up for me."). The Terravex employees also try to intimidate Tripp and his dad ("They want their truck back.").

title: How to Be a Latin Lover
justification: Several characters exert dominance. Maximo is kicked out and begs to stay, showing a loss of power. Sara confronts Maximo, asserting her authority and kicking him out, highlighting a power shift.

title: Lady Bird
justification: The film contains instances of characters asserting authority, such as the teacher correcting Lady Bird's name and telling her to 'take it away'. There are also instances of parental control, such as the mother telling Lady Bird to 'stop' and later scolding her for the state of her room and clothes, emphasizing her role as the 'bad guy'.

title: Kidnap
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting dominance are present. Examples include the restaurant scene where customers demand specific treatment ("Dale, where's my eggs over?") and the mother's increasingly desperate commands to the kidnappers ("Let him out! Let him out!"). The kidnappers also exert control through threats and demands.

title: Underworld: Blood Wars
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays. Examples include Semira relieving council members of their duties and Marius ordering his Lycans. There are constant struggles for dominance between vampires and Lycans, and within their own factions.

title: The Mountain Between Us
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. For example, a flight attendant directs passengers, and Ben takes charge in survival situations, telling Alex what to do. The pilot Walter also asserts his authority as the pilot.

title: Rings
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Sir, please stay in your seat," and "Come on, Holt! Supposed to be on the road an hour ago."

title: Logan Lucky
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. For example, the brothers are clearly in charge of Sadie, giving her a to-do list. Also, the warden at the prison has complete control over the inmates.

title: Home Again
justification: Alice is clearly in charge of her household, setting rules for the guests. Harry and George's interactions with producers and agents show a struggle for control over their creative work. Austen's sudden appearance and attempts to win Alice back also highlight a power struggle in their relationship.

title: Resident Evil: The Final Chapter
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, giving orders, and asserting dominance. Examples include Dr. Isaacs's control over the Umbrella Corporation and his clones, the Red Queen's directives, and the power struggles within the survivor groups. Lines like "Security level to maximum" and "You're fired" highlight the hierarchical structure and the exercise of authority.

title: The House
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Frank's increasingly aggressive behavior as 'The Butcher,' and the general control exerted over the illegal casino's patrons and operations. The town officials also exert their authority, attempting to shut down the casino.

title: Three Billboards Outside Ebbing Missouri
justification: Several characters exert authority, like the police chief over Dixon ('Hand me your gun and your badge.') and Mildred's confrontational interactions ('So why don't you just finish up your tea there, Father, and get the fuck outta my kitchen.'). There are also instances of defiance and resistance to authority, indicating a struggle for control.

title: The Bye Bye Man
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or asserting control. For example, Sasha tells John, "You got the whole upstairs to make girly, okay?" and later demands, "Elliot, come on. What? We all know you don't believe in this stuff, okay? But can you just please let her do it?"

title: Victoria and Abdul
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, requests phrased as commands ('Have one sent'), and constant reminders of hierarchy ('I am the Queen of England'). Characters like the Prime Minister and Dr. Reid are constantly trying to manage the Queen's behavior and relationships, highlighting the power struggles within the court.

title: My Little Pony: The Movie
justification: The Storm King and Tempest exert control through threats and demands, highlighted by lines like "Give me three days. I'll have everything ready for your arrival" and "Fail me, and your horn won't be the only thing that's broken." The princesses initially resist, but are quickly subdued, demonstrating a clear hierarchy.

title: Black Panther
justification: The dialogue is filled with challenges to authority, declarations of loyalty, and characters giving orders. Examples include M'Baku's challenge for the throne, T'Challa's commands to his Dora Milaje, and Killmonger's seizing of power and subsequent orders to weaponize vibranium.

title: Avengers: Infinity War
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Tony Stark directing Peter Parker ("Kid, that's the wizard. Get on it."), Thor commanding Rocket and Groot, and Thanos demanding Gamora's loyalty and the Soul Stone.

title: Incredibles 2
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Elastigirl giving orders to the police ('Follow them and get me close!') and Bob trying to assert authority over his children ('Stop it! Don't touch the buttons!'). However, most interactions are fairly egalitarian.

title: Deadpool 2
justification: Several characters give orders or assert dominance. Colossus orders Wade around, Cable interrogates and threatens, and various characters attempt to control Russell's actions. Examples: "Collar him, too." "Be at the X-Jet in five."

title: Dr. Seuss’ The Grinch
justification: The Grinch gives orders to his dog Max, such as "Come on, Max" and "Max, what is this depressing bean?". Cindy-Lou is told what to do by her mother, such as "Cindy-Lou. Sweetheart, come eat.". These examples show a mild power dynamic.

title: Mission: Impossible—Fallout
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and asserting dominance. Examples include Sloane's control over the IMF team, Walker's defiance of Hunt, and the White Widow's manipulation of others for her own gain. Lines like "Make the call. Shut 'em down," and "I have operational authority here, direct from the president," highlight the constant struggle for control.

title: Ant-Man and the Wasp
justification: Sonny Burch attempts to control Hope and Hank by threatening their business and demanding a partnership. Hope resists his control, asserting her own authority by refusing his demands and ultimately outsmarting him. The dialogue is filled with power plays and attempts to assert dominance.

title: Solo: A Star Wars Story
justification: Characters frequently give orders and express doubts about each other's competence. Examples include Beckett's instructions to Han, Val's criticisms of Beckett's choices, and Dryden Vos's dominance over Beckett, highlighting a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Venom
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and threatening each other. Examples include Carlton Drake's control over his employees ("Cut the camera off, please.") and Venom's possessive and controlling relationship with Eddie ("You are mine.").

title: A Star is Born
justification: Throughout the film, Jack exerts control over Ally, inviting her on stage despite her initial reluctance ('No, I can't do that. I'm sorry. No, Jack, please.'). Later, Rez attempts to control Ally's career and image, leading to conflict ('Okay, but you can't go rogue on me.').

title: Aquaman
justification: The film features constant struggles for power, particularly the throne of Atlantis. Orm's ambition to become Ocean Master and his challenge to Arthur, along with the political maneuvering between kingdoms, highlights the central role of power dynamics. Dialogue like "You may sit on the throne of Atlantis, but your claim to it is weak" and "I am the one true king!" underscores this theme.

title: Bohemian Rhapsody
justification: Freddie's interactions with Paul show a clear power imbalance, with Freddie often dictating terms and dismissing others' opinions. The band dynamic also involves power struggles, such as arguments over song choices and creative direction, with Freddie often asserting his dominance. The firing of Reid and the solo deal announcement further highlight Freddie's unilateral decision-making and control within the band.

title: A Quiet Place
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or instructions, such as "Go find your mother," "Listen to me," and "You cannot go down there!" indicate a clear hierarchy. The dialogue also reveals a protective dynamic, with characters emphasizing the need to protect others, as in "Your father will always protect you" and "You have to protect them."

title: Ralph Breaks The Internet
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. For example, Shank commands her crew ("Pyro. Give those punks the works."), and Ralph directs Vanellope ("Kid, fire!"). There's also a clear power dynamic in the auction scene, with the auctioneer controlling the bidding process.

title: Crazy Rich Asians
justification: Several scenes highlight the Young family's wealth and status, creating a clear hierarchy. Eleanor's disapproval of Rachel and attempts to assert dominance are evident: "You will never be enough." The Goh family also displays a hierarchy, with the father making demeaning comments about Rachel's appearance and career.

title: Hotel Transylvania 3: Summer Vacation
justification: Captain Ericka is giving orders to the crew, and Van Helsing is commanding Ericka to kill Dracula. Dracula is seen as a leader and protector of his family and friends, and he is trying to protect them from Van Helsing.

title: Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald
justification: Dumbledore manipulates Newt into doing his bidding, highlighting his own inability to act directly. Grindelwald exerts control over his followers, demanding obedience and loyalty, as seen in his interactions with Krall and Queenie. The hierarchy within the Ministry is also evident, with Travers asserting his authority over Dumbledore and other characters.

title: The Meg
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Blow it up now," "Copy that, Mac," and "Origin, recommend an immediate right turn to three-five-zero."

title: Ocean’s 8
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the heist team, with Debbie Ocean as the leader giving instructions and making decisions. Examples include: "So go home, get your affairs in order, because tomorrow, we begin pulling off one of the biggest jewelry heists in history." and "In a minute, we're gonna stand up. She's gonna sit down."

title: The Nun
justification: The Bishop directs Father Burke to investigate, indicating a clear hierarchy within the Church. Father Burke gives orders to Frenchie and Sister Irene, establishing his authority during the investigation. The demon Valak attempts to dominate the nuns and others, showcasing a struggle for control.

title: Peter Rabbit
