justification: The dialogue includes characters giving orders ("Come here!"), vying for positions ("Give me the promotion, June"), and asserting authority ("Get out! Stay out of my house!"). There are also instances of characters apologizing and showing deference to others, indicating a hierarchical structure.

title: Creed II
justification: The dialogue is filled with challenges to authority and assertions of dominance, especially between Creed and Drago, and Creed and Rocky. Examples include Drago's constant challenges to Creed's status as champion and Rocky's attempts to guide and control Creed's decisions, which Creed resists: "If he doesn't fight you? Then he's no champion." and "I'm taking this fight with or without you."

title: Spider-Man: Into The Spider-Verse 3D
justification: Kingpin gives orders like "Get rid of the body" and "Kill that guy," demonstrating his authority. The police also assert their power, shouting, "Police! Put your hands up!" and "Stop!".

title: The Equalizer 2
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. The opening scene shows a soldier deferring to a superior officer ('Yes, sir.'). Later, a man violently forces a woman to open her mouth, demonstrating extreme dominance ('Open your mouth.').

title: Rampage
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and struggling for control. Examples include: "Put it down," "Get outta here, you big lug," and "Boss. Wheels up! You boys are Oscar Mike."

title: A Wrinkle in Time
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance, give orders, and manipulate others. Examples include Mrs. Whatsit's cryptic commands, Charles Wallace's attempts to control situations, and The IT's manipulation of Charles Wallace and Meg.

title: Fifty Shades Freed
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of Christian exerting control over Ana, such as dictating her schedule ("You're coming with me.") and expressing disapproval of her choices. Ana also asserts her independence and challenges Christian's authority, like when she insists on using her maiden name at work and confronts Gia about her behavior towards Christian.

title: Christopher Robin
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Christopher Robin's boss expecting him to deliver a presentation and Madeline being told what to do by her mother. However, most of the dialogue revolves around friendship and helping each other.

title: I Can Only Imagine
justification: Miss Fincher demands Bart sing, stating, "You can. And you will. And there'll be no further discussion about it." Bart's father is verbally abusive and controlling, demonstrated by lines like, "Sit down and eat. C'mon, sit down and eat. Getting cold."

title: Smallfoot
justification: The Stonekeeper exerts significant control over the yeti community by manipulating information and enforcing strict rules. Migo's initial banishment and the Stonekeeper's manipulation of the stones to maintain order demonstrate a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: The Post
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of people trying to exert control or influence. Ben is constantly pushing Kay to publish, despite her reservations, and there are multiple instances of characters referencing powerful figures like Kennedy and Johnson to either intimidate or persuade.

title: Night School
justification: Carrie asserts her authority over Teddy multiple times, stating, "You're gonna do what I told you to do." Stewart also exerts control, warning Teddy, "I look forward to seeing how you do on the midterm. My midterm," highlighting his role in evaluating Teddy's progress.

title: Bumblebee
justification: Several instances of authority and obedience are present. The mother gives orders to Charlie ('Feed the dog'), and military personnel give orders to each other ('Take it down!'). There's also a clear hierarchy in the Decepticon scenes, with one robot commanding another ('Set course for Earth').

title: The First Purge
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and navigating hierarchical structures. Dmitri's control over his crew is evident in lines like, "If you so much as blink, Blaise will remove the skin from your face, fat man. She does exactly what I say." and "Yo, pocket that money quick, son. And then send these niggas on their way, a'ight?"

title: Book Club
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control over others. For example, the pilot tries to get a woman's number by using his authority, and Carol's friends try to control her dating life. Also, Carol tries to control Bruce's sex life.

title: The House with a Clock in its Walls
justification: Throughout the movie, characters are giving orders and asserting authority. Examples include the coach directing the basketball team ('Goggles, get up! Come on, guys!'), Jonathan instructing Lewis ('First you get the book, then you get the key.'), and Isaac demanding the key ('Give me the key.').

title: Skyscraper
justification: The film features several instances of characters asserting dominance. Ray Hutchinson demands, "I want everyone gone... you, your men, snipers, everyone." Later, Kores Botha holds Georgia hostage, forcing Will to comply with his demands, stating, "Or I'm gonna throw your daughter off the fucking roof."

title: Insidious: The Last Key
justification: The dialogue is replete with examples of power dynamics. Gerald's abusive behavior towards his daughters, marked by commands like "Put your hands on the wall" and threats of punishment, highlights a stark power imbalance. Elise's father's controlling nature is evident in his statement: "You can either follow my rules...or you can break them and sleep under my floor."

title: Instant Family
justification: The foster parents, Pete and Ellie, struggle to establish authority with the new children, especially Lizzy, who resists their attempts to parent. Examples include the conflict over the black bedroom, the dinner table confrontation, and the grounding incident, showing a clear power struggle.

title: The Mule
justification: The DEA agents exert authority over Luis, forcing him to work for them. Earl is given orders by the cartel members, and they threaten him with violence if he disobeys: "New boss says, you show up late again and you're done."

title: Blockers
justification: Several instances show parents attempting to control their daughters' choices, like preventing a 'sex pact'. Dialogue such as "I'm gonna stop her" and the physical altercations demonstrate a struggle for control and authority.

title: Pacific Rim: Uprising
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and assertions of authority. Examples include "Malikova, get Namani squared away and prepped for training. Yes, sir! As you were." and "Gipsy Avenger, this is Marshal Quan. All you have to do is stand there and look pretty. Stay focused, try not to fall over."

title: Maze Runner: The Death Cure
justification: Characters frequently give orders and make demands, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include: "Move it, Immunes," "Follow the roads where we can," and "Get Janson."

title: Tag
justification: The game of tag itself is a constant struggle for dominance, with characters strategizing and manipulating each other to avoid being 'it'. Jerry's elaborate traps and the group's willingness to go to extreme lengths (like waterboarding) highlight the intense competition and desire to 'win' or, more accurately, avoid losing. Dialogue like 'I will never let you tag me' and 'You're gonna die before that ever happens' emphasizes the high stakes and personal investment in maintaining control.

title: The Nutcracker and the Four Realms
justification: Several scenes show characters giving orders and others obeying. For example, the father tells Clara, "Please get your sister ready," and Captain Hoffman repeatedly asks Clara, "Is that an order?"

title: Life of the Party
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to assert dominance or control. For example, the divorce mediation is filled with attempts to 'win' and insult each other, and Maddie's friends kidnap Deanna to force her to join their sorority.

title: Overboard
justification: Several characters give orders or express frustration with their lack of control. Kate directs Leo to do chores, saying, "While I'm studying for my exam, you keep the house running." Bobby, the construction boss, barks orders at his employees, demonstrating a clear hierarchy.

title: Sicario: Day of the Soldado
justification: The dialogue is dominated by characters giving orders, asserting authority, and threatening violence to achieve compliance. Examples include: "Get on your knees and put your hands up," "I can do whatever the fuck I want here," and "No rules today, sport, just orders."

title: I Feel Pretty
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Renee's interactions with Helen Grey and Avery LeClaire show her navigating a hierarchical work environment, while her assertive behavior with Ethan and in the bikini contest demonstrates her attempts to assert control and confidence. The dialogue reveals a constant negotiation of status and influence.

title: BlacKkKlansman
justification: The dialogue is filled with racial slurs and assertions of white supremacy, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. Characters like Felix exert dominance through threats and intimidation, demanding obedience and loyalty. The presence of David Duke and the reverence shown towards him further highlight the hierarchical structure and the pursuit of power within the Klan.

title: The Shape of Water
justification: Characters give orders and expect obedience, such as 'Say what I sign' and 'Repeat'. There are threats and implied consequences for disobedience, like 'Moscow will not support your plan' and the discussion of killing the asset. The dialogue reveals a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Red Sparrow
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and manipulating others. Examples include Matron's control over the recruits, the training to exploit weaknesses, and the power dynamics in the SVR.

title: Breaking In
justification: The entire plot revolves around criminals invading a home to find money, establishing immediate dominance through violence and threats. The dialogue is filled with orders, threats, and attempts to control the situation, such as "Calm the fuck down!" and "From this moment on, you are going to have to do exactly what I say, or you and your kids will not survive this night."

title: Goosebumps 2: Haunted Halloween
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or dominance over others. Examples include the Junk Bros bullying, Slappy ordering people around, and the mother setting rules.

title: Den of Thieves
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and threatening each other. Examples include: "Sit down. You sit right there," "You need to fucking look at me when I'm talking to you," and "Get down on the ground! Get down on the fucking ground!". These exchanges highlight a constant struggle for control and status.

title: First Man
justification: There are instances of hierarchy and control, particularly within the space program. Examples include the selection of Armstrong for Gemini 8 ("We're putting you in command of Gemini 8.") and the interactions between astronauts and mission control, where orders are given and followed ("8, stand by for a correction.").

title: Hereditary
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or demanding obedience, such as "Charlie, shoes off" and "You are going to this...party with your brother." The mother's controlling behavior and attempts to manipulate situations also highlight power imbalances within the family.

title: Uncle Drew
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and challenging each other's authority. Examples include the older man setting 'new rules' in his car, the preacher commanding others, and constant verbal sparring for status.

title: Truth or Dare
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving each other orders and attempting to exert control. Examples include "Hey, Tyson, shut up!" and "Don't tell me to shut up." The game "Truth or Dare" itself becomes a tool for manipulation and control, with characters being forced to comply with its demands under threat of death.

title: Love, Simon
justification: Martin blackmails Simon to get closer to Abby, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. He uses Simon's secret against him: "Now, why the hell did you screenshot my emails?" and "Well, I need you to help me talk with her...and hang out with her and stuff, you know?"

title: Darkest Hour
justification: The film depicts constant power struggles: Churchill fights to maintain his position as Prime Minister against Halifax's attempts to negotiate peace with Germany and replace him. There are also scenes of Churchill giving orders to his staff and military personnel, highlighting his authority, such as when he commands Nicholson to hold Calais at all costs.

title: The Commuter
justification: The film features multiple instances of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and struggling for control. Examples include the woman, Joanna, who manipulates Michael into finding a specific passenger, and the various authority figures (police, conductors) who exert control over others. The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and attempts to intimidate, highlighting the power struggles at play.

title: The 15:17 to Paris
justification: The subtitles show a clear military hierarchy with sergeants giving orders and airmen obeying. Examples include: "Drop. On the podium." and "Airman Stone, why are you doing push-ups? I'm late, Sergeant."

title: Alpha
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the tribe, with the chief giving orders and expectations to his son, Keda. Dialogue such as "Prove you can lead" and "He must do his part" highlights the pressure to earn his place. Later, Keda establishes dominance over the wolf, Alpha, commanding it with phrases like "Get in the water!" and eventually leading the pack.

title: Peppermint
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy, especially within the criminal organization. Diego Garcia gives orders to his subordinates, demanding results and threatening consequences for failure: "Smoke him. Make an example. A loud one." Riley North also exerts power, interrogating and threatening individuals to get information or force compliance.

title: Death Wish
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance through threats and violence. Examples include the home invasion scene where the robber barks orders like "Put the fucking phone down right now" and the torture scene where the doctor inflicts pain to extract information.

title: The Spy Who Dumped Me
justification: Characters give orders and assert dominance, such as 'Get out! Abort! Mission abort!' and 'Just drive, please.' There are also struggles for control, like the assassin's demand, 'Where is drive?' and the power plays within the intelligence agency.

title: Annihilation
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy within the military and scientific teams. Dr. Ventress leads the team and makes decisions, while others follow her orders. There are also instances of interrogation and control, such as the questioning of Lena about her husband's mission and the attempts to understand the nature of the Shimmer.

title: Green Book
justification: The film showcases a clear power dynamic between Dr. Shirley and Tony Lip. Dr. Shirley gives Tony instructions and expects him to follow them, such as dictating driving speeds and correcting Tony's diction. Tony, despite his initial resistance, ultimately complies, highlighting Dr. Shirley's authority.

title: Nobody’s Fool
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. Frank, the coffee shop owner, holds power over Tanya as her employer, demonstrated by his ability to give her a job and later advise her. There are also instances of Tanya attempting to assert dominance, such as when she demands a three-week vacation after only working for a short time.

title: Adrift
justification: The film shows some power dynamics, but it is not a central theme. Richard is more experienced with sailing, so he often gives Tami instructions, such as "Let the sheet go!" and "Get below now!". Christine and Peter also exert some power by offering Richard a job and setting the terms.

title: Robin Hood
justification: The Sheriff constantly asserts his authority, demanding taxes and obedience: "By the order of the Sheriff of Nottingham, you need to pay the toll." He also threatens and punishes those who defy him, highlighting a clear power imbalance: "Nothing's sacred till I've caught that thief and drowned him in a cage."

title: Super Troopers 2
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of authority and attempts to assert dominance. Examples include Farva's constant need for radio checks and the Captain giving orders to the officers. The interactions between the American officers and the Canadian Mounties also highlight a struggle for status and control.

title: Slender Man
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or making demands, such as "Hurry up!" and "Don't make any noise." There are also instances of characters being excluded or denied access, like "Not a chance" and "Yeah, not tonight, grasshopper."

title: Teen Titans Go! To The Movies
justification: The entire plot revolves around Robin's desire for a movie, which he sees as a status symbol. Characters like Jade Wilson and Slade exert control through manipulation and deception, highlighting a constant struggle for dominance within the superhero hierarchy. Robin's willingness to betray his friends for fame underscores the importance of status in this world.

title: Hostiles
justification: The film is driven by the power dynamic between Captain Blocker and his superiors, who force him to escort Chief Yellow Hawk. Blocker's initial refusal and the Colonel's manipulation of his pension highlight the struggle for control. The dialogue is filled with orders and resistance, showcasing a clear hierarchy.

title: The Hate U Give
justification: The film features multiple instances of power dynamics. Police officers exert authority through commands like "Do not move" and "Where's the weapon?" Gang leader King displays dominance, threatening Starr's father and demanding obedience: "Keep my kids out your mouth, King."

title: Avengers: Endgame
justification: Several characters give orders or express authority. Tony directs Scott during the time travel test ('Scott, fire up... the van thing.') and later instructs him ('Scott, get this back to the compound. Suit up.'). Thanos asserts his dominance and inevitability ('I am inevitable.').

title: The Lion King
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, obedience, and challenges to authority. Examples include Mufasa instructing Simba, Zazu's attempts to control Simba and Nala, and Scar's manipulation of the hyenas and his attempts to dominate Sarabi.

title: Toy Story 4
justification: The dialogue shows Woody giving orders to Forky ('Be quiet!') and trying to control his actions ('Forky, slow down!'). Gabby Gabby also exerts control over Benson and attempts to manipulate Woody ('You can't leave yet. You have what I need.').

title: Frozen II
justification: Elsa is the Queen and makes decisions for Arendelle, but Anna challenges her and insists on being involved. There are also power dynamics between the Arendellian soldiers and the Northuldra people, with both sides initially distrustful and defensive, as well as the historical context of King Runeard's actions and his desire to control the Northuldra.

title: Captain Marvel
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and questioning authority. Examples include Yon-Rogg's control over Carol, the military hierarchy within Starforce and S.H.I.E.L.D., and the power struggles between the Kree and Skrulls.

title: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker
justification: The provided text is an error message. There is no dialogue or interaction to analyze for power dynamics.

title: Spider-Man: Far From Home
justification: Nick Fury and Maria Hill are constantly giving Peter Parker orders, showing their authority. Beck also asserts control, manipulating Peter and his team, as seen when he says, "With our technology and with EDITH, Mysterio will be the greatest hero on Earth! Then everyone will listen!"

title: Aladdin
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy, with characters like Jafar vying for control of Agrabah and Aladdin struggling to gain status to impress Princess Jasmine. Dialogue such as "You're either the most powerful man in the room, or you're nothing" and the Genie's servitude highlight the importance of power and status.

title: Joker
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between employers and employees, as seen in Arthur's interactions with Hoyt, who berates and fires him. Thomas Wayne's condescending remarks about the less fortunate also highlight a power imbalance. The subway scene shows the rich looking down on the poor.

title: It: Chapter Two
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, like Richie's aggressive humor and Beverly's father's abusive behavior. The dialogue also shows Pennywise's manipulation and attempts to instill fear, demonstrating a clear power imbalance. Mike's drugging of Bill to force a vision also highlights a struggle for control.

title: Jumanji: The Next Level
justification: Several characters give orders and express authority. For example, Bravestone tells the others, "Come on! Follow me!" and Jurgen the Brutal commands his hyena master, demonstrating a clear hierarchy.

title: Us
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting control. Examples include parents telling children what to do ('Bags in the house first', 'Jason, eat something'), characters demanding obedience ('Can you watch your daughter, please?'), and the Tethered asserting their dominance ('We want to take our time').

title: Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include: "If she moves, I want you to shoot her," and "Get your greasy sausage fingers off of her."

title: John Wick: Chapter 3 — Parabellum
justification: The film is saturated with power dynamics. Characters constantly reference 'the High Table' and its rules, demonstrating a rigid hierarchy. Dialogue such as 'I have served, I will be of service' and threats like 'Your penance will be paid in blood' highlight the constant struggle for status and obedience.

title: How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World
justification: The dialogue includes many instances of characters giving orders and asserting authority. For example, Hiccup directs the dragon riders, and Grimmel commands the Deathgrippers. There are also power struggles, such as Gobber's attempts to advise Hiccup and the warlords' interactions with Grimmel.

title: The Secret Life of Pets 2
justification: Several characters exert authority: Snowball commands his superhero team, Rooster bosses Max around on the farm, and Pops runs a puppy school. Examples include Snowball saying, "Commander Horsey, please read the minutes" and Rooster telling Max, "Dogs sleep outside."

title: Pokémon: Detective Pikachu
justification: Several instances show characters giving orders or expressing dominance. Examples include: "You hold the door," "Run! Rabid Aipom!", and the general dynamic between Tim and Pikachu, where Pikachu often directs Tim's actions and expresses his authority as a detective.

title: Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood
justification: Several scenes highlight power dynamics. Randy's control over stuntmen ('you don't stunt, I don't pay you') and the Manson family's manipulation of George Spahn ('Squeaky sent me to bed') are clear examples. Rick's struggle with his fading career and his agent's harsh pep talk ('You don't get these lines right, I'm gonna blow your fucking brains out tonight') also demonstrate power imbalances.

title: Shazam!
justification: The movie features several instances of power dynamics. There are bullies who try to dominate Freddy, and the wizard Shazam holds immense power over Billy, dictating his destiny. Sivana also seeks power, threatening and manipulating others to achieve his goals.

title: Dumbo
justification: The circus owner, Max, constantly gives orders and asserts his authority over his employees and family. Vandevere, the wealthy businessman, exerts control through financial power and manipulation, dictating terms and dismissing those who displease him. Examples include Max telling Holt what to do and Vandevere firing Max's troupe.

title: Maleficent: Mistress of Evil
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and power plays, such as "Tie it off, come on!", "Stay close", and "Get on his back." Queen Ingrith's manipulative behavior and Maleficent's initial dominance also highlight the theme.

title: Glass
justification: The film features multiple characters vying for control. Dr. Staple attempts to control the protagonists through therapy and manipulation, while the characters with powers struggle for dominance amongst themselves and over others, as seen in lines like "You will learn to kneel before the broken."

title: Godzilla: King of the Monsters
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience, such as Colonel Foster directing G-Team ("G-Team. Barnes, Martinez, Hendricks, I want you on those CROWS now!") and Serizawa commanding the team on the submarine. Emma Russell also exerts control through the ORCA, manipulating Titans, and Alan Jonah commands his mercenary forces.

title: The Upside
justification: The dialogue shows a clear power dynamic between Philip and Dell, with Philip often giving orders and Dell reluctantly complying. Examples include Philip's demands regarding music, personal care, and Dell's business ideas. The 'strike one' interaction further highlights Philip's authority.

title: Ford v. Ferrari
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting authority, giving orders, and maneuvering for control. For example, Leo Beebe's role as a senior executive and his interactions with Carroll Shelby, where he attempts to exert control over the racing program, demonstrate this dynamic. Henry Ford II's interactions with Shelby also highlight the power he wields, emphasizing the hierarchy within the Ford Motor Company.

title: The LEGO Movie 2: The Second Part
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and trying to assert control. Queen Watevra attempts to control the narrative and force a wedding, while Rex Dangervest tries to manipulate Emmet into becoming tougher and following his lead. Examples include 'Take them to get changed for the ceremony' and 'Raptors, re-coordinate'.

title: The Addams Family
justification: Margaux Needler is constantly giving orders and expecting compliance, such as "Double the balloons. And I want a blizzard of confetti." Gomez and Morticia also exert authority over their children, as seen when Morticia commands Wednesday to dig up Pugsley: "Dig up your brother. At once."

title: Downton Abbey
justification: The dialogue shows a clear hierarchy between the family and the servants, with commands being given and obedience expected. Examples include Mrs. Webb and Mrs. Hughes's constant struggle for control over the staff, and Carson's attempts to maintain authority even in retirement. The royal visit amplifies these dynamics, with everyone scrambling to please their superiors.

title: Rocketman
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over Elton. Dick James tries to control Elton's career, saying, "You fuck up and I'll kill ya." John Reid manipulates Elton, and Sheila tries to control Elton's life and career.

title: Alita: Battle Angel
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders and asserting dominance. Examples include Ido telling Alita, "For now, I don't want you out after dark. Is that understood?" and Vector's control over Motorball, stating, "I don't want my players losing unless I tell them to."

title: Good Boys
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. For example, the 'Daddy' character in the fraternity scene barks orders, and the girls assert dominance over the boys at the playground, demanding the drone back. The constant negotiation and manipulation to get what they want also highlights the power struggles.

title: Men in Black: International
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and jockeying for position. Examples include High T's interactions with Agents H and M, Riza's control over her henchmen, and the general hierarchy within the MIB organization.

title: Annabelle Comes Home
justification: The Warrens are seen as authority figures, with others seeking their help and guidance ('We need another barrier of protection. A holy one.'). Judy's parents set rules and expectations for her and her babysitter ('Behave? Yes. And you'll remember to go to...'). There are also instances of bullying and social hierarchy among the teenagers.

title: Yesterday
justification: Ed Sheeran's arrival and subsequent offer of a support act position immediately shifts the power dynamic. Jack is initially in awe and then becomes subservient, agreeing to Sheeran's impromptu songwriting challenge and accepting his manager's offer. Debra Hammer's controlling management style and the record label's attempts to manipulate Jack's image and music further highlight the power dynamics at play.

title: Tyler Perry’s A Madea Family Funeral
justification: Characters are constantly trying to control each other through direct commands ('Hattie, you ain't finna say nothing'), insults ('Where was you hoes back in the day'), and physical intimidation (Ma hitting Hattie). There are also power struggles within the family, especially regarding the deceased's secrets and the handling of the funeral.

title: Zombieland: Double Tap
justification: Several characters attempt to assert dominance. Tallahassee frequently gives orders and expresses his opinions forcefully, such as when he declares "We ride at dawn." Albuquerque and Flagstaff's relationship also shows a clear hierarchy, with Albuquerque in charge.

title: Angel Has Fallen
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders and obedience, especially within the Secret Service and military teams. Examples include "Yes, sir," "Delta Team, engage," and various commands given to secure the president and investigate the assassination attempt. The interactions between the president and his staff, and the acting president and his advisors, also highlight the hierarchical structure and the exercise of authority.

title: Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark
justification: Characters frequently give orders (e.g., "Let's go, girls," "Tommy, slow down," "Move!"). There are also instances of defiance and resistance to authority (e.g., "Eat shit, Harold," "Mom, okay, jeez," "Hey, get out of my car.").

title: Dark Phoenix
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Kurt, take Peter. Go!', 'Scott, I need you to blast that thruster'), asserting authority ('I am not putting this team in more danger'), and struggling for control ('Get out of my head'). Charles Xavier's manipulation of Jean's mind also highlights a significant power imbalance.

title: Terminator: Dark Fate
justification: The film features a clear power dynamic between protectors (Grace, Sarah, and the T-800) and the protected (Dani), with constant orders and sacrifices made to ensure Dani's survival. Examples include Grace's repeated commands to Dani ('Stay behind me!', 'Move!') and Sarah's authoritative instructions ('I drive.'). The Rev-9 also exerts power through its relentless pursuit and attempts to control the situation ('Give me the girl.').

title: Dora and the Lost City of Gold
justification: Several characters exert authority: the teacher ("Okay, let's see who did the reading last night."), Sammy as class president, and Alejandro as the adult rescuer. Dora also displays a degree of control in jungle situations, guiding her peers.

title: Escape Room
justification: Characters frequently give orders and express frustration when others don't comply. Examples include: "Turn it off, please," "Don't touch anything else, okay?" and "Ladies, come on, enough with the water. Get over here and help us look."

title: A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood
justification: The journalist Lloyd's editor, Ellen, assigns him a puff piece despite his investigative background, stating, "Didn't I hire you to do whatever I tell you to do?" This shows a clear power dynamic. Also, the TV director is shown to be in charge on set, telling people what to do.

title: Midway
justification: The dialogue is filled with orders, commands, and discussions of rank. Examples include: "Fly a grid on bearing 185," "Lindsey has command," and "Take us back to Enterprise, lieutenant. That's an order."

title: The Curse of La Llorona
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Anna's boss transferring her cases due to her husband's death, and the police officer ordering Anna to take an officer with her are examples of authority. La Llorona's power over the children and Patricia's desperate attempts to regain control over her life also highlight power dynamics.

title: Pet Sematary
justification: Several instances of parental authority are evident, such as when Louis tells Ellie, "You get down from there!" and when Rachel scolds her, "Honey, you can't wander off like that." The resurrected Ellie exhibits a twisted form of dominance, ordering Rachel, "Hug your daughter, Rach," and later taunting her with "Now you'll never get out of bed again."

title: What Men Want
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include: "Look straight ahead," "Move!", and "Do something." The negotiation between Jamal Barry and the sports agents also highlights power dynamics, as they compete for his representation.

title: Ad Astra
justification: The film features a clear military hierarchy with characters giving and receiving orders ('Major, what can you tell us about the Lima Project, sir?'). Roy's journey is driven by the need to confront his father, a figure of immense authority and control, and the film explores the power he holds over Roy's life.

title: Isn’t it Romantic
justification: Whitney asserts her authority over Natalie, stating, "I don't have to explain shit to you. I don't work for you. Technically, actually, you're my assistant so..." Later, Natalie declares, "You're going down, bitch," indicating a power struggle.

title: Gemini Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, questioning authority, and struggling for control. Examples include: "Get out of there, now," "You can tell me now, or you can tell me in five minutes minus your teeth," and Verris's manipulation of Junior.

title: MA
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, from the cop ordering the teens around to Sue Ann setting rules in her basement and manipulating the teens. Ben's aggressive confrontation with Sue Ann and his controlling behavior towards his daughter further exemplify the power struggles at play.

title: Five Feet Apart
justification: Several characters exert control over others, such as Barb's strict enforcement of rules and Stella's initial attempts to control Will's behavior. Dialogue like "Will, get back to your room" and "Six feet at all times. I got it" demonstrates this dynamic. Stella's later control over Will's regimen also highlights this theme.

title: Wonder Park
justification: The film features multiple instances of characters giving orders and others following them, indicating a clear hierarchy. Examples include the father telling June to go to Math Camp, and June bossing around the Wonderland characters to fix the park.

title: Rambo: Last Blood
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "Just do the fucking job all day and night!", "If one of you bitches wants to run away go ahead...run, But I will find you...and I will kill you...I swear", and "Next time do what I tell you, bro."

title: Playing with Fire
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's status. Examples include Jake's interactions with the children ('Rest of the depot's off-limits, are we clear?') and Commander Richards's berating of Jake ('Great optics for the department, Carson.').

title: Harriet
justification: The dialogue is dominated by commands, obedience, and assertions of ownership. Examples include: "You got to be miles away from here fore dawn," "Come on back peaceful. Family's worried about you," and "If your niggers helped my slave escape, I'm holding you responsible."

title: A Dog’s Way Home
justification: Several instances show characters asserting authority or control. Gunter Beckenbauer attempts to intimidate Terri Ray, saying they 'do not want to go to war with me.' Later, Animal Control officers arrive to impound Bella, asserting their legal authority and threatening arrest.

title: The Angry Birds Movie 2
justification: Several characters give orders or express authority, such as Red telling others what to do and Zeta commanding her subordinates. There are also instances of characters questioning or challenging authority, like Silver questioning Red's plans and the pigs' engineer being threatened for not meeting deadlines. The dialogue highlights a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: Queen & Slim
justification: Characters frequently give orders ('Get in the driver's seat,' 'Pop the trunk,' 'Slow down') and assert dominance through threats and intimidation ('I could kill you right now,' 'Nigga, I'll call you what the fuck I want'). There are also instances of characters asserting authority or control in various situations, such as the lawyer's professional confidence and Earl's control over his property and associates.

title: Breakthrough
justification: The parents and medical staff have a power struggle over John's treatment. Joyce demands the doctor be 'the best' and later insists they wake John up, showing her desire to control the situation. The medical staff, particularly Dr. Garrett, initially assert their authority based on expertise, but Joyce challenges this.

title: Crawl
justification: The father-daughter relationship is central, with the father often pushing Haley, a swimmer, to excel using phrases like "apex predator." There's also a clear dynamic of Haley defying authority, such as ignoring evacuation orders and Wayne's instructions, indicating a struggle for control.

title: Little Women
justification: Aunt March's dialogue is full of power assertions, such as "You're not paid to think" and her insistence that women need to marry well. Jo's interactions with Mr. Davis at school also show a clear power imbalance, with him hitting her for a drawing.

title: The Hustle
justification: Josephine is clearly in charge, manipulating Penny and others. Examples include Josephine's control over Brigitte and Albert ('Everything is fine, Brigitte. You and Albert may go.') and her manipulation of Penny ('I've invested in you, Penny. And I must see a robust return before I can share the profits.').

title: The Intruder
justification: The dialogue reveals a struggle for control and dominance, particularly between Scott and Charlie. Scott repeatedly asserts his ownership and boundaries, stating, "No guns on my property ever." Charlie's actions, like mowing the lawn and showing up unannounced, suggest a desire to maintain influence and a connection to the house, creating tension and a power struggle.

title: Last Christmas
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the audition scene where the director and others hold power over the auditionees. Also, Crăciun, the shop owner, holds power over Kate, her employee, scolding her for mistakes and threatening to fire her: "Curăţă-ţi mizeria, fată proastă!".

title: Overcomer
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. The coach instructs players ('You guys get to class'), and later faces pressure from parents about a player's future. John and Amy's marital dynamic involves Amy's attempts to 'fix' John, leading to conflict and John's frustration with his job and pay cut.

title: Cold Pursuit
justification: Several characters give orders or make demands, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include Viking's control over his drug operation and Nels's interrogation of potential leads, such as when he demands information from Dante and Speedo.

title: Dragon Ball Super: Broly
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, expressing fear of authority figures like Freeza, and striving for dominance. Examples include Freeza's control over his army, Paragus's manipulation of Broly, and Vegeta's desire to surpass Goku.

title: Long Shot
justification: The movie features a clear hierarchy, with Charlotte Field, the Secretary of State, holding significant power. This is evident in her interactions with Fred, whom she hires as a speechwriter, and the President, whose endorsement she needs. Dialogue like "Right now." and "You're a punch-up writer, you're not Maya Angelou!" highlights the power imbalance and Charlotte's control over Fred.

title: Spies in Disguise
justification: The dialogue is filled with examples of characters asserting dominance and control. Sterling fires Wilbur immediately after Wilbur disagrees with him, stating "Wrong answer, Willy. You're fired." Later, Jenkins asserts authority over Sterling, ordering him into custody despite his protests.

title: Child’s Play
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and assertions of control. Examples include: "I want you to finish this one, and then I want you GONE," and "Andy, I told you to unpack those boxes."

title: Ready or Not
justification: The Le Domas family exerts control through wealth and tradition, demanding Grace participate in a deadly game. Dialogue like "Stand tall and fuck 'em. The only thing that matters is what Alex thinks" and "He will decide that, my dear" highlights the family's dominance and Grace's outsider status.

title: Happy Death Day 2U
justification: Several characters give orders or try to exert control. Examples include the main character ordering Ryan to fix the time loop, and the police officer ordering Tree to face the wall. There are also instances of characters trying to persuade others to follow their plans, indicating a struggle for influence.

title: Vice
justification: The dialogue showcases a clear hierarchy, with Dick Cheney strategically positioning himself for influence. Examples include Cheney directing staff, overriding protocols ('They're not going anywhere. Just, uh, tell them, um, we have all the helicopters.'), and manipulating situations to expand executive power.

title: 21 Bridges
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders ('Move!', 'Shut up. On your knees.', 'Drive.', 'Cover me.'). There are also power struggles between cops and criminals ('We're the guys that are taking your cocaine.', 'Not smart. You guys are gonna fucking die.'). The police captain exerts authority over his detectives ('Guys, I need you to get up. You're sitting in my crime scene.').

title: Midsommar
justification: Several interactions reveal a subtle power dynamic. Christian's academic competitiveness with Josh, and his dismissive attitude towards Dani's feelings, highlight a struggle for dominance. Pelle's influence over the group and the villagers' deference to the elders also contribute to the theme.

title: The Art of Racing in the Rain
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control. Denny promises his father-in-law he will prioritize safety, showing deference. Later, Eve's parents attempt to take custody of Zoë, asserting their perceived authority over Denny's parenting.

title: Countdown
justification: Several characters give orders or instructions, indicating a hierarchy. Examples include a nurse telling an intern to take over an IV, a supervisor telling a nurse to do a room, and a doctor telling a nurse to get vitals. Also, the attempted sexual assault shows a clear abuse of power.

title: Uncut Gems
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, demands, and displays of dominance. Examples include 'Give me the keys to your fucking car!', 'Take his clothes off', and 'Monday, I want the money. Arno gets the money. All right? I'm not fucking around anymore.'

title: Judy
justification: Several scenes depict power dynamics. Judy is often told what to do, such as "Don't you dare!" and "Get up." There are also scenes where she asserts her authority, such as when she tells Burt, "He can stay."

title: Fighting With My Family
justification: The Rock's dialogue is a clear display of dominance, berating the aspiring wrestlers and asserting his authority. Later, the WWE coach holds tryouts where he decides who has the skills and spark to be a WWE superstar, demonstrating his power to make or break careers.

title: On the Basis of Sex
justification: The dialogue reveals power dynamics in several relationships. Ruth challenges Marty's dismissive behavior ("But all the little brush-offs, the dismissive pats on the head, it-it matters, Marty."). Tom, Marty's boss, exerts authority over Marty's career choices ("when you lose and you embarrass our firm, just be ready for your career to come crashing back to earth.").

title: A Dog’s Journey
justification: Gloria exerts control over CJ, demonstrated by dictating CJ's actions and finances: "You're not allowed to have a dog. You understand me?" and admitting to spending CJ's inheritance: "How do you think we have a house? And a car?". There are also instances of CJ asserting herself, such as when she confronts Gloria about her behavior and declares her intention to leave: "So you can't... You can't push me around."

title: Booksmart
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others, such as Jared trying to force the girls to enjoy his party and the mayor ordering people around at the murder mystery party. There are also instances of characters resisting authority, like the girls ditching Jared's boat party and Amy standing up to Nick's casual dismissal of her. The pizza delivery guy also holds power over the girls when he threatens them with a gun.

title: Parasite
justification: The wealthy family exerts control over their employees, issuing commands and setting expectations. The Kim family, in turn, manipulates and deceives to gain and maintain their positions, highlighting a struggle for status and control. Examples include the mother telling the housekeeper to boil water for ram-don and the father firing the driver.

title: Stuber
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to assert dominance or control. Examples include Vic's aggressive interrogation tactics and manipulation of Stu, Amber's bossy and demeaning behavior towards her employees, and the general disrespect shown towards Stu as an Uber driver.

title: 47 Meters Down: Uncaged
justification: Several instances of power dynamics are present. The father figure, Grant, exerts authority over his daughters, telling them to "rearrange your plans" and "watch your tone." There's also a clear social hierarchy among the teenagers, with some girls bullying Mia, demonstrated by their taunts and actions like pushing her into the pool.

title: Bad Boys For Life
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and challenging authority. Examples include Mike's constant disregard for rules and Rita's attempts to control him, as well as the power struggles within AMMO.

The film displays a clear military hierarchy. Characters frequently address superiors as "Sir" or "Sarge" and follow orders without question, such as "Yes, Sarge" and "No, Sarge." General Erinmore's orders carry significant weight, dictating the mission and overriding local command decisions, as seen when Colonel Mackenzie is forced to stand down his troops.

title: Sonic The Hedgehog
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance and challenging authority. Robotnik constantly belittles others and demands obedience, while Sonic's interactions involve struggles for control and playful challenges to authority figures.

title: Birds of Prey (And the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn)
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and vying for control. Examples include Roman Sionis's interactions with his subordinates, Montoya's attempts to assert authority in the police department, and the general struggle for control of Gotham's criminal underworld.

title: Dolittle
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience. Examples include Dolittle directing the animals, Müdfly commanding soldiers, and Rassouli's control over his kingdom. The dialogue highlights the hierarchical relationships and the struggle for control.

title: The Invisible Man
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control and dominate, especially by Adrian. Examples include: "Open the fucking door, Cecilia!", Adrian's control over Cecilia's life detailed in her monologue, and the lawyer's attempts to manipulate Cecilia regarding the trust fund and her pregnancy.

title: The Call of the Wild
justification: The film depicts Buck's journey through various hierarchical structures, from Judge Miller's estate where he is 'king' to the brutal world of sled dogs where 'Spitz' is his 'new boss'. Dialogue such as 'He leads, you follow' and scenes of Buck being beaten into submission highlight the struggle for dominance.

title: Onward
justification: Barley often directs Ian, especially regarding quests and magic, creating a hierarchical dynamic. Examples include: "First, let me do the talking." and "This book is for a game. I told you, everything in Quests of Yore is historically accurate."

title: Tenet
justification: Several characters give orders and expect obedience. Sator's control over Kat is a major plot point, demonstrated by his threats and manipulation: "If I can't have you... no one else can." The Protagonist is also directed by Priya and Ives, highlighting a clear hierarchy.

title: The Gentlemen
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, negotiations for power, and characters asserting dominance. Examples include Dry Eye's attempts to buy Michael out, Michael's threats to Dry Eye, and Coach's control over his trainees. The constant struggle for control and respect is evident throughout the interactions.

title: The Croods: A New Age
justification: The Bettermans exert control through their home and rules, such as 'We don't eat the bananas.' Grug and Phil compete for dominance, with Phil manipulating Grug in his 'man cave.' Eep and Guy's relationship is strained by differing views on 'Tomorrow,' highlighting a power struggle over their future.

title: Fantasy Island
justification: Several characters exert authority, such as Roarke giving instructions and controlling the island's events. The soldier barks orders at the protagonist, and Kalashov's men threaten and interrogate the guests. These interactions highlight a clear hierarchy and struggle for control.

title: The New Mutants
justification: Dr. Reyes exerts control over the young mutants, dictating their treatment and confinement: "Until I decide you're not a danger." Illyana also displays dominance through intimidation and physical altercations, such as her fight with Dani and her general bullying behavior: "Keep behaving exactly like you are right now...and we can all just spend the day in solitary."

title: Wonder Woman 1984
justification: Maxwell Lord's interactions are driven by a desire for control and influence, demonstrated by his manipulation of investors and his wish to gain power from the President. The dialogue highlights his need to dominate situations and people, such as when he tells his son, 'Don't you wish I had an audience with the President today?'

title: Like a Boss
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters vying for control, especially Claire Luna. She manipulates Mel and Mia with offers and threats, demanding 51% of their company and later threatening to take controlling interest if they falter. The interactions between Mel and Mia also show a power struggle, with Mel often trying to assert her dominance.

title: Unhinged
justification: Several characters exert authority, like Rachel's boss firing her: "Deborah, no, wait. I'm sorry, okay?" and the road-raging man demanding an apology: "Ma'am, I was saying, if you could just apologize...". The escalating conflict shows a struggle for control and dominance.

title: The Photograph
justification: Several instances show characters asserting control or questioning others' decisions. Examples include Denise telling Christina she's too old to live with her and should move out, and Kyle's repeated attempts to advise Michael on his relationships, even when unwanted.

title: The War with Grandpa
justification: The central conflict revolves around a grandfather and grandson battling for control of a bedroom, using increasingly aggressive tactics. Dialogue such as "You took something of mine, and I want it back" and the establishment of "rules of engagement" highlight the struggle for dominance. The constant one-upmanship and attempts to outsmart each other further emphasize the power dynamics at play.

title: Underwater
justification: The captain gives orders to the crew, such as "Rodrigo, Paul. I need you two to check where we are on submersible. Now." and "I'm sending Norah to the control room." There is also a clear hierarchy in the crew, with the captain making decisions and the others following his lead, even when they disagree.

title: The Turning
justification: Several characters exert authority over others. Mrs. Grose frequently directs Kate, saying, "You need to take charge here, Kate." Miles also attempts to dominate Kate, challenging her with phrases like, "If you can handle it." Quint's influence is also shown through Miles's behavior.

title: Gretel & Hansel
justification: The film explores power dynamics through the witch's manipulation and control over Gretel, evident in lines like, "It's not for you to agree or disagree, my pretty. It's already inside of you." and "You will be. Will I have mastery and dominion over everything? Nearly everything.". The story also shows the powerlessness of Gretel and Hansel in the face of poverty and the witch's influence.

title: Honest Thief
justification: The dialogue between the In-and-Out Bandit and the FBI agents showcases a power struggle. The bandit attempts to negotiate a deal, while the agents maintain control by dictating the terms and expressing skepticism. Also, the corrupt agents Hall and Nivens exert their authority by stealing the money and attempting to silence witnesses.

title: The Way Back
justification: The coach exerts authority over the players, dictating plays and scolding them for mistakes: "Marcus, this time your feet don't leave the paint." There are also instances of players challenging each other's status and skills, like when Marcus's poor shooting percentage is revealed and mocked.

title: My Hero Academia: Heroes: Rising
justification: The film features several instances of characters attempting to assert dominance. Mahoro frequently scolds Deku, highlighting his perceived incompetence. Bakugo constantly gives orders and asserts his superiority, especially towards Deku and other heroes.

title: Brahms: The Boy II
justification: The film explores power dynamics through Jude's selective mutism and the influence of the Brahms doll. Dialogue such as "Your dad and I make the rules in this house, not your doll" and "He wants me to live in the big house with him forever. He said he'd kill you and Daddy if I didn't do it" highlight the struggle for control and the doll's manipulation.

title: Jojo Rabbit
justification: The film depicts a society steeped in Nazi ideology, where authority figures like Captain Klenzendorf exert control through propaganda and intimidation. Jojo's interactions with Elsa also highlight power imbalances, as she initially holds a position of vulnerability but gradually gains influence over him. The dialogue is filled with commands, threats, and attempts to assert dominance, reflecting a constant struggle for control.

title: Impractical Jokers: The Movie
justification: There are many instances of power dynamics. For example, one person tells another, "You answer the questions we ask you." Another example is when one person is told to say, "Murr's funnier, smarter, and better than me."

title: I Still Believe
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Melissa telling Jeremy, "That's why I should just never look at you again." and Jeremy's father telling him to slow down and take his time with Melissa. However, these are not the main focus of the dialogue.

title: Emma.
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters attempting to exert control over others, whether through direct commands ('Come along.') or subtle manipulations ('I lay it down as a general rule...'). Mr. Knightley frequently criticizes Emma's actions, highlighting a power struggle in their relationship ('Emma, your infatuation about that girl blinds you.').

title: Bloodshot
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and directives, especially from Dr. Harting to Ray and his team. Examples include "Commence bioelectrical charge," "Jimmy, will you walk him to his room, please?", and "I need you to come back here right now."

title: Let Him Go
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters asserting dominance, issuing threats, and attempting to control each other. Blanche Weboy clearly controls her family, and George and Margaret are constantly trying to assert their will against the Weboys and Lorna.

title: Freaky
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting control are present. Examples include "You're going. That's final," and the teacher, Mr. Bernardi, repeatedly scolding Millie for being late and unprepared, saying, "Late again, Miss Kessler," and "Once again, Miss Kessler is unprepared."

title: Downhill
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. For example, Pete tries to dictate the family's activities, and Billie confronts the resort staff about the avalanche, demanding acknowledgment of their poor handling of the situation. The interaction between Billie and Guglielmo also explores power dynamics through sexual experience.

title: Weathering With You
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as the older man, Keisuke, seemingly having some authority over Hodaka, his employee. Also, the police officers exert their authority over Hodaka when they question him and eventually try to arrest him.

title: It's a Wonderful Life
justification: Potter attempts to exert financial dominance by offering George a job and trying to take over the Building and Loan. George resists Potter's influence, asserting his own values and community ties: "You sit around here, and you spin your little webs, and you think the whole world revolves around you and your money. Well, it doesn't, Mr. Potter."

title: The Hunt
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting dominance, and struggling for control. Examples include Athena directing others in the 'hunt,' characters being captured and controlled, and the constant threat of violence to enforce compliance. The power dynamic is a central theme, driving the plot and character interactions.

title: The Rhythm Section
justification: The dialogue includes direct commands like "Open the doors... Now!" and "Everyone get out!!" which indicates a clear power dynamic. The refusal to comply ("I can't let you off here, sir.") and subsequent forceful commands further emphasize the struggle for control.

title: Monster Hunter
justification: The dialogue shows a clear military hierarchy with commands being given and obeyed. Examples include "Man the 50. Yes, boss," and "Axe, get on one of those dunes and set up an observation point. Yes, boss." The Captain gives orders and the team follows them.

title: The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge on the Run
justification: The dialogue is filled with commands and obedience, especially between Krabs and his employees ("Oui, oui, Monsieur Boss Man Krabs.", "Right away, Mr. K!"). King Poseidon's interactions with his Chancellor also highlight a clear power dynamic, with the king demanding attention and service ("Chancellor! Chancellor! Chancellor!").

title: Richard Jewell
justification: Several scenes depict law enforcement (FBI, police) exerting authority over Richard Jewell, directing his actions and questioning him. Examples include the FBI agents instructing Jewell to follow them to the field office and the aggressive questioning by journalists. Also, the news media dictates the narrative, influencing public perception and putting pressure on law enforcement.

title: The Broken Hearts Gallery
justification: There are multiple instances of power dynamics. Lucy commands Nick to get coffee, and Nick is clearly in a subordinate position to Lucy, as evidenced by his eagerness to please her and Marcos's comment, "Her Majesty looks a little upset this morning, so tread lightly." There are also instances of Jeff's friends teasing him and telling him what to do.

title: Infidel
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters attempting to exert control over others, whether through legal authority (police, lawyers), religious authority (Rawlins' preaching, the Iranian clerics), or physical intimidation (kidnappers). Examples include the police demanding Rawlins' client 'back off,' the kidnappers demanding Rawlins' blog password, and the Iranian government putting Rawlins on trial.

title: News of the World
justification: Several scenes depict characters asserting authority, such as the interactions with the soldiers demanding loyalty oaths and the encounter with Almay who attempts to buy Johanna. The most salient example is Farley's control over the town and his demand that Kidd read only his approved news, culminating in violence when Kidd defies him.

title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
justification: The film explores power dynamics subtly. There are instances of command, such as "Tell me about it" and "Turn around," but these are balanced by moments of equality and shared experiences. The mother's control over Héloïse's marriage is a significant power dynamic.

title: Bill & Ted Face the Music
justification: The Great Leader and her robot enforcer show a clear hierarchy. The Great Ones issue commands to Bill and Ted, setting a deadline to save reality: 'We need to hear the song in 77 minutes and 25 seconds. You have everything you require. Get to work.'

title: My Boyfriend’s Meds
justification: Several scenes depict characters attempting to exert control or influence over others. Examples include Chase trying to impress Morales with marketing ideas, and the retreat leader directing participants in exercises, demanding obedience and participation. Hank's doctor also exerts control by giving him orders regarding his medication and behavior.

title: The Last Full Measure
justification: Several characters exert authority, like the nurse telling Huffman how to treat Jimmy, and Jimmy himself interrogating Huffman with loaded questions and threats. The military hierarchy is evident in the flashbacks, with soldiers following orders and deferring to superiors ('Lieutenant, what the hell is going on up there?').

title: Words on Bathroom Walls
justification: Several characters exert authority or seek dominance. For example, the mother attempts to control Adam's medication, and Sister Catherine holds power over Maya's future at the school.  Also, the mean students try to dominate Adam through physical intimidation.

title: Fatale
justification: Several characters exert control over others. Val manipulates Darren by withholding his phone and demanding more from him. Derrick's interactions with Tyrin involve financial control and veiled threats.

title: After We Collided
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters exert control and dominance. Hardin frequently attempts to dictate Tessa's actions ('No, you're not,' 'Stop!'). Kimberly's interactions with her assistant also show a clear hierarchy ('Five minutes?' 'Problem?' 'Don't be late.').

title: The Lodge
justification: The film revolves around Richard's attempts to assert control over his children's lives by introducing Grace, leading to conflicts. Aiden and Mia resist Grace's presence and authority, culminating in a struggle for dominance within the isolated setting, as evidenced by Grace's increasingly erratic behavior and attempts to impose her religious beliefs.

title: IP Man: The Finale
justification: The film explores power dynamics through several lenses: martial arts mastery, cultural dominance, and racial prejudice. Characters constantly vie for respect and control, as seen in the challenges to Ip Man's authority and the Marines' attempts to assert dominance through physical force. Dialogue such as "Drink this cup of tea... and you are one of us" and the Marine drill instructor's racist tirades highlight the struggle for power and acceptance.

title: Half Brothers
justification: Throughout the dialogue, characters assert dominance and control. Flavio manipulates his sons with promises and guilt, while Asher and Renato constantly bicker and try to one-up each other. The border patrol officer and the rednecks at the gas station also exert authority.

title: The Personal History of David Copperfield
justification: Several characters exert authority: Aunt Betsey controls David's finances and renames him, Steerforth commands other students, and Wickfield is manipulated by Uriah Heep who eventually becomes his partner and controls his actions. Examples include: 'If I'm to financially support my nephew, I want to like his name.' and 'Uriah has been very good for our business.'

title: The Wretched
justification: Several characters exert authority: a mother sets strict rules for her daughter ("I want you home right after. That's the rule."), a father pressures his son ("You... are on dish duty."), and a marina worker enforces regulations ("You can't take that out on the water, alright? It's gotta stay in the picnic area."). There are also instances of resistance and defiance, indicating a struggle for control.

title: The Rental
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or expressing control. Examples include: "Will you hide your dog." "Let me show you out back and then I'll get outta your hair." "We'll figure it out."

title: 2 Hearts
justification: Several scenes depict characters giving orders or asserting control. Examples include the father telling the sons to "Focus! Let's get to work," and Chris initially dominating the Safety Buddies conversation with Sam, dictating her role as his "first safety driver."

title: Jay and Silent Bob Reboot
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. For example, Millennium threatens Jay and Silent Bob: "Either you take us to Hollywood or I stab you both to death." Also, Jihad threatens Underhill: "If you fuck with any of us, I live up to my name and I put you underground."

title: Train to Busan Presents: Peninsula
justification: The film features several instances of characters vying for power and control. Unit 631 soldiers exert authority over civilians, exemplified by the line, "You'd have been locked up for insubordination if it were the old days!" Gang leaders also display dominance, as seen when one says, "The boss wants to see you."

title: Promising Young Woman
justification: Several interactions involve attempts to exert control or gain an advantage. For example, Cassie manipulates Dean Walker by threatening his daughter, and Gail's comments to Ryan are laced with dominance. The dialogue reveals a constant negotiation of status and authority.

title: Met Opera — Agrippina
justification: The dialogue is filled with power struggles, commands, and betrayals. Examples include Agrippina's plot to make Nero emperor ('I want Claudius out of the way to secure Nero as Emperor') and Nero's eventual order to kill his own mother ('Then kill her'). The entire narrative revolves around who holds power and how they maintain or lose it.

title: True to the Game 2: Gena’s Story
justification: Several characters exert authority: Saleem controls his crew with threats ('When we hit 'em, we're gonna hit 'em all at once. So, chill the fuck out, nigga. No loose ends.') and Vaughn intimidates Mark ('Stay the fuck away from Gena!'). Even seemingly softer characters like Gah Git display a matriarchal authority ('You can't be laying your hands on these kids nowadays.').

title: The Assistant
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, demanding information, and navigating complex hierarchical relationships. Examples include demands for reports by rank, controlling travel arrangements, blocking credit cards as a power play, and the constant need to manage schedules and access to superiors. The assistant's interactions with her boss and other employees highlight the imbalance of power and the struggle to maintain status.

title: Love and Monsters
justification: The dialogue shows Joel's initial dependence on others for survival advice ('Don't fight. Just run and hide.') and later, his interactions with Clyde and Minnow, where Clyde gives orders and teaches him survival skills ('Always survey from high ground when possible.'). The arrival of Captain Wilkinson introduces a clear hierarchy, with him giving orders and taking charge ('Come help us get a fire started.').

title: Relic
justification: The dialogue shows characters trying to control each other, especially Edna and her daughters. For example, Kay tries to convince Edna to move into a retirement home, while Edna resists and accuses Sam of stealing from her. There are also instances of characters giving orders, such as when Kay tells Sam to go get the phone.

title: The Tax Collector
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, commands, and assertions of dominance. Examples include: "Don't forget you work for Wizard," "When you say it, you say it with respect," and "Gata, bring her to me."

title: Becky
justification: The film features escaped convicts who exert dominance through violence and threats, giving orders like "Take him and walk out the side door now." Becky also struggles for control, defying authority and ultimately killing the convicts, demonstrating a shift in power.

title: The Song of Names
justification: There are instances of commands being given, such as "Take him" and "Go fetch your father," indicating a hierarchy. However, much of the dialogue is informational or welcoming, diluting the overall sense of power struggle.

title: Break the Silence The Movie
justification: There are some instances of hierarchy, such as Jin buying clothes for the crew and the members teasing each other. However, the dialogue mainly focuses on shared experiences and memories, with no strong power dynamics present.

title: All My Life
justification: There are some instances of power dynamics, such as Yasmin's demands at work and Gigi's bossing around in the kitchen. Jenn and Sol also negotiate rules for living together, indicating a balance of power. However, the overall focus is on support and collaboration, reducing the salience of power dynamics.

title: Met Opera: Wozzeck
justification: The Captain repeatedly asserts his authority over Woyzeck, giving him orders and criticizing his morality. Examples include: "Slowly, Woyzeck. Slowly. One thing at a time!" and "Woyzeck, you have no virtue. You are not a virtuous man."

title: A Hidden Life
justification: The film depicts Franz's struggle against the Nazi regime, showcasing the power imbalance between the individual and the state. Dialogue such as "I am not your friend. I am your Mayor!" and the constant pressure on Franz to conform and swear loyalty to Hitler highlight this struggle for dominance and control.

title: Yogi Bear
justification: Ranger Smith is clearly in charge, giving orders to Jones and trying to control Yogi. The Mayor exerts authority by threatening to close the park and later reassigning Ranger Smith. Jones is eager to gain power and status, seeking the Head Ranger position.

title: The Last Song
justification: Several instances show characters attempting to exert control or dominance. For example, Marcus pressures Blaze for money, and Will's father's wealth creates a social hierarchy. There are also instances of characters giving orders, such as when Scott tells Ronnie to get him a drink.

title: Easy A
justification: The dialogue shows a clear struggle for status and control, especially through rumor-spreading and social manipulation. Olive's interactions with Brandon and other students reveal attempts to navigate and subvert the school's social hierarchy, while characters like Marianne try to enforce moral authority.

title: No Strings Attached
justification: Several interactions involve one character directing or ordering another. Examples include Emma telling Adam, "You have 45 seconds to pull your shit together, OK?" and later, "Emma, time to go!" There are also instances of characters asserting dominance or control in relationships, such as when Adam tries to dictate the terms of his casual relationship with Emma.

title: Paul
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting authority, such as the agent telling his subordinates, "Listen to me, Frik and Fuck." There are also instances of characters seeking permission or approval, like when Ruth asks, "May I come in?"

title: Colombiana
justification: The film features a clear hierarchy within the criminal underworld, with characters like Don Luis issuing commands and expecting obedience. Examples include "Kill this motherfucker" and "Don Luis said kill everyone."

title: War Horse
justification: The film depicts a clear hierarchy between Albert's father and him, as well as between the officers and soldiers in the war. Albert's father gives him orders like "Go back to the house" and the officers command the soldiers with phrases like "Walk on, Joey, walk on!" and "Draw swords!"

title: Argo
justification: Several instances of characters giving orders or asserting authority are present. Examples include 'Stay inside the fucking house,' and 'Don't fuck up. The whole country is watching you.' There are also instances of characters deferring to authority, such as 'No, sir' and 'Yes, sir, it will be done.'

title: Contraband
justification: The dialogue is filled with threats, demands, and displays of dominance. Examples include: "I'm going to come after the both of you. Then, all the way down the line. I'll come asking your wife for it, your kids..." and "Get the fuck out of my house!". Captain Camp also asserts his authority over the crew, highlighting a clear hierarchy.

title: The Dictator
justification: The dialogue is filled with instances of characters asserting dominance, giving orders, and making demands. Examples include Aladeen's dictatorial pronouncements, his interactions with subordinates, and his attempts to control situations, such as 'Get me clothes, little man' and 'Then unpopulate them'. Even in seemingly egalitarian settings, characters like Aladeen attempt to establish control, highlighting a constant struggle for power.

title: Jack Reacher
justification: Several characters attempt to exert control over others. Helen's father, the D.A., tries to control her actions and career choices, saying, "You're making a terrible mistake. You cannot win this case." Reacher uses intimidation and physical force to get information from Sandy and others, demonstrating his dominance.

title: Mr. Peabody & Sherman
justification: The conflict between Sherman and Penny is driven by Penny's desire to assert dominance, calling Sherman a dog and ordering him to beg. Ms. Grunion attempts to assert authority over Mr. Peabody, threatening to take Sherman away. Mr. Peabody also exerts control over Sherman, forbidding him from certain actions and expressing disappointment when Sherman disobeys.

title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
justification: Frank-N-Furter exerts control through commands and manipulation: "Come up to the lab and see what's on the slab" and "You're going to kill him? What's his crime? You saw what became of Eddie. Society must be protected." Riff Raff and Magenta ultimately overthrow Frank, declaring "I'm your new commander. You now are my prisoner."

title: Sinister 2
justification: The film features several instances of power dynamics. Clint's abusive behavior towards Courtney and Dylan, demonstrated by his command to "Eat!" and the revelation that "Clint beat him real bad," highlights a clear power imbalance. Additionally, the state troopers' initial attempt to remove the children without proper legal authority, asserting "I'm in charge, asshole," showcases an abuse of power.

title: Sausage Party
justification: Characters frequently give orders and assert dominance. Examples include: "Sausage, control your insolent bun," and El Douche demanding, "Spill the beans!"

title: Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children
justification: Miss Peregrine clearly holds authority over the children, dictating their actions and schedules: "Children! Would you make your way down the stairs, please?" and "I give the orders in this house, Mr. Barron." Barron also exerts control, demanding obedience and making threats: "If you value his life, I suggest everyone does as they're told."

title: The Purge: Election Year
justification: The dialogue is filled with characters giving orders, asserting authority, and challenging each other's positions. Examples include the Senator demanding security measures, Joe's interactions with those trying to take advantage of him, and the power plays within Dante Bishop's organization.

title: Lights Out
justification: The dialogue shows characters giving orders and asserting control. Examples include Becca telling the man to leave her apartment ('Get out of here.') and the social worker Emma questioning Becca about Martin's well-being and living situation, implying authority.

title: Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising
justification: The dialogue is filled with attempts to control the sorority's behavior, reflecting a struggle for dominance between the neighbors and the sorority.
